nodes.name: Brahman
nodes.description: Brahman is the ultimate, unchanging reality underlying the universe in the Upanishads and the Vedanta schools. It is described as being, consciousness and bliss (sat-chit-ananda) and, in the Upanishadic teaching, as identical with the innermost self (atman).
nodes.story: In the Chandogya Upanishad the sage Uddalaka Aruni finds his son Shvetaketu returning from twelve years of study proud but unable to explain what makes all things known. He asks the boy to drop a lump of salt into water overnight. In the morning the salt cannot be found, yet every sip, from the top, the middle and the bottom, tastes of salt. So too, says Uddalaka, the one subtle essence pervades everything though it cannot be seen; it is the reality, it is the self, and that, Shvetaketu, you are (tat tvam asi). Through nine such lessons, a banyan seed whose invisible core holds the whole tree, rivers that lose their names in the sea, Uddalaka leads his son to recognise Brahman as the unseen ground of his own being.
variations: In the Rig Veda and Brahmanas 'brahman' mainly means the sacred formulation or its power; the sense of an absolute reality develops in the Upanishads.
Advaita Vedanta holds Brahman to be attributeless (nirguna) and the world an appearance; Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita identify Brahman with a personal God, usually Vishnu-Narayana.
Shaiva traditions identify Brahman with Shiva and Shakta traditions (e.g. the Devi Gita of the Devi Bhagavata) with the Goddess.
Gaudiya Vaishnavism treats impersonal Brahman as the effulgence of Krishna, with Bhagavan as the fuller aspect.

nodes.name: Hiranyagarbha
nodes.description: Hiranyagarbha, the 'golden germ' or 'golden womb', is the first-born source of creation praised in Rig Veda 10.121. In later texts the golden cosmic egg floating on the primordial waters becomes the birthplace of Brahma, and in Vedanta Hiranyagarbha denotes the cosmic mind, the subtle totality of all beings.
nodes.story: Rig Veda 10.121 opens with the Golden Germ arising in the beginning, born as the one lord of all that exists, who fixed earth and heaven in place. Each verse praises his deeds, giving breath and strength, ruling men and beasts, spreading out the mountains, the sea and the directions, and each ends with the haunting refrain: to which god shall we offer our oblation? When the great waters came, bearing the germ and generating fire, from them arose the one life-breath of the gods. Only in the last verse does the poet answer, naming Prajapati as lord of creatures. Centuries later the Manusmriti retells the image: the self-existent one placed a seed in the waters, it became a golden egg bright as the sun, and in it Brahma was born, splitting it after a year into heaven and earth.
variations: The final verse of Rig Veda 10.121, naming Prajapati, is often considered a later addition; the refrain's 'ka' ('who?') was later read as a proper name of Prajapati.
Puranas and the Manusmriti make the golden egg the womb from which Brahma is born; Vedanta uses Hiranyagarbha for the collective subtle body of the universe.

nodes.name: Purusha
nodes.description: Purusha is the cosmic person of the Purusha Sukta (Rig Veda 10.90), whose sacrifice by the gods produced the universe, the Vedas and society. Later traditions read him as the Supreme Self, and Vaishnavas identify him with Narayana-Vishnu.
nodes.story: The Purusha Sukta describes a being with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes and a thousand feet, who covers the earth on every side and extends ten fingers beyond it. Only a quarter of him is all creatures; three quarters are immortal in heaven. The gods performed a sacrifice with Purusha himself as the offering, spring its butter, summer its fuel, autumn its oblation. From that great sacrifice came the verses, chants and metres, the horses, cattle, goats and sheep. From his mind the moon was born, from his eye the sun, from his mouth Indra and Agni, from his breath the wind; from his navel the atmosphere, from his head the sky, from his feet the earth. The hymn also derives the four social orders from his mouth, arms, thighs and feet.
variations: Scholars generally consider the Purusha Sukta one of the latest hymns of the Rig Veda; its varna verse (10.90.12) is much discussed.
In Samkhya philosophy purusha means the plural, passive conscious self distinct from matter (prakriti), a different technical sense.
The Shatapatha Brahmana speaks of Purusha Narayana, and Vaishnava texts such as the Bhagavata identify the cosmic Purusha with Vishnu's first purusha-avatara.

nodes.name: Prajapati
nodes.description: Prajapati, 'lord of creatures', is the creator god who dominates the Brahmanas, where he produces the worlds, gods, asuras and humans through heat (tapas) and sacrifice, and is identified with the year and the sacrifice itself. His role and titles later pass largely to Brahma; the plural prajapatis also denotes Brahma's mind-born progenitor sons.
nodes.story: In the Chandogya Upanishad Prajapati proclaims that whoever finds the self free from sin, age and death gains all worlds. Indra of the gods and Virochana of the asuras come to him as students and live chastely for thirty-two years. Prajapati tells them to look into a pan of water: the self is what is seen there. Both depart satisfied, adorned and dressed, but Virochana teaches the asuras that the body is the self. Indra, troubled that such a self would suffer when the body suffers, returns. Prajapati gives him further teachings, the self of dreams, then of deep sleep, and each time Indra finds a flaw and returns, until after one hundred and one years in all Prajapati reveals the self that dwells in the body yet is bodiless and immortal.
variations: In the Rig Veda Prajapati is rare and appears mainly in late hymns; he becomes the supreme creator only in the later Vedic literature.
In the Epics and Puranas the name is a title of Brahma, and the plural refers to progenitors such as Daksha, Kashyapa and the mind-born sons of Brahma.
The Brihadaranyaka's 'Da Da Da' teaching (5.2) has Prajapati instructing gods, humans and asuras with a single syllable understood three ways.

nodes.name: Nasadiya Sukta — Hymn of Creation
nodes.description: The Nasadiya Sukta (Rig Veda 10.129) is a philosophical hymn on the origin of the universe, famous for ending in open questions rather than a creator's decree. It speaks of a primordial 'That One' (tad ekam) arising through heat and desire before the gods themselves.
nodes.story: Then there was neither non-existence nor existence, the hymn begins; neither the air nor the sky beyond it. What covered everything, and where, in whose keeping? Was there water, deep and unfathomable? There was neither death nor immortality, no sign dividing night from day. That One breathed, without wind, by its own impulse; other than that there was nothing. Darkness was hidden by darkness, all was undistinguished water, and That One was born through the power of heat (tapas). In the beginning desire arose, the first seed of mind, and sages searching their hearts found the bond of the existent in the non-existent. But who truly knows, the poet asks, whence this creation came? The gods came afterwards. Perhaps the one who oversees it in the highest heaven knows, or perhaps he does not know.
variations: Vedantic commentators read 'That One' as Brahman; others see links to Prajapati or Hiranyagarbha, but the hymn itself names no deity.
The 'desire' (kama) of verse 4 is cosmic desire, later personified as the god Kamadeva.

nodes.name: Svayambhuva Manu
nodes.description: Svayambhuva Manu, 'Manu of the Self-born', is the first of the fourteen Manus and progenitor of humankind in the first manvantara. Born from Brahma together with his consort Shatarupa, he fathered Priyavrata, Uttanapada, Akuti, Devahuti and Prasuti, and the Manusmriti is attributed to him.
nodes.story: The Bhagavata Purana tells that when Brahma had brought forth Svayambhuva Manu and Shatarupa, the new couple bowed and asked their father how they might serve him. Brahma told them to beget children and rule the earth with righteousness. But Manu pointed to a problem: the earth, the home of all beings, lay sunk beneath the waters of the cosmic ocean, so where could his children live? As Brahma pondered, a tiny boar the size of a thumb emerged from his nostril and in moments swelled to the size of an elephant, then a mountain. Roaring, it dived into the waters and raised the earth on its tusks. With the ground restored, Manu ruled from his capital Barhishmati, and his sons and daughters peopled the world.
variations: Vishnu Purana 1.7 has Brahma divide his own body into the male Manu and the female Shatarupa; the Matsya Purana makes Manu the son of Brahma and Shatarupa.
The Manusmriti presents itself as Manu's teaching recited by Bhrigu; modern scholarship dates it to around the turn of the Common Era.

nodes.name: Shatarupa
nodes.description: Shatarupa, 'she of a hundred forms', is the first woman in Puranic cosmogony and the consort of Svayambhuva Manu. Their children included the kings Priyavrata and Uttanapada and the daughters Akuti, Devahuti and Prasuti, through whom much of creation descends.
nodes.story: The Matsya Purana tells that Brahma produced from his own body a woman of dazzling beauty, known as Shatarupa, Savitri and Saraswati. Captivated, he could not stop gazing at her. As she respectfully circled him, a new face sprang up to the right, behind and to the left so that he never lost sight of her, and when she rose into the sky a fifth face appeared above. His mind-born sons were dismayed at their father's infatuation. In this telling Brahma took her as his consort, and after a hundred years their son Svayambhuva Manu was born. Other Puranas instead describe Brahma dividing himself into Manu and Shatarupa as the first couple, whose daughters became the mothers of the sages' lineages and of Daksha's many children.
variations: In the Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas Shatarupa is Manu's wife, born with him from Brahma; in the Matsya Purana she is Brahma's own consort and Manu's mother.
The Matsya Purana identifies her with Savitri, Gayatri and Saraswati; the story of Brahma's fifth head is linked in other texts to Shiva severing it.

nodes.name: Vaivasvata Manu
nodes.description: Vaivasvata Manu, son of the sun god Vivasvat (Surya), is the seventh Manu and progenitor of the present age of humanity. Saved from the great flood by the fish Matsya, he became father of Ikshvaku, founder of the Solar dynasty, and of Ila, from whom the Lunar dynasty descends.
nodes.story: The Shatapatha Brahmana tells that after the waters of the flood subsided, Manu found himself alone on the northern mountain, the last of the living. Longing for offspring, he worshipped and performed austerities, and poured into the waters an offering of clarified butter, sour milk, whey and curds. After a year a woman arose from it, walking with butter gathering in her footprints. Mitra and Varuna asked who she was, and she answered that she was Manu's daughter. Manu too asked, and she said: I am the blessing you offered; use me in the sacrifice and you will be rich in offspring and cattle. She was Ida, the sacred offering itself, and through her Manu generated this race of men, which is therefore called the race of Manu.
variations: The Bhagavata Purana calls him Satyavrata, a king of Dravida who became Vaivasvata Manu after the flood.
Yaska's Nirukta makes Manu the son of Vivasvat by the substitute wife (Savarna, later Chhaya); the Puranas make him Sanjna's son and assign Chhaya's son as Savarni Manu.

Ila is variously born from his offering (Shatapatha), from a sacrifice whose priest erred so that a daughter was born instead of a son (Bhagavata 9.1), or, in the Ramayana, as a son of Kardama transformed into a woman.
Ikshvaku is said in the Vishnu Purana to have been born from Manu's nostril as he sneezed.

nodes.name: The Great Flood (Manu and the Fish)
nodes.description: The flood legend tells how a small fish rescued by Manu warned him of a coming deluge and towed his boat to safety, so that life could begin again. First recorded in the Shatapatha Brahmana, it grows in the Mahabharata and the Puranas into the story of Matsya, the first avatar of Vishnu.
nodes.story: In the Bhagavata Purana, King Satyavrata was offering water to his ancestors in the Kritamala river when a tiny fish appeared in his cupped hands and begged not to be thrown back among bigger fish. He carried it home in his water-pot, but overnight it outgrew the pot, then a pond, then a lake, until he released it into the ocean. Realising that no ordinary creature could grow so, the king recognised Vishnu. The fish foretold that in seven days the worlds would sink beneath the waters of dissolution; a boat would come, and he must board it with the seven sages, all plants and seeds. When the flood rose, a great horned fish appeared; Satyavrata tied the boat to its horn with the serpent Vasuki, and as they sailed Matsya taught him the highest truth. He became Vaivasvata Manu.
variations: In the Shatapatha Brahmana the fish is unnamed, Manu alone survives, and the ship comes to rest on the northern mountain, called Manu's Descent.
In the Mahabharata the fish reveals itself as Brahma Prajapati, Manu takes the seven sages and seeds aboard, and the boat is moored to a Himalayan peak called Naubandhana.
In the Matsya and Bhagavata Puranas the fish is Vishnu; the Bhagavata adds the rope-serpent Vasuki and Matsya's slaying of the asura Hayagriva who stole the Vedas.
Comparative mythologists note parallels with Mesopotamian and biblical flood stories; the relationship between them is debated.

nodes.name: Saptarishi (Seven Sages)
nodes.description: The Saptarishi are the seven great seers who preside over each cosmic age and are identified with the seven stars of the Great Bear (Ursa Major). The Rig Veda already speaks of 'the seven rishis', but the names differ between the Vedic list and the Puranic list of Brahma's mind-born sons.
nodes.story: The Mahabharata tells that when the Seven Sages performed a sacrifice, Agni rose from the fire and was overcome with longing for their wives. Knowing his love was improper, he withdrew to the forest in despair. Svaha, a daughter of Daksha who loved Agni, took on the forms of the sages' wives one by one, visiting him as each in turn. She could assume six of their forms, but not that of Arundhati, the wife of Vashistha, so great was her devotion to her husband. Each time Svaha carried Agni's seed to a golden pot on the White Mountain, where the child Skanda was born. Rumours spread that the sages' wives had been unfaithful, and six sages parted from their wives, who became the Krittikas (Pleiades); Arundhati alone remained with Vashistha in the sky.
symbols: Seven stars of the Great Bear
variations: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad and Shatapatha Brahmana list Gotama, Bharadvaja, Vishvamitra, Jamadagni, Vashistha, Kashyapa and Atri.
The Mahabharata and Puranas give Marichi, Atri, Angiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu and Vashistha, the mind-born sons of Brahma.

The Puranas assign a different set of seven sages to each manvantara; the Puranic list above belongs to the first (Svayambhuva) manvantara, while the present (Vaivasvata) age is usually given as Kashyapa, Atri, Vashistha, Vishvamitra, Gautama, Jamadagni and Bharadvaja.
In some tellings of the Krittika story Arundhati is suspected too, or the number of wives who become the Pleiades differs.

nodes.name: Adityas
nodes.description: The Adityas are the sons of the goddess Aditi, a group of sovereign gods who uphold cosmic order (rita), led by Varuna and Mitra. The Rig Veda counts six to eight of them, while later texts fix the number at twelve and link them with the months and the sun.
nodes.story: Rig Veda 10.72 tells that eight sons were born from Aditi's body. With seven she went to the gods, but the eighth, Martanda, she cast away, for he was born misshapen, a lifeless 'dead egg'. The Shatapatha Brahmana continues that the brothers shaped him into proper form, and from the flesh they cut away the elephant arose; he became Vivasvat, the sun, from whom humankind descends. So, says the hymn, Aditi brought Martanda back for the sake of birth and death, for mortals and their fate. The Adityas themselves, Mitra, Varuna, Aryaman, Bhaga, Daksha and Amsha in one early list, are praised as far-seeing guardians who hate deceit and bind the wicked, keepers of the moral order of the world.
variations: Rig Veda 2.27 names six: Mitra, Aryaman, Bhaga, Varuna, Daksha and Amsha; RV 9.114 speaks of seven and RV 10.72 of eight including Martanda.
The Brahmanas and Upanishads count twelve, equated with the months (Brihadaranyaka 3.9.5).
Epic and Puranic lists of twelve vary, typically Dhatri, Mitra, Aryaman, Indra (Shakra), Varuna, Amsha, Bhaga, Vivasvat, Pushan, Savitr, Tvashtr and Vishnu (Vamana/Urukrama) as the youngest.
Together with the eight Vasus, eleven Rudras and two others (Indra and Prajapati, or the Ashvins) they make up the thirty-three gods.

nodes.name: Vasus
nodes.description: The Vasus, 'the good' or 'bright ones', are a class of eight elemental gods attendant on Indra (or Agni), representing aspects of nature such as fire, earth, wind and the heavens. In the Mahabharata they are cursed by Vashistha and born as sons of Ganga, the eighth becoming Bhishma.
nodes.story: The Mahabharata tells that the eight Vasus once wandered with their wives near the hermitage of the sage Vashistha. The wife of Dyu saw the sage's wish-fulfilling cow Nandini and begged her husband to steal it for a human friend. Urged on by his brothers, Dyu took the cow. Vashistha, finding Nandini gone, cursed the Vasus to be born as mortals. They pleaded for mercy, and he softened the curse: seven would be freed within a year of their birth, but Dyu, who had committed the theft, would live long on earth, virtuous but childless. The Vasus asked the river goddess Ganga to be their mother. Married to King Shantanu, she drowned seven infants at birth to release them, until Shantanu stopped her with the eighth, who grew up to be Bhishma.
variations: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad lists them as fire (Agni), earth (Prithivi), wind (Vayu), atmosphere, sun (Aditya), sky (Dyaus), moon (Chandramas) and stars.
The Mahabharata lists Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Aha, Anila, Anala, Pratyusha and Prabhasa, sons of Dharma and Vasu, a daughter of Daksha.
The thieving Vasu reborn as Bhishma is named Dyu (Dyaus) in the Adi Parva account and Prabhasa in other versions.

nodes.name: Ekadasha Rudras
nodes.description: The Rudras are a group of storm and life-breath deities associated with the god Rudra. In the Rig Veda the plural 'Rudras' usually refers to the Maruts, Rudra's sons; later Vedic texts fix them at eleven, and the Puranas treat the Eleven Rudras as forms of Shiva.
nodes.story: In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, at the court of King Janaka, the learned Vidagdha Shakalya presses the sage Yajnavalkya with question after question about the number of the gods. Thirty-three, says Yajnavalkya: eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, twelve Adityas, Indra and Prajapati. And which are the Rudras? The ten vital breaths in a person, answers the sage, with the self as the eleventh. When they depart from this mortal body, they make people weep; and because they cause weeping (from rud, to cry), they are called Rudras. The Vishnu Purana tells another origin: at the beginning of creation a being half male and half female, blazing like the sun, sprang from Brahma's anger, and at his command divided itself into the eleven Rudras.
variations: In the Rig Veda 'the Rudras' are generally the Maruts, sons of Rudra, rather than a fixed group of eleven.
Name lists of the eleven vary widely between the Mahabharata and the Puranas; recurring names include Aja Ekapad, Ahirbudhnya, Hara, Tryambaka, Kapalin and Pinakin.
Their parentage varies: emanations of Brahma's anger, sons of Kashyapa and Surabhi, or forms of Shiva; popular tradition regards Hanuman as the eleventh Rudra.

nodes.name: Maruts
nodes.description: The Maruts are a troop of young, boisterous storm gods, sons of Rudra and the dappled cow Prishni in the Rig Veda, who ride golden chariots with lightning and accompany Indra in his battle with Vritra. The Puranas make them the forty-nine sons of Diti, divided in the womb by Indra.
nodes.story: The Ramayana and the Puranas tell that Diti, grieving for her sons slain by the gods, asked her husband Kashyapa for a son who would kill Indra. He granted it on condition that she keep a strict vow of purity for a thousand years. Indra came to serve her with seeming devotion, bringing fuel, water and fruit, while watching for a lapse. Near the end, Diti fell asleep with her head where her feet should have been and her hair unbound. Indra seized the moment, entered her womb and cut the embryo into seven pieces, and each piece into seven more. When the unborn children cried, he told them, do not weep (ma ruda). Diti awoke and, seeing the outcome, asked that the forty-nine become Indra's companions, the Maruts of the winds.
variations: In the Rig Veda they are sons of Rudra and Prishni, their number varying between hymns; the Ramayana and Puranas make them 49 sons of Diti and Kashyapa.
The Ramayana has Diti keep her vow for a thousand years; the Bhagavata Purana describes a one-year vow (pumsavana vrata).
Some Rig Vedic hymns (the Agastya cycle, 1.165–171) record tension between the Maruts and Indra before their reconciliation.

nodes.name: Aditi
nodes.description: Aditi, 'the boundless' or 'unbound', is the Vedic mother of the gods, especially of the Adityas, and a personification of limitless space, freedom from guilt and the nourishing earth-cow. In the Puranas she is a daughter of Daksha and wife of the sage Kashyapa, mother of Indra and of Vishnu in his Vamana avatar.
nodes.story: The Bhagavata Purana tells that when the asura king Bali drove the gods from heaven, Aditi grieved for her exiled sons. Her husband Kashyapa taught her the payovrata, a twelve-day vow of worship to Vishnu sustained on milk alone. Aditi kept it with perfect devotion, and at its end Vishnu appeared before her, four-armed and radiant. Moved by her love, he promised that he himself would be born as her son to restore her children. In due time he was born to Aditi and Kashyapa, and at once took the form of a small, bright-faced brahmin boy, Vamana. Going to Bali's sacrifice, the dwarf asked for three paces of land, and with three strides reclaimed the worlds, returning heaven to Indra, Aditi's eldest.
variations: Rig Veda 10.72 contains the paradox that Daksha was born from Aditi and Aditi from Daksha.
Puranic genealogies make her one of the daughters of Daksha (by Asikni or by Prasuti, depending on the text) married to Kashyapa.
The Harivamsha and Bhagavata make Devaki a rebirth of Aditi, so that Krishna's birth repeats Vamana's.

nodes.name: Diti
nodes.description: Diti is a daughter of Daksha and wife of Kashyapa, and the mother of the Daityas, the asura line that includes Hiranyakashipu and Hiranyaksha. In the Rig Veda she appears only briefly, often paired with Aditi, and in the Puranas she is also the mother of the Maruts.
nodes.story: The Bhagavata Purana tells that one evening, at the hour of twilight when Shiva and his spirit-hosts roam abroad, Diti approached her husband Kashyapa, overcome with desire for a son. Kashyapa begged her to wait, for the hour was inauspicious, but she would not be refused, and he yielded. Afterwards Diti was stricken with remorse and feared what she had done. Kashyapa foretold that she would bear two mighty sons who would torment the three worlds until Vishnu himself descended to slay them; yet, he consoled her, one of her grandsons would be a great devotee of the Lord. For a hundred years Diti held back the birth, and the darkness of the unborn twins spread through the worlds. They were born as Hiranyakashipu and Hiranyaksha, and her grandson was Prahlada.
variations: In the Rig Veda Diti is a shadowy figure mentioned a few times alongside Aditi; her role as mother of the Daityas is post-Vedic.
The Bhagavata identifies her twin sons as rebirths of Jaya and Vijaya, Vishnu's gatekeepers cursed by the Kumaras.

nodes.name: Danu
nodes.description: Danu is the mother of the Danavas. In the Rig Veda she is the mother of the serpent-demon Vritra and is struck down by Indra together with her son; in the Epics and Puranas she is a daughter of Daksha and a wife of Kashyapa, mother of many Danava lords.
nodes.story: The great Indra hymn of the Rig Veda (1.32) describes the climax of Indra's battle with Vritra, the serpent who had penned up the waters. When Indra's vajra shattered Vritra, the demon's mother Danu bent low over her son to shield him. Indra hurled his weapon at her too. The mother lay above and the son below, says the poet, and Danu lay like a cow beside her calf. Vritra's body sank into the midst of the endless, restless waters, and the released rivers flowed over it towards the sea. In later genealogies Danu, daughter of Daksha and wife of Kashyapa, became the mother of the Danava clans, including Namuchi, Shambara and Puloman, perennial rivals of the gods who were also their half-brothers.
variations: In the Rig Veda she is Vritra's mother; in later texts Vritra is usually the son of Tvashtr, created to avenge Vishvarupa.
Puranic lists of her sons differ considerably in names and number.

nodes.name: Prithvi (Bhudevi)
nodes.description: Prithvi, 'the broad one', is the Earth goddess. In the Rig Veda she is paired with Dyaus (Heaven) as the primal parents, and the Atharva Veda's Bhumi Sukta praises her as mother of all; in the Puranas she is Bhudevi, consort of Vishnu in his Varaha form and one of his two principal consorts beside Shri.
nodes.story: The Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas tell that under the wicked king Vena the earth withheld her bounty, and when Prithu was crowned, his people were starving. Taking up his bow in anger, Prithu pursued the Earth, who fled from him in the form of a cow through all the worlds. Finding no refuge, she turned and pleaded: to kill a female was a sin, and if she perished, where would his subjects live? Prithu relented, and she offered to yield all nourishment if he would provide a calf and level the land so the rains could settle. With Svayambhuva Manu as the calf, Prithu milked her of every grain and plant; then gods, sages, serpents and others milked her in turn. Because he spared her as a father would, the Earth became known as Prithvi.
variations: In the Vedas she is mainly a cosmic mother paired with Dyaus; as Bhudevi she becomes a consort of Vishnu, especially of Varaha, and in Sri Vaishnavism appears beside Shri with Vishnu.
Narakasura is her son by Varaha in the Bhagavata and Kalika Puranas; in some regional traditions Satyabhama, who helps defeat him, is Bhudevi's incarnation.
Mangala (Mars) is her son in most accounts, though the Skanda and other texts give him an origin from Shiva's sweat falling on the earth.
The Tamil saint Andal is revered in Sri Vaishnavism as an incarnation of Bhudevi.

nodes.name: Dyaus Pita
nodes.description: Dyaus Pita, 'Father Heaven', is the Rig Vedic sky god, paired with Prithvi (Earth) as the primordial parents of the gods, and father of Ushas and other deities. He is the linguistic cousin of the Greek Zeus and Latin Jupiter, but in India his cult faded early, surviving mainly as one of the Vasus.
nodes.story: The Rig Veda addresses Heaven and Earth together as a dual deity, Dyavaprithivi, the two broad, unfailing parents who hold all creatures between them like a vast bowl. In the hymns (1.159, 1.160, 1.185) the poets ask which of the two was born first, and how; none can say. Heaven the father and Earth the mother, ever young, rich in milk and seed, are called upon to guard the worshipper from distress, as parents guard a child on their lap. Dyaus himself is the bull who bellows in thunder, the father who begot Indra, and his daughter is the radiant Dawn. In the Mahabharata he reappears as Dyu, one of the eight Vasus, whose theft of the sage Vashistha's cow led to his birth on earth as Bhishma.
variations: The Rig Veda calls him father of Indra (4.17.4), of Ushas and of the Ashvins ('grandsons/offspring of Dyaus'); later genealogies assign these gods to Kashyapa and Aditi or to Surya.
Some Vedic passages make Dyaus female or grammatically feminine; the pairing with Earth is his most stable role.
Scholars link the name to Proto-Indo-European *Dyeus ph2ter, cognate with Zeus Pater and Jupiter.

nodes.name: Prishni
nodes.description: Prishni, 'the dappled' or 'speckled one', is the Rig Vedic mother of the Maruts, usually imagined as a dappled cow and interpreted as the storm cloud or the earth. The Maruts are called prishni-matarah, 'those whose mother is Prishni', and Rudra is their father.
nodes.story: The Rig Veda sings of the Maruts as the sons of Rudra born from the udder of Prishni, the dappled cow. Their mother bore them for great battle, the poets say, and the young storm gods leapt forth in splendour, with golden ornaments on their breasts and spears on their shoulders. Harnessing spotted deer to their chariots, they roar across the sky, shaking the mountains and bending the forests, pouring rain from the udder of heaven. Prishni's milk, like the rain, nourishes the world, and some hymns link it to the soma drink itself. Later texts reuse her name for a different figure: in the Bhagavata Purana, Prishni is the wife of Prajapati Sutapas who, after long austerity, received Vishnu as her son and was later reborn as Aditi and then as Devaki.
variations: Scholars variously interpret Prishni as the storm cloud, the starry night sky or the earth.
The Prishni of the Bhagavata Purana (a past life of Devaki, mother of Prishnigarbha) is a namesake rather than the Vedic mother of the Maruts.

nodes.name: Vak
nodes.description: Vak is the goddess of speech, the sacred word through which the gods act and the cosmos is ordered. In Rig Veda 10.125 she speaks in her own voice as the queen who sustains all the gods; in the Brahmanas she is Prajapati's partner in creation and is identified with Saraswati.
nodes.story: In Rig Veda 10.125, the hymn attributed to the seer Vak, daughter of Ambhrina, the goddess herself speaks. I move with the Rudras and the Vasus, she declares, with the Adityas and all the gods; I support Mitra and Varuna, Indra and Agni, and the two Ashvins. I am the queen, the gatherer of treasures, the first of those worthy of worship. The gods have set me in many places. Through me alone one eats, sees, breathes and hears; whom I love I make mighty, a sage or a seer. I bend the bow for Rudra so that his arrow strikes the hater of the sacred word. My birthplace is in the waters, in the ocean, and I blow forth like the wind, reaching beyond heaven and beyond this earth, so vast have I become.
variations: The Brahmanas identify Vak with Saraswati (e.g. 'Vak is Saraswati'), and later tradition merges the two.
Rig Veda 10.125 is recited in Shakta worship as the Devi Sukta, read as the self-proclamation of the supreme Goddess.
Some Brahmana passages describe Prajapati creating together with Vak, others describe Vak as his daughter.

nodes.name: Ratri
nodes.description: Ratri is the Vedic goddess of night, sister of Ushas (Dawn), who adorns the dark with stars and gives rest and protection to living beings. The Ratri Sukta (Rig Veda 10.127) is her main hymn, and later Shakta tradition links her with the Goddess as Kalaratri and Mahamaya.
nodes.story: In Rig Veda 10.127 the goddess Night draws near and looks about with many eyes, the stars, putting on all her glories. Immortal, she fills the wide space, the depths and the heights, and drives away darkness with her light. Coming, she makes room for her sister Dawn, and darkness too will pass. At her approach the villages settle to rest, and so do all who walk, all who fly and even the swift falcons. The poet asks her to ward off the she-wolf and the wolf, to keep away the thief, and to be easy to pass through. A Yajur Veda legend adds that when Yama died, his sister Yami could not stop grieving, for there was only day; so the gods created night, and with the coming of tomorrow she began to forget.
variations: The Rig Veda presents Night as benign and protective; later tradition also knows a fearsome aspect, Kalaratri.
In Shakta usage the Ratri Sukta is recited before the Devi Mahatmya, where the Goddess is praised as Yoganidra, Kalaratri and Mahamaya.

nodes.name: Ushas
nodes.description: Ushas is the goddess of dawn, the most celebrated goddess of the Rig Veda, praised in some twenty hymns as the radiant daughter of Heaven who awakens all beings and opens the way for the sun. Ever young herself, she reminds mortals of the passing of their days.
nodes.story: The Rig Veda pictures Dawn arriving each morning in a shining chariot drawn by ruddy horses or cows, clothed in light like a dancer or a bride who displays her beauty. She drives away her sister Night, rouses every creature to its work, and uncovers the treasures that darkness hid. She is the same each day, yet by her coming she wears away the lives of men, so the poets pray to her for long life and wealth. One hymn (4.30) tells a darker tale: Indra struck Dawn's cart with his vajra, and the daughter of Heaven fled in terror, her shattered chariot lying by the river Vipash. In the Rig Veda's great Ushas hymns (1.113, 1.123) she is also the sister of Bhaga and the kin of Varuna.
nodes.vahana: Chariot drawn by ruddy horses or cows
variations: Several hymns describe the Sun following Dawn as a lover or husband, while others make her the mother who bears the Sun and Agni.
The Aitareya Brahmana's story of Prajapati and his daughter identifies the daughter as either the sky or Ushas.
She is cognate with the Greek Eos and Latin Aurora; her worship faded after the Vedic period.

nodes.name: Ashvins
nodes.description: The Ashvins are twin horsemen gods of the morning, divine physicians and rescuers who appear at dawn in a golden chariot. Children of Vivasvat (Surya) and Saranyu (Sanjna), they heal the sick, restore youth and save those in distress; in the Mahabharata they are the fathers of Nakula and Sahadeva.
nodes.story: The Mahabharata tells that the princess Sukanya was married to the aged sage Chyavana. One day the Ashvins saw her bathing and urged her to leave the old man for one of them. She refused, faithful to her husband. Pleased, the twins offered to make Chyavana young and handsome, but she would then have to choose among the three. All three entered a pool and rose as identical youths of radiant beauty. Sukanya, looking carefully, chose her own husband. In gratitude Chyavana promised to win the twins a share of soma, from which the gods had excluded them as mere healers. When Indra raised his vajra to stop the offering, Chyavana conjured the terrible demon Mada, and Indra yielded, admitting the Ashvins among the soma-drinking gods.
nodes.vahana: Three-wheeled golden chariot drawn by horses or birds
variations: The Rig Veda calls them 'offspring of Dyaus' as well as children of Vivasvat and Saranyu; the Puranas say Sanjna bore them in the form of a mare to Surya as a horse.
In the Shatapatha Brahmana the Chyavana story is told with the Ashvins receiving their share through a sacrificial secret; the Mahabharata adds the conflict with Indra and the demon Mada.
In some reckonings the two Ashvins complete the thirty-three gods with the Vasus, Rudras and Adityas.

nodes.name: Indra
nodes.description: King of the devas and wielder of the thunderbolt, Indra is the most-praised deity of the Rig Veda, where about a quarter of the hymns celebrate his soma-fuelled victories over Vritra and other foes. In the epics and Puranas he remains lord of Svarga and the rains, but becomes a more fallible figure who loses his throne, is cursed by sages and is outshone by Vishnu, Shiva and Krishna.
nodes.story: Having drunk deep of soma, Indra took up the vajra that Tvashtr had forged and went out against Vritra, the serpent who lay coiled upon the mountains holding back the waters. He struck the dragon between the shoulders and split him like a tree felled by an axe. Vritra's mother Danu fell over her son, lying above him like a cow with her calf, and was struck down too. Then the imprisoned waters, lowing like cows rushing to their stalls, streamed over the dragon's body toward the sea, and Indra, 'king of what moves and what rests', set the sun in the sky. The Rig Veda sings this victory again and again; later texts add that the killing brought on Indra the stain of brahmin-slaying, which drove him into hiding.
nodes.vahana: Airavata (white elephant); the horse Uchchaihshravas in later texts
variations: Rig Veda: supreme warrior-king and soma-drinker; epics and Puranas: a lesser king of the gods, often proud, lustful or fearful and dependent on Vishnu or Shiva.

Parentage: the Rig Veda hints at Dyaus as his father and speaks of a mother who bore him (later commentary names her Nishtigri); the epics and Puranas make him a son of Kashyapa and Aditi and one of the twelve Adityas.
In Puranic cosmology 'Indra' is an office held by a different being in each Manvantara; the Indra of the present age is Purandara.
His slaying of Vritra and Vishvarupa is heroic in the Rig Veda, but the Brahmanas and Mahabharata treat it as incurring brahmahatya (the sin of killing a brahmin).

nodes.name: Shachi (Indrani)
nodes.description: Shachi, called Indrani, is the queen of Indra and daughter of the Danava Puloman. Her name means 'might' or 'divine power', and a Rig Vedic hymn (10.159) in which she exults over her rivals is ascribed to 'Shachi Paulomi'. In the epics she is the model of the faithful wife, most famously in her resistance to Nahusha.
nodes.story: When Indra hid himself in a lotus stalk to escape the sin of killing Vishvarupa, the gods crowned the virtuous mortal king Nahusha in his place. Power made Nahusha arrogant, and he demanded Shachi as his queen. She took refuge with Brihaspati, then asked Nahusha for time. Praying to the goddess of rumour, Upashruti, she was led across the Himalaya to a lake where Indra lay hidden in the fibres of a lotus. On Indra's advice she told Nahusha she would receive him only if he came in a palanquin borne by the great seers. Impatient, Nahusha drove the sages on and touched Agastya with his foot; the sage cursed him to fall to earth as a serpent, and Indra returned to his throne and his queen.
variations: Rig Veda 10.86 (the Vrishakapi hymn) shows Indrani as outspoken and jealous; epic tradition presents her as the ideal chaste queen.
She is often identified with Aindri, the Matrika who is Indra's shakti, though Matrika lists treat Aindri as a separate battle-goddess.
Some Puranas name her children as Jayanta, Jayanti and Devasena; Devasena's parentage differs widely between texts.

nodes.name: Agni
nodes.description: Agni, the god of fire, opens the Rig Veda (1.1) and is its second most-praised deity: the priest of the gods and the messenger who carries offerings from the sacrificial fire to heaven. He dwells in the hearth, the lightning, the sun and the waters, and remains central to every Hindu rite, from marriage to cremation. Later he becomes guardian of the south-east and a figure in epic tales such as the burning of the Khandava forest.
nodes.story: Once Agni was asked by the rakshasa Puloman whether the woman in the ashram was Puloma, wife of the sage Bhrigu, whom the demon had long ago claimed. Bound to truth, Agni admitted that she was. The demon carried her off, and her unborn child Chyavana fell from her womb blazing so brightly that the demon was burnt to ash. Bhrigu, enraged that Agni had betrayed his wife, cursed him to devour everything, clean and unclean alike. Agni protested that he had only spoken the truth, and withdrew from the world, so that all sacrifices ceased. Brahma then softened the curse: whatever Agni touches would be made pure, and his hunger would purify rather than defile the world.
variations: Rig Veda: born of heaven and earth, of the waters (as Apam Napat) or of the fire-drills; Vishnu Purana: eldest son of Brahma; other lists make him one of the eight Vasus (Anala).
Agni's role in Kartikeya's birth varies: the Mahabharata makes Agni and Svaha his parents, while the Ramayana and Shaiva Puranas have Agni only carry Shiva's seed.
The Brahmanas sometimes identify Agni with Rudra, reflecting Rudra's fiery nature.

nodes.name: Svaha
nodes.description: Svaha is the wife of Agni and the personification of the sacred exclamation svaha, uttered as each offering is poured into the fire. The word is Vedic, but her story as a goddess first appears in the Mahabharata and the Puranas, which make her a daughter of Daksha and Prasuti.
nodes.story: Agni once fell in love with the wives of the Seven Sages, and wasted away with longing he could not honourably fulfil. Svaha, Daksha's daughter, had long loved Agni. She took the form of Shiva, wife of Angiras, and came to him; then, one by one, she assumed the forms of five more of the sages' wives. Each time she flew away in the shape of a bird to a white mountain and cast Agni's seed into a golden vessel among the reeds. Only the form of Arundhati, the steadfast wife of Vasishtha, she could not take. From the seed collected six times a radiant child was born with six heads: Skanda. Agni accepted Svaha as his wife, and ever since offerings are made to the fire with her name.
nodes.abode: With Agni in the sacrificial fire
variations: Mahabharata: Svaha takes the forms of six sages' wives and is Skanda's mother; Shaiva Puranas make Skanda the son of Shiva and Parvati, with Agni only a carrier of the seed.
The Brahmavaivarta and Devi Bhagavata Puranas treat Svaha as a part-form of Prakriti, the supreme Goddess.
Her sons with Agni are named as Pavaka, Pavamana and Shuchi in the Vishnu Purana.

nodes.name: Varuna
nodes.description: In the Rig Veda Varuna is the sovereign guardian of rita, the cosmic and moral order: an all-seeing king who binds wrongdoers with his noose and forgives the penitent. Over time he loses this ethical supremacy and becomes chiefly lord of the waters and the ocean, guardian of the west among the Dikpalas.
nodes.story: King Harishchandra had a hundred wives but no son. On Narada's advice he prayed to Varuna, promising that if a son were born he would sacrifice him to the god. Rohita was born, but each time Varuna came to claim him the king found an excuse, until the boy, grown, took his bow and fled to the forest. Varuna struck Harishchandra with dropsy. After years of wandering, Rohita bought Shunahshepa, a brahmin boy, from his poor father Ajigarta for a hundred cows as a substitute. Bound to the sacrificial post, Shunahshepa praised Prajapati, Agni, Savitr, Varuna and Ushas in turn. With each verse a fetter loosened and the king's belly shrank, until the boy was free and Harishchandra was healed. Vishvamitra then adopted Shunahshepa as his son.
nodes.abode: A palace of a thousand doors in heaven (Vedic); the ocean and Sukha in the west (Puranic)
variations: Rig Veda: supreme moral sovereign paired with Mitra; epics and Puranas: lord of the waters and a regional guardian (west).
Bhrigu is called Varuni, son of Varuna, in the Taittiriya Upanishad and Brahmanas, but a mind-born son of Brahma in the Puranas.
Some scholars link Varuna with the Greek Ouranos; the etymology is debated.

nodes.name: Mitra
nodes.description: Mitra, whose name means both 'friend' and 'contract', is the Aditya of alliances, treaties and social harmony, almost always invoked together with Varuna as Mitra-Varuna. He is one of the oldest attested Indo-Iranian gods: he appears with Varuna, Indra and the Nasatyas in a Mitanni treaty of the fourteenth century BCE, and as Mithra in Iran.
nodes.story: The Shatapatha Brahmana tells that when the gods resolved to press and so 'slay' King Soma for the sacrifice, they called on Mitra to join them. Mitra refused, saying 'I am the friend of all beings'. Yet the gods insisted he take a share, and when he did, the cattle turned away from him, murmuring that he who was called Friend had done a cruel deed. The Rig Veda paints a warmer picture: Mitra, speaking, brings people together; he upholds earth and sky and watches the tillers of the soil with unwinking eye. With Varuna he guards rita, the true order, and the pair are the joint fathers of the sages Vasishtha and Agastya, born when their seed fell into a jar at the sight of the apsara Urvashi.
variations: Later Vedic texts pair Mitra with day and Varuna with night.
In the Puranas Mitra is simply one of twelve Adityas presiding over a month of the solar year, with little independent mythology.

nodes.name: Surya (Vivasvat)
nodes.description: Surya is the Sun god, the visible eye of Mitra and Varuna in the Rig Veda, crossing the sky in a chariot drawn by seven horses. Vivasvat, originally a separate Vedic figure and father of Yama and Manu, merged with Surya, so that in the epics and Puranas the Sun is the ancestor of the Solar dynasty and father of Yama, Yami, Manu, the Ashvins, Shani, Karna and Sugriva. He is worshipped daily in the Gayatri and at sunrise, and in his own cults at Konark and Multan.
nodes.story: Sanjna, daughter of Vishvakarma, could not bear the blazing heat of her husband Surya. Leaving behind a shadow-double, Chhaya, to care for their children, she fled to her father and then to the northern lands, where she practised austerities in the form of a mare. Chhaya bore Surya children of her own and favoured them, until Yama, in anger, raised his foot against her and she cursed him. Surya, seeing that no true mother would curse her son, forced Chhaya to confess. He went to Vishvakarma, who set him on his lathe and trimmed away part of his brilliance, fashioning weapons for the gods from the shavings. Surya then took the form of a stallion and found Sanjna; from their union were born the twin Ashvins.
nodes.vahana: Chariot of seven horses driven by Aruna
variations: Vivasvat and Surya are distinct in the Rig Veda; the epics and Puranas treat them as one.
The Sun's wife is Sanjna (Saranyu) with her shadow Chhaya in the Puranas; in Rig Veda 10.17 the substitute is an unnamed 'savarna' (look-alike).
Sugriva is Surya's son in the Valmiki Ramayana; later retellings add that both Vali and Sugriva were born to Riksharaja.
Shani and Savarni Manu are sons of Chhaya, while Yama, Yami, Vaivasvata Manu and the Ashvins are sons of Sanjna; some Puranas differ on individual children.
The Aditya Hridayam hymn, taught to Rama by Agastya, is placed by the Critical Edition of the Ramayana among later additions.

nodes.name: Sanjna (Saranyu)
nodes.description: Sanjna, the Vedic Saranyu, is the daughter of the divine artisan Tvashtr (Vishvakarma in the Puranas) and the wife of the Sun, Vivasvat. She is the mother of Yama and Yami, of Vaivasvata Manu and of the twin Ashvins, and her flight from her husband, leaving a substitute behind, is one of the oldest stories in Indian literature.
nodes.story: The Rig Veda preserves the tale in two riddling verses. Tvashtr held a wedding for his daughter Saranyu, and the whole world gathered. But the mother of Yama, once wed to the great Vivasvat, vanished. The immortals hid her away from mortals, fashioned a woman of like appearance and gave her to Vivasvat; and Saranyu bore the Ashvins and abandoned the twins. Later commentators fill in the gaps: Saranyu, having borne Yama and Yami, left a look-alike and fled in the form of a mare. Vivasvat, discovering the deceit, became a stallion and followed her, and from their union the Ashvins were born. The Puranas retell the same story with the shadow-wife named Chhaya and the Sun's unbearable brightness as the reason for Sanjna's flight.
variations: Rig Veda: daughter of Tvashtr; Puranas: daughter of Vishvakarma (the two craftsmen being identified).
In Rig Veda 10.17 the substitute is unnamed; the Puranas call her Chhaya ('shadow').
The Vaivasvata Manu is Sanjna's son in the Puranas; some interpreters of Rig Veda 10.17 make Manu the son of the substitute.

nodes.name: Chhaya
nodes.description: Chhaya, 'Shadow', is the double whom Sanjna created from herself to take her place beside the Sun. She became Surya's second wife and the mother of Shani, Savarni Manu and the river-goddess Tapati. The figure grows out of the unnamed look-alike wife (savarna) of Rig Veda 10.17.
nodes.story: Sanjna made Chhaya from her own shadow and asked her to keep the secret and care for her children. Chhaya served Surya faithfully and bore him children of her own, but she could not love Sanjna's children as she loved hers. Yama, hurt by her partiality, raised his foot to kick her, and Chhaya cursed him that his leg would rot and fall. Yama ran to his father. Surya, unable to undo the curse, softened it so that worms would carry flesh from the wound to the earth and Yama would be healed. Then he confronted Chhaya: no mother curses her own son. Threatened with his anger, she confessed the truth, and Surya set out to find Sanjna. Chhaya's son Shani, the slow planet Saturn, inherited her dark complexion.
variations: Rig Veda 10.17 speaks only of an unnamed substitute 'of like appearance' (savarna); the name Chhaya appears in the Harivamsha and Puranas.
Details of Yama's curse and Surya's remedy differ between the Harivamsha, Markandeya and other Puranas.
Later popular tradition attributes Shani's darkness to Chhaya's penance in the sun while pregnant with him.

nodes.name: Soma (Chandra)
nodes.description: In the Rig Veda Soma is the sacred plant, the drink pressed from it and the god who embodies it; the entire ninth book is devoted to Soma Pavamana, 'the purifying'. Already in late Vedic texts Soma is identified with the Moon, the cup from which the gods drink the elixir, and in the epics and Puranas he is Chandra, son of Atri, husband of the twenty-seven Nakshatras and ancestor of the Lunar dynasty through his son Budha.
nodes.story: Soma performed a great royal sacrifice and, intoxicated by power, carried off Tara, wife of Brihaspati, guru of the gods. Brihaspati demanded her back, but Soma refused. Shukra, rival guru of the asuras, took Soma's side, and Rudra, a pupil of Angiras, took Brihaspati's, so that gods and asuras were drawn into the Tarakamaya war. Brahma finally intervened and restored Tara to her husband, but she was pregnant. When a child of dazzling beauty was born, both Soma and Brihaspati claimed him. Tara, ashamed, would not speak until Brahma asked her gently, and she confessed that the child was Soma's. Soma named his son Budha, the planet Mercury, and through Budha's son Pururavas the Lunar dynasty began.
symbols: chariot drawn by ten white horses or antelope
nodes.vahana: Chariot drawn by ten white horses (or an antelope)
nodes.abode: Chandraloka; in the Vedic view, the highest heaven and the mountains where the soma plant grows
variations: Origin: the Rig Veda has the soma plant brought from heaven by an eagle; the Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas make Chandra the son of Atri (and Anasuya), born from Atri's eyes; other Puranas have him rise from the Churning of the Ocean.

Daksha cursed Soma to waste away for favouring Rohini above her 26 sisters; the curse was softened into the monthly waxing and waning, and Soma is said to have been restored at Prabhasa (Somnath) by worshipping Shiva.
In Rig Veda 10.85 Soma marries Surya, daughter of Savitr; the later husband of the Nakshatras reflects the lunar identification.
Some Vedic texts name Soma, not Kubera, as guardian of the north.

nodes.name: Vayu
nodes.description: Vayu is the god of the wind and of breath (prana), in the Rig Veda a swift, beautiful charioteer who has the right to drink the first draught of soma, often paired with Indra. In the Upanishads he is the vital breath and in the epics he is guardian of the north-west and the divine father of Hanuman and Bhima.
nodes.story: After a victory over the asuras, the gods grew proud, thinking it their own doing. Brahman appeared before them as a mysterious spirit (yaksha). They sent Agni to find out who it was, and when Agni boasted he could burn anything on earth, the spirit set down a blade of grass; Agni could not burn it. Then Vayu went, declaring, 'I am Matarishvan; I can carry off whatever there is on earth'. The spirit placed the blade of grass before him, and Vayu rushed at it with all his force but could not stir it. Humbled, he returned. Only when Indra approached did the spirit vanish, and the goddess Uma Haimavati revealed that it was Brahman, the power behind every victory.
nodes.vahana: Gazelle or antelope; a chariot of red or purple horses (Vedic)
nodes.abode: The atmosphere (antariksha); Vayuloka in the north-west
variations: The Rig Veda distinguishes Vayu (wind as a god) from Vata (the physical wind); later texts merge them.
Madhva's Dvaita tradition holds that Hanuman, Bhima and Madhvacharya himself are successive incarnations of Vayu.
Regional and Puranic tales tell of a contest between Vayu and Shesha in which Vayu blew a peak off Mount Meru, which became Lanka's Trikuta or a sacred hill in the south; versions vary.

nodes.name: Rudra
nodes.description: Rudra, the 'roarer' or 'howler', is the fierce Vedic god of storms, wild places, disease and healing, father of the Maruts, whose arrows are feared and whose medicines are prayed for. The Yajur Veda's Shatarudriya litany and the Brahmanas expand his many names, and the Shvetashvatara Upanishad proclaims him the one supreme lord; through these stages the Vedic Rudra becomes the Shiva of the epics and Puranas.
nodes.story: The Shatapatha Brahmana tells that when Prajapati brought forth the creatures, a boy was born at the end of a year, and he cried. Prajapati asked him why he wept, when he had been born out of toil and austerity. 'Because I have no name,' said the boy; 'give me a name.' Prajapati called him Rudra, and because he still cried, he gave him name after name: Sharva, Pashupati, Ugra, Ashani, Bhava, Mahadeva and Ishana. Each name was a form of Agni: the waters, the plants, the wind, the lightning, the rain, the moon and the sun. With eight names the boy became Kumara. The Rig Veda addresses the same god with awe, begging him to spare children and cattle and to heal with his thousand remedies.
nodes.abode: Mountains and wild places (Vedic); Mount Mujavat
variations: Rig Veda: a secondary but feared and healing god; Yajur Veda and Brahmanas: an outsider god excluded from the main sacrifice and given leftover offerings; Shvetashvatara Upanishad: the supreme lord, identified with Shiva.
Puranic accounts make Rudra born from Brahma's anger or forehead and divided into eleven Rudras; Shaiva texts instead hold Shiva to be the unborn source of Brahma and Vishnu.
The Brahmanas equate Rudra with Agni; the Aitareya Brahmana tells of Rudra (as Bhutavat) shooting Prajapati for pursuing his own daughter.

nodes.name: Yama (Dharmaraja)
nodes.description: In the Rig Veda Yama, son of Vivasvat, is the first mortal to die and the king who rules the blissful world of the ancestors. In later literature he becomes the stern but just lord of death and judge of the dead, guardian of the south, and is identified with Dharma, the divine father of Yudhishthira in the Mahabharata.
nodes.story: The Rig Veda's funeral hymn honours Yama as the one who first went down the great slopes and found the path for many, the way by which our fathers of old departed. The dead are sent along those ancient paths to meet the fathers and King Yama in the highest heaven, and are told to run past the two four-eyed, broad-nosed dogs, sons of Sarama, who guard the way and watch over men. Later tradition gives Yama a darker, stricter office: seated in his hall with his scribe Chitragupta reading out each soul's deeds, he assigns reward and punishment. Yet he is never merely cruel; to Nachiketa he teaches the secret of the deathless Self, and to Savitri he returns her husband's life in reward for her wisdom and steadfastness.
nodes.abode: Yamaloka and the city Samyamani in the south
variations: Rig Veda: a benign king of the ancestors in heaven; epics and Puranas: the judge of the dead presiding over the hells.
The Mahabharata usually identifies Yama with Dharma (father of Yudhishthira and, through Mandavya's curse, born as Vidura), but some passages treat Dharma as a distinct deity, son of Brahma.
Comparative scholars link Yama with the Iranian Yima, the first king of a golden age.

nodes.name: Yami (Yamuna)
nodes.description: Yami is the twin sister of Yama and daughter of Vivasvat and Saranyu, known from a famous Rig Vedic dialogue with her brother. Later tradition identifies her with the river-goddess Yamuna, and the festival of Yama Dvitiya (Bhai Dooj) celebrates her love for her brother.
nodes.story: In a Rig Vedic dialogue the twins speak as the first pair of humans. Yami urges Yama to unite with her so that their line may continue; Yama refuses, saying that what is right among kin forbids it and that the watchers of the gods never rest, and he bids her seek another. A later Vedic text tells what followed Yama's death. Yami grieved without end, and when the gods tried to console her she would only say, 'Today he died.' Since there was as yet only day, her grief could never grow old. So the gods created night; after night came a new morning, and she forgot her sorrow. Thus, it is said, day and night together make people forget grief. In later lore Yami flows as the Yamuna, whom Yama visits each year for her blessing.
nodes.abode: The Yamuna river; Yamunotri in the Himalaya
variations: The identification of the Vedic Yami with the river Yamuna is post-Vedic.
The Bhagavata Purana's Kalindi, daughter of the Sun who marries Krishna, is identified with the Yamuna by many traditions, though not all equate her with Yami.
Yama Dvitiya legends of Yami feeding her brother are regional and late.

nodes.name: Savitr
nodes.description: Savitr, 'the Impeller', is the golden Vedic god who rouses all beings to activity at dawn and lays them to rest at dusk. He is the deity of the Gayatri mantra (Rig Veda 3.62.10), recited daily by twice-born Hindus. Later he merges with Surya and is listed among the twelve Adityas.
nodes.story: The Rig Veda pictures Savitr as a golden god with golden arms and hands, riding a golden chariot along ancient dustless paths. At morning he raises his arms and all creatures stir and go to their work; at evening he spreads out his arms again and the weaver rolls up her cloth, the traveller turns home and the birds return to their nests, for none can transgress his ordinances. It was to him that the seer Vishvamitra addressed the verse that became the holiest of all mantras: 'May we meditate on the adorable splendour of the god Savitr, who shall stimulate our thoughts.' Known as the Gayatri or Savitri, it is taught to every boy at his sacred-thread initiation and recited at dawn and dusk to this day.
nodes.vahana: Golden chariot drawn by brown, white-footed horses
nodes.abode: The heavens and the paths of the sun
variations: In the Rig Veda Savitr is distinct from Surya; later texts identify the two.
A Brahmana legend explains his golden hands as a replacement for hands lost at the sacrifice; versions differ.
Savitr's daughter Surya marries Soma in Rig Veda 10.85.

nodes.name: Pushan
nodes.description: Pushan, 'the Nourisher', is the Vedic god of roads, journeys and herds, who finds lost cattle, protects travellers and guides the souls of the dead. He rides a chariot drawn by goats and eats gruel (karambha), and later becomes one of the twelve Adityas with solar associations.
nodes.story: The Rig Veda knows Pushan as the god who eats mashed gruel, and later tradition explains why. At Daksha's great sacrifice, when Daksha insulted Shiva, Pushan laughed and showed his teeth in approval. When Sati gave up her life and Shiva's fury took form as Virabhadra, the ganas fell upon the assembly: Bhrigu's beard was torn out, Bhaga was blinded and Pushan's teeth were knocked out. Afterwards the gods begged Shiva to restore the sacrifice. Shiva relented and ruled that Pushan would henceforth eat through the teeth of the sacrificer, taking only soft, ground offerings. Yet the Vedic Pushan is gentle and helpful: he knows every path, drives away wolves and robbers, and leads the departed safely to the fathers.
nodes.abode: The roads and the paths between worlds
variations: The Brahmanas attribute Pushan's lost teeth to eating a dangerous portion of Rudra's (or Prajapati's) sacrifice; the Puranas to Virabhadra's attack on Daksha's yajna.
Pushan appears among the twelve Adityas only in later lists; in the Rig Veda he is not usually called an Aditya.

nodes.name: Bhaga
nodes.description: Bhaga, 'the Dispenser' or 'Share', is the Aditya who apportions wealth, good fortune and marital happiness. His name lies at the root of the title Bhagavan, 'the fortunate' or 'blessed one', and is cognate with Slavic bog, 'god'.
nodes.story: The Rig Veda invokes Bhaga at dawn, for the morning is the time of apportioning; Ushas is called his sister, and people pray that they may be 'rich in Bhaga'. The Brahmanas tell how, at a sacrifice, a dangerous portion was set before Bhaga, and when he looked at it his eyes were destroyed; therefore, they say, Bhaga is blind, and fortune is dealt out without seeing. The Puranas give the tale a new setting. At Daksha's sacrifice Bhaga signalled his approval with his eyes when Daksha reviled Shiva, and Virabhadra plucked them out. When Shiva was appeased, he granted that Bhaga would see through the eyes of Mitra, and so good fortune was restored to the world.
variations: The Brahmanas blame his blindness on a sacrificial portion; the Puranas on Virabhadra at Daksha's yajna.
The Bhagavata Purana names Siddhi as Bhaga's wife and gives him children; this is absent from Vedic sources.

nodes.name: Aryaman
nodes.description: Aryaman is the Aditya of hospitality, custom, marriage and the bonds between clans, the third of the great Adityas alongside Mitra and Varuna. Later he becomes chief of the Pitris (ancestors), and in the Bhagavad Gita Krishna says, 'Among the ancestors I am Aryaman' (10.29).
nodes.story: Aryaman's greatest role is at the wedding. In the Rig Veda's marriage hymn the bride is freed from her father's house and bound to her husband's, and the couple pray that Aryaman will unite them in harmony until old age. In later rites the bride offers parched grain to Aryaman as she circles the sacred fire, asking that the bond be firm and long. As keeper of hospitality he oversees the exchange of gifts and the welcome of guests between clans. Later Vedic texts speak of the Milky Way as 'Aryaman's path', and in time he becomes king of the ancestors, to whom offerings are made at shraddha rites, a role the Bhagavad Gita recalls when Krishna names Aryaman as his own glory among the Pitris.
variations: Rig Veda: god of hospitality and alliance; epics and Puranas: chief of the Pitris.
His Iranian counterpart Airyaman is a god of healing and friendship.

nodes.name: Tvashtr
nodes.description: Tvashtr is the Vedic divine craftsman who shapes living forms in the womb, forged Indra's vajra and made the cup of the gods. He is father of Saranyu and of the three-headed Vishvarupa, whose killing turned him into Indra's enemy. Epics and Puranas list him among the twelve Adityas and often merge him with Vishvakarma.
nodes.story: Tvashtr's three-headed son Vishvarupa served as priest of the gods, but his mother was of the asuras, and he secretly offered part of the sacrifice to them. Indra, fearing his power, cut off his three heads, which flew off as birds: the francolin, the sparrow and the partridge. Grieving, Tvashtr held a soma sacrifice from which he excluded Indra, but Indra seized the soma and drank it by force. Tvashtr poured what remained into the fire, crying 'Grow, you whose foe is Indra!' From the fire arose Vritra, who grew an arrow's length each day. But Tvashtr had misplaced the accent of his words, so that they meant 'you whom Indra shall slay', and the curse turned back upon his own creation.
variations: In the Rig Veda Tvashtr is Indra's armourer; the Brahmanas and Mahabharata make him Indra's enemy after Vishvarupa's death.
The Bhagavata Purana has Vritra rise from Tvashtr's fire with the mis-accented mantra, as in the Brahmanas, while the Mahabharata varies the details.
Epics and Puranas often identify Tvashtr with Vishvakarma; he is also listed as one of the twelve Adityas.

nodes.name: Vishvakarma
nodes.description: In two hymns of the Rig Veda (10.81-82) Vishvakarman, the 'All-Maker', is a cosmic creator who sacrifices the worlds into being. In the epics and Puranas he becomes the architect and engineer of the gods, builder of cities such as Lanka and Dvaraka and maker of celestial weapons and chariots. He is widely worshipped by craftspeople on Vishvakarma Puja.
nodes.story: The Rig Veda asks: what was the ground, what the wood and what the tree from which the All-Maker, seeing all, fashioned heaven and earth? He is the seer and priest who offered all the worlds in sacrifice and, with eyes, faces, arms and feet on every side, forged sky and earth together with his arms and wings. In later ages he becomes the craftsman of the gods. When his daughter Sanjna could not bear her husband's brilliance, he placed Surya on his lathe and trimmed away an eighth of his light, and from the glowing shavings fashioned Vishnu's Sudarshana discus, Shiva's trident and other weapons of the gods. He built the golden city of Lanka, the Pushpaka chariot and, at Krishna's request, the island fortress-city of Dvaraka.
nodes.vahana: Hamsa (swan) or elephant in popular iconography
variations: Rig Veda: a supreme creator, sometimes equated with Prajapati; epics and Puranas: the artisan of the gods.
Parentage differs: the Vishnu Purana makes him son of the Vasu Prabhasa and Yogasiddha, sister of Brihaspati.
He is frequently identified with Tvashtr, which makes him Sanjna's father in the Puranas.
Maya, not Vishvakarma, is the architect of the asuras and of the Pandavas' hall at Indraprastha.

nodes.name: Parjanya
nodes.description: Parjanya is the Vedic god of the rain-cloud, who roars like a bull, quickens plants, cattle and women with his seed and makes the earth fruitful. Three Rig Vedic hymns are addressed to him; later his rain-giving role passes largely to Indra, while Parjanya survives as an Aditya and as a word for rain-cloud.
nodes.story: When Parjanya comes, the Rig Veda sings, the winds rush out, the lightning flies, the plants shoot up and the sky swells; the earth becomes ready for every creature when he quickens her with his seed. Like a charioteer lashing his horses he drives forth the messengers of rain; from afar the lion's roar of thunder rises. Trees are shattered, demons are struck down, and even the innocent flee before the mighty one, while the wicked tremble. Then the singer asks him to rest: you have poured the rain, now hold it back; you have made the deserts passable and the plants grow. Another hymn describes the frogs, silent through the dry year like brahmins keeping a vow, bursting into chant at the first rains Parjanya brings.
variations: Rig Veda: son of Dyaus and husband of the earth; later lexicons give Parjanya as a name of Indra.
Some epic and Puranic lists of the twelve Adityas include Parjanya; others do not.

nodes.name: Brihaspati
nodes.description: Brihaspati, 'Lord of Prayer', is the Vedic priest of the gods, embodiment of the power of sacred speech. In the epics and Puranas he is the guru of the devas, son of the sage Angiras, rival of the asura teacher Shukra, husband of Tara, and the planet Jupiter (Guru) among the Navagraha.
nodes.story: The Panis had hidden the cattle of the gods in the rock-cave of Vala. Brihaspati, leading the Angiras seers, came singing to the mountain. With his roaring chant, the Rig Veda says, he split the rock as easily as a bird's egg is broken; he drove out the cows from the cave like the kernel from a husk, and with them brought forth the dawn, the sun and the light. As a seer takes honey from a stone, he drew the treasure from the hollow mountain, and Vala mourned his lost cattle like a tree its fallen leaves. The Rig Veda gives the same deed to Indra, who shatters Vala with the Angirases' help. Later Brihaspati is the wise counsellor of the gods and the teacher who seeks to regain the lore of reviving the dead.
nodes.vahana: Chariot drawn by eight horses (Puranic); elephant in some iconography
variations: In the Rig Veda Brihaspati is a form of priestly power closely linked with Agni and Indra; the epics make him a son of Angiras and guru of the gods.
The Puranas agree that Tara bore Budha to Soma, but differ on how the paternity dispute with Brihaspati was settled and on Budha's own reaction.
Later tradition attributes the materialist Barhaspatya (Charvaka) doctrine to Brihaspati, sometimes as a ruse to mislead the asuras.

nodes.name: Brahma
nodes.description: Brahma is the four-faced creator god of the Trimurti, who fashions the worlds and their creatures at the start of each cosmic cycle. He inherits the role of the Vedic creator Prajapati and first appears as a personal god in the Upanishads (Mundaka calls him the first of the gods). Although revered as the grandsire (Pitamaha) of all beings, he has very few temples and receives little independent worship.
nodes.story: At the end of a cosmic night, when Vishnu lay asleep on the serpent Shesha upon the causal waters, a golden lotus rose from his navel, and on it Brahma awoke. Seeing nothing but water and darkness, he turned to look in every direction, and so gained four faces. Not knowing who he was or where he came from, he climbed down the lotus stalk for ages without finding its root, then returned to his seat. There he heard a voice sound two syllables, 'tapa, tapa' (austerity), and he sat in meditation for a thousand divine years. When his mind became clear, the Lord revealed himself, and Brahma, empowered, began to create: first the mind-born sages, then the Prajapatis, gods, demons, humans and all living things.
variations: Vaishnava Puranas (Bhagavata, Vishnu) have Brahma born from the lotus of Vishnu's navel; Shaiva texts (Shiva Purana, Linga Purana) have Brahma and Vishnu both emanate from Shiva; Shakta texts (Devi Bhagavata) make all three gods creations of the Great Goddess.
Manusmriti and several Puranas describe him as born within the golden cosmic egg (Hiranyagarbha) that floated on the primordial waters.
He is said to have once had five heads; Shaiva texts say Shiva (as Bhairava) cut off the fifth for its arrogance or for a false claim during the pillar-of-light contest.

Legends explaining his lack of worship vary: Shiva's curse after Brahma lied about seeing the top of the fiery linga, or Savitri's curse at Pushkar (Padma Purana), where one of his few temples stands.

nodes.name: Vishnu
nodes.description: Vishnu is the preserver of the Trimurti and the supreme deity of Vaishnavism, who descends as avatars whenever dharma declines. In the Rig Veda he is a comparatively minor but exalted god, the friend of Indra famed for his three strides across the cosmos, and he later rises to cosmic supremacy in the epics and Puranas. His consorts are Lakshmi (Shri) and Bhudevi, his mount is Garuda and he rests on the serpent Shesha in the ocean of milk.
nodes.story: Between two ages of creation Vishnu lay in yogic sleep on the coils of Shesha, floating on the endless ocean. From the wax of his ears two mighty demons, Madhu and Kaitabha, sprang up and rushed at Brahma, who sat trembling on the lotus from Vishnu's navel. Brahma praised Yoganidra, the goddess of sleep, and she withdrew from Vishnu's eyes. The Lord awoke and wrestled the demons with his bare arms for five thousand years. Drunk with pride, they offered him any boon he wished. 'Then be slain by me,' said Vishnu. Trapped by their own word, they asked to be killed where the earth was not flooded. Vishnu smiled, laid them across his thighs, and severed their heads with his discus, earning the name Madhusudana.
variations: In the Rig Veda Vishnu has only a handful of hymns and is chiefly Indra's ally; his supremacy develops in the Brahmanas (where he is identified with the sacrifice) and the epics.
Vaishnava traditions identify Vishnu (Narayana) with the supreme Brahman; Shaiva and Shakta texts place him below Shiva or the Devi respectively.
In the Devi Mahatmya the slaying of Madhu and Kaitabha is made possible by the Goddess as Yoganidra; in the Mahabharata and Harivamsha versions the emphasis is on Vishnu alone.
Some Tamil traditions make Vishnu the brother of Parvati (as Minakshi's brother Alagar), who gives her away in marriage to Shiva.

nodes.name: Shiva
nodes.description: Shiva is the destroyer and transformer of the Trimurti and the supreme deity of Shaivism, at once the ash-smeared ascetic of Mount Kailasa and the householder with Parvati and their sons. He grows out of the Vedic storm god Rudra, and the Shvetashvatara Upanishad is the first text to exalt Rudra-Shiva as the supreme lord. He is worshipped above all in the form of the linga.
nodes.story: When the gods and asuras churned the ocean of milk for the nectar of immortality, the first thing to rise from the waters was not treasure but Halahala, a black poison whose fumes began to scorch the three worlds. Gods, demons and every creature fled in terror, and Prajapati's creatures cried out for help. Moved by compassion, Shiva took the poison in his cupped palm and drank it. Parvati, alarmed, pressed his throat so it would go no further, or in other tellings Shiva simply held it there by his own power. The venom stained his throat a deep blue, and from that day he has been called Nilakantha, the blue-throated one, the god who swallows the world's suffering so that others may live.
variations: The word shiva ('auspicious') is used in the Rig Veda as an epithet of Rudra and other gods; the identification of Rudra with a supreme Shiva is first explicit in the Shvetashvatara Upanishad.

Shaiva Siddhanta, Kashmir Shaivism and the Pashupata and Lingayat traditions describe his nature and relation to the soul differently; Vaishnava texts sometimes make him subordinate to or a devotee of Vishnu.

In the Halahala episode, some versions have Parvati stop the poison at his throat, others have Shiva hold it by his own yogic power; Vishnu and Brahma are sometimes said to have asked him to drink it.

nodes.name: Saraswati
nodes.description: Saraswati is the goddess of knowledge, speech, music and the arts and the consort of Brahma. In the Rig Veda she is a mighty sacred river, praised as 'best of mothers, best of rivers, best of goddesses', and the Brahmanas identify her with Vak, sacred speech. In later Hinduism she becomes the white-clad patron of learning, worshipped especially at Vasant Panchami.
nodes.story: The Matsya Purana tells how Brahma, meditating on creation, brought forth from his own body a radiant woman, known by many names: Shatarupa, Savitri, Gayatri, Sarasvati. Captivated by her, he could not take his eyes from her; as she moved respectfully around him, a new face sprang up on each side so that he might keep gazing, and a fifth appeared above. Though she was born from him, she became his consort, and from their union came Svayambhuva Manu and the order of human life. Theologians have long read the episode as a mystery rather than a scandal: the creator and his own creative Word, speech and knowledge, must unite before the worlds can be named and ordered. Other texts, troubled by it, have Shiva sever Brahma's fifth head.
nodes.abode: Brahmaloka; the banks of the river Sarasvati
variations: In the Rig Veda she is chiefly a river goddess (Sarasvati river) linked with purification, fertility and the Ashvins; the later texts describe the river as vanishing into the desert.

Matsya Purana and others make her Brahma's daughter and consort; many traditions simply call her Brahma's wife, and some (Pushkar legend, Padma Purana) separate her from Savitri and Gayatri as distinct consorts.
The Brahmavaivarta Purana makes Sarasvati one of the three wives of Vishnu (with Lakshmi and Ganga), whose quarrel led to mutual curses turning them into rivers.
In Shakta theology (Devi Mahatmya, Devi Bhagavata) she is Mahasarasvati, one of the three great forms of the supreme Goddess.

nodes.name: Lakshmi (Shri)
nodes.description: Lakshmi, also called Shri, is the goddess of prosperity, fortune, beauty and sovereignty and the eternal consort of Vishnu. The Shri Sukta and the Shatapatha Brahmana already praise Shri as a radiant goddess of abundance, and in the Puranas she rises from the churning of the ocean of milk. She incarnates alongside Vishnu's avatars, most famously as Sita and Rukmini.
nodes.story: Once the sage Durvasa gave Indra a garland of heavenly flowers, but Indra tossed it onto his elephant, who trampled it. Durvasa cursed him, and Shri, fortune herself, departed from the heavens: the gods grew weak, sacrifices ceased and the asuras triumphed. On Vishnu's advice, gods and asuras churned the ocean of milk. Among the wonders that rose, the most dazzling was Lakshmi, seated on a full-blown lotus and holding lotuses in her hands. The sages sang the Shri Sukta, the rivers came to bathe her, and the elephants of the quarters poured water over her from golden vessels. The ocean gave her a garland of unfading lotuses. Ignoring every other suitor, she went straight to Vishnu and made her home on his chest, and fortune returned to the worlds.
symbols: gold coins flowing from her hand
nodes.vahana: Owl (uluka); sometimes an elephant; seated on a lotus
nodes.abode: Vaikuntha (on Vishnu's chest, the Shrivatsa); Kshira Sagara
variations: The Vishnu Purana first makes Shri the daughter of the sage Bhrigu and Khyati, and then describes her re-emergence from the ocean after Durvasa's curse.
In the Shatapatha Brahmana Shri emerges from Prajapati's austerities and the other gods take her qualities from her.

Vaishnava traditions hold she incarnates with each avatar: as Padma with Vamana, Dharani with Parashurama, Sita with Rama, Rukmini with Krishna; Sri Vaishnavism makes her the mediator (purushakara) between devotee and God.
In Shakta theology (Devi Mahatmya) Mahalakshmi is the supreme Goddess herself, source of all three great goddesses.
Her mount is given as the owl in eastern India (Bengal, Odisha); elsewhere she is shown seated on a lotus flanked by elephants.

nodes.name: Parvati (Uma)
nodes.description: Parvati, 'daughter of the mountain', is the consort of Shiva, the daughter of Himavan and Mena and the rebirth of Sati. First glimpsed as Uma Haimavati in the Kena Upanishad, she becomes the model of devoted love won through austerity and the mother of Ganesha and Kartikeya. In Shakta traditions she is a gentle form of the supreme Goddess, whose fierce aspects include Durga and Kali.
nodes.story: After Sati's death, Shiva withdrew into deep meditation, and the demon Taraka, who could be killed only by a son of Shiva, terrorized the gods. Sati was reborn as Parvati, and at the gods' urging Kama shot his flower arrow at Shiva while she served him, only to be burnt to ashes by the third eye. Undaunted, Parvati resolved to win Shiva by her own austerity. She gave up food, then even leaves, and was called Aparna.
