His name also means banner or bright sign, and trailing comets, dhumaketu or smoke-bannered, were counted among his many forms.
variations: In early texts ketu means a comet or bright sign; its role as the headless body of Svarbhanu and as the ninth graha develops in Puranic and astrological texts.
Some Puranas speak of many Ketus (comets) rather than a single graha.
In Jyotisha Ketu is the south (descending) lunar node, often linked with Ganesha as presiding deity.

nodes.name: Narakasura
nodes.description: The asura king of Pragjyotisha (associated with ancient Assam), son of the Earth goddess Bhudevi, fathered in many accounts by Vishnu as Varaha. He stole the earrings of Aditi and imprisoned thousands of princesses until Krishna, with Satyabhama, slew him; his death is celebrated as Naraka Chaturdashi on the eve of Diwali.
nodes.story: Naraka, son of the Earth, grew arrogant in his impregnable city of Pragjyotisha. He seized the umbrella of Varuna and the jewelled earrings of Aditi, mother of the gods, and carried off sixteen thousand maidens to his palace. Indra went to Dvaraka to plead for help, and Krishna rode out on Garuda with Satyabhama beside him. He smashed the mountain forts and the fields of nooses, slew the five-headed Mura who guarded the city, and destroyed Naraka's army. When Naraka hurled his spear, Krishna cut off his head with the discus. Bhudevi herself then came forward, returned Aditi's earrings and asked Krishna to protect Naraka's son Bhagadatta. Krishna freed the captive women and, to spare them from shame, accepted them all as his wives.
sources: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva and Udyoga Parva (references to Krishna slaying Naraka)
variations: The Kalika Purana makes him the son of Varaha and Bhudevi, raised by King Janaka, installed as guardian of the goddess Kamakhya, and later cursed by Vasishtha after turning impious.
In many South Indian and Deepavali tellings Satyabhama, as an incarnation of Bhudevi, delivers the fatal blow, since he could be killed only by his mother.
The number of captive women is given as sixteen thousand or sixteen thousand one hundred.
At his request, his death day is observed as Naraka Chaturdashi with lamps and ritual baths.

nodes.name: Kalanemi
nodes.description: A mighty Danava who led the asuras in the Tarakamaya war against the gods and was slain by Vishnu; the Harivamsha and Bhagavata say he was reborn as Kamsa. A different Kalanemi, a rakshasa uncle of Ravana, appears in later Ramayana traditions trying to stop Hanuman.
nodes.story: In the great war over Tara, wife of Brihaspati, the Danava Kalanemi rose against the devas like a mountain of darkness. The Harivamsha describes how he scattered the gods and took over the functions of the guardians of the world, claiming the sacrificial offerings for himself. The gods fled to Vishnu, who came mounted on Garuda. Kalanemi hurled his weapons at him, but Vishnu cut off the Danava's head with the Sudarshana discus. In another age, the Bhagavata and Harivamsha say, this same Kalanemi was born as Kamsa, the tyrant of Mathura, once again to be slain by Vishnu, now as Krishna. Later Ramayana retellings add a rakshasa Kalanemi who, disguised as a hermit, tried to delay Hanuman on his journey to the healing herb, and was killed by him.
variations: The Danava of the Harivamsha and the rakshasa who opposes Hanuman are usually regarded as different beings sharing a name.
The Vishnu Purana and Harivamsha say the six sons of Devaki killed by Kamsa had been sons of Kalanemi in an earlier birth.
The rakshasa Kalanemi is absent from Valmiki's Ramayana.

nodes.name: Vatapi
nodes.description: A Daitya who could take the form of a ram or goat and be cooked and eaten, then burst alive out of the eater's belly at his brother Ilvala's call. He met his end when the sage Agastya ate him and digested him completely.
nodes.story: Ilvala and Vatapi hated brahmins and devised a cruel trick. Ilvala would invite a brahmin guest to a feast and serve him a meal of meat, which was Vatapi transformed into a ram. When the guest had eaten, Ilvala would call out his brother's name, and Vatapi would tear his way out of the guest's belly, killing him. Many brahmins died this way, until the sage Agastya came to their house. He ate the whole dish with calm contentment. Ilvala called, 'Vatapi, come out!', but nothing happened. Agastya smiled, patted his stomach and said that Vatapi had already been digested; the words 'Vatapi, be digested' became a proverb. The Chalukya capital Vatapi, modern Badami, bears his name.
variations: The Bhagavata makes Vatapi and Ilvala sons of Hlada, brother of Prahlada, and his wife Dhamani.
In the Mahabharata Agastya comes to Ilvala seeking wealth to satisfy Lopamudra; in the Ramayana the tale is told as one of Agastya's great deeds for the forest-dwelling sages.

nodes.name: Ilvala
nodes.description: A Daitya king, brother of Vatapi, who used his brother's shape-shifting to murder brahmin guests at feasts. The Ramayana says the sage Agastya burned him with a glance after digesting Vatapi; the Mahabharata says he gave Agastya great wealth instead.
nodes.story: The Mahabharata explains Ilvala's hatred: he once asked a brahmin to give him a son equal to Indra, and when the brahmin refused, he vowed revenge on all brahmins. When Agastya needed wealth to provide the ornaments his bride Lopamudra asked for, he went with three kings to Ilvala, who was famed for his riches. Ilvala welcomed them with his usual feast of Vatapi, but the sage ate it all and digested it. Stunned and afraid, Ilvala asked what they wanted, and Agastya asked for wealth. Ilvala gave each king a fortune in cows and gold, and gave Agastya even more, with a golden chariot drawn by two swift horses. In the Ramayana, however, when Ilvala rushed at the sage in rage, Agastya reduced him to ashes with the fire of his gaze.
variations: Ramayana: Agastya burns Ilvala to death; Mahabharata: Ilvala survives and pays Agastya tribute.
The Bhagavata makes him a grandson of Hiranyakashipu through Hlada.

nodes.name: Sunda
nodes.description: An asura of Hiranyakashipu's line, son of Nikumbha, who with his inseparable brother Upasunda won from Brahma a boon that nothing but each other could kill them. The gods had the apsara Tilottama created to set them against each other, and the brothers destroyed one another.
nodes.story: Sunda and Upasunda shared everything: one kingdom, one bed, one meal, one will. They performed such austerities on the Vindhya mountains that Brahma granted them mastery of every art and freedom from death at the hands of any being except each other. Secure in this boon, they conquered the three worlds, drove the gods from heaven and harassed the sages. Brahma then asked Vishvakarma to create a woman from the finest particle of every beautiful thing in creation; she was named Tilottama. She appeared, gathering flowers, where the brothers were drinking and feasting on the Vindhya slopes. Each seized one of her hands and claimed her as his wife. Their unbroken love turned to fury; they grabbed their maces and struck each other dead. Tilottama returned to Brahma, and the worlds were at peace.
sources: Mahabharata, Adi Parva 201-204 (Sunda and Upasunda episode)
variations: Narada tells the story to the Pandavas so that they will agree on a rule for sharing Draupadi and avoid quarrelling over her.
A different Sunda appears in the Ramayana as the husband of the yakshini Tataka and father of Maricha.

nodes.name: Upasunda
nodes.description: The younger brother of Sunda, son of the asura Nikumbha in Hiranyakashipu's line. He shared a boon of near-invincibility with his brother, and the two killed each other in a quarrel over the apsara Tilottama.
nodes.story: When the Pandavas married Draupadi together, the sage Narada came to them with a warning drawn from the tale of Upasunda and his elder brother Sunda. The two asura brothers had never been apart and never disagreed. Their austerities won them Brahma's promise that only they could kill each other, which seemed a harmless condition for brothers so united. After they had overrun heaven and earth, the gods sent Tilottama, the most beautiful woman ever fashioned. The moment she walked into their garden, Sunda declared her his wife, and so an elder sister-in-law to Upasunda; Upasunda declared her his own, and so a younger brother's wife to Sunda. Soon they were fighting. Blinded by desire, the inseparable pair beat each other to death with maces. Hearing this, the Pandavas agreed that whoever intruded on a brother alone with Draupadi would go into exile for twelve years.
sources: Mahabharata, Adi Parva 201-204 (Sunda and Upasunda episode)
variations: The story is a teaching tale within the Mahabharata; Upasunda is not significant outside it.

nodes.name: Kali (spirit of the Kali Yuga)
nodes.description: Kali (with a short 'a', distinct from the goddess Kali) is the personification of the Kali Yuga, the dark age of strife, and of the losing throw of the dice. He possesses King Nala in the Mahabharata, is restrained by King Parikshit in the Bhagavata, and is destined to be destroyed by Kalki at the end of the age.
nodes.story: Kali arrived too late for Damayanti's svayamvara and learned, to his fury, that she had chosen the mortal Nala over the gods themselves. He vowed to ruin Nala and waited twelve years for a lapse in the king's purity. When Nala once performed his evening rites without washing his feet properly, Kali entered him. Possessed, Nala gambled away his kingdom to his brother Pushkara and wandered in the forest, even abandoning Damayanti as she slept. Damayanti's grief-stricken curse and the venom of the serpent Karkotaka, who bit Nala, tormented the spirit within him. At last, when Nala learned the secret of dice from King Rituparna, Kali was forced out, trembling, and took refuge in a vibhitaka tree. Kali begged forgiveness and promised that those who recite Nala's story would be free from his influence.
nodes.abode: Places of gambling, drinking, lust, slaughter and gold (Bhagavata); the vibhitaka tree (Mahabharata)
sources: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Duryodhana as a portion of Kali)
variations: In the Bhagavata Purana Parikshit finds Kali beating the bull of Dharma, raises his sword, but spares him when he surrenders and assigns him places to dwell.
The Mahabharata says Duryodhana was born from a portion of Kali.
The Kalki Purana gives Kali a genealogy descended from Adharma and describes his final defeat by Kalki.
He must not be confused with the goddess Kali (Kālī), with whom he has no connection.

nodes.name: Madhu
nodes.description: One of the twin primordial asuras, Madhu and Kaitabha, who sprang from the ear-wax of Vishnu as he slept on the cosmic ocean and threatened Brahma. Vishnu slew them, earning the name Madhusudana, 'slayer of Madhu'.
nodes.story: At the end of a cosmic age, Vishnu slept on the serpent Shesha upon the endless waters, and from the wax of his ears two terrible asuras were born, Madhu and Kaitabha. Seeing Brahma seated on the lotus that rose from Vishnu's navel, they rushed to kill him. Brahma, terrified, sang praises to Yoganidra, the Great Goddess of sleep who held Vishnu's eyes closed. She withdrew from him, and Vishnu awoke and fought the brothers with his bare arms for five thousand years. Bewildered by the Goddess, the proud asuras offered to grant him a boon; Vishnu asked only that they die by his hand. Seeing water everywhere, they agreed on condition that he kill them where the earth was not flooded. Vishnu laid them on his thighs and struck off their heads with his discus.
variations: In the Narayaniya of the Shanti Parva Madhu and Kaitabha steal the Vedas from Brahma, and Vishnu, having recovered them in the horse-headed form of Hayagriva, slays the pair.
The Devi Bhagavata says they had won from the Goddess the boon of dying only when they chose.
The earth is called Medini because it was formed from their fat or marrow (Devi Bhagavata and other Puranas).
The Ramayana's Uttara Kanda has a different Madhu, a Danava father of Lavana, who is slain by Shatrughna.

nodes.name: Kaitabha
nodes.description: Twin of Madhu, the second of the primordial asuras born from the ear-wax of the sleeping Vishnu. With his brother he attacked Brahma and was slain by Vishnu once the goddess Yoganidra released him from sleep; Vishnu is thus called Kaitabhajit.
nodes.story: The Narayaniya of the Mahabharata tells another version of the twins' career. When Brahma was creating the worlds from the lotus of Vishnu's navel, the four Vedas lay before him in embodied form. Madhu and Kaitabha, born from two drops of water on the lotus, seized the Vedas and dived with them into the depths of Rasatala, leaving Brahma blind to the knowledge he needed to create. Grieving, Brahma prayed to Vishnu, who took the horse-headed form of Hayagriva. Chanting the Sama Veda in a deep voice, he descended into the netherworld, recovered the Vedas and returned them to Brahma. When the asuras came back and found them gone, they searched for the thief and challenged Vishnu, who slew them both, and Brahma could resume creation.
variations: In the Devi Mahatmya they arise from Vishnu's ear-wax; in the Narayaniya from drops of water on the lotus.
The Mahabharata's Vana Parva makes the asura Dhundhu, slain by King Kuvalashva (Dhundhumara), the son of Madhu and Kaitabha.

nodes.name: Mahishasura
nodes.description: The shape-shifting buffalo-demon whose defeat by the Goddess is the central episode of the Devi Mahatmya and the mythic basis of Navaratri and Durga Puja. He conquered heaven and drove out the gods. An earlier Mahabharata passage already has a Mahisha slain by Skanda.
nodes.story: Having routed Indra and the devas, Mahisha seated himself on the throne of heaven. The exiled gods went to Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, and from the blazing anger of all of them a single mass of light gathered into the form of a Goddess. Each god gave her a weapon — Shiva his trident, Vishnu his discus, Indra his thunderbolt — and Himavan gave her a lion. Her laughter shook the worlds. Mahisha's generals fell one by one; then he himself charged, changing from buffalo to lion, to a sword-bearing man, to an elephant and back to a buffalo, hurling mountains with his horns. The Goddess drank divine wine, laughed, leapt upon him, pressed his neck under her foot and pierced him with her trident; as he half-emerged from the buffalo's mouth in his own form, she struck off his head with her great sword.
nodes.abode: Svarga (usurped from Indra); Mysore (Mahishuru) in Karnataka tradition
variations: Mahabharata (Vana Parva): Mahisha attacks the gods and is killed by the young Skanda, whose spear splits his head.
Devi Bhagavata: Brahma's boon made him invulnerable to every male, so only a woman could kill him; he proposes marriage to the Goddess before the battle.
Vamana Purana names the slayer Katyayani, the goddess born from the gods' combined radiance at the hermitage of the sage Katyayana.
Kalika Purana makes Mahisha a devotee of Shiva who, slain by the Goddess in successive births, asks to remain forever at her feet — explaining his presence in her images.
Karnataka tradition links him with Mysore (Mahishuru), where the goddess Chamundeshwari slew him.

nodes.name: Shumbha
nodes.description: Asura king who, with his younger brother Nishumbha, seized the three worlds and the gods' shares of sacrifice in the final episode of the Devi Mahatmya. Told of the Goddess's beauty, he demanded her in marriage; when she replied that she would wed only one who defeated her in battle, he sent army after army and was finally slain by her in single combat.
nodes.story: Having taken Indra's realm and the gods' sacrificial shares, Shumbha heard from his servants Chanda and Munda of a woman of peerless beauty on the Himalaya, and sent a messenger to claim her. Smiling, the Goddess replied that in her folly she had once vowed to marry only one who conquered her in battle. Enraged, Shumbha sent Dhumralochana, then Chanda and Munda, then Raktabija — all destroyed — and then his brother Nishumbha, who also fell. He taunted her for relying on the strength of other goddesses. 'I alone exist here in the world; who else is there beside me?' she answered, and the Mothers vanished into her body. They fought with weapons, then hand to hand, rising into the sky; at last she hurled him to the earth and pierced his chest with her spear, and the whole world grew calm.
sources: Harivamsha, Vishnu Parva (Vishnu's charge to the goddess Nidra)
variations: The Harivamsha already foretells that the goddess Nidra, dwelling in the Vindhyas, will slay the danavas Shumbha and Nishumbha.
Devi Bhagavata: the brothers won from Brahma invulnerability against gods, men and beasts, disdaining to ask protection from women.
Vamana Purana tells the episode with Kaushiki, born from the dark sheath shed by Parvati, as the victorious goddess.

nodes.name: Nishumbha
nodes.description: Younger brother of Shumbha and co-ruler of the asura empire in the Devi Mahatmya. A formidable warrior, he was the last champion to face the Goddess before Shumbha himself.
nodes.story: After Raktabija's fall, Nishumbha led the asura host against the Goddess while Shumbha followed with his own army. He showered her with arrows and struck her lion on the head with his sword; she shattered his sword and shield with a sharp arrow and split his hurled spear with her discus. Struck down, he rose again, took up a club, and then, multiplying himself into ten thousand arms, covered her with discuses. At last she pierced his heart; from his breast another mighty being emerged crying 'Stop!' — laughing, the Goddess cut off its head with her sword, and Nishumbha fell lifeless to the earth. Maddened with grief and fury at his brother's death, Shumbha rode out for the final battle.
sources: Harivamsha, Vishnu Parva (Vishnu's charge to the goddess Nidra)
variations: Devi Bhagavata: the brothers' boon from Brahma left them vulnerable only to a woman.
Vamana Purana tells the parallel story with Kaushiki as the slayer.

nodes.name: Chanda
nodes.description: Asura general and servant of Shumbha who, with his companion Munda, first saw the Goddess on the Himalaya and praised her to their king. Sent to seize her by force, he was beheaded by Kali, and from the slaying of the pair the Goddess took the name Chamunda.
nodes.story: Chanda and Munda, marching with a fourfold army, found the Goddess seated smiling on her lion on a golden peak of the Himalaya. When they rushed at her with bows and drawn swords, her face darkened with anger, and from her brow sprang Kali — gaunt and black, clad in a tiger skin, garlanded with skulls, her tongue lolling, armed with sword, noose and skull-topped staff. She tore through the army, crushing elephants, chariots and riders in her jaws. Chanda covered her with arrows and Munda hurled thousands of discuses, which vanished into her mouth like suns into a cloud. Laughing terribly, she seized Chanda by the hair and cut off his head; when Munda rushed at her, she struck him down too. She laid both heads before the Goddess, who declared: 'Because you have brought Chanda and Munda, you shall be famed as Chamunda.'
variations: The Devi Bhagavata tells the episode with Kalika as their slayer.
Popular tradition makes Chanda and Munda brothers; the Devi Mahatmya simply pairs them as Shumbha's servants.
The derivation of the name Chamunda from Chanda and Munda is the Devi Mahatmya's own; Chamunda is also counted among the Matrikas.

nodes.name: Munda
nodes.description: Asura general, companion of Chanda and servant of the brothers Shumbha and Nishumbha. Their praise of the Goddess's beauty set the war in motion, and he fell to Kali after Chanda.
nodes.story: Wandering on the Himalaya, Chanda and Munda saw the radiant Goddess and hurried to their master. 'Great king,' they said, 'you already possess every jewel of the three worlds — Indra's elephant Airavata, the horse Uchchaihshravas, the Parijata tree, Kubera's great treasure, Varuna's umbrella and noose, the swan-chariot of Brahma. Why not take this jewel among women as well?' Their words kindled Shumbha's desire and set the whole war in motion. Later, sent to drag her back by force, Munda watched Kali spring from the Goddess's brow and devour their army. He hurled thousands of discuses, but they vanished into her mouth; when she beheaded Chanda, Munda rushed at her in rage, and she cut him down with her sword. Kali laid both heads at the Goddess's feet, and she was named Chamunda.
variations: Popular tradition treats Chanda and Munda as brothers.
The Devi Bhagavata names the slayer Kalika.

nodes.name: Raktabija
nodes.description: Asura general of Shumbha from each drop of whose blood that touched the ground a new warrior equal to him sprang up. In the Devi Mahatmya he was destroyed when Kali, as Chamunda, drank his blood before it could fall while the Goddess struck him down.
nodes.story: When Raktabija advanced, the Mothers — Brahmani, Maheshvari, Kaumari, Vaishnavi, Varahi, Narasimhi and Aindri — struck him with their weapons; but from every drop of his blood that fell, a new Raktabija arose, until the world was filled with his doubles and the gods despaired. Then Chandika laughed and said to Kali: 'Open wide your mouth, Chamunda, and quickly take in the drops of blood and the great asuras born of them.' As the Goddess pierced him with spear, sword and arrows, Kali caught every drop on her vast tongue and devoured the new-born asuras before they could multiply. Drained of blood, Raktabija sank to the earth and died, and the gods rejoiced while the Mothers danced, drunk with his blood.
variations: The Devi Mahatmya presents his power as innate; later and popular retellings attribute it to a boon from Shiva or Brahma.
The Vamana Purana is said to make him arise from the funeral pyre of Rambha, Mahishasura's father.
A similar blood-multiplying power belongs to Andhaka in the Matsya Purana, where too the Mothers are created to drink the blood.

nodes.name: Dhumralochana
nodes.description: The 'smoke-eyed' asura chieftain, the first general Shumbha sent to seize the Goddess by force. She reduced him to ashes with a single angry sound, 'hum', and her lion destroyed his army.
nodes.story: When the Goddess refused Shumbha's proposal, the asura king turned in fury to Dhumralochana, a lord of his army: 'Go at once with your troops and drag that insolent woman here by the hair. If anyone — god, yaksha or gandharva — rises to protect her, kill him.' Dhumralochana marched to the Himalaya with sixty thousand asuras and ordered her to come willingly to his master or be dragged. 'You are sent by the lord of the asuras, mighty and with an army at your back,' she replied calmly; 'if you take me by force, what can I do to you?' As he rushed at her, she merely uttered the sound 'hum' — and he was burnt to ashes. Her lion, shaking its mane, fell upon his army and tore it apart.

nodes.name: Durgamasura
nodes.description: Asura who, by a boon from Brahma, took possession of the Vedas, so that sacrifice ceased, the gods weakened and a hundred-year drought fell upon the earth. He was slain by the Goddess who, having appeared as Shatakshi and Shakambhari, thereby became known as Durga.
nodes.story: Durgama, son of Ruru, performed fierce austerities in the Himalaya and asked Brahma for the Vedas. Once they were his, sacred knowledge vanished from the world: brahmins forgot the hymns, fire-offerings stopped, the gods lost their strength and no rain fell for a hundred years. Rivers and wells dried up and living beings perished. The sages prayed to the Goddess, who appeared with countless eyes as Shatakshi and wept for nine days and nights at the suffering until her tears became rivers. As Shakambhari she fed the starving with vegetables, fruits and roots from her own body. Then Durgama marched against her; many shaktis sprang from her body, and after a fierce battle she killed him with her arrows and returned the Vedas to the world. Because she slew Durgama, she is called Durga.
variations: The Devi Mahatmya only foretells his death in a single verse; the full narrative is in the Devi Bhagavata.
The Devi Bhagavata treats Shatakshi, Shakambhari and Durga as successive names of one manifestation.

nodes.name: Arunasura
nodes.description: Daitya king who won a boon of invulnerability from Brahma through long devotion to the Gayatri mantra and then conquered the gods. The Goddess slew him as Bhramari, sending forth countless bees — creatures neither two- nor four-legged.
nodes.story: In the netherworld the daitya Aruna resolved to conquer the gods and performed austerities for thousands of years on the banks of the Ganga in the Himalaya, repeating the Gayatri. Brahma granted his wish: he would not die in battle or by any weapon, by man or woman, nor by any creature with two legs or four. He drove the gods from heaven. Since his strength flowed from the Gayatri, Brihaspati went to him and persuaded him to abandon it. Then the gods prayed to the Devi, who appeared surrounded by innumerable bees, bumblebees and hornets, holding them in her hands. Swarming across the worlds like a dark cloud, the bees tore open the breasts of Aruna and his armies, and the demons perished. Praised by the gods as Bhramari, the Goddess vanished.
variations: The Devi Mahatmya foretells the episode in one verse; the Devi Bhagavata gives the full narrative.
Not to be confused with Aruna, the charioteer of Surya.

nodes.name: Tarakasura
nodes.description: Mighty daitya whose boon made him vulnerable only to a son of Shiva, forcing the gods to bring about Shiva's marriage to Parvati. He was slain by the young war god Kartikeya (Skanda), a story told in the Mahabharata, the Shiva and Skanda Puranas and Kalidasa's Kumarasambhava.
nodes.story: Taraka, son of the daitya Vajranga, performed ever more terrible austerities for centuries until Brahma came to grant a boon. He asked to be unconquerable, and to die, if at all, only at the hands of a son of Shiva — for Shiva, mourning Sati, sat lost in meditation and seemed unlikely ever to father a child. Taraka seized heaven and made the gods his servants. At Brahma's counsel they sent Kama to stir Shiva's heart; Kama was burnt to ashes by Shiva's third eye, but Parvati's austerities won Shiva, and their son Kartikeya, born of Shiva's fiery seed and nursed by the Krittikas, was made commander of the divine army. The boy-general met Taraka on the battlefield and, after a fierce duel, pierced him with his spear, restoring heaven to the gods.
sources: Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita (Parvati and Kumara Khandas)
variations: Matsya Purana: the boon made him vulnerable only to a child seven days old.
Andhra tradition holds that Taraka wore a Shiva linga on his body; Kartikeya shattered it, and its five pieces are worshipped at the Pancharama shrines.
The Mahabharata (Karna Parva) and Shiva Purana make him the father of the three Tripura brothers.

nodes.name: Andhaka
nodes.description: Blind asura born of Shiva and Parvati's play and raised as the son of the daitya Hiranyaksha. Driven by desire for Parvati — unaware that she was his own mother — he warred against Shiva, who impaled him on his trident; purified, he became Shiva's devotee and a leader of his ganas, identified in several accounts with the skeletal Bhringi.
nodes.story: Once, on Mount Mandara, Parvati playfully covered Shiva's eyes with her hands; the world fell dark, and from the sweat of Shiva's brow, warmed by her touch, a blind, black, fearsome child was born. Shiva gave him to the childless daitya Hiranyaksha. Grown mighty through Brahma's boon, Andhaka ruled the asuras, and when his ministers told him of a peerless woman on Mandara, he demanded her for himself. War followed: Shukracharya revived the fallen asuras with his secret lore until Nandi carried him off and Shiva swallowed him, and every drop of Andhaka's blood sprang up as a new Andhaka. At last Shiva impaled him on his trident and held him aloft for ages. Burnt dry of sin, Andhaka sang Shiva's praises; forgiven, he was made a chief of the ganas and called Bhringi.
nodes.abode: The asura realm; later Kailasa, as Shiva's gana
sources: Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Yuddha Khanda
variations: Shiva Purana: born from Shiva's sweat when Parvati covered his eyes and given to Hiranyaksha; other Puranas (Matsya, Kurma, Vamana) make him Hiranyaksha's own son.

Matsya Purana: Shiva emanated the Mothers (Matrikas) to drink the blood from which new Andhakas sprang; when the Mothers then threatened the world, Vishnu as Narasimha brought forth goddesses to restrain them.
Most accounts end with his redemption rather than death; some name the redeemed Andhaka Bhringi, whereas elsewhere Bhringi is an independent sage devoted solely to Shiva.
Shiva impaling Andhaka (Andhakasura-vadha) is a major theme of temple sculpture, notably at Ellora and Elephanta.

nodes.name: Jalandhara
nodes.description: Mighty asura born from the fire of Shiva's anger when it was cast into the ocean, and raised as the Ocean's son. Protected by the fidelity of his devoted wife Vrinda, he conquered the gods, but was slain by Shiva after Vishnu's deception broke that protection.
nodes.story: When Indra, failing to recognise Shiva in the guise of a naked ascetic, raised his thunderbolt against him, fire blazed from Shiva's third eye; at Brihaspati's plea Shiva cast it into the ocean where the Ganga meets the sea. There it became a wailing child, raised by the Ocean. When Brahma took him on his lap, the boy gripped the creator's neck until tears streamed from his eyes, and so he was named Jalandhara, 'he who holds water'. Crowned by Shukracharya and wedded to the virtuous Vrinda, he avenged the churning of his father the Ocean by conquering heaven. Inflamed by Narada's praise of Parvati, he sent Rahu to demand her from Shiva and even approached her in Shiva's form. The war was decided only when Vishnu broke Vrinda's fidelity; then Shiva's discus struck off Jalandhara's head, and his radiance merged into Shiva.
nodes.abode: The ocean; his capital is traditionally identified with Jalandhar in Punjab
sources: Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Yuddha Khanda
variations: Several versions say Shiva created the Sudarshana discus to kill him — drawing a wheel in the water with his toe — and later gave it to Vishnu.
Lakshmi, also born of the ocean, regards him as her brother and persuades Vishnu not to kill him in their duel.
The Padma Purana tells the story from a Vaishnava standpoint, dwelling on Vishnu's grief at Vrinda's pyre.

nodes.name: Vrinda (Tulasi)
nodes.description: Virtuous wife of the asura Jalandhara, whose unwavering fidelity (pativrata) made her husband invincible. Deceived by Vishnu in the form of Jalandhara, she cursed him and gave up her life; she is revered as the holy basil plant Tulasi, sacred to Vishnu and ritually married to him each year in the Tulasi Vivah.
nodes.story: Vrinda, daughter of the asura Kalanemi, loved Jalandhara with such devotion that no god could slay him while her fidelity held. As his war with Shiva raged, Vishnu came to her in Jalandhara's form — some tellings add illusory demons and a severed head he seemed to revive — and she embraced him as her husband. Her virtue broken, Jalandhara fell to Shiva. Discovering the deception, Vrinda cursed Vishnu: as he had parted her from her husband, he too would lose his wife and need the help of monkeys — fulfilled when he came as Rama. Then she entered the fire. From the ground of her pyre sprang Tulasi, Amalaki and Malati, and devotees say she lives on as Tulasi, without whose leaves no offering to Vishnu is complete. Her story still raises hard questions about divine deception and its cost to the innocent.
nodes.abode: Jalandhara's city; as Tulasi, the courtyard shrine (tulasi-vrindavana) of Hindu homes
sources: Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Yuddha Khanda
variations: Shiva Purana: her curse condemns Vishnu to separation from his wife and dependence on monkeys; the curse that he become the Shaligram stone belongs to the parallel story of Tulasi and Shankhachuda (Brahmavaivarta, Devi Bhagavata), which popular tradition merges with hers.

In the Brahmavaivarta and Devi Bhagavata, Tulasi is a partial manifestation of Lakshmi, daughter of King Dharmadhvaja and wife of the asura Shankhachuda; the Gandaki river flows from her body and Vishnu becomes the Shaligram stones found in it.
The annual Tulasi Vivah celebrates her marriage to Vishnu as Shaligram, or to Krishna.
Vrindavan, Krishna's forest, is traditionally linked with her name, though Gaudiya tradition also knows a separate forest-goddess Vrinda.

nodes.name: Bhasmasura (Vrikasura)
nodes.description: Asura who won from Shiva the power to destroy anyone by touching their head, and then tried to use it on Shiva himself. Vishnu tricked him into placing his hand on his own head — as a young brahmin student in the Bhagavata, and as the enchantress Mohini in popular retellings.
nodes.story: Vrika, son of Shakuni, asked Narada which god was quickest to please and was told: Shiva. At Kedara he cut pieces of his own flesh and offered them into the fire; on the seventh day, as he was about to sever his head, Shiva rose from the flames and offered a boon. Vrika chose the power to kill anyone on whose head he laid his hand — and at once tried it on Shiva, meaning to carry off Parvati. Shiva fled to the ends of the world, pursued, until Vishnu came to meet the demon as a radiant young brahmachari. 'Why trust the word of Shiva, lord of ghosts, cursed by Daksha?' the boy asked sweetly. 'Test the boon on your own head.' Deluded, Vrika did so, and his head burst apart. The gods rained flowers, and Shiva was saved.
variations: Bhagavata: the demon is Vrika, son of Shakuni (an asura, not the Gandhara prince), whose touch makes heads burst; Vishnu comes as a brahmachari.
In South Indian and popular retellings he is Bhasmasura, whose touch reduces to ash; Vishnu as Mohini lures him into a dance in which he copies her gesture of placing a hand on the head.
Some Kerala retellings set the union of Shiva and Mohini that produced Ayyappa just after this episode.

nodes.name: Tripurasura (the Three Cities' lords)
nodes.description: Collective node for the three asura brothers Tarakaksha, Kamalaksha and Vidyunmali, sons of Tarakasura, who ruled three flying cities of gold, silver and iron built by Maya. Their destruction by a single arrow of Shiva, the Tripura-dahana, earned him the name Tripurantaka; the core of the myth already appears in the Vedic Brahmanas.
nodes.story: After Taraka's death his three sons performed austerities and asked Brahma for immortality; refused, they asked instead for three cities that would come into line only once in a thousand years and could be destroyed only then, by a single arrow. Maya built them fortresses of gold in heaven, silver in the sky and iron on earth, and the brothers, devout worshippers of Shiva, at first ruled well — until pride corrupted them and they oppressed the worlds. The gods fashioned for Shiva a cosmic chariot: the earth its body, sun and moon its wheels, Brahma its charioteer, Mount Meru the bow, the serpent Vasuki the bowstring, and Vishnu himself the arrow, with Agni at its tip. When the three cities aligned, Shiva loosed a single shaft and burned them to ashes.
symbols: three flying cities of gold, silver and iron
nodes.abode: Tripura, the three cities in heaven, sky and earth
sources: Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Yuddha Khanda
variations: In the Vedic Brahmanas the asuras' three forts of iron, silver and gold are destroyed with an arrow made of Agni, Soma and Vishnu, shot by Rudra; the named brothers and Shiva's lone arrow appear from the Mahabharata onward.
Shiva Purana: because the brothers were devout Shaivas, Vishnu first created a heretical teacher who led them away from Vedic and Shaiva worship; only then could Shiva strike.
Matsya Purana centres the story on Maya, the architect, whom Shiva spares.
Later tradition says Shiva's chariot broke down because he had not first worshipped Ganesha.

nodes.name: Gayasura
nodes.description: Pious, giant asura devoted to Vishnu, whose austerities made his body so holy that all who saw or touched him were liberated, emptying the realm of Yama. When he lay down to give his body for Brahma's sacrifice, Vishnu held him still beneath a sacred stone; the place became Gaya in Bihar, the foremost site of offerings to the ancestors.
nodes.story: Gaya, a giant asura devoted to Vishnu, performed austerities so fierce that the gods trembled. Vishnu granted his wish: his body became holier than every tirtha, so that all who touched or beheld him went straight to heaven, and Yama's realm stood empty. At Vishnu's counsel Brahma asked Gaya for his pure body as the ground for a great sacrifice, and Gaya lay down gladly. Even after the rite his body kept quivering. The gods set a great stone, the Dharmashila, upon him, and still he moved; at last Vishnu himself stood upon it as Gadadhara, the mace-bearer, together with the other gods. Gaya grew still and asked only that they remain there forever and that pinda offerings made on that spot should liberate the ancestors. So Gaya became the holiest place of shraddha, and Vishnu's footprint is worshipped there at the Vishnupada temple.
variations: Vayu Purana: Vishnu subdues but does not kill Gaya; he lies forever beneath the site, which his body sanctifies.
Popular retellings say Vishnu pressed him down into the netherworld with his foot, or killed him with his mace.
Some scholars read the myth as the Brahmanical absorption of an older, possibly Buddhist or local, pilgrimage centre.

nodes.name: Rambha (father of Mahishasura)
nodes.description: Danava, son of Danu and brother of Karambha, who became the father of Mahishasura through union with a she-buffalo. His story, told in the Vamana and Devi Bhagavata Puranas, explains the buffalo-demon's origin; he is distinct from the apsara Rambha.
nodes.story: Rambha and his brother Karambha, sons of Danu, longed for mighty sons and began austerities — Karambha standing in the waters of the Panchanada, Rambha amid fires. Indra, taking the form of a crocodile, seized Karambha by the feet and killed him. Grief-stricken, Rambha resolved to cut off his own head as an offering into the fire, but Agni appeared, restrained him and granted him a son who would be unconquerable and able to take any form at will. Returning home, Rambha saw a beautiful she-buffalo and desired her, and from their union Mahisha was born. Soon afterwards a jealous buffalo gored Rambha to death, and as his body burned on the pyre the grieving she-buffalo entered the flames. Accounts differ on what followed: in some Mahisha himself emerges from the pyre, in others a fierce warrior rises from it.
variations: The Vamana Purana and Devi Bhagavata differ on whether Mahisha was born directly of the she-buffalo or emerged from Rambha's funeral pyre.
The Vamana Purana is said to make Raktabija arise from Rambha's pyre.
The Devi Bhagavata names Agni as the giver of his boon; retellings vary.

nodes.name: Mahishi
nodes.description: Buffalo-headed demoness of Kerala's Sabarimala tradition who sought to avenge Mahishasura and won a boon that only a son born of Shiva and Vishnu could kill her. She was slain by the child-hero Ayyappa (Manikandan); her story is regional and attested in late texts and temple lore.
nodes.story: After the Goddess slew Mahishasura, his kinswoman Mahishi performed severe austerities to Brahma and obtained a boon: none could kill her but a son born of Shiva and Vishnu — an impossibility, she thought. She overran heaven and tormented the gods. But when Vishnu took the enchanting form of Mohini, a child was born of her union with Shiva: Hariharaputra, left by the Pampa river with a bell around his neck and raised by the king of Pandalam as Manikandan. Journeying through the forest as a boy of twelve, he met Mahishi, fought her and threw her down, dancing upon her body until she died on the banks of the Azhutha river. From the demon's form emerged a beautiful woman, freed from a curse, who asked to marry him; bound by celibacy, he instead gave her a place beside his shrine as Malikappurathamma.
nodes.abode: Forests of the Western Ghats around Sabarimala
variations: Kerala tellings variously make her Mahishasura's sister, his cousin (a daughter of Karambha) or his widow.
In her previous life she was Leela, wife of the sage Dattatreya, cursed by him to be born as a buffalo-demoness; freed by Ayyappa, she became Malikappurathamma.
She does not appear in the pan-Indian Sanskrit Puranas; the story is a regional Kerala tradition.

nodes.name: Jaya
nodes.description: One of the two gatekeepers (dvarapalas) of Vishnu's Vaikuntha, with his brother Vijaya. Cursed by the four Kumaras for barring their way, he was born three times as a great enemy of Vishnu, returning to his post after being slain by Vishnu's avatars.
nodes.story: The four Kumaras, eternal sages who look like small boys, passed through six gates of Vaikuntha to see Vishnu. At the seventh, the doorkeepers Jaya and Vijaya, mistaking them for mere naked children, barred their way with their staffs. Angered that such pride could exist even in Vaikuntha, the sages cursed them to fall into births in the world where lust, anger and greed prevail. Vishnu himself hurried to the gate with Lakshmi, honoured the sages and accepted the curse as his own will, assuring the brothers they would soon return. Tradition adds that he offered them a choice — seven births as his devotees or three as his enemies — and, unable to bear long separation, they chose enmity. So they were born as Hiranyakashipu and Hiranyaksha, then Ravana and Kumbhakarna, then Shishupala and Dantavakra.
variations: Bhagavata 7.1 assigns the three births to the pair without saying which brother became which; one common mapping gives Jaya the elder roles (Hiranyakashipu, Ravana, Shishupala), but other retellings reverse it.
The choice between seven births as devotees and three as enemies is a popular elaboration not found in the Bhagavata.
Images of the pair guard the sanctum doors of South Indian Vishnu temples.

nodes.name: Vijaya
nodes.description: Brother of Jaya and co-gatekeeper of Vishnu's Vaikuntha. Under the Kumaras' curse he passed through three demonic births, each ended by an avatar of Vishnu, and then returned to his post.
nodes.story: In the mapping that makes him the younger of each pair, Vijaya's first birth was as Hiranyaksha, who dragged the earth into the cosmic waters and was slain by Varaha, while his brother as Hiranyakashipu died at the claws of Narasimha. Reborn in the Treta age as Kumbhakarna, Ravana's giant brother, he slept for months on end and fell to Rama's arrows at Lanka. In the Dvapara age he came as Dantavakra, ally of Shishupala, and was killed by Krishna with his mace. In the Bhagavata, Narada tells Yudhishthira that by fixing their minds on Vishnu with unbroken hatred, the brothers thought of him as constantly as any devotee, and so each death at his hands was a liberation; after the third life they returned to the gates of Vaikuntha. Narada tells the story to explain how Shishupala, who reviled Krishna, could merge into him at death.
variations: Which brother took which birth is not specified in the Bhagavata; some retellings make Vijaya Hiranyakashipu, Ravana and Shishupala instead.
Dantavakra (Vijaya's third birth in the common mapping) is killed by Krishna in the Bhagavata's tenth book.

nodes.name: Bhrigu
nodes.description: Bhrigu is the ancestor of the Bhargava priestly clan, whom the Rig Veda credits with bringing fire to humankind. The Brahmanas and Taittiriya Upanishad know him as Bhrigu Varuni, son and pupil of Varuna, while the Puranas count him among the mind-born sons of Brahma. His line includes Chyavana, Shukracharya, Jamadagni and Parashurama.
nodes.story: Once the sages gathered on the Sarasvati argued about which of the three great gods was supreme, and they sent Bhrigu to find out. At Brahma's court he pointedly failed to bow, and Brahma flushed with anger but held back for the sake of his son. On Kailasa, Shiva rose to embrace him, but Bhrigu rebuffed him as an impure wanderer of cremation grounds; Shiva raised his trident until Parvati calmed him. In Vaikuntha, Bhrigu found Vishnu resting with Lakshmi and kicked him in the chest. Vishnu rose at once, begged pardon for not greeting his guest, and pressed the sage's foot, asking whether it was hurt. He said he would wear the mark on his chest forever. Overwhelmed, Bhrigu went back and declared Vishnu the greatest of the gods.
nodes.abode: Bhrigu's hermitage (associated with Bhrigukaccha / Bharuch on the Narmada)
variations: Vedic texts make him the son of Varuna; the Mahabharata (Anushasana Parva) has him born from the fire of Varuna's sacrifice; the Puranas make him a mind-born son of Brahma.

The test of the Trimurti (Bhagavata 10.89) ends in praise of Vishnu; the Padma Purana version has Bhrigu curse Shiva and Brahma, and the Matsya Purana tells of him cursing Vishnu to be born among mortals.
Astrological tradition attributes the Bhrigu Samhita to him.

nodes.name: Atri
nodes.description: Atri is the seer-family behind the fifth mandala of the Rig Veda and one of the Saptarishis in both the Vedic and Puranic lists. The Rig Veda remembers the Ashvins rescuing him from a burning pit and his restoring the eclipsed Sun. In the Puranas he and his wife Anasuya are the parents of Soma, Dattatreya and Durvasa.
nodes.story: Atri and Anasuya withdrew to Mount Riksha to beg the Lord of the universe for a son like himself. Atri stood on one leg, living on air, for a hundred years, until the heat of his tapas rose from his head as fire and scorched the three worlds. Then Brahma on his swan, Vishnu on Garuda and Shiva on his bull appeared before him together. Astonished, Atri asked why three had come when he had prayed to one. The gods smiled and said they were one reality, and since he had meditated on that one, each would be born as his son. So Soma was born from Brahma's portion, Dattatreya from Vishnu's, and the fiery Durvasa from Shiva's.
sources: Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Rama at Atri's hermitage)
variations: The Vishnu Purana and Harivamsha say Soma was born from Atri's eyes; the Bhagavata makes Soma, Dattatreya and Durvasa sons of Atri and Anasuya as portions of Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva.
Later tradition identifies the Svarbhanu of Rig Veda 5.40 with Rahu, the eclipse demon.

nodes.name: Anasuya
nodes.description: Anasuya ('free from envy') is the wife of the sage Atri and a model of chastity and ascetic power. In the Ramayana she welcomes Sita at Chitrakuta and gives her gifts that never fade. The Puranas make her the mother of Soma, Dattatreya and Durvasa.
nodes.story: When Rama, Sita and Lakshmana reached Atri's hermitage, the sage introduced his aged wife, whose tapas was legendary. During a ten-year drought she had brought forth fruits and roots and made the Ganga flow through the forest as the Mandakini; at the gods' request she had even turned ten nights into one. Sita bowed to her, and Anasuya praised her for following her husband into exile, teaching her that a devoted wife is her husband's truest companion in dharma. Pleased by Sita's humility, she gave her a celestial garland, garments, ornaments and an unguent that would never fade or lose its fragrance. Then she asked Sita to tell how Rama had won her at the svayamvara, and listened with delight as night fell on the forest.
sources: Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (sargas 117–119 in the vulgate)
variations: The Bhagavata makes her a daughter of Kardama and Devahuti; the Vishnu Purana a daughter of Daksha and Prasuti.
A popular later legend (in Dattatreya traditions) tells how Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva came to test her chastity and she turned them into infants, after which they were born as her sons.

nodes.name: Kashyapa
nodes.description: Kashyapa is a Vedic seer and, in the epics and Puranas, the great progenitor: son of Marichi and husband of thirteen daughters of Daksha. Through Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kadru and Vinata he fathered the Adityas, Daityas, Danavas, Nagas, Garuda and Aruna, so gods and demons alike are Kashyapas. He is one of the Saptarishis in the Vedic list and in the list of the present age.
nodes.story: One evening Diti, burning with desire for a son, came to Kashyapa just as he had finished his sacrificial offerings. He begged her to wait, for it was twilight, the hour when Shiva and his ghostly hosts roam and people must be pure and watchful. Diti would not be put off, and Kashyapa gave in. Afterwards, ashamed, she feared Shiva's anger, and Kashyapa told her sadly that because she had conceived at that forbidden hour she would bear two fearsome sons who would torment the worlds, until the Lord himself descended to destroy them. Yet, moved by her repentance, he promised that one grandson would be a great devotee of Vishnu. The twins were Hiranyaksha and Hiranyakashipu, and the grandson was Prahlada.
nodes.abode: Hermitage in the Himalaya; Kashmir (Kashyapa-mira) is traditionally named after him
variations: The number and names of his wives vary; the Mahabharata and Puranas usually give thirteen daughters of Daksha.
In the Rig Veda the Maruts are sons of Rudra and Prishni, but in the Ramayana and Puranas they are born from Diti's embryo, which Indra split.

nodes.name: Angiras
nodes.description: Angiras is the ancestor of the Angirasa priestly clan, which the Rig Veda calls the ancient fathers who won back the hidden cows and the light. Agni himself is called the first Angiras, and the Atharva Veda was once known as the Atharvangirasa. Later tradition counts Angiras among Brahma's mind-born sons and the Saptarishis, and makes him the father of Brihaspati.
nodes.story: In the time of the fathers, the Panis hid the cows of the gods, and with them the dawn's light, deep inside the rock-cave of Vala. The divine bitch Sarama tracked them across the waters, but the Panis only mocked her. Then the Angirases, the ancient singers, came with Indra and Brihaspati to the mountain. They sang their sacred hymns, and the power of their chant, together with Indra's might, split the rock. Vala broke open, the bellowing cows came out into the light, and the dawn and the Sun shone on the world again. The Rig Veda returns to this deed again and again, for the Angirases' song showed that a true prayer can open what force alone cannot.
variations: In the Rig Veda the Angirases are mostly a group of ancestral priests; the epics and Puranas turn Angiras into a single Prajapati.
His wife is Shraddha (Kardama's daughter) in the Bhagavata and Smriti (Daksha's daughter) in the Vishnu Purana.

nodes.name: Pulastya
nodes.description: Pulastya is one of Brahma's mind-born sons and a Saptarishi in the Puranic list for the first age. Through his son Vishrava he is the grandfather of Kubera, Ravana, Kumbhakarna and Vibhishana, so the rakshasas of Lanka are called Paulastyas. He also appears as a teacher of Bhishma and as the sage who blessed Parashara to compose a Purana.
nodes.story: Pulastya went to do tapas on the slopes of Meru, near the hermitage of the royal sage Trinabindu. The daughters of nearby sages and nymphs kept coming there to sing, dance and play, breaking his concentration. Annoyed, Pulastya declared that any maiden who came into his sight would become pregnant. The others stayed away, but Trinabindu's daughter had not heard the warning and wandered there looking for her friends. She saw the sage, found herself with child and ran home in dismay. Trinabindu understood what had happened and gave her to Pulastya as his wife. Pleased with her devoted service, the sage promised her a son as learned as himself, and she bore Vishrava, who became the father of Kubera and Ravana.
variations: The Mahabharata says the rakshasas, vanaras and yakshas were all Pulastya's offspring.
The Bhagavata names his wife Havirbhu (Kardama's daughter) and his sons Agastya and Vishrava; the Vishnu Purana names his wife Priti (Daksha's daughter).

nodes.name: Pulaha
nodes.description: Pulaha is one of the six (later seven or ten) mind-born sons of Brahma and a Saptarishi in the Puranic list for the first age. The Mahabharata makes him the progenitor of wild creatures and the Kimpurushas. His hermitage on the Gandaki, Pulahashrama, is a holy place in the Puranas.
nodes.story: When Brahma wanted to populate the world, sons sprang from his mind, and Pulaha was born from his navel, some say, or from his ear. Unlike his brothers, whose children were sages and gods, Pulaha became the father of the wild world. The Mahabharata says his offspring were the sharabhas, lions, tigers, bears and wolves, along with the Kimpurushas, the half-human beings of the mountains. Pulaha later withdrew to a hermitage on the banks of the Gandaki, where the river's stones carry the marks of Vishnu. The Bhagavata tells that King Bharata, giving up his throne, came to this Pulahashrama to spend his last years in worship, and it has remained a place of pilgrimage ever since.
variations: The Bhagavata (3.12) says Pulaha was born from Brahma's navel; other Puranas give different parts of Brahma's body.
The Vishnu Purana makes Kardama a son of Pulaha and Kshama; the Bhagavata makes Kardama born from Brahma's shadow and has Pulaha marry Kardama's daughter Gati.

nodes.name: Kratu
nodes.description: Kratu is one of Brahma's mind-born sons and a Saptarishi in the Puranic list for the first age. His name means 'willpower' or 'sacrificial intent'. He is best known as the father of the Valakhilyas, sixty thousand thumb-sized ascetics who attend the Sun's chariot.
nodes.story: Kratu's sons, the Valakhilyas, were each no bigger than a thumb, yet their tapas was immense. When Kashyapa held a sacrifice to gain a son, Indra carried a mountain of firewood while the Valakhilyas struggled together under a single leaf-stalk. Indra laughed and stepped over them. Stung, the tiny sages began a new sacrifice to bring forth a second Indra who would be a terror to the first. The frightened king of the gods ran to Kashyapa, who persuaded the ascetics not to overturn Brahma's order. The power of their rite would instead go into a son who would be 'Indra' of the birds. So the Valakhilyas' tapas went into the birth of Garuda, and they themselves withdrew to follow the chariot of the Sun.
variations: His wife is Sannati (Daksha's daughter) in the Vishnu Purana and Kriya (Kardama's daughter) in the Bhagavata.
The Mahabharata tells the Valakhilya episode without naming Kratu as their father; the Puranas supply the link.

nodes.name: Marichi
nodes.description: Marichi ('ray of light') is usually named first among Brahma's mind-born sons and heads the Puranic list of Saptarishis for the first age. He is the father of Kashyapa and so the forefather of gods, asuras and the Solar dynasty. The Bhagavad Gita names a Marichi as chief of the Maruts.
nodes.story: At the wedding of Rama and Sita in Mithila, the family priest Vashistha stood up to recite the lineage of the Ikshvakus, as custom required. He began at the very beginning: the eternal Brahma, born of the unmanifest, had a son Marichi. Marichi's son was Kashyapa, and Kashyapa's son was Vivasvan, the Sun. From Vivasvan came Manu, the first king, and from Manu came Ikshvaku, founder of Ayodhya's royal line. Generation by generation Vashistha named the kings down to Dasharatha and his sons. The genealogy shows why Marichi is so honoured, for this ray of Brahma's mind stands at the head of the solar kings and, through Kashyapa, of the Adityas and Daityas alike.
sources: Ramayana, Bala Kanda 1.70 and Ayodhya Kanda 2.110 (Ikshvaku genealogy)
variations: His wife is Kala (Kardama's daughter) in the Bhagavata and Sambhuti (Daksha's daughter) in the Vishnu Purana.
Commentators often treat the Marichi of Gita 10.21, chief of the Maruts, as distinct from the Prajapati.
In Jain tradition a Marichi, grandson of Rishabhanatha, is an earlier birth of Mahavira; this figure is unrelated to the Puranic Prajapati.

nodes.name: Vashistha
nodes.description: Vashistha is the seer-family of the seventh mandala of the Rig Veda, where he is priest to King Sudas and is said to be born of Mitra and Varuna. In the epics he is the royal priest of the Ikshvakus, guru of Rama, owner of the wish-granting cow and the great rival of Vishvamitra. He is a Saptarishi in every list, and his wife Arundhati is the model of marital devotion.
nodes.story: King Vishvamitra, returning from a campaign, stopped at Vashistha's hermitage, and the sage fed his whole army with delicacies produced by his cow Shabala. Amazed, the king demanded the cow, offering thousands of cattle and even his kingdom. Vashistha refused, and Vishvamitra had her dragged away. Weeping, Shabala broke free and ran back to her master, and at his word she poured out armies of warriors who destroyed the king's forces. Vishvamitra's sons attacked Vashistha, and he burned them to ashes with a single cry. The king then won divine weapons from Shiva and loosed them all, even the Brahmastra, but Vashistha stood firm with only his staff, which swallowed every weapon. Vishvamitra cried out that a kshatriya's strength is worthless beside a brahmin's power, and set out to become a brahmarshi himself.
nodes.abode: Hermitage in the Himalaya; royal court of Ayodhya; the star Mizar in Ursa Major
sources: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Vashistha–Vishvamitra and Vasus episodes)
variations: In the Rig Veda he is born of Mitra and Varuna at the sight of Urvashi; the Puranas make him Brahma's mind-born son, and explain the two births by saying Nimi's curse forced him to be reborn from Mitra and Varuna.
The cow is Shabala in the Ramayana and Nandini (Kamadhenu's daughter) in the Mahabharata.
The rivalry with Vishvamitra may reflect the two sages' competition for King Sudas's patronage in the Rig Veda; later texts turn it into a contest between brahmin and kshatriya power.
The Yoga Vasishtha, a late philosophical work, is framed as his teaching to Rama.

nodes.name: Arundhati
nodes.description: Arundhati is the wife of Vashistha and the ideal of marital fidelity. In Vedic domestic ritual the bride is shown the star Arundhati (Alcor) beside Vashistha (Mizar) in the Great Bear as a sign of constancy. The Mahabharata praises her tapas and says she alone among the sages' wives could not be impersonated.
nodes.story: Agni once fell in love with the wives of the Seven Sages as he blazed in their sacrificial fires, and he wasted away with longing. Svaha, daughter of Daksha, loved Agni and wanted to win him, so she took the form of each wife in turn and went to him, flying off afterwards as a bird. She took the shapes of six of the wives, but she could not take the form of Arundhati, whose devotion to Vashistha and whose tapas were beyond imitation. Rumour soon spread that the sages' wives had been with Agni, and six of the rishis gave up their wives, who became the Krittikas, the Pleiades. Only Arundhati stayed at her husband's side, and so she shines beside him in the northern sky.
nodes.abode: Vashistha's hermitage; the star Alcor beside Mizar
sources: Grihya Sutras (marriage rite: showing the bride Dhruva and Arundhati)
Mahabharata, Vana Parva (birth of Skanda, Svaha episode)
variations: The Bhagavata makes her a daughter of Kardama and Devahuti; the Vishnu Purana names Vashistha's wife Urja, daughter of Daksha.
The Shiva Purana says she was once Sandhya, a mind-born daughter of Brahma, who was reborn as Arundhati, daughter of the sage Medhatithi.
The Atharva Veda uses arundhati as the name of a healing plant; her identity as Vashistha's wife comes from later ritual and epic texts.

nodes.name: Vishvamitra
nodes.description: Vishvamitra is the seer-family of the third mandala of the Rig Veda, which contains the Gayatri mantra (3.62.10). The epics tell how this king of the Kushika line gave up his throne after being humbled by Vashistha and, through enormous tapas, became a brahmarshi. He is Rama's teacher in the Ramayana and a Saptarishi in the Vedic list and in the list of the present age.
nodes.story: King Trishanku wanted to go to heaven in his own body. Vashistha refused to perform the rite, and Vashistha's sons cursed the king to become an outcaste. Vishvamitra, still at odds with Vashistha, took pity on him and began the sacrifice himself. By the strength of his tapas Trishanku rose into the sky, but Indra pushed him back, and the king came tumbling down crying for help. Vishvamitra shouted 'Stop!', and Trishanku hung in mid-air. In fury the sage began to create a second universe, with new constellations in the southern sky and even a new set of gods. The frightened gods came to terms. Trishanku would stay, head downward, shining among the new stars Vishvamitra had made, and those stars would last as long as the worlds endure.
weapons: divine astras (won from Shiva and passed to Rama)
nodes.abode: Siddhashrama; hermitage on the Kaushiki river
variations: The Ramayana tells his rise to brahmarshi in stages (rajarshi, rishi, maharshi, brahmarshi); the Mahabharata and Puranas differ in detail.
In the Aitareya Brahmana he adopts Shunahshepa as his eldest son Devarata; in the Ramayana he teaches Shunahshepa the hymns that save him.
The Harishchandra ordeal is told in the Markandeya and Devi Bhagavata Puranas; the Aitareya Brahmana's Harishchandra story does not include Vishvamitra's persecution.

nodes.name: Jamadagni
nodes.description: Jamadagni is a Rig Vedic seer of the Bhrigu clan and one of the Saptarishis in the Vedic list and in the list of the present age. In the epics he is the son of Richika, husband of Renuka and father of Parashurama. His murder by the sons of Kartavirya Arjuna led Parashurama to wage war on the kshatriyas.
nodes.story: Renuka went to the river to fetch water and saw King Chitraratha sporting with his wives. For a moment she was stirred with longing. When she returned, Jamadagni saw by his ascetic insight what had passed in her mind and, in anger, ordered his sons one by one to kill her. The four eldest froze in horror, and he cursed them to lose their reason. Then the youngest, Rama (Parashurama), came in and at his father's word struck off his mother's head with his axe. The sage's anger cooled, and he offered his obedient son any boon. Parashurama asked that his mother live again with no memory of what had happened, that his brothers be restored, and that he himself be unconquered in battle and long-lived. All was granted.
nodes.abode: Hermitage on the Narmada; traditionally linked with Jamadagni-ashrama sites
sources: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva (Surya's umbrella and sandals)
variations: The Mahabharata says Kartavirya carried off the calf of Jamadagni's sacrificial cow; later Puranas and folk tellings call the cow Kamadhenu or Sushila.
In the Bhagavata, Kartavirya's sons behead Jamadagni to avenge their father; in some versions Renuka is also wounded.
His mother Satyavati was Vishvamitra's sister, and the Mahabharata's story of the swapped sacrificial porridge links the two sages' natures.

nodes.name: Gautama Maharishi
nodes.description: Gotama Rahugana is the seer of Rig Veda hymns 1.74–93, and a Gotama is one of the seven sages in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad's list. In the epics Gautama is the husband of Ahalya, who curses her and Indra, and the Puranas credit him with bringing the Godavari to earth. Tradition generally treats these as one sage, though the identification is not certain.
nodes.story: During a long drought, Gautama's tapas kept his hermitage at Brahmagiri green, and he fed the sages who came to him for shelter. When the rains returned, some of them wanted to leave, and they set loose an illusory cow in his rice-field. The Brahma Purana says Ganesha, acting for Parvati, sent it to draw Ganga away from Shiva. When Gautama drove it away with a blade of grass, the cow fell dead, and he was blamed for killing a cow. To cleanse the sin, Gautama worshipped Shiva with great devotion until Shiva released a stream of the Ganga from his matted hair onto Brahmagiri. There it became the Godavari, also called Gautami, which flows past Tryambakeshwar to the eastern sea.
variations: Whether the Rig Vedic Gotama Rahugana, Ahalya's husband and the Gautama of the Godavari legend are one sage is uncertain; tradition tends to merge them.
Akshapada Gautama, author of the Nyaya Sutras, and the Gautama of the Dharmasutra are usually treated as different figures.

nodes.name: Ahalya
nodes.description: Ahalya is the wife of the sage Gautama, whom Indra seduced in her husband's form. Gautama's curse and her release by Rama is one of the best-known episodes of the Ramayana. She is counted among the Panchakanya, five women whose names are recited at dawn to remove sin.
nodes.story: One morning, while Gautama was away, Indra came to the hermitage disguised as the sage and asked Ahalya to lie with him. In Valmiki's telling she knew who he was and agreed out of curiosity about the king of the gods. As Indra slipped away, the real Gautama came back from his bath. Seeing everything, he cursed Indra to lose his manhood and cursed Ahalya to live invisible in the hermitage for thousands of years, living on air and lying in ashes, until Rama came. Long afterwards Vishvamitra brought Rama and Lakshmana to the silent hermitage. As Rama entered, Ahalya appeared again, radiant. The princes touched her feet, she welcomed them as guests, flowers rained from the sky, and Gautama returned to take her back.
variations: The Brahmanas only mention Indra as Ahalya's lover in a ritual formula, without condemning either of them.
In Valmiki's Bala Kanda she knowingly consents; in the Uttara Kanda, many Puranas and later retellings she is deceived and innocent.
Valmiki's curse makes her invisible and ascetic; from the Raghuvamsha, Adhyatma Ramayana and Ramcharitmanas onward she is turned to stone and freed by the touch of Rama's foot.
The Uttara Kanda says Brahma created her and gave her to Gautama; the Mahabharata and Harivamsha make her the daughter of the Puru king Mudgala.

nodes.name: Bharadvaja
nodes.description: Bharadvaja is the seer-family of the sixth mandala of the Rig Veda, son of Brihaspati and a Saptarishi in the Vedic list and in the list of the present age. In the Ramayana he hosts Rama and later Bharata at his hermitage at Prayaga. In the Mahabharata he is the father of Drona, and Ayurvedic tradition says he received medicine from Indra.
nodes.story: Bharadvaja was so devoted to the Vedas that he spent three whole lifetimes studying them in celibacy. As he lay old and weak at the end of the third, Indra came and asked what he would do with a fourth life. 'I would spend it studying the Veda,' said Bharadvaja. Indra then showed him three huge mountains that had never been seen before, took a handful from each, and said: 'These mountains are the three Vedas, and these three handfuls are all you have learned. The Veda is endless.' Indra then taught him the Savitra fire rite, by which he could know the infinite Veda through the fire. Bharadvaja performed it and reached the world of heaven.
nodes.abode: Hermitage at Prayaga, at the confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna
variations: The Puranas say he was born to Brihaspati and Mamata, his brother Utathya's wife, abandoned, and given by the Maruts to King Bharata, who adopted him.
A disciple named Bharadvaja goes with Valmiki in the opening of the Ramayana; whether he is the same as the Vedic seer is unclear.

nodes.name: Dadhichi (Dadhyanch)
nodes.description: Dadhyanch Atharvana appears in the Rig Veda as the seer who taught the Ashvins the secret Madhu-vidya through a horse's head, and with whose bones Indra struck down his enemies. In the epics and Puranas, as Dadhichi, he gives up his life so that his bones can be made into the vajra that kills Vritra. Shaiva Puranas also praise him as a devotee of Shiva who opposed Daksha.
nodes.story: The demon Vritra had swallowed the waters and driven the gods from heaven, and no weapon could harm him. Vishnu told the gods that only a weapon made from the bones of the sage Dadhichi could defeat him. Ashamed but desperate, Indra and the gods went to his hermitage and asked him for his body. Dadhichi smiled and said the body is only lent to us and is best given for the good of the worlds. Seated in yoga, he withdrew his life-breath and left his body. The divine craftsman Vishvakarma then shaped his bones into the vajra, the thunderbolt. Armed with it, Indra fought Vritra, killed him and set free the waters, and Dadhichi's gift has been a byword for sacrifice ever since.
nodes.abode: Hermitage on the Sarasvati; Naimisharanya (in later tradition)
variations: In the Rig Veda, Indra slays foes with the bones of Dadhyanch; the full self-sacrifice story comes from the Mahabharata and Puranas.
The Rig Veda calls Dadhyanch a son of Atharvan; some Puranas make Dadhichi a son of Chyavana and Sukanya.
The Linga Purana says he defeated Vishnu in a dispute over King Kshuva; Vaishnava texts do not share this episode.

nodes.name: Chyavana
nodes.description: Chyavana is the aged sage whom the Rig Veda praises the Ashvins for making young again. The Brahmanas and the Mahabharata tell how he married Princess Sukanya and won the Ashvins a share of the soma sacrifice. He is a son of Bhrigu and an ancestor of Jamadagni and Parashurama.
nodes.story: Having been restored to youth by the Ashvins, Chyavana kept his promise to them. At King Sharyati's sacrifice he rose to offer the divine physicians a cup of soma, which the gods had always refused them. Indra objected that the Ashvins were only healers who mixed with mortals, not worthy of soma. Chyavana ignored him, and as he lifted the cup Indra raised the thunderbolt to strike. With one glance Chyavana froze Indra's arm. From the sacrificial fire he then called forth Mada, 'Intoxication', a monster so huge its jaws spanned earth and sky, which rushed at Indra to swallow him. Terrified, Indra gave in and granted the Ashvins their share. Chyavana then divided Mada into drink, women, dice and hunting.
nodes.abode: Hermitage by a lake near the Narmada (Sharyati's land)
variations: In the Shatapatha Brahmana the Ashvins win their soma share by learning from Sukanya that they are 'incomplete'; the Mahabharata adds Indra's opposition and the demon Mada.
The Mahabharata names Chyavana's son Aurva by Arushi; some Puranas give his sons by Sukanya as Apnavana and Dadhicha.

nodes.name: Sukanya
nodes.description: Sukanya is the daughter of King Sharyati, son of Manu, and the wife of the aged sage Chyavana. Her loyalty, even when tempted by the Ashvins, led to her husband being made young again. Her story is first told in the Shatapatha Brahmana and retold in the Mahabharata and Puranas.
nodes.story: Sukanya was playing in the forest when she saw two lights shining from an anthill and poked them with a thorn. They were the eyes of the ancient sage Chyavana, buried in his tapas. Her father's army was struck with sickness until King Sharyati made amends by giving Sukanya to the blinded old man. One day the Ashvins, the handsome twin physicians, found her bathing and urged her to leave her withered husband for one of them. She refused and told them they were themselves 'incomplete'. Curious, they promised to make Chyavana young if she would explain. She agreed, and the three went into a pool. Three identical youths came out, and Sukanya picked out her husband. Then she told the Ashvins they had been left out of the gods' sacrifice at Kurukshetra.
variations: In the Shatapatha Brahmana she wins the rejuvenation by telling the Ashvins why they are incomplete; in the Mahabharata and Bhagavata she must identify her husband among three identical youths.
In the Devi Bhagavata she recognises Chyavana through the grace of the Goddess.

nodes.name: Agastya
nodes.description: Agastya is the seer of Rig Veda hymns 1.165–191, born with Vashistha from the seed of Mitra and Varuna in a jar. The epics tell how he humbled the Vindhya mountains, drank the ocean, digested the demon Vatapi and armed Rama with divine weapons. In Tamil tradition he is Agathiyar, father of Tamil grammar and the Siddha tradition.
nodes.story: In the forest the asura brothers Ilvala and Vatapi killed brahmins by a cruel trick. Vatapi would turn himself into a goat, Ilvala would cook him and serve him to a guest, and then Ilvala would call his brother's name. Vatapi would burst out of the guest's belly, killing him. Agastya, needing wealth for his wife Lopamudra, came to Ilvala, who served him the usual meal. Agastya ate every bite, and when Ilvala called out, 'Vatapi, come out!', the sage just smiled, patted his stomach and said, 'He has been digested.' Only a belch came out. In the Ramayana, Ilvala then rushed at him in fury, and Agastya burned him to ashes with a blazing look, freeing the southern forests from their terror.
nodes.abode: Hermitage south of the Vindhyas (Panchavati region); Pothigai hills (Tamil tradition); the star Canopus
sources: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva and Anushasana Parva (Nahusha)
variations: In the Mahabharata Ilvala is subdued and gives Agastya wealth; in the Ramayana Agastya burns him to death.
The Aditya Hridaya, which Agastya teaches Rama before the final battle, is in the vulgate Yuddha Kanda but not in the Critical Edition.
The Bhagavata makes him a son of Pulastya and Havirbhu, unlike the Vedic birth from Mitra and Varuna.
Tamil tradition, and the Skanda Purana, say Shiva sent him south to balance the earth during Shiva's wedding, and that Murugan taught him Tamil.

nodes.name: Lopamudra
nodes.description: Lopamudra is the wife of Agastya and the woman who speaks in Rig Veda 1.179, where she urges her ascetic husband to turn to married love. The Mahabharata says Agastya created her from the finest features of all creatures and gave her to the king of Vidarbha to raise. Shri Vidya tradition honours her as a great devotee of the goddess Lalita Tripura Sundari.
nodes.story: Agastya once saw his ancestors hanging head-down in a pit. They told him they would fall unless he had a son to carry on their line. Finding no woman worthy of him, the sage made a girl from the most beautiful parts of every creature and gave her secretly to the childless king of Vidarbha, who raised her as Lopamudra. When she grew up, Agastya asked for her hand, and she left the palace for a life of bark garments. When he finally came to her, she spoke up. She would come to him only in the comforts she had grown up with, dressed in jewels on a fine bed, and not in rags. So the great ascetic went to kings to ask for wealth. The journey took him to Ilvala, and at last their son Dridhasyu was born.
variations: In Rig Veda 1.179 she speaks as the aging wife of an ascetic; the Mahabharata supplies the story of her creation and her demand for wealth.
Shri Vidya tradition names one form of the Panchadashi mantra, the Hadi-vidya, the Lopamudra-vidya after her.
Some Tamil and Kodava traditions identify her with the river Kaveri.

nodes.name: Narada
nodes.description: Narada is the wandering divine sage (devarshi), a mind-born son of Brahma who travels between the worlds singing the name of Narayana on his vina. He carries news and counsel between gods, sages and kings, and in bhakti tradition is the model devotee and teacher of devotion. His meddling sometimes sets events in motion, earning him the playful epithet 'lover of quarrels'.
nodes.story: In the Bhagavata Purana Narada tells Vyasa of his previous life. In an earlier cycle of creation he was the young son of a maidservant who waited on wandering sages during the rainy season. Eating the remnants of their meals and listening to their songs about Hari, the boy's heart turned wholly towards God. When his mother died of a snakebite, he wandered alone into a forest, sat beneath a pippala tree and meditated. The form of the Lord flashed within his heart and vanished, leaving him aching with longing. A divine voice told him he would not see that form again in this life, but that his devotion would never fade. At the dissolution he entered Narayana, and in the next creation he was born from Brahma, to roam the worlds forever singing the Lord's names.
variations: The Rig Vedic Anukramani attributes hymns 8.13 and 9.104–105 to a seer Narada Kanva, but this is a later attribution.
The Bhagavata makes Narada born from Brahma's lap; the Mahabharata and Puranas elsewhere count him among the gandharvas or as a son of Kashyapa in a different birth.

The Shiva Purana and Tulsidas' Ramcharitmanas tell of Narada's pride over conquering desire, after which Vishnu gave him a monkey's face and Narada cursed Vishnu to suffer separation from his wife as Rama.

nodes.name: Durvasa
nodes.description: Durvasa is the famously irascible sage, son of Atri and Anasuya and regarded as born of a portion of Shiva. His curses and boons are turning points in many stories: the loss of the gods' fortune before the churning of the ocean, Kunti's mantra for summoning gods, and, in Kalidasa's drama, Shakuntala's forgotten ring. Though quick to anger, he is equally quick to reward sincere hospitality.
nodes.story: Wandering the earth, Durvasa received from a Vidyadhari a fragrant garland of celestial flowers. Meeting Indra riding his elephant Airavata, the sage offered it to the king of the gods. Indra carelessly placed it on the elephant's head; drawn by the scent, Airavata pulled it down with his trunk and trampled it. Durvasa blazed with anger: because Indra, drunk with his own splendour, had scorned a gift given in reverence, the prosperity of the three worlds would desert him. Lakshmi withdrew, the gods lost their vigour, plants withered and sacrifices ceased, and the asuras rose against heaven. Desperate, the devas went to Vishnu, who counselled them to churn the Ocean of Milk together with the asuras to regain their lost fortune and win the nectar of immortality.
sources: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (visit to the exiled Pandavas)
Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva (Durvasa's stay with Krishna)
variations: The curse on Shakuntala is Kalidasa's invention; in the Mahabharata Dushyanta simply pretends not to know her.
In the Uttara Kanda, Durvasa's demand to see Rama at once forces Lakshmana to break Rama's vow, leading to Lakshmana's departure.
Some Puranas say the garland was a gift from Shiva or Vishnu's prasada rather than from a Vidyadhari.

nodes.name: Vyasa (Krishna Dvaipayana)
nodes.description: Vyasa, 'the arranger', is the sage credited with dividing the one Veda into four, composing the Mahabharata and, in tradition, the Puranas and the Brahma Sutras. Son of Parashara and Satyavati, he is also the biological grandfather of both the Kauravas and the Pandavas, and appears throughout the epic he narrates. He is revered as a partial incarnation of Vishnu and one of the Chiranjivis.
nodes.story: Born on an island in the Yamuna to the fisher-maiden Satyavati and the sage Parashara, the dark-skinned child grew up at once and left for the forest, promising his mother he would come whenever she thought of him. Years later, when her son Vichitravirya died childless, Satyavati summoned him to raise heirs for the Kuru line by niyoga with the widowed queens. Ambika shut her eyes at the sight of the gaunt, matted ascetic, and her son Dhritarashtra was born blind; Ambalika turned pale with fear, and Pandu was born pale. When Ambika later sent a maidservant in her place, the woman received him calmly and bore the wise Vidura.
