So the grandfather of both warring houses later composed the Mahabharata, the story of his own descendants.
sources: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva (Moksha-dharma; birth of Shuka)
variations: The Vishnu Purana (3.3) lists twenty-eight Vyasas, one for each dvapara yuga of this manvantara; Krishna Dvaipayana is the latest.
The story of Ganesha writing the Mahabharata to Vyasa's dictation appears in some manuscripts but was excluded from the Critical Edition as an interpolation.
Tradition identifies him with Badarayana, author of the Brahma Sutras; many scholars treat them as different people.

nodes.name: Valmiki
nodes.description: Valmiki is the adikavi, the first poet, author of the Ramayana and a character within it. He shelters the banished Sita in his hermitage, raises her twin sons Lava and Kusha and teaches them to sing his poem. His name is traditionally derived from valmika, the anthill that grew over him during long meditation.
nodes.story: Valmiki once asked Narada whether any man then living possessed every virtue, and Narada told him the story of Rama. Later, walking to the Tamasa river with his disciple Bharadvaja, Valmiki watched a pair of krauncha birds absorbed in each other when a hunter's arrow struck the male. As the female cried over her dying mate, grief welled up in the sage and poured out as a curse in a new, measured verse: 'Hunter, may you never find rest for endless years.' Troubled that he had spoken in anger, he wondered at the form his words had taken. Brahma then appeared, told him the metre had come by his will, and commanded him to tell the whole story of Rama in it. So, it is said, grief (shoka) became verse (shloka), and the first poem was born.
nodes.abode: Hermitage on the Tamasa river, near the Ganga
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Rama's visit at Chitrakuta)
Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda (Sita's exile and the twins)
variations: His earlier life as the highway robber Ratnakara, who repeated 'mara' until it became 'Rama', is a later tradition (Adhyatma Ramayana, Skanda Purana and folk retellings); it is not in the Valmiki Ramayana.
In the Uttara Kanda he calls himself the tenth son of Prachetas; some later traditions identify Prachetas with Varuna.
Communities such as the Balmikis venerate him as their guru and ancestor.

nodes.name: Markandeya
nodes.description: Markandeya is an ageless sage of the Bhrigu line who survives the cosmic dissolution. In the Mahabharata he narrates long cycles of tales to the exiled Pandavas and recounts his vision of the divine child floating on a banyan leaf amid the flood. The Markandeya Purana, including the Devi Mahatmya, is placed in his mouth, and later Shaiva tradition celebrates Shiva's rescue of the boy Markandeya from Yama.
nodes.story: In a widely loved Puranic tale, the sage Mrikandu and his wife Marudvati, long childless, worshipped Shiva and were offered a choice: a dull son who would live long, or a brilliant, virtuous son who would live only sixteen years. They chose the latter. As the boy's sixteenth year closed, Markandeya went to a Shiva linga and worshipped without pause. When Yama's messengers could not approach him, Yama came himself and cast his noose; it fell around both the boy and the linga he embraced. Shiva burst forth from the linga in fury, struck down the god of death and blessed Markandeya to remain sixteen forever. The episode gave Shiva the name Kalantaka, 'ender of Time', and is popularly associated with the Mahamrityunjaya prayer.
nodes.abode: Hermitages in the Himalaya; survives the pralaya on the cosmic waters
sources: Later Puranic and Tamil temple tradition (Kalantaka legend, Thirukkadaiyur)
variations: The rescue from Yama is Puranic and temple tradition; the Mahabharata presents Markandeya as a long-lived sage who witnessed many dissolutions.
The Linga Purana tells a parallel rescue from Kala of a devotee named Shveta.
In the Mahabharata the child on the banyan leaf is Narayana/Krishna; the Bhagavata places the vision after a boon from Nara-Narayana.

nodes.name: Parashara
nodes.description: Parashara is a Vedic seer, grandson of Vashistha and son of Shakti, to whom a group of Rig Vedic hymns to Agni is attributed. In the epics he is the father of Vyasa by Satyavati, and he narrates the Vishnu Purana to his disciple Maitreya. The Parashara Smriti and an early astrological tradition are also attached to his name.
nodes.story: Travelling on pilgrimage, Parashara boarded a ferry on the Yamuna rowed by Satyavati, the fisher-chief's foster daughter, whose body smelled of fish. Captivated, he asked for her love. She hesitated, fearing for her maidenhood and the sages watching from the banks, so Parashara raised a thick mist to veil them and promised that her virginity would be restored. He also granted that the fishy odour would give way to a fragrance carried a whole yojana, earning her the names Gandhavati and Yojanagandha. On an island in the river she gave birth to Krishna Dvaipayana, who grew at once to manhood and departed for the forest. Parashara went on his way, and Satyavati later became the queen of King Shantanu.
sources: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Parashara's sacrifice against the rakshasas)
variations: In the Mahabharata and Vishnu Purana, Parashara begins a sacrifice to burn all rakshasas to avenge his father, but is persuaded by Vashistha and Pulastya to stop.
Attribution of the Brihat Parashara Hora Shastra (astrology) to him is traditional and much later.

nodes.name: Shakti (son of Vashistha)
nodes.description: Shakti is the eldest of Vashistha's hundred sons and the father of Parashara. Verses of the Rig Veda are attributed to him, and in the Mahabharata his curse on King Kalmashapada sets off the tragic destruction of Vashistha's sons amid the feud with Vishvamitra.
nodes.story: King Kalmashapada of the Ikshvaku line, returning from a hunt, met Shakti on a narrow forest path. Neither would give way. The king ordered the sage aside, and when Shakti replied that the path belonged to the brahmana, the king struck him with a whip. Shakti cursed him to roam the earth as a man-eating rakshasa. Vishvamitra, who coveted the king's patronage and bore enmity to Vashistha's house, sent a rakshasa named Kinkara to enter the cursed king. Maddened, Kalmashapada devoured Shakti first and then all of Vashistha's other sons. Shakti's widow Adrishyanti was then carrying their child; when the grieving Vashistha tried again and again to end his life, he heard the unborn Parashara reciting the Veda from her womb and chose to live.
sources: Rig Veda 9.108 (verses attributed to Shakti Vasishtha in the Anukramani)
variations: Some versions say Vishvamitra himself, rather than a hired rakshasa, drove the king to devour Shakti.

nodes.name: Yajnavalkya
nodes.description: Yajnavalkya is the great ritualist and philosopher of the Shatapatha Brahmana and the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, the seer of the White (Shukla) Yajurveda. His dialogues with King Janaka, with his wife Maitreyi and with the scholars of Janaka's court, including Gargi, are among the foundations of Vedanta. A law code, the Yajnavalkya Smriti, bears his name.
nodes.story: King Janaka of Videha once held a sacrifice with lavish gifts and, wishing to learn who was most learned among the brahmins of Kuru and Panchala, set apart a thousand cows with gold pieces tied to their horns. When no one dared claim them, Yajnavalkya told his pupil Samashravas to drive them home. Challenged for his presumption, he replied that he bowed to the most learned, but simply wanted the cows. One after another the great scholars questioned him: Ashvala, Artabhaga, Bhujyu, Ushasta, Kahola, Gargi twice, Uddalaka Aruni and finally Vidagdha Shakalya, who pressed him on the number of gods and, failing to answer the sage's last question, lost his head as warned. Through these answers Yajnavalkya unfolded the Self as the inner controller, describable only as 'not this, not this' (neti neti).
variations: In the Vishnu Purana, after a quarrel with his teacher Vaishampayana, he vomits the Yajurveda, which other pupils eat as partridges (tittiri), giving the Taittiriya (Black) recension; Surya in the form of a horse then teaches him the White Yajurveda.
Brihadaranyaka 6.3.7 and 6.5 place him in a line of teachers after Uddalaka Aruni.

nodes.name: Uddalaka Aruni
nodes.description: Uddalaka Aruni is one of the most important teachers of the Brahmanas and Upanishads, father of Shvetaketu. His teaching in the sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad, with its refrain tat tvam asi ('you are that'), is among the most celebrated passages in Indian philosophy. He also appears questioning Yajnavalkya in Janaka's court.
nodes.story: When his son Shvetaketu returned at twenty-four from twelve years of study, proud and thinking himself learned, Uddalaka asked whether he had sought that teaching by which the unheard becomes heard and the unknown known. Shvetaketu admitted he had not. So his father taught him through homely examples. He had him drop a lump of salt into water overnight and in the morning asked him to find it; it could not be seen, yet every sip tasted of salt. He had him split a banyan fruit, then a seed within it, until nothing visible remained, and showed that from that unseen essence the great tree grows. Each lesson ended with the same refrain: that subtlest essence is the Self of all this; that is the real, that is the Self; you are that, Shvetaketu.
variations: The Mahabharata (Adi Parva 1.3) tells of Aruni of Panchala, pupil of Ayoda Dhaumya, who lay in a breach of a field embankment to stop the water and was renamed Uddalaka; this Aruni is traditionally identified with the Upanishadic teacher.
He is addressed by the clan name Gautama in the Upanishads.

nodes.name: Shvetaketu
nodes.description: Shvetaketu is the son and pupil of Uddalaka Aruni, the listener to whom 'tat tvam asi' is addressed in the Chandogya Upanishad. He appears in the Shatapatha Brahmana and several Upanishads as a proud young scholar humbled into learning, and the Mahabharata credits him with establishing the rule of marital fidelity.
nodes.story: According to a tale Pandu tells Kunti in the Mahabharata, in ancient times women were free to go with any man. One day, as the young Shvetaketu sat with his parents, a brahmin came, took his mother by the hand and led her away. Uddalaka calmly explained that this was the ancient custom, but Shvetaketu was outraged and laid down a new rule: from then on a wife who strayed from her husband, or a husband who betrayed a faithful wife, would incur a sin as grave as killing an unborn child. The Upanishads remember him differently, as the proud graduate humbled when King Pravahana Jaivali asked him five questions on the soul's journey after death that he could not answer, and he returned to ask his father for the teaching.
variations: The Mahabharata makes him the maternal uncle and companion of Ashtavakra.

nodes.name: Nachiketa
nodes.description: Nachiketa is the boy who went to the house of Death and won from Yama the teaching on the immortal Self. His story first appears in the Taittiriya Brahmana and is the frame of the Katha Upanishad, where his refusal of every worldly temptation makes him an enduring model of the earnest seeker.
nodes.story: Vajashravasa performed a sacrifice in which he was to give away all he owned, but he gave only old, barren cows. His young son Nachiketa, troubled, asked again and again, 'To whom will you give me?' Irritated, his father snapped, 'To Death I give you!' Nachiketa went to the house of Yama and, finding him away, waited three nights without food. On his return Yama, anxious at having neglected a brahmin guest, offered three boons. Nachiketa asked that his father be calm and welcome him back, then for knowledge of the fire ritual that leads to heaven, which Yama named after him. For the third he asked what becomes of a man after death. Yama tried to dissuade him with long life, wealth and celestial maidens, but the boy refused them all, and Yama taught him the imperishable Self.
symbols: chain of gold given by Yama
sources: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva (Nachiketa and Yama, on the gift of cows)
variations: The Taittiriya Brahmana version centres on the fire ritual; the Katha Upanishad adds the teaching on the Self.
His father is called Vajashravasa, Ushan Vajashravasa, and (Katha 1.11) Auddalaki Aruni; commentators disagree on whether this is Uddalaka Aruni himself.

nodes.name: Maitreyi
nodes.description: Maitreyi is the wife of Yajnavalkya whose dialogue with him in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad is one of the classic statements on the Self. The Upanishad calls her a brahmavadini, a woman who discoursed on Brahman, in contrast to his other wife Katyayani, and she chooses knowledge of immortality over a share of his wealth.
nodes.story: Preparing to leave household life, Yajnavalkya told his wife Maitreyi that he would divide his property between her and his other wife, Katyayani. Maitreyi asked whether the whole earth filled with wealth would make her immortal. 'No,' he said, 'your life would be like the life of the wealthy, but there is no hope of immortality through wealth.' 'What should I do with that which will not make me immortal?' she replied. 'Tell me what you know.' Delighted, Yajnavalkya taught her that husband, wife, sons, wealth and worlds are dear not for their own sake but for the sake of the Self, which is to be seen, heard, reflected upon and meditated upon. When she was bewildered by his words that after death there is no awareness, he explained that where there is no duality, there is no second to be known.
variations: The Ashvalayana Grihya Sutra honours a Sulabha Maitreyi among women teachers; whether she is the same person is uncertain.

nodes.name: Gargi Vachaknavi
nodes.description: Gargi Vachaknavi, daughter of the sage Vachaknu of the Garga clan, is the philosopher who twice questioned Yajnavalkya before King Janaka's assembly in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. Her probing questions on what the world is 'woven' upon drew out the teaching of the Imperishable (akshara), and she is remembered as one of the great women thinkers of the Vedic age.
nodes.story: At the assembly in Janaka's court, Gargi pressed Yajnavalkya with a chain of questions: if all this is woven on water, on what is water woven? On air, he replied; and air on the intermediate regions, and those on the worlds of the gandharvas, sun, moon, stars, gods, Indra and Prajapati, until she asked on what the worlds of Brahman are woven. 'Gargi, do not question too far, lest your head fall off,' he warned, and she fell silent. Later she rose again, telling the brahmins she would ask him two questions like arrows fitted to a warrior's bow. On what is woven that which is above the sky and below the earth, past, present and future? On space, he said; and space on the Imperishable, at whose command sun and moon stand apart. Satisfied, she declared that none of them would defeat him.
variations: The later Yoga Yajnavalkya presents Gargi as Yajnavalkya's wife and pupil; this is not found in the Upanishad.

nodes.name: Ashtavakra
nodes.description: Ashtavakra, 'bent in eight places', is the sage born crooked because of his father's curse, who as a boy defeated the court scholar Bandin in King Janaka's assembly. He is the grandson of Uddalaka Aruni, and the late non-dual classic, the Ashtavakra Gita, presents him instructing Janaka on the Self.
nodes.story: While still in the womb, Ashtavakra corrected his father Kahoda's recitation of the Veda; stung, Kahoda cursed him to be born bent in eight places. Kahoda later went to King Janaka's court, was defeated in debate by Bandin, and was drowned according to the terms of the contest. At twelve, learning the truth, Ashtavakra set out for Mithila with his uncle Shvetaketu. Barred at the gate as a mere boy, he argued his way in, declaring that neither years nor grey hair make one great, but learning. Before the assembled scholars he defeated Bandin in a contest of verse. Bandin then revealed that he was a son of Varuna and had sent the brahmins to his father's sacrifice. Kahoda returned, and after bathing in the Samanga river, Ashtavakra's limbs became straight.
variations: The Ashtavakra Gita is a much later Advaita text (dated variously between the 8th and 14th centuries CE).
In the Vishnu Purana, apsaras who laughed at his form are cursed to fall into the hands of robbers as Krishna's widows, though he blesses them to regain heaven afterwards.

nodes.name: Shuka
nodes.description: Shuka is the son of Vyasa, a sage born already detached and illumined, who attains liberation in the Mahabharata's Moksha-dharma. In the Bhagavata Purana he recites the entire Bhagavata to King Parikshit during the king's last seven days, and so is revered as the paramount narrator of Krishna's story.
nodes.story: Vyasa performed long austerities to Shiva on Mount Meru for a son as pure as the elements. As he churned the fire-sticks (arani), he saw the apsara Ghritachi, who had taken the form of a female parrot, and his seed fell upon the sticks; from them Shuka, 'the parrot', was born, radiant as fire. He mastered the Vedas and, at his father's bidding, went to King Janaka of Mithila, who tested his detachment and confirmed his wisdom. In the Bhagavata, Shuka wanders naked and unconcerned; bathing apsaras do not cover themselves before the youth, yet grow shy before his aged father, for they see that Shuka perceives no difference. Later he sat before King Parikshit, cursed to die within seven days, and recited the whole Bhagavata Purana on the banks of the Ganga.
nodes.abode: Wanders freely; ultimately merges into the Absolute
sources: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva (Moksha-dharma: birth and liberation of Shuka)
variations: In the Mahabharata Shuka departs from the world and merges into the sky, while his father calls after him; the Bhagavata keeps him present to narrate to Parikshit.
Some Puranic versions give Shuka a wife and children; the Mahabharata and Bhagavata present him as a lifelong renunciate.

nodes.name: Kanva
nodes.description: Kanva is the forest sage on the Malini river who found the abandoned infant Shakuntala and raised her as his daughter. Dushyanta's marriage to Shakuntala and the birth of Bharata, the eponymous ancestor of the Bharatas, take place in his hermitage. He also appears as a counsellor to Duryodhana and, with Vishvamitra and Narada, as one of the sages whose curse doomed the Yadavas.
nodes.story: King Dushyanta, hunting on the banks of the Malini, entered the peaceful hermitage of the sage Kanva and found only a young woman, Shakuntala. She told him that Kanva was away gathering fruit, and explained her origin: born to Vishvamitra and the apsara Menaka, abandoned in the forest and guarded by shakunta birds, she had been found and raised by Kanva as his daughter. Dushyanta married her there by the gandharva rite and returned to his capital. When Kanva came back he knew by his inner vision what had happened and approved the union, foretelling that her son would be a great king. After the boy Bharata was born and had grown strong in the hermitage, subduing wild beasts, Kanva sent mother and son to Dushyanta's court with his disciples.
variations: Distinct from, though often associated with, the Rig Vedic seer Kanva Ghaura, eponym of the Kanva family of Rig Veda Book 8; the epic sage is called Kashyapa.
In Kalidasa's drama, Kanva is away on pilgrimage to Somatirtha when Dushyanta arrives, and his farewell to Shakuntala in Act 4 is one of its most celebrated scenes.

nodes.name: Vishrava
nodes.description: Vishrava is a sage, son of Pulastya, and father of both Kubera, the lord of wealth, and the rakshasa siblings Ravana, Kumbhakarna, Vibhishana and Shurpanakha. Through him the rakshasa royal house of Lanka descends from a mind-born son of Brahma, which is why Ravana is called Paulastya.
nodes.story: After the rakshasas were driven from Lanka to the underworld by Vishnu, their elder Sumali saw the splendour of Kubera, Vishrava's son, and resolved that his own line should produce a son as mighty. He sent his daughter Kaikesi to the sage. She approached Vishrava at dusk, as he tended his sacred fire, and asked him for children. Vishrava consented but warned that, having come at so dreadful an hour, she would bear fearsome and cruel sons. When she pleaded, he promised that her last son would be righteous and devoted to dharma. So Kaikesi bore the ten-headed Ravana, the giant Kumbhakarna, the rakshasi Shurpanakha and finally the gentle Vibhishana. Kubera, his son by Devavarnini, daughter of Bharadvaja, had already received Lanka and the Pushpaka chariot, and the rivalry between his sons would shape the Ramayana.
variations: In the Mahabharata (Vana Parva), Kubera is Pulastya's son who leaves him for Brahma; Pulastya then generates Vishrava from half of himself, and Kubera gives him three rakshasis: Pushpotkata (mother of Ravana and Kumbhakarna), Raka (mother of Khara and Shurpanakha) and Malini (mother of Vibhishana).
Puranas name Kubera's mother Ilavida rather than Devavarnini.

nodes.name: Rishyashringa
nodes.description: Rishyashringa, 'the deer-horned', is the son of the sage Vibhandaka, raised in the wilderness without ever seeing a woman. Lured to the drought-stricken kingdom of Anga, he brought the rains and married Princess Shanta, and later performed the sacrifice that gave King Dasharatha his four sons.
nodes.story: Rishyashringa, son of the sage Vibhandaka, grew up in a remote forest hermitage with no knowledge of women or of the world. When drought struck the kingdom of Anga because of a fault of King Romapada, the ministers learned that rain would return only if this innocent ascetic came to the land. Courtesans were sent to the forest; the youth, thinking them strange young ascetics, was charmed by their sweets and embraces and followed them. In the Mahabharata he is carried away on a floating hermitage built on a raft. As soon as he set foot in Anga the rains fell. Romapada gave him his daughter Shanta in marriage. Later, at King Dasharatha's request, Rishyashringa presided over the sacrifice for sons from which Rama and his brothers were born.
variations: The Mahabharata says he was born of a doe after Vibhandaka's seed was stirred by the sight of the apsara Urvashi.
Some later retellings make Shanta Dasharatha's own daughter adopted by Romapada; the Bala Kanda calls her Romapada's daughter.
A Buddhist parallel is the Nalinika / Alambusa Jataka; some scholars have linked the tale to the later unicorn legend.

nodes.name: Dhruva
nodes.description: Dhruva is the prince, son of King Uttanapada and grandson of Svayambhuva Manu, whose childhood austerities won him from Vishnu the fixed position of the pole star (dhruva), around which the heavens revolve. He is a model of steadfast devotion, and later ruled as a righteous king before ascending to his eternal station.
nodes.story: Prince Dhruva, son of King Uttanapada by his neglected queen Suniti, once tried to climb onto his father's lap, but his stepmother Suruchi pulled him away, telling him that only her son Uttama deserved that seat, and that he should have been born from her womb. Stung, the five-year-old ran to his mother, who told him to seek refuge in Vishnu. Leaving the palace, he met sages who taught him to meditate on the Lord: Narada in the Bhagavata, the seven rishis in the Vishnu Purana. In the Madhuvana forest by the Yamuna he performed austerities so fierce that the worlds trembled. Vishnu appeared, touched his cheek with the conch, and granted him the pole-star position, a fixed abode around which the stars and planets revolve, higher than any other.
symbols: child ascetic standing on one leg
variations: In the Vishnu Purana, Dhruva is instructed by the Saptarishi (Marichi and the others); in the Bhagavata, by Narada, who teaches him the twelve-syllable mantra.
The Bhagavata adds his later war with the yakshas after his brother Uttama is killed, halted by Svayambhuva Manu, and a boon from Kubera.

nodes.name: Vaishampayana
nodes.description: Vaishampayana is a disciple of Vyasa who recited the Mahabharata to King Janamejaya at his snake sacrifice; that recitation forms the inner frame of the epic. The Puranas also make him the first teacher of the Yajurveda, from whose school the Taittiriya (Black) Yajurveda descends.
nodes.story: When King Janamejaya held his great snake sacrifice to avenge his father Parikshit, Vyasa came to the assembly with his disciples. The king asked him about the deeds of his ancestors, the Pandavas and the Kauravas, and the cause of their quarrel. Vyasa turned to his pupil Vaishampayana, who had learned the whole Bharata from him, and told him to recite it. In the intervals of the sacrifice Vaishampayana narrated the epic, answering the king's questions as he went. The bard Ugrashravas heard that recitation and later retold it to the sages of the Naimisha forest, in the frame in which the Mahabharata reaches us. In the Vishnu Purana, Vaishampayana appears also as the teacher of the Yajurveda whose quarrel with his pupil Yajnavalkya led to the Black and White Yajurveda.
variations: The Mahabharata says Vyasa taught the epic to five disciples (Sumantu, Jaimini, Paila, Shuka and Vaishampayana), and different versions circulated among them.
The Vishnu Purana says he incurred the sin of killing a brahmin (his nephew, by accident), which his pupils expiated for him.

nodes.name: Rama
nodes.description: Rama, prince of Ayodhya and eldest son of King Dasharatha of the Ikshvaku (Solar) dynasty, is the hero of Valmiki's Ramayana and the seventh avatar of Vishnu. Revered as maryada purushottama, the ideal of dharma in word and deed, he is worshipped across South and Southeast Asia together with Sita, Lakshmana and Hanuman.
nodes.story: On the eve of his consecration as heir, Rama learned that Queen Kaikeyi had claimed two boons long owed her by Dasharatha: that her son Bharata be crowned, and that Rama live fourteen years in the forest. Without a word of protest he set aside the royal insignia, put on bark garments and walked out of Ayodhya, followed by Sita and Lakshmana while the whole city wept. In the Dandaka forest Ravana carried Sita away, and Rama's search led him to the vanara king Sugriva and to Hanuman, who found her in Lanka. A causeway of stones was built across the sea; in the great war Rama slew Ravana with a weapon of Brahma, regained Sita and returned in the Pushpaka chariot to be crowned, beginning the reign remembered as Rama-rajya, a golden age of justice.
symbols: bark garments and matted hair in exile
accompanied by Sita, Lakshmana and Hanuman
weapons: bow (Kodanda in later tradition; Vishnu's bow received from Parashurama and Agastya)
nodes.abode: Ayodhya; Vaikuntha (or Saketa in later devotional tradition)
variations: Many scholars (e.g. J. L. Brockington) regard the Bala and Uttara Kandas as later layers; Rama's explicit identity with Vishnu is concentrated in them, though whether the core books already present him as divine is debated (e.g. Sheldon Pollock argues it is integral).
The Buddhist Dasharatha Jataka has no abduction or war: Rama-pandita is exiled to the Himalaya, and Sita is his sister who becomes his queen.
In Jain versions such as Vimalasuri's Paumacariya, Rama (Padma) is a non-violent Baladeva who attains liberation, and it is Lakshmana who kills Ravana.
The Adhyatma Ramayana and Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas present Rama as the supreme Brahman himself, and the Sita whom Ravana abducts as a shadow (Maya Sita).

The Bengali Krittivasi Ramayan adds Rama's untimely worship of Durga (Akal Bodhan) before the final battle; Kamban's Tamil Ramavataram and southern traditions add Rama's worship of Shiva at Rameshwaram.
The Uttara Kanda's banishment of Sita and killing of the shudra ascetic Shambuka are ethically debated episodes; the Mahabharata's Ramopakhyana ends with the coronation.
Southeast Asian retellings include the Thai Ramakien, the Khmer Reamker and the Malay Hikayat Seri Rama.

nodes.name: Sita
nodes.description: Sita, princess of Videha (Mithila) and wife of Rama, is the heroine of the Ramayana, revered as the ideal of steadfast virtue and as an incarnation of the goddess Lakshmi. Found by King Janaka in a ploughed furrow, she is called Bhumija, daughter of the Earth, to whom she finally returns.
nodes.story: King Janaka was ploughing a field to prepare a sacrificial ground when a girl rose from the furrow; he raised her as his own and named her Sita, 'furrow'. He vowed to give her only to the man who could string Shiva's mighty bow, and Rama not only strung it but broke it. When Rama was exiled, Sita refused to stay behind, insisting that a wife's place was at her husband's side, even in the wilderness. Abducted by Ravana and held in the ashoka grove of Lanka, she rejected his every threat and temptation. After the war she proved her purity by entering fire, from which Agni himself returned her unharmed. Later, banished while pregnant, she raised her twin sons in Valmiki's hermitage; when asked to prove herself once more, she called upon the Earth, who opened and received her.
symbols: crest-jewel (chudamani) sent to Rama through Hanuman
nodes.abode: Mithila and Ayodhya; returned into the Earth
sources: Valmiki Ramayana (Bala, Ayodhya, Aranya, Sundara, Yuddha and Uttara Kandas)
variations: The Rig Veda (4.57) invokes Sita, the personified furrow, as an agricultural goddess, and later ritual texts pair her with Indra or Parjanya; scholars see this as background to the epic heroine's birth from the furrow.
In the Uttara Kanda, Sita is the rebirth of Vedavati, who immolated herself after Ravana molested her, vowing to be born again for his destruction.
In the Adhyatma Ramayana and the Ramcharitmanas, the real Sita remains in Agni's keeping and Ravana abducts only her shadow (Maya or Chhaya Sita); the fire-ordeal restores the real Sita.

The Adbhuta Ramayana has her born of Mandodari and, as a fierce goddess, slaying a thousand-headed Ravana; Jain texts such as Gunabhadra's Uttarapurana and the Vasudevahindi make her Ravana's daughter, abandoned because of a prophecy.

In Valmiki the bow is a bride-price of valour (viryashulka) rather than a formal svayamvara; later retellings such as the Ramcharitmanas stage an assembly of kings and add Sita's first sight of Rama in Janaka's garden.
The 'Lakshmana-rekha', a protective line drawn around the hut, does not occur in Valmiki and belongs to later tellings.
The Buddhist Dasharatha Jataka makes Sita Rama's sister and queen.
The banishment and her return into the Earth belong to the Uttara Kanda, widely regarded as a later layer; the Mahabharata's Ramopakhyana ends with the reunion.

nodes.name: Lakshmana
nodes.description: Lakshmana, son of Dasharatha and Sumitra and twin of Shatrughna, is Rama's inseparable companion who shared his fourteen years of exile. Valmiki makes him a portion of Vishnu; later tradition identifies him with the serpent Shesha, on whom Vishnu rests.
nodes.story: When Rama was banished, Lakshmana at first raged against his father and Kaikeyi, then asked only to follow as Rama's servant and bow-bearer. In the forest he built the hut at Panchavati and kept watch night after night. When the rakshasi Shurpanakha attacked Sita, Lakshmana cut off her nose and ears, setting the war in motion. In Lanka he fell more than once to the weapons of Indrajit and Ravana and was revived by herbs that Hanuman carried from the Himalaya. At last he faced Indrajit, the conqueror of Indra, and after a long duel severed his head with an arrow he charged with an oath on Rama's truth and righteousness. In the Uttara Kanda, to save Rama from breaking his word, he accepted banishment and gave up his life on the banks of the Sarayu.
sources: Valmiki Ramayana (Bala, Ayodhya, Aranya, Yuddha and Uttara Kandas)
variations: Valmiki's Bala Kanda makes Lakshmana and Shatrughna portions of Vishnu; the identification of Lakshmana with the serpent Shesha is found in later texts such as the Adhyatma Ramayana and the Puranas (where Balarama is also Shesha).
In Jain versions (Paumacariya), Lakshmana is the Vasudeva who kills Ravana, the Prati-vasudeva, and in consequence descends to hell, while Rama attains liberation.
The Ramcharitmanas moves Parashurama's confrontation to Janaka's court, where Lakshmana mocks the angry sage.
A folk tradition holds that Lakshmana did not sleep for the fourteen years of exile, Urmila sleeping in his place by a boon of the goddess Nidra; this is absent from Valmiki.
The 'Lakshmana-rekha' drawn to protect Sita is a later addition not found in Valmiki.

nodes.name: Urmila
nodes.description: Urmila is the daughter of King Janaka of Mithila and younger sister of Sita, married to Lakshmana at the same ceremony in which Sita wed Rama. Valmiki says little of her; later poets celebrated her silent sacrifice in remaining behind during Lakshmana's fourteen-year exile.
nodes.story: After Rama broke Shiva's bow, Janaka offered not only Sita but also his own daughter Urmila, and she was given to Lakshmana, while Kushadhvaja's daughters Mandavi and Shrutakirti were married to Bharata and Shatrughna on the same day. Valmiki names her in the Bala Kanda, but she vanishes from the narrative when Lakshmana follows Rama to the forest. Later tradition filled the silence. A popular legend, found in folk and regional retellings rather than in Valmiki, tells that Nidra, the goddess of sleep, came to Lakshmana in the forest; he begged to be allowed to guard Rama and Sita unsleeping, and Urmila took his share of sleep, slumbering through the fourteen years. Modern poets revived her memory: Rabindranath Tagore lamented her neglect in his essay Kavye Upekshita, and Maithilisharan Gupta made her the heroine of Saket.
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda (Lakshmana's sons Angada and Chandraketu)
variations: The Nidra legend of Urmila sleeping for fourteen years is a folk and regional tradition (notably in Telugu and Hindi retellings) with no basis in Valmiki.
Valmiki calls Urmila Janaka's own daughter, whereas Sita was found in the furrow; later tellings sometimes treat them simply as sisters born to Janaka's queen.
The Uttara Kanda gives Lakshmana two sons, Angada and Chandraketu, whom tradition counts as Urmila's children.

nodes.name: Bharata
nodes.description: Bharata, son of Dasharatha and Kaikeyi, is the brother for whose sake Rama was exiled and who refused the throne his mother's scheme had won him. Ruling from Nandigrama as Rama's regent, with Rama's sandals on the throne, he is the epic's model of selfless fraternal devotion.
nodes.story: Bharata was away at his grandfather's court in Kekaya when Dasharatha died. Returning to a silent Ayodhya, he learned that his mother had gained him the kingdom by exiling Rama; he denounced Kaikeyi bitterly and refused the crown. With the royal priests, the queens and an army he marched to Chitrakuta to beg Rama to come back. Rama, bound by his father's word, would not break the promise, so Bharata asked for his brother's sandals (paduka). Carrying them on his head, he installed them on the throne and governed from the village of Nandigrama, wearing matted hair and bark, vowing to enter fire if Rama did not return when the fourteen years were over. When Hanuman brought news of Rama's approach, Bharata went out on foot to welcome him and handed back the kingdom.
symbols: royal umbrella held over the sandals
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha and Uttara Kandas
variations: Valmiki's Bala Kanda makes Bharata a quarter-portion of Vishnu; later traditions identify him with Vishnu's discus (Sudarshana) or conch (Panchajanya), assigning the other emblem to Shatrughna, and the assignments differ between texts.
In the Uttara Kanda Bharata conquers the Gandharva country, where his sons Taksha and Pushkala found Takshashila and Pushkalavati.
In the Ramcharitmanas, Bharata's arrow brings down Hanuman as he flies over Nandigrama with the mountain of herbs.

nodes.name: Mandavi
nodes.description: Mandavi is the elder daughter of Kushadhvaja, Janaka's younger brother, and the wife of Bharata. Valmiki names her only at the fourfold wedding in Mithila; later tellings give her a quiet role during Bharata's austere regency.
nodes.story: When Rama had broken Shiva's bow and his marriage to Sita was settled, the sage Vishvamitra and the royal priest Vashistha proposed that the two houses be bound more closely still. Janaka gave his daughter Urmila to Lakshmana, and his brother Kushadhvaja, king of Sankashya, gave his daughters Mandavi and Shrutakirti to Bharata and Shatrughna. The four princes took their brides' hands before the sacred fire on the same auspicious day as Dasharatha looked on, and the procession returned to Ayodhya amid rejoicing. Valmiki tells little more of her. Later devotional retellings imagine Mandavi sharing her husband's penance, living simply while Bharata dwelt at Nandigrama as an ascetic with Rama's sandals on the throne, awaiting the end of the exile. Bharata's sons Taksha and Pushkala, founders of Takshashila and Pushkalavati, are traditionally reckoned her children.
variations: Valmiki names Bharata's sons but does not dwell on their mother; the attribution to Mandavi is traditional.
Her role during the exile is elaborated only in later devotional and regional retellings.

nodes.name: Shatrughna
nodes.description: Shatrughna, son of Dasharatha and Sumitra and twin of Lakshmana, was as closely attached to Bharata as Lakshmana was to Rama. In the Uttara Kanda he slays the demon Lavana and founds the city of Madhura (Mathura).
nodes.story: While Rama was in exile, Shatrughna stood beside Bharata. When the brothers returned from Kekaya and found the hunchbacked Manthara decked in finery, Shatrughna seized her and dragged her across the floor in fury, until Bharata reminded him that Rama would never forgive the killing of a woman, and he let her go. Years later, after Rama's coronation, the sages of the Yamuna banks complained of Lavana, son of the demon Madhu, who held an invincible trident first given to his father by Shiva. Rama sent Shatrughna against him. On the way Shatrughna spent a night in Valmiki's hermitage, the very night Sita bore her twin sons. Catching Lavana outside his city without his trident, Shatrughna killed him with a divine arrow and founded the city of Madhura on the site.
weapons: divine arrow used to slay Lavana
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala and Ayodhya Kandas
Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda (slaying of Lavana)
Padma Purana, Patala Khanda (the horse sacrifice)
variations: Valmiki makes him, with Lakshmana, a portion of Vishnu; later traditions identify him with Vishnu's conch (Panchajanya) or discus (Sudarshana), the opposite emblem to Bharata's.
In the Padma Purana and Jaimini's Ashvamedha he leads Rama's sacrificial horse and is defeated by Lava and Kusha.
The Uttara Kanda, where his conquest of Lavana is told, is widely regarded as a later layer of the epic.

nodes.name: Shrutakirti
nodes.description: Shrutakirti is the younger daughter of Kushadhvaja of Sankashya and the wife of Shatrughna. She appears in Valmiki only at the fourfold marriage in Mithila.
nodes.story: Kushadhvaja, younger brother of King Siradhvaja Janaka, had been made king of Sankashya after Janaka killed King Sudhanva, who had besieged Mithila demanding both Shiva's bow and Sita. When Rama's marriage to Sita was agreed, Vishvamitra and Vashistha asked that Kushadhvaja's two daughters be given to Rama's remaining brothers. The elder, Mandavi, was wedded to Bharata, and the younger, Shrutakirti, to Shatrughna, on the same day that Rama and Lakshmana married Sita and Urmila. Valmiki describes the four couples circling the sacred fire while flowers fell from the sky and celestial music sounded, and then Shrutakirti steps quietly out of the epic. Later tradition counts Shatrughna's sons Subahu and Shatrughati, to whom he gave the cities of Madhura and Vidisha, as her children.
variations: The attribution of Shatrughna's sons to Shrutakirti is traditional rather than explicit in Valmiki.

nodes.name: Dasharatha
nodes.description: Dasharatha, king of Kosala at Ayodhya and son of Aja of the Ikshvaku line, was the father of Rama, Lakshmana, Bharata and Shatrughna. Bound by two boons owed to his queen Kaikeyi, he exiled his beloved eldest son and died of grief soon after.
nodes.story: Childless for many years, Dasharatha performed a horse sacrifice and, with the sage Rishyashringa officiating, a rite for sons; from the fire rose a radiant being bearing a vessel of divine payasa, which the king shared among Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra, and four sons were born. Long before, however, as a young prince hunting by night on the Sarayu, he had shot at a sound he took for an elephant drinking and killed an ascetic youth filling a water-pot for his blind, aged parents. The grieving father cursed him to die, like himself, sorrowing for a son. The curse ripened when Kaikeyi claimed the two boons she had earned by saving him in the gods' war against the asura Shambara. Dasharatha banished Rama and, a few nights later, confessing the old sin to Kausalya, died calling Rama's name.
symbols: royal umbrella and throne of Ayodhya
variations: Valmiki names Aja as his father; Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha names his mother as Indumati.
In the Buddhist Dasharatha Jataka he is a king of Varanasi.
The Ramcharitmanas says Dasharatha and Kausalya were Svayambhuva Manu and Shatarupa reborn, and also identifies them with Kashyapa and Aditi, to whom Vishnu had promised to be born as a son.
The Padma Purana tells how Dasharatha confronted Shani to stop a ruinous planetary transit, praised him with the Dasharatha Shani Stotra and received a boon.
The popular story that Kaikeyi saved him by thrusting her finger into a broken chariot axle is a later folk elaboration; Valmiki says only that she carried the wounded king from the battlefield.
Valmiki mentions some 350 lesser wives besides the three chief queens.

nodes.name: Kausalya
nodes.description: Kausalya, chief queen of Dasharatha and mother of Rama, is portrayed as a devout and dignified matriarch whose grief at her son's exile is one of the Ayodhya Kanda's most moving themes. Her name marks her as a princess of the Kosala country.
nodes.story: On the morning Rama was to be consecrated, Kausalya had kept a night-long vigil, offering oblations to Vishnu for her son's welfare. Rama came to her dressed not for coronation but for exile. Stunned, she fell to the ground like a felled tree, then begged him to stay or to take her with him, reminding him of a mother's claim upon her son. Rama gently answered that her place lay with her husband, the stricken king. Accepting it, she blessed him with a long benediction for his safety in the forest, invoking the gods, the seasons, the rivers and the sages. Left behind, she turned her anguish on Dasharatha, and the king, begging forgiveness with folded hands, confessed to her his killing of the ascetic youth long ago before he died.
variations: The Ramcharitmanas identifies her with Shatarupa, wife of Svayambhuva Manu, and with Aditi, reborn to have Vishnu as her son; in the Adhyatma Ramayana and Ramcharitmanas the newborn Rama first shows her his four-armed divine form.
Regional tradition in Chhattisgarh makes her a princess of Dakshina Kosala and honours her at the Kausalya temple of Chandkhuri.

nodes.name: Kaikeyi
nodes.description: Kaikeyi, princess of Kekaya and Dasharatha's favourite queen, was the mother of Bharata. Incited by her maid Manthara, she used two boons to have Rama exiled and Bharata crowned, an act that made her name a byword for scheming, though later tradition often softens her role.
nodes.story: Kaikeyi had once saved Dasharatha's life, carrying the wounded king from the battlefield during the gods' war against the asura Shambara; in gratitude he granted her two boons, which she kept in reserve. Hearing of Rama's coming consecration, the hunchbacked Manthara warned her that she and Bharata would be reduced to servants of Kausalya. At first Kaikeyi rejoiced and gave the maid a jewel, for she loved Rama; but Manthara's words took hold. Casting off her ornaments, she lay on the floor of the chamber of anger. When the anxious king swore by Rama to grant her wish, she named her boons: Bharata's coronation and Rama's exile for fourteen years. Her own son repudiated her, and she went with him to Chitrakuta, where later tellings such as the Ramcharitmanas show her repentant.
variations: The popular tale that she drove Dasharatha's chariot and kept it running by thrusting her finger into a broken axle is a later folk addition.

In the Adhyatma Ramayana and the Ramcharitmanas, the gods have Saraswati turn Manthara's (and so Kaikeyi's) mind, so that Rama may go to the forest and destroy Ravana; Kaikeyi's act thus serves a divine purpose.
Some later devotional and modern retellings present her as knowingly sacrificing her reputation for the gods' plan.

nodes.name: Sumitra
nodes.description: Sumitra, the third of Dasharatha's chief queens, was mother of the twins Lakshmana and Shatrughna. Valmiki portrays her as wise and self-effacing, sending Lakshmana into exile with words that became proverbial.
nodes.story: When Rama left for the forest, Lakshmana came to take leave of his mother. Sumitra did not hold him back. Instead she blessed him with counsel that later generations learned by heart: he was to regard Rama as his father Dasharatha, Sita as his mother, and the forest as Ayodhya, and so go forth in happiness. Afterwards, when Kausalya was overwhelmed by grief and anger, it was Sumitra who consoled her, reminding her of Rama's virtue, his strength and his certain return. According to the Bala Kanda, Sumitra had received the divine payasa of Dasharatha's sacrifice twice over, which is why she bore twins; a popular explanation adds that one son was drawn to Rama and the other to Bharata because her portions had come from the shares of their mothers.
variations: Accounts of how the payasa was divided differ: in some tellings Kausalya and Kaikeyi each give part of their share to Sumitra, explaining the twins' attachments to Rama and Bharata.
Later traditions assign her various royal birthplaces, none attested in Valmiki.

nodes.name: Manthara
nodes.description: Manthara is the hunchbacked maidservant who came from Kekaya with Queen Kaikeyi and persuaded her to demand Rama's exile. Her whispered counsel sets the Ramayana's central crisis in motion.
nodes.story: From the palace terrace Manthara saw Ayodhya hung with banners and learned that Rama was to be made heir the next morning. She hurried to Kaikeyi, who lay resting, and warned her that once Rama was king, Bharata would be banished or killed, and Kaikeyi herself would wait on Kausalya as a handmaid. Kaikeyi at first answered with joy and gave her a jewel; Manthara flung it aside and pressed on, reminding her of the two boons the king had promised long ago and teaching her to enter the chamber of anger and refuse all comfort until they were granted. When Bharata returned to find his father dead and his brother exiled, Shatrughna seized the richly adorned maid and dragged her along the ground, until Bharata restrained him.
variations: In the Mahabharata's Ramopakhyana, Brahma sends the gandharvi Dundubhi to be born as Manthara to bring about Rama's exile.
In the Adhyatma Ramayana and the Ramcharitmanas, the goddess Saraswati, at the gods' request, clouds Manthara's mind so that Rama's divine mission may proceed.
Kamban's Tamil Ramavataram traces her grudge to Rama's boyhood, when he struck her hump with a pellet from his bow in play.

nodes.name: Shanta
nodes.description: Shanta is the wife of the sage Rishyashringa, whose arrival ended a drought in Anga and who later officiated at Dasharatha's sacrifice for sons. Valmiki calls her the daughter of King Romapada (Lomapada) of Anga; later tradition makes her Dasharatha's own daughter, given in adoption to his friend Romapada, and so Rama's elder sister.
nodes.story: The kingdom of Anga was stricken by drought because its king Romapada had offended the brahmins. His counsellors advised him to bring to the city the young sage Rishyashringa, raised in the forest by his father Vibhandaka without ever seeing a woman. Courtesans lured the innocent youth onto a boat and carried him to Anga, and as soon as he arrived the rain poured down. Romapada gave him his daughter Shanta in marriage, and the couple lived honoured at court. Later Dasharatha, longing for sons, travelled to Anga and invited Rishyashringa and Shanta to Ayodhya, where the sage performed the rites from which Rama and his brothers were born. Temples to Rishyashringa, such as the one at Kigga near Sringeri, keep the couple's memory alive.
variations: Valmiki's Bala Kanda and the Mahabharata make Shanta the daughter of Romapada (Lomapada) of Anga.
The Bhagavata Purana and other Puranic and regional traditions say Dasharatha gave his daughter Shanta to his childless friend Romapada; some folk tellings make her Kausalya's daughter.

nodes.name: Janaka
nodes.description: Janaka is the royal title of the kings of Videha (Mithila). Sita's father, whom the Ramayana calls Siradhvaja Janaka, was renowned as a royal sage (rajarshi) who ruled with detachment; the philosopher-king Janaka Vaideha of the Shatapatha Brahmana and Brihadaranyaka Upanishad is traditionally conflated with him, though the texts suggest different kings of one dynasty.
nodes.story: Janaka was ploughing the ground for a sacrifice when he found an infant girl in the furrow and raised her as Sita. In his palace lay the great bow of Shiva, entrusted to his ancestor Devarata after the gods' quarrel at Daksha's sacrifice; so heavy was it that it had to be drawn on an eight-wheeled cart by thousands of men. Janaka declared that Sita would be given only to one who could string it. Kings came and failed, and some even besieged Mithila in anger. When Vishvamitra brought the young Rama, the prince lifted the bow, strung it and drew it until it snapped with a crash like thunder. Overjoyed, Janaka sent messengers to Dasharatha and gave his daughters and nieces in marriage to the four princes of Ayodhya.
sources: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ashtavakra episode) and Shanti Parva
variations: Janaka is a dynastic title: Valmiki's Bala Kanda traces the Videha line from Nimi and Mithi to Siradhvaja, son of Hrasvaroman. The Upanishadic Janaka Vaideha, patron of Yajnavalkya, and the Janaka of Ashtavakra's tale are not securely the same king as Sita's father.
The Mahabharata's Shanti Parva attributes to Janaka the saying that if Mithila burns, nothing of his is burnt, the classic statement of royal detachment.
The name of his queen, Sunaina (Sunayana), is not given in Valmiki and comes from later tradition.

nodes.name: Sunaina
nodes.description: Sunaina (Sunayana) is the name later tradition gives to the queen of Janaka and mother of Sita and Urmila. She is not named in Valmiki's Ramayana and is best known from medieval retellings, above all Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas.
nodes.story: In the Ramcharitmanas, Sunayana watches anxiously as the kings of the earth fail one after another to move Shiva's bow. Seeing the youthful Rama step forward, she grieves to her companions that her husband's vow is heartless: how could so tender a boy bend a bow that mighty warriors could not stir? A wise companion answers that the power of the great is not measured by their size, for the pot-born sage Agastya drank up the ocean. Then the bow breaks, and her fear turns to joy. Later, when the court of Ayodhya gathers at Chitrakuta around the exiled Rama, Tulsidas brings Janaka and Sunayana to the forest too, and the queen of Mithila meets Kausalya, the two mothers sharing their sorrow for their children.
variations: Valmiki leaves Janaka's queen unnamed; the name Sunaina or Sunayana belongs to later tradition.
Since Sita was found in the furrow, Sunaina's motherhood of Sita is adoptive; Urmila is Janaka's own daughter.

nodes.name: Kushadhvaja
nodes.description: Kushadhvaja is the younger brother of King Siradhvaja Janaka and king of Sankashya, and the father of Mandavi and Shrutakirti. He appears in the Bala Kanda of Valmiki's Ramayana.
nodes.story: When Dasharatha's party arrived in Mithila for Rama's wedding, Janaka summoned his brother Kushadhvaja from Sankashya, the city on the river Ikshumati, and recited their lineage from Nimi. He told how, after their father Hrasvaroman retired to the forest, King Sudhanva of Sankashya had besieged Mithila demanding Shiva's bow and the lotus-eyed Sita; Janaka killed Sudhanva in battle and installed Kushadhvaja on the throne of Sankashya. Vishvamitra and Vashistha then proposed that Kushadhvaja's two daughters, as virtuous as they were beautiful, be married to Bharata and Shatrughna. Kushadhvaja gladly agreed, and Mandavi and Shrutakirti were wedded alongside Sita and Urmila, binding the houses of Mithila and Ayodhya in a fourfold alliance.
variations: Not to be confused with Kushadhvaja, son of Brihaspati, whom the Uttara Kanda names as the father of Vedavati.

nodes.name: Lava
nodes.description: Lava is the younger of the twin sons of Rama and Sita, born in the hermitage of Valmiki after Sita's banishment. With his brother Kusha he learned the Ramayana from Valmiki and sang it at Rama's court; he later ruled from Shravasti in the north.
nodes.story: According to the Padma Purana and later tellings such as Jaimini's Ashvamedha and the Bengali Krittivasi Ramayan, when Rama loosed the horse of his horse sacrifice it wandered near Valmiki's hermitage. The boy Lava read the golden plate on its forehead proclaiming Rama's sovereignty over all who let it pass and, indignant at the challenge, tied the horse to a tree. Rama's army under Shatrughna came to reclaim it; single-handed, Lava held them off until he was overpowered and taken captive. Kusha, returning, rushed to his rescue, and together the twins routed the army, in some versions even binding Hanuman. Only Sita's intervention ended the fight. Valmiki's Uttara Kanda knows nothing of this battle: there the twins simply sing the epic at the sacrifice, and Rama recognises them as his sons.
symbols: vina (as a singer of the Ramayana)
variations: The capture of the sacrificial horse and the battle with Rama's army are found in the Padma Purana, Jaimini's Ashvamedha, Bhavabhuti's Uttararamacharita and regional retellings, not in Valmiki.
A popular folk tale says that only Lava was born to Sita, and that Valmiki created Kusha from kusha grass when he feared the child lost.
In the Uttara Kanda, Rama gives Lava the northern city of Shravasti; the Punjabi tradition links Lahore (Lavapura) with his name.

nodes.name: Kusha
nodes.description: Kusha is the elder of Rama and Sita's twin sons, born in Valmiki's hermitage. He received southern Kosala with its capital Kushavati, and according to Kalidasa later restored Ayodhya as the seat of the Ikshvaku line.
nodes.story: On the night Shatrughna lodged at Valmiki's hermitage, Sita gave birth to twin sons. The sage took a handful of sacred kusha grass: with its tips he performed the protective rites for the first-born, naming him Kusha, and with its lower part, lava, he protected the younger, naming him Lava. Valmiki taught the boys the epic he had composed, and they sang it at Rama's horse sacrifice, where the king recognised his sons. When Rama left the world he gave Kusha the kingdom of southern Kosala at Kushavati. In Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha, the deserted Ayodhya appears to Kusha at night as a mourning woman, the city's presiding goddess, and begs him to come home; he moves his court back and restores her splendour.
symbols: vina (as a singer of the Ramayana)
variations: The Raghuvamsha adds Kusha's return to Ayodhya and his marriage to the naga princess Kumudvati; their son Atithi continues the line.
In the Padma Purana and Jaimini's Ashvamedha he rescues Lava and fights Rama's army over the sacrificial horse.
A folk tale says Valmiki created Kusha from kusha grass as a substitute for Lava.

nodes.name: Guha
nodes.description: Guha is the king of the Nishadas, a forest people, at Shringaverapura on the Ganga, and a close friend of Rama. He welcomed the exiles and ferried them across the river, and later helped Bharata's army to cross.
nodes.story: When Rama reached Shringaverapura on the first stage of his exile, Guha, lord of the Nishadas, came out with his elders and offered him his kingdom and every comfort. Rama embraced his friend but, bound by his vow, accepted only fodder for the horses and slept on a bed of grass beneath an ingudi tree, while Guha and Lakshmana kept watch through the night, speaking of Ayodhya's sorrow. At dawn Guha's boatmen ferried the exiles across the Ganga. Later, seeing Bharata approach with a great army, Guha suspected he meant to harm Rama and readied his warriors; but when Bharata's grief and loyalty became plain, Guha wept, showed him the place where Rama had slept, and brought five hundred boats to carry his host over the river.
variations: The Ramcharitmanas distinguishes Guha (Nishadraj) from the boatman Kevat, who insists on washing Rama's feet before ferrying him; popular tradition often merges the two.
In Kamban's Tamil Ramavataram, Rama embraces Guhan as a brother, saying that the four brothers have now become five.

nodes.name: Shabari
nodes.description: Shabari is an aged female ascetic of the forest, a Shabara by birth, who served the sages of Matanga's hermitage near Lake Pampa and waited years for Rama's coming. In devotional tradition she became the supreme example of bhakti that transcends birth and caste.
nodes.story: Directed by the freed Kabandha, Rama and Lakshmana reached the hermitage of Matanga on the western shore of Lake Pampa. There the ascetic woman Shabari, who had served the sages until they ascended to heaven, rose to greet them and touched their feet. Her teachers had told her to await Rama, and she had gathered the fruits of the Pampa forest for him. She showed the brothers the altar where the sages had worshipped and the lakes they had brought into being by their thought. Then, with Rama's leave, she cast her body into the fire and rose to heaven in radiant form, to the realm of the sages she had served. Later devotional tradition adds that she tasted each berry first so as to offer Rama only the sweetest, and that Rama ate them with love.
symbols: ascetic's bark garments and matted hair
variations: The episode of the pre-tasted berries is a later devotional addition, popular in North Indian bhakti tradition and folk retellings, and is not in Valmiki.
In the Ramcharitmanas Rama teaches Shabari the nine forms of devotion (navadha bhakti) and grants her liberation.
In the Adhyatma Ramayana Shabari herself tells Rama that Sita is in Lanka and advises him to seek Sugriva's friendship.

nodes.name: Jatayu
nodes.description: Jatayu is the aged vulture king, son of Aruna and younger brother of Sampati, and an old friend of Dasharatha. He fought Ravana to rescue the abducted Sita and died in Rama's arms, becoming a model of selfless sacrifice.
nodes.story: Meeting Rama at Panchavati, Jatayu declared himself a friend of his father and offered to guard Sita when the brothers were away. When Ravana flew off with the weeping Sita in his chariot, the old bird rose to challenge him, rebuking him for his crime. In a fierce battle in the sky Jatayu shattered Ravana's chariot, killed the asses that drew it and the charioteer, and broke his bow; but the rakshasa drew his sword and cut off the aged vulture's wings, and Jatayu fell to earth. Searching for Sita, Rama and Lakshmana found him lying in his blood. With his last breaths he told them that Ravana had carried her away to the south, and then he died. Rama, grieving as for a father, cremated him with full rites and offered water for his spirit.
variations: In the Adhyatma Ramayana and the Ramcharitmanas Jatayu praises Rama as Vishnu and attains a divine form and Vishnu's abode.
Local traditions place his fall at several sites, including Lepakshi in Andhra Pradesh and Jatayupara at Chadayamangalam in Kerala.
Valmiki calls him the son of Aruna and Shyeni; some later texts make the vulture brothers sons of Garuda instead.

nodes.name: Sampati
nodes.description: Sampati is the elder brother of Jatayu, a great vulture whose wings were burned by the sun when he shielded his brother in their youth. Wingless on a mountain by the southern sea, he told the searching vanaras that Sita was held in Lanka.
nodes.story: Long ago the two vulture brothers, proud of their strength, raced towards the sun. As Jatayu faltered in the scorching heat, Sampati spread his wings over him; they were burnt away and he fell onto the Vindhya mountains, where the sage Nishakara consoled him and foretold that he would regain his wings by helping Rama's messengers. Ages later the vanaras under Angada, despairing of finding Sita, sat down on the southern shore to fast unto death, lamenting Jatayu's fate. Hearing of his brother's death, Sampati asked to be carried to the sea to offer him water. Then, with his far-seeing vulture's eyes, he saw Sita across the ocean in Lanka and told them so; as he spoke, new wings sprang from his body and he soared away.
nodes.abode: Vindhya mountains by the southern ocean
variations: In Valmiki, Sampati's son Suparshva had seen Ravana carrying off a woman and reported it to his father.
Some retellings compress the story so that Sampati's wings regrow as soon as he offers water to Jatayu.

nodes.name: Kabandha
nodes.description: Kabandha is a headless, gigantic monster of the Krauncha forest whose mouth gaped in his belly and whose single eye burned in his chest. Slain and cremated by Rama and Lakshmana, he was freed from a curse, regained his celestial form and guided Rama towards Sugriva and Shabari.
nodes.story: Wandering the Krauncha forest in search of Sita, Rama and Lakshmana were suddenly seized by a monstrous being with no head or neck: a single eye burned in his chest, a huge mouth gaped in his belly, and his arms stretched a league long to snatch whatever passed. The brothers drew their swords and cut off his arms. Dying, the creature told his story. He had once been radiant and handsome but terrified sages in fearsome forms, until the sage Sthulashira cursed him to keep one; then, proud of a boon of long life from Brahma, he attacked Indra, whose thunderbolt drove his head and thighs into his body. Only when Rama severed his arms and burned him would he be free. Rama cremated him, and from the pyre he rose in shining form, counselling Rama to seek the friendship of Sugriva.
variations: Valmiki has him call himself Danu, son of Shri, of the Danava race; the Mahabharata and the Adhyatma Ramayana make him the gandharva Vishvavasu.
Retellings differ on the curse-giver and on whether the brothers kill him with swords or arrows.

nodes.name: Viradha
nodes.description: Viradha is a monstrous rakshasa of the Dandaka forest who seized Sita soon after the exiles entered the wilderness. Invulnerable to weapons by Brahma's boon, he was buried alive by Rama and Lakshmana and so released from a curse, regaining his true form as the gandharva Tumburu.
nodes.story: As the exiles entered the Dandaka forest, a towering man-eater wearing a tiger skin and carrying a spear hung with the carcasses of lions and elephants rushed on them, snatched up Sita and threatened to drink the brothers' blood. Their arrows only wounded him, for Brahma had made him proof against weapons. He hoisted the two princes onto his shoulders and strode away, until they broke his arms and beat him down. Seeing that no weapon could kill him, Rama had Lakshmana dig a great pit. Viradha then recognised Rama: he was the gandharva Tumburu, cursed by Kubera for neglecting his service out of love for the apsara Rambha, and could be freed only by Rama. He directed the brothers to the hermitage of the sage Sharabhanga and was buried in the pit.
variations: Some later retellings give a different origin for his curse or compress the episode into a brief encounter (as in the Ramcharitmanas).
Valmiki names his parents as Java and Shatahrada.

nodes.name: Shravana Kumara
nodes.description: Shravana Kumara is the popular name of the young ascetic whom Dasharatha accidentally killed while hunting, and whose bereaved parents cursed the king to die grieving for a son. Valmiki leaves the youth unnamed; the name comes from later retellings, in which he became India's ideal of filial devotion.
nodes.story: Valmiki tells the tale through Dasharatha's dying words. In the rainy season the young prince, proud of his skill at shooting by sound, lay in wait by the Sarayu at night. Hearing a gurgling he took for an elephant drinking, he loosed an arrow and heard a human cry. He found a young ascetic with matted hair, pierced through beside his water-pot; the youth said his blind, aged parents were waiting thirsty in their hermitage, and that he was not a brahmin, so the king was spared that sin. When the arrow was drawn out, he died. Dasharatha carried water to the parents and confessed. They performed their son's funeral rites, the father cursed the king to die, like him, grieving for a son, and both entered the pyre. The youth rose to heaven in a celestial body.
symbols: carrying pole with two baskets (kavad) bearing his parents, in later iconography
variations: Valmiki does not name the youth and describes him as the son of a vaishya father and a shudra mother; the name Shravana and the image of him carrying his parents on pilgrimage in two baskets slung from a pole come from later retellings and folk tradition.
Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha retells the hunting accident briefly and without the later name.

nodes.name: Hanuman
nodes.description: The mighty vanara son of the Wind god Vayu and Anjana (and, as her husband, of the vanara chief Kesari), minister to Sugriva and the foremost messenger and devotee of Rama. In the Valmiki Ramayana he leaps the ocean to find Sita, burns Lanka and fetches the healing herbs that revive Lakshmana. Later tradition venerates him as a chiranjivi (deathless one), as an avatar of Shiva (Rudra), and as the embodiment of strength, learning, celibacy and selfless devotion.
nodes.story: When the southern search party despaired on the ocean shore, the aged Jambavan reminded Hanuman of his birth from the Wind and of the powers he had forgotten. Swelling to mountainous size, Hanuman pressed Mount Mahendra until its springs gushed, then sprang into the sky. Over the sea the golden mountain Mainaka rose to offer him rest; he touched it courteously and flew on. Surasa, mother of the nagas, blocked his path with gaping jaws; he grew vast, then shrank to the size of a thumb, darted in and out of her mouth, and won her blessing. The shadow-seizing Simhika dragged him down by his shadow, and he tore her apart from within. Alighting on Mount Lamba, he shrank to the size of a cat and slipped into Lanka at dusk to search for Sita.
symbols: Dronagiri mountain bearing the Sanjivani herb, held aloft
chest opened to reveal Rama and Sita
vermilion (sindoor) and red or saffron complexion
weapons: immense strength and power to change size at will
nodes.abode: Kishkindha; as a chiranjivi, Gandhamadana mountain (and, in devotion, wherever Rama's name is sung)
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda (childhood and boons)
variations: Shiva Purana and much later tradition: Hanuman is an avatar of Shiva (Rudra), Vayu carrying Shiva's energy into Anjana's womb.
Some later and regional tellings link his birth to Rama's: a bird carried a portion of Dasharatha's sacred payasa to Anjana, who ate it and conceived.
The infant leap at the Sun, Indra's vajra and the gods' boons appear in the Uttara Kanda, which many scholars regard as a later layer of the Valmiki text.
Madhva (Dvaita) tradition: Hanuman is the first manifestation of Vayu (Mukhyaprana), followed by Bhima and by Madhvacharya himself.
Jain Paumacariya (Vimalasuri): Hanuman is a vidyadhara prince, son of Pavanamjaya and Anjanasundari, who marries several wives and finally renounces the world as a Jain monk.
Thai Ramakien and other Southeast Asian versions: Hanuman is a playful, amorous hero with wives, including the mermaid Suvannamaccha, mother of his son Macchanu.
Pan-Indian devotion holds him a lifelong brahmachari; the Makardhvaja and Ahiravana (Mahiravana) episodes come from later regional Ramayanas such as the Krittivasi.
The image of Hanuman tearing open his chest to show Rama and Sita derives from later devotional legend about Sita's pearl necklace, not from Valmiki.

nodes.name: Anjana
nodes.description: The mother of Hanuman and wife of the vanara chief Kesari. In the Valmiki Ramayana she was once the apsara Punjikasthala, born as a vanari through a curse, who conceived Hanuman through the Wind god Vayu. Hills at Anjaneri (near Nashik) and Anjanadri (near Hampi) are revered locally as her home and Hanuman's birthplace.
nodes.story: Anjana was once Punjikasthala, a celebrated apsara, who through a curse was born on earth as a vanari, daughter of the vanara Kunjara, and became the wife of Kesari. One day, taking a lovely human form, she wandered on a mountain peak in fine garments and garlands, glowing like a rain-cloud touched by lightning. The Wind god Vayu, captivated, gently stirred her robe and embraced her with his subtle, invisible form. Alarmed, she cried out, asking who dared violate her vow of fidelity. Vayu reassured her that her chastity was untouched: he had entered her only through his mind and energy, and she would bear a son equal to him in speed and leaping, mighty and wise. In a mountain cave she gave birth to Hanuman.
nodes.abode: Mountain home of Kesari; local traditions name Anjaneri (Nashik) or Anjanadri (Hampi)
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda (Jambavan's account of Hanuman's birth)
variations: Shiva Purana and Shaiva tradition: Anjana performed austerities to Shiva, whose energy Vayu placed in her womb, so that Hanuman is Rudra's avatar.
Some regional tellings make Anjana the daughter of the sage Gautama and Ahalya.
Some later accounts have her conceive after eating a portion of Dasharatha's sacred payasa dropped by a bird.
Jain Paumacariya: Anjanasundari, a vidyadhara princess wrongly banished by her husband Pavanamjaya, gives birth to Hanuman in exile; her story is a major Jain narrative in its own right.

nodes.name: Kesari
nodes.description: A powerful vanara chief, husband of Anjana and father of Hanuman, who is called Kesarinandana, son of Kesari, after him. Valmiki credits him with slaying the demon Shambasadana at Gokarna and lists him among the vanara leaders who fought for Rama at Lanka.
nodes.story: Seeking to win Sita's trust in the ashoka grove, Hanuman introduced himself through his father. He told her of Kesari, a vanara lord who dwelt on Malyavan, finest of mountains, and who once journeyed to sacred Gokarna by the sea. There, at the bidding of the divine sages, he fought and slew Shambasadana, a demon who had been tormenting the holy men at that shrine. Hanuman declared that he himself had been born in Kesari's field of the Wind god, and was known throughout the world by his own deeds as Hanuman. When Rama's army later marched on Lanka, Kesari himself was counted among the great vanara chiefs leading their troops, and Ravana's spies pointed him out among the host arrayed before the city.
weapons: trees and rocks, as a vanara warrior
nodes.abode: Mount Malyavan (Sundara Kanda); Mount Sumeru (Uttara Kanda)
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda (Hanuman's self-introduction to Sita)
variations: Popular tradition names Kesari as a son of Brihaspati; this is not found in Valmiki.
Jain Paumacariya replaces him with the vidyadhara prince Pavanamjaya as Hanuman's father.

nodes.name: Sugriva
nodes.description: The vanara king of Kishkindha, son of the Sun god Surya and younger brother of Vali. Exiled by Vali, he allied with Rama by a vow sworn before fire: Rama slew Vali and restored his throne, and Sugriva sent the vanara hosts to find Sita and fight at Lanka.
nodes.story: Driven out by his brother Vali and robbed of his wife Ruma, Sugriva hid on Mount Rishyamuka, the one place Vali dared not enter because of the sage Matanga's curse. When two bow-bearing princes approached, he sent Hanuman to learn who they were. Hanuman brought Rama and Lakshmana to him, and before a kindled fire Rama and Sugriva swore friendship: Rama would kill Vali, and Sugriva would search out Sita. Sugriva showed Rama the jewels Sita had dropped from Ravana's chariot, and Rama wept. To reassure Sugriva, Rama pierced seven sala trees with a single arrow. Yet once crowned in Kishkindha, Sugriva lost himself in pleasures through the rainy season, until Lakshmana's fury, softened by Tara's words, roused him to summon vanaras from every quarter of the earth.
symbols: golden garland of Kishkindha's kings (inherited from Vali)
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda (birth from Surya)
Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda (birth of Vali and Sugriva from Riksharaja)
variations: Uttara Kanda: Vali and Sugriva are born to the vanara Riksharaja, who had been transformed into a woman; Indra fathered Vali and Surya fathered Sugriva.
Kamba Ramayanam and Ramcharitmanas soften Sugriva's lapse and stress his repentance and devotion to Rama.
In the Jain Paumacariya Sugriva is a vidyadhara king whose throne is usurped by an impostor, Sahasagati, whom Rama defeats.

nodes.name: Vali
nodes.description: The mighty vanara king of Kishkindha, son of Indra, husband of Tara and father of Angada. Estranged from his brother Sugriva after a misunderstanding in the demon Mayavi's cave, he was slain by Rama, an act Valmiki presents as justice yet leaves open to Vali's own sharp protest.
nodes.story: Challenged by Sugriva at the gates of Kishkindha, Vali brushed aside Tara's warning that his brother now had a powerful ally. In the first fight Rama could not tell the brothers apart and held back; the second time Sugriva wore a flowering creeper so that Rama could know him. As the brothers grappled, Rama shot Vali in the chest from behind a tree. Dying, Vali reproached Rama for striking unseen a warrior who had done him no wrong. Rama answered that the earth belonged to the Ikshvakus, and that Vali, by taking his younger brother's wife, had committed a crime deserving death. Vali accepted the judgement, entrusted Angada and Tara to Sugriva and Rama, and gave Sugriva his golden garland, Indra's gift, before he died.
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda (birth from Indra)
Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda (Vali and Ravana)
variations: Later retellings add a boon by which Vali drew half the strength of anyone who faced him, explaining why Rama shot from hiding; Valmiki does not mention it.
Uttara Kanda: Vali seized Ravana, who had come to challenge him, tucked him under his arm while performing his evening rites at the four oceans, and then made friends with him.
A popular tradition holds that Vali was reborn as the hunter Jara, whose arrow ended Krishna's earthly life, balancing Rama's hidden shot.
Jain Paumacariya: Vali defeats Ravana but then renounces kingship to become an ascetic; he is not killed by Rama.
Kamba Ramayanam gives Vali a moving death scene in which he recognises Rama's divinity and asks his forgiveness.

nodes.name: Tara (queen of Kishkindha)
nodes.description: The wise queen of Kishkindha, daughter of the vanara physician Sushena, wife of Vali and mother of Angada, and after Vali's death the consort of Sugriva. Famed for political insight, she is counted among the Panchakanya, the five exemplary women whose names are recited at dawn.
nodes.story: When Sugriva roared a second challenge at the gates of Kishkindha, Tara held her husband back. A defeated foe, she reasoned, would not return so boldly without a mighty protector, and she reported what Angada had learned from spies: Sugriva had allied himself with Rama, prince of Ayodhya. She urged Vali to make peace, name Sugriva his heir and befriend Rama. Proud and unafraid, Vali went out and fell to Rama's arrow. Tara ran to the battlefield and lamented over his body with a grief that moved even the victors. Later, when Lakshmana stormed into Kishkindha, furious at Sugriva's delay, it was Tara, calm and dignified, who went out to meet him, soothed his anger with measured words and saved the kingdom.
variations: Some later traditions say Tara emerged from the churning of the ocean and was claimed by Vali.
Adhyatma Ramayana: Rama consoles the grieving Tara with teaching on the Self, and she attains wisdom.
Some regional tellings have Tara curse Rama that he too would lose Sita soon after regaining her.
She is named with Ahalya, Draupadi, Sita (or Kunti) and Mandodari in the Panchakanya verse.

nodes.name: Ruma
nodes.description: The wife of Sugriva, seized by Vali when he drove his brother into exile. Her abduction parallels Sita's and is the wrong Rama cites to justify slaying Vali; she was restored to Sugriva when he became king.
nodes.story: Ruma was the beloved wife of Sugriva. When Vali, believing his brother had sealed him inside the cave of the demon Mayavi to seize the throne, returned victorious and drove Sugriva into exile, he also took Ruma for himself. Sugriva fled to Mount Rishyamuka with Hanuman and a few loyal ministers, grieving for his lost wife and kingdom. When he met Rama, whose own wife had been carried off by Ravana, the shared sorrow of two husbands torn from their wives became the bond of their alliance. As Vali lay dying, Rama named the seizure of Ruma, his younger brother's wife, as the crime that justified his punishment. With Vali dead, Sugriva was crowned in Kishkindha and Ruma was restored to his side.
variations: Some retellings name her father as the vanara Panasa; Valmiki gives few details of her lineage.

nodes.name: Angada
nodes.description: The son of Vali and Tara, made crown prince of Kishkindha by Sugriva at Rama's wish. He led the southern search party that included Hanuman and Jambavan, and served as Rama's envoy to Ravana's court before the war.
nodes.story: Before the final assault on Lanka, Rama chose Angada as his envoy. Leaping over the walls, the young prince entered Ravana's court and delivered Rama's message: give back Sita or perish with your whole race. Ravana ordered him seized; four rakshasas grabbed his arms, but Angada sprang up to the palace roof carrying them, shook them off to fall to the ground, shattered the rooftop pinnacle with his foot and flew back to Rama. Later retellings expand the scene: in the Ramcharitmanas and other versions, Angada plants his foot in the assembly and dares any warrior to shift it. One champion after another fails, and when Ravana himself bends down to try, Angada withdraws his foot and tells him to clasp Rama's feet instead.
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (embassy to Ravana)
variations: The famous planted-foot challenge (Angad ka pair) belongs to the Ramcharitmanas and other later retellings, not to Valmiki.
In the Kishkindha Kanda, despairing of finding Sita within Sugriva's deadline, Angada resolves to fast to death until Sampati's news revives the party.

nodes.name: Jambavan
nodes.description: The ancient and wise king of the rikshas (bears), created by Brahma, who counselled Sugriva's army and reminded Hanuman of his forgotten powers. His life spans the ages: in the Puranas and Harivamsha he fights Krishna over the Syamantaka jewel and gives him his daughter Jambavati in marriage.
