nodes.story: Indra feared Vishvamitra's austerities and sent the apsara Menaka to distract him. Their union produced a daughter, whom Menaka left on the banks of the Malini. Shakunta birds sheltered the infant until the sage Kanva found her, and he named her Shakuntala after them. She grew up in his hermitage and married King Dushyanta. When she brought their son to court, the king claimed not to know her. Shakuntala did not beg. She told him that a wife is half of a man, that a son is himself reborn, and that truth outweighs a thousand horse sacrifices. If he would not accept her, she said, her son would still rule the earth. A heavenly voice confirmed her words. In Kalidasa's version the sage Durvasa, ignored by the lovesick girl, curses her to be forgotten by the one she is thinking of. Only the lost ring can break the curse.
nodes.abode: Kanva's hermitage on the Malini river
variations: The Shatapatha Brahmana calls her an apsaras who conceived Bharata at Nadapit.
Durvasa's curse, the lost ring and the reunion in Marica's heavenly hermitage come from Kalidasa. They are not in the Mahabharata, where Dushyanta knowingly denies her.
The Padma Purana version is close to Kalidasa's play.

nodes.name: Bharata (son of Dushyanta)
nodes.description: Son of Dushyanta and Shakuntala, a universal emperor after whom the Bharata lineage (and, in many texts, Bharatavarsha, India) is named. The Shatapatha and Aitareya Brahmanas praise Bharata Dauhshanti for his countless horse sacrifices. He is the ancestor of Kuru and the Pandavas.
nodes.story: Raised in Kanva's hermitage, Shakuntala's son was so strong as a child that he tied lions, tigers and elephants to the trees around the ashram and rode on their backs. The hermits called him Sarvadamana, 'tamer of all'. In Kalidasa's play he forces open the mouth of a lion cub to count its teeth. After Dushyanta accepted him, he was named Bharata and in time became a chakravartin. The Brahmanas say he performed horse sacrifices beside the Ganga and the Yamuna, and that no king before or after could match his deeds, 'as no mortal can touch the sky with his arms'. The Puranas add a sad story. Bharata's queens killed their own sons because he said the children did not look like him. With his line in danger, he held a sacrifice to the Maruts, and they gave him Bharadvaja as an adopted heir.
nodes.abode: The Paurava capital (later tradition places it at Hastinapura)
variations: Many Puranas (e.g. the Bhagavata, Canto 5) say Bharatavarsha is named after a different Bharata, the son of Rishabha. Others name it after Dushyanta's son.
In the Mahabharata his son is Bhumanyu, and the line continues from father to son. The Puranas insert the adopted Bharadvaja (Vitatha).
The Aitareya Brahmana says the sage Dirghatamas Mamateya performed his great consecration (aindra mahabhisheka).

nodes.name: Kuru
nodes.description: Paurava king, son of Samvarana and Tapati (daughter of Surya). The Kuru dynasty and the sacred field of Kurukshetra are named after him. He is the ancestor of Pratipa, Shantanu, and so of both the Kauravas and the Pandavas.
nodes.story: King Kuru went to a stretch of land and began to plough it himself with a golden plough, drawn by Shiva's bull and Yama's buffalo. Indra came down and asked what he was doing. Kuru answered that he was cultivating the eight virtues there: austerity, truth, forgiveness, compassion, purity, charity, yoga and celibacy. Indra laughed and went away. But Kuru kept ploughing day after day. At last Indra came back and offered him a boon. Kuru asked that anyone who died on that ground, whether fasting or fighting bravely, would go straight to heaven. Indra granted it. The field became Kurukshetra, the 'field of Kuru', also called Dharmakshetra, the field of dharma. Generations later his descendants would fight the great war there. The Mahabharata remembers his line simply as the Kurus.
variations: The detailed story of ploughing with Shiva's bull and Yama's buffalo is in the Vamana Purana. The Mahabharata tells the origin of Kurukshetra more briefly.
The Kurus as a people appear in late Vedic literature (Kuru-Panchala). The individual king Kuru is known from the epic and the Puranas.

nodes.name: Pratipa
nodes.description: A righteous Kuru king of the Lunar dynasty and father of Devapi, Bahlika and Shantanu. His encounter with the river goddess Ganga sets in motion the birth of Bhishma and the whole Kuru story of the Mahabharata.
nodes.story: Old King Pratipa was sitting in meditation on the bank of the Ganga when a radiant woman rose from the water and sat down on his right thigh, asking him to take her as his wife. Pratipa, bound by dharma, gently refused: the right thigh, he explained, is the seat of a daughter or daughter-in-law, while the left belongs to a wife. He therefore promised her to his future son. The woman was Ganga herself, and she agreed. When Shantanu was born to the aged Pratipa and his queen, the king told him that a celestial woman would one day come to him, and that he should marry her without asking who she was. Having crowned Shantanu, Pratipa retired to the forest, leaving the stage set for the birth of Bhishma.
variations: Devapi, Pratipa's eldest son, renounced the throne because of a skin disease, which is why the younger Shantanu became king; the Rig Veda (10.98) knows a Devapi and a Shantanu, whose link to the epic princes is debated.

nodes.name: Shantanu
nodes.description: King of Hastinapura, son of Pratipa and husband first of the river goddess Ganga and then of the fisherwoman Satyavati. He was the father of Bhishma, Chitrangada and Vichitravirya, and it was said that whatever old thing he touched became young again.
nodes.story: Shantanu married a mysterious woman on the bank of the Ganga after promising never to question or oppose her. Seven times she bore him a son, and seven times she carried the infant to the river and drowned it, laughing. Bound by his word, Shantanu kept silent, but when she lifted the eighth child he finally cried out. She revealed herself as Ganga: the babies were the eight Vasus, cursed by Vashistha to be born as men, and she had freed them at once. The eighth, Devavrata, would live long on earth. Years later Shantanu fell in love with Satyavati, but her father demanded that her son inherit the throne. Devavrata renounced both kingship and marriage for his father's sake, and the grateful Shantanu gave him the boon of choosing the hour of his own death.
variations: In the Mahabharata Shantanu is the rebirth of King Mahabhisha, cursed by Brahma for gazing at Ganga in the divine assembly.
The Rig Veda's Shantanu, for whom his brother Devapi performs a rain rite, is usually identified with the epic king, but the identification is not certain.

nodes.name: Bhishma
nodes.description: Son of Shantanu and Ganga, the incarnation of one of the eight Vasus, famed for his terrible vow of lifelong celibacy and renunciation of the throne. The grandsire of both Kauravas and Pandavas, he commanded the Kaurava army for the first ten days of the Kurukshetra war and, lying on a bed of arrows, taught Yudhishthira the dharma of kings.
nodes.story: When King Shantanu pined for the fisher-maiden Satyavati, the prince Devavrata went to her father himself. The fisher chief asked that Satyavati's son become king. Devavrata renounced the throne; and when the chief worried that Devavrata's own sons might one day claim it, the prince swore before the assembled elders never to marry or father children. The gods rained flowers and a voice cried 'Bhishma!', the one of the terrible vow. Decades later, as commander of the Kaurava host, he was unbeatable until he told the Pandavas how he could be brought down: he would not fight Shikhandi, who had been born a woman. With Shikhandi before him, Arjuna's arrows covered him so thickly that he fell without touching the ground. Holding off death by his father's boon, he lay on that bed of arrows until the winter solstice.
nodes.vahana: silver chariot with a palm-tree banner
variations: The Mahabharata names the Vasu born as Bhishma Dyaus, the one who stole Vashistha's cow Nandini; later retellings often call him Prabhasa.
The Bhishma-stava-raja, his hymn to Krishna on the bed of arrows (Shanti Parva), and the Vishnu Sahasranama recited to Yudhishthira (Anushasana Parva) are central to Vaishnava devotion.

nodes.name: Satyavati
nodes.description: Daughter of King Uparichara Vasu, born from a fish (the cursed apsara Adrika) and raised by a fisher chief. Mother of Vyasa by the sage Parashara and of Chitrangada and Vichitravirya by King Shantanu, she became the matriarch who secured the continuation of the Kuru line.
nodes.story: As a young woman Satyavati ferried travellers across the Yamuna, and her body smelled of fish. One day the sage Parashara stepped into her boat and desired her. She hesitated, fearing for her honour; he wrapped the island in mist, promised that she would remain a maiden, and granted her a fragrance that could be smelled for a yojana. On an island in the river she bore Krishna Dvaipayana, Vyasa, who promised to come whenever she called him. Later she became the queen of Shantanu. When her son Vichitravirya died childless, the widowed Satyavati first asked Bhishma to father heirs, and when he refused to break his vow, she summoned Vyasa to beget sons on the widowed queens. From that niyoga came Dhritarashtra, Pandu and Vidura.
variations: After Pandu's death Satyavati retired to the forest with her daughters-in-law Ambika and Ambalika, foreseeing the ruin of the dynasty.

nodes.name: Chitrangada (son of Shantanu)
nodes.description: Elder son of Shantanu and Satyavati, who became king of Hastinapura after his father's death. He died young in a duel with a Gandharva of the same name; he is distinct from Chitrangada, the princess of Manipura who married Arjuna.
nodes.story: When Shantanu died, Bhishma, true to his vow, placed Satyavati's elder son Chitrangada on the throne of Hastinapura. The young king was a mighty warrior and proud of it, and he held all other men to be his inferiors. A king of the Gandharvas, who also bore the name Chitrangada, came to challenge him, unwilling that a mortal should share his name. The two fought for three years on the field of Kurukshetra, beside the river Sarasvati, in a fierce duel of magic and arms. In the end the Gandharva, more skilled in illusion, killed the Kuru prince. Bhishma performed his funeral rites and crowned the younger brother Vichitravirya, still a boy, ruling in his name.

nodes.name: Vichitravirya
nodes.description: Younger son of Shantanu and Satyavati, king of Hastinapura after his brother Chitrangada. He married Ambika and Ambalika, the princesses of Kashi won for him by Bhishma, but died childless; Dhritarashtra and Pandu were born to his widows by niyoga and counted as his legal sons.
nodes.story: Vichitravirya was still a boy when he became king, and Bhishma ruled for him. When he came of age, Bhishma heard that the king of Kashi was holding a svayamvara for his three daughters. He drove there alone, seized the princesses Amba, Ambika and Ambalika, and defeated all the assembled kings who tried to stop him. Amba confessed that her heart belonged to King Shalva and was sent to him, but Ambika and Ambalika were married to Vichitravirya. The young king lived for seven years in pleasure with his lovely wives, until he wasted away from consumption. He died without a son, leaving the Kuru throne empty and Satyavati desperate for an heir.

nodes.name: Amba
nodes.description: Eldest princess of Kashi, abducted by Bhishma for Vichitravirya and then rejected by her beloved King Shalva. Blaming Bhishma for her ruin, she performed austerities to destroy him and was reborn as Shikhandi, before whom Bhishma laid down his arms.
nodes.story: Amba told Bhishma she had already chosen King Shalva, so he let her go. But Shalva refused her: she had been won by another man in front of all the kings. Returning to Hastinapura, she found Bhishma bound by his vow and unable to marry her. With nowhere to go, she turned her grief into a single purpose: the death of Bhishma. On her behalf Bhishma's own teacher Parashurama fought him for days, but could not win. Amba then undertook fierce austerities, fasting and standing in the water, until Shiva appeared and promised that in another life she would kill Bhishma. Unable to wait, she built a pyre on the bank of the Yamuna and entered it. She was reborn as the daughter of King Drupada, who became the warrior Shikhandi.
variations: A widespread retelling adds that Skanda gave her a garland of ever-fresh lotuses, promising that whoever wore it would kill Bhishma; she hung it on Drupada's gate, where Shikhandi later put it on.

nodes.name: Ambika
nodes.description: Second princess of Kashi and senior wife of Vichitravirya. By niyoga with Vyasa she became the mother of the blind Dhritarashtra.
nodes.story: When Vichitravirya died childless, Satyavati summoned her son Vyasa to raise heirs on his brother's widows. The sage came as he was, dark-skinned, his hair matted, his body smelling of the forest after long austerity. When he entered Ambika's chamber at night, she was so frightened by his fierce look that she shut her eyes and kept them closed. Vyasa told Satyavati that the son would be as strong as ten thousand elephants but, because of his mother's fault, born blind. So Dhritarashtra came into the world. Asked to go to Vyasa a second time, Ambika could not bear it and sent one of her maids, adorned in her own clothes, in her place; that maid bore the wise Vidura.

nodes.name: Ambalika
nodes.description: Youngest princess of Kashi and junior wife of Vichitravirya. By niyoga with Vyasa she became the mother of Pandu, the father of the Pandavas.
nodes.story: After the birth of the blind Dhritarashtra, Satyavati knew that a blind man could not easily rule, and she sent Vyasa to her second widowed daughter-in-law, Ambalika. Ambalika had been warned not to shut her eyes as her sister had done. She kept them open, but when she saw the terrifying ascetic she turned pale with fear. Vyasa said that because she had grown pale, her son would be pale as well, and he would be called Pandu, the pale one. The child was born healthy and brave, and although pale of skin he grew into a great archer and conqueror. Through him Ambalika became the grandmother of the five Pandavas.

nodes.name: Dhritarashtra
nodes.description: The blind elder son of Vichitravirya's widow Ambika, fathered by Vyasa through niyoga, and king of Hastinapura. Husband of Gandhari and father of Duryodhana and the hundred Kauravas, his inability to restrain his sons led to the Kurukshetra war.
nodes.story: Passed over for the throne because of his blindness, Dhritarashtra came to rule after his brother Pandu withdrew to the forest. He loved his son Duryodhana beyond reason. When Duryodhana and Shakuni planned the dice game, Vidura warned him again and again, but the king allowed it, and he stayed silent while Draupadi was dragged into the hall. Only when jackals howled and evil omens filled the palace did he grant her boons and free the Pandavas. Before the war, Sanjaya was given divine sight to narrate the battle to him, and so he heard of the deaths of all his sons. Afterwards, embracing an iron figure in place of Bhima, he crushed it in his grief. He ended his days in the forest with Gandhari and Kunti, dying in a forest fire.
variations: A Dhritarashtra Vaichitravirya appears in the Kathaka Samhita of the Black Yajur Veda in a dispute with the sage Vaka Dalbhya; whether he is the epic king is debated.
Before the war, in some recensions, Krishna gives him sight for a moment so he can behold the cosmic form.

nodes.name: Gandhari
nodes.description: Princess of Gandhara, daughter of King Subala and sister of Shakuni, who blindfolded herself for life on learning that her husband Dhritarashtra was blind. Mother of Duryodhana, the hundred Kauravas and Dushala, she is remembered for her devotion, her righteous counsel and her curse on Krishna.
nodes.story: Pleased by her service, Vyasa granted Gandhari a boon of a hundred sons. After two years of pregnancy she heard that Kunti had already borne a son, and in anguish she struck her womb, delivering a hard lump of flesh. Vyasa had it sprinkled with water and divided into a hundred and one pieces, each kept in a pot of ghee; from them came Duryodhana, his brothers and a daughter, Dushala. Though she often told Duryodhana 'where there is dharma, there is victory', he never listened. After the war, standing over the field of the dead, she turned her grief on Krishna, who could have stopped the slaughter. She cursed him that in thirty-six years his own clan would destroy itself and he would die alone. Krishna accepted the curse with a smile.
variations: Some later retellings say her boon of a hundred sons came from Shiva rather than Vyasa.
A popular tale, absent from the Critical Edition, says she removed her blindfold to make Duryodhana's body invulnerable with her gaze, all but his thighs, which he had covered.

nodes.name: Pandu
nodes.description: Son of Ambalika by Vyasa through niyoga, king of Hastinapura and a great conqueror. Cursed by the sage Kindama to die if he ever embraced a woman in love, he withdrew to the forest, where his wives Kunti and Madri bore the five Pandavas by invoking the gods.
nodes.story: Out hunting in the forest, Pandu shot a stag and its doe who were mating. The stag was the sage Kindama, who had taken that form to make love to his wife. Dying, he cursed the king: the day Pandu lay with a woman in desire, he too would die. Heartbroken, Pandu gave up his kingdom and lived as an ascetic in the Himalayas with Kunti and Madri. Longing for sons, he learned that Kunti could summon any god with a mantra, and so the five Pandavas were born, his legal sons. Years later, one spring day, overcome by Madri's beauty, Pandu embraced her against her pleading, and died in that moment as the curse had foretold. Madri followed him onto his funeral pyre.
nodes.abode: Hastinapura; later the forest of Shatashringa

nodes.name: Kunti (Pritha)
nodes.description: Daughter of the Yadava Shura (Shurasena), sister of Vasudeva and aunt of Krishna, given in adoption to King Kuntibhoja, from whom she took her name. First wife of Pandu, she bore Karna by Surya before marriage and Yudhishthira, Bhima and Arjuna by Dharma, Vayu and Indra.
nodes.story: As a young girl in Kuntibhoja's house, Pritha served the irascible sage Durvasa so faithfully that he taught her a mantra to call any god and receive a son from him. Curious, she tried it on the rising Sun. Surya appeared and, despite her fear, gave her a son born wearing golden armour and earrings. Unmarried and ashamed, she placed the baby in a basket and set him adrift on the river; he became Karna. Years later, as Pandu's widow, she raised her sons and Madri's twins through exile, the burning of the lac house and the forest years. On the eve of war she went to Karna and revealed that he was her firstborn. He would not change sides, but promised that she would still have five sons: either he or Arjuna would survive.
variations: Her prayer to Krishna asking for adversity, so that she might always remember him, is found in the Bhagavata Purana (Canto 1) rather than the Mahabharata.
Only after the war, at the water rites, did she reveal Karna's birth to the Pandavas.

nodes.name: Madri
nodes.description: Princess of Madra, sister of King Shalya and second wife of Pandu. Using Kunti's mantra she invoked the twin Ashvins and bore Nakula and Sahadeva; she ascended Pandu's funeral pyre after his death.
nodes.story: Bhishma obtained Madri for Pandu by paying a rich bride-price to her brother Shalya, as was the custom of the Madra people. When Kunti had borne three sons by the gods, Madri asked Pandu to persuade Kunti to share her mantra. Kunti agreed to let her use it once. Madri cleverly called on the Ashvins, the twin gods, and bore twins, Nakula and Sahadeva. Kunti, a little alarmed, refused to give her a second chance. On a spring day in the forest Pandu, overcome with desire, seized Madri despite her protests, and died in her arms by Kindama's curse. Holding herself responsible and wishing to follow him, Madri entrusted her sons to Kunti and entered Pandu's funeral pyre.

nodes.name: Vidura
nodes.description: Half-brother of Dhritarashtra and Pandu, born to a maid of the Kuru queens by Vyasa through niyoga, and chief minister of Hastinapura. The incarnation of Dharma (Yama), he was renowned for wisdom and impartial counsel, preserved in the Vidura Niti.
nodes.story: Long ago the sage Mandavya was wrongly impaled as a thief. When he later asked Dharma, the god of justice, why he had suffered, Dharma said that as a child he had pierced an insect with a blade of grass. Outraged that a child's act should be punished so harshly, Mandavya cursed Dharma to be born as a man of a low mother. So Dharma became Vidura, son of Vyasa and a palace maid. Though barred from the throne by birth, he was the conscience of the court. He warned Yudhishthira of the lac house in a riddle only he understood, and pleaded with Dhritarashtra to stop the dice game. At the end of his life, meeting Yudhishthira in the forest, he fixed his gaze on him and passed his life-breath into his nephew.
variations: The Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva) records his night-long advice to Dhritarashtra.
The Bhagavata Purana tells of his pilgrimage during the war and his conversations with Uddhava and the sage Maitreya.

nodes.name: Yudhishthira
nodes.description: Eldest of the Pandavas, son of Kunti by Dharma (Yama) and legal son of Pandu, famed for his truthfulness and devotion to dharma. His weakness for dice cost the Pandavas their kingdom and led to thirteen years of exile; after the Kurukshetra war he ruled Hastinapura for thirty-six years.
nodes.story: Near the end of the forest exile, the thirsty Pandavas came one by one to a lake where an unseen voice said, 'Answer my questions before you drink.' Each brother ignored it, drank and fell dead. When Yudhishthira arrived, a Yaksha appeared and put riddles to him: What is swifter than the wind? The mind. What is the greatest wonder? That every day creatures go to death, yet the living think they will live forever. Satisfied, the Yaksha offered to revive one brother. Yudhishthira chose Nakula, so that Madri too would have a living son, as Kunti did. Moved by this impartiality, the Yaksha revealed himself as Dharma, Yudhishthira's own father, restored all four brothers and granted him boons, including that the Pandavas would pass their final year in disguise unrecognised.
symbols: chariot that floated above the ground
variations: His one lie, 'Ashwatthama is dead', spoken to Drona while muttering 'the elephant', made his chariot, which had always floated above the earth, touch the ground.
At the end of the Mahaprasthana he refused to enter heaven without the faithful dog that had followed him, which was Dharma in disguise.

nodes.name: Bhima
nodes.description: Second of the Pandavas, son of Kunti by the wind god Vayu and legal son of Pandu, renowned for his immense strength, appetite and mastery of the mace. He killed the rakshasas Hidimba and Baka, King Jarasandha, Kichaka, Dushasana and finally Duryodhana, fulfilling the vows he swore in the dice hall.
nodes.story: Jealous of Bhima's strength, the young Duryodhana poisoned his food during a festival at Pramanakoti on the Ganga, tied him up with creepers while he slept, and threw him into the river. Bhima sank down to the realm of the Nagas, where the serpents bit him; their venom destroyed the poison in his body, and he woke and began crushing them. The serpents ran to their king Vasuki. There the Naga elder Aryaka, a kinsman of Kunti's family, recognised the boy, and Vasuki had him drink from bowls of a strengthening elixir, each giving the strength of a thousand elephants. Bhima drank eight bowls, slept for eight days, and returned to his anxious mother and brothers stronger than ever, but warned by Vidura to keep silent about Duryodhana's plot.
variations: In the Vana Parva he meets his half-brother Hanuman, also a son of Vayu, while fetching Saugandhika flowers for Draupadi, and cannot lift the old monkey's tail.
His blow to Duryodhana's thighs, against the rules of mace combat, was prompted by Krishna and angered Balarama.

nodes.name: Arjuna
nodes.description: Third of the Pandavas, son of Kunti by Indra and legal son of Pandu, the peerless archer and wielder of the Gandiva bow. The incarnation of the sage Nara and the dearest friend of Krishna, he received the Bhagavad Gita on the field of Kurukshetra and killed Bhishma, Karna and Jayadratha in the war.
nodes.story: During the exile, Arjuna went to the Himalayas to win divine weapons and performed austerities so fierce that the sages begged Shiva to intervene. A boar charged at him; Arjuna shot it, and at the same instant a wild Kirata hunter shot it too. They quarrelled over the kill. Arjuna emptied his inexhaustible quivers at the hunter, who swallowed the arrows and snatched the Gandiva from his hands. They wrestled until Arjuna fell senseless. Coming to, he worshipped a clay image of Shiva with a garland, and saw the garland appear on the hunter's head. Recognising the god, he fell at his feet. Delighted by his courage, Shiva appeared with Parvati and gave him the Pashupata weapon, and soon after the guardians of the directions gave him their astras.
nodes.vahana: chariot with white horses and Hanuman's banner, driven by Krishna
nodes.abode: Indraprastha; Amaravati during his stay in Indra's heaven
variations: During the war Krishna's vision of the cosmic form and the teaching of the Gita (Bhishma Parva) are given to Arjuna alone.
In the Ashvamedhika Parva he is killed by his son Babruvahana and revived by Ulupi with a Naga gem, ending the Vasus' curse for Bhishma's death.
Bharavi's Kiratarjuniya (6th century CE) is the classic poetic retelling of the Kirata episode.

nodes.name: Nakula
nodes.description: Fourth of the Pandavas and elder of the twins, son of Madri by the Ashvins and legal son of Pandu. Considered the handsomest man of his age, he was a master swordsman and an expert in the care and training of horses.
nodes.story: When the Pandavas were to live their thirteenth year in disguise at the court of King Virata, Nakula chose the role he knew best: he became Granthika, keeper of the king's horses, promising that no horse under his care would ever be vicious or fall sick. His skill kept him unrecognised while his brothers served elsewhere in the palace. Nakula also has a quiet but decisive place in the story of the Yaksha at the enchanted lake. Offered the life of one brother, Yudhishthira chose him over the mighty Bhima and Arjuna, reasoning that Kunti already had a surviving son and that Madri too deserved one. That choice, proof of Yudhishthira's even-handed dharma, persuaded the god to revive all four brothers.
variations: Besides Draupadi, he married Karenumati, a princess of Chedi, by whom he had a son Niramitra.

nodes.name: Sahadeva
nodes.description: Youngest of the Pandavas, twin of Nakula, son of Madri by the Ashvins and legal son of Pandu. Wise and learned, he was skilled in statecraft and astronomy, and he killed Shakuni, the architect of the dice game, on the last day of the war.
nodes.story: In the dice hall at Hastinapura, as Draupadi was insulted before the Kuru elders, each of the Pandavas swore a vow of vengeance. Bhima vowed to kill Duryodhana and Dushasana, Arjuna to kill Karna, and the quiet Sahadeva swore that he would slay Shakuni, the gambler whose loaded throws had stripped them of everything. For thirteen years he carried that vow through the forest and through his disguise as Tantipala, keeper of King Virata's cattle. On the eighteenth day of the Kurukshetra war, as the Kaurava army was collapsing, Sahadeva sought out Shakuni, reminded him of the dice hall, and cut off his head with a broad-headed arrow, keeping his word.
variations: He also married Vijaya, a daughter of the Madra king Dyutimat, by whom he had a son Suhotra.
Popular traditions credit him with knowing the future but being forbidden to reveal it unasked; this is not found in the Critical Edition.

nodes.name: Draupadi
nodes.description: Daughter of King Drupada of Panchala, born from the sacrificial fire, and common wife of the five Pandavas. Won by Arjuna at her svayamvara, she was humiliated in the Kuru assembly after the game of dice, and her demand for justice became a driving force of the war.
nodes.story: Staked and lost by Yudhishthira in the game of dice, Draupadi was dragged by her hair into the assembly by Dushasana. She stood before the elders and asked a question none could answer: had Yudhishthira lost himself before he staked her, and if so, what right had he to wager her? Bhishma confessed that the point of dharma was too subtle for him. Karna called her a woman with many husbands and ordered her stripped. Yet as Dushasana pulled at her garment, cloth after cloth appeared, until a mountain of garments lay in the hall and he sank down exhausted. Terrible omens broke out, and the frightened Dhritarashtra offered her boons. She asked only for the freedom of her husbands, refusing any more, for she said greed destroys dharma.
variations: In the Critical Edition the endless garments appear without any named cause; the vulgate adds Draupadi's prayer to Krishna, and later tradition credits the miracle directly to him.
The scene in which Draupadi rejects Karna at her svayamvara as a charioteer's son is in the vulgate but relegated to the apparatus of the Critical Edition.
Her famous taunt that Duryodhana was a blind man's son, after he fell into a pool in the Maya Sabha, is absent from the Critical Edition; there it is Bhima and others who laugh.
The Adi Parva explains her five husbands through a previous life in which she asked Shiva five times for a husband; she is also said to be a portion of Shri (Lakshmi).
In South Indian worship she is a goddess in her own right (Draupadi Amman), with fire-walking festivals.

nodes.name: Karna
nodes.description: Firstborn son of Kunti by the sun god Surya, born with golden armour and earrings, abandoned at birth and raised by the charioteer Adhiratha and his wife Radha. Made king of Anga by his friend Duryodhana, he became Arjuna's great rival and was killed by him on the seventeenth day of the Kurukshetra war.
nodes.story: Karna was famed for never refusing a Brahmin who asked him for anything at his midday worship of the Sun. Knowing that Karna could never be killed while he wore his natural armour and earrings, Indra, father of Arjuna, planned to take them from him disguised as a Brahmin. Surya warned his son in a dream, but Karna would not break his vow. When Indra came and asked, Karna cut the armour and earrings from his own body and gave them, yet he bargained for something in return. Shamed, Indra gave him the Vasavi Shakti, an unfailing spear that would kill any one enemy but return to Indra after one use. Karna saved it for Arjuna, but was forced to spend it on Ghatotkacha, whose night attack was destroying the Kaurava army.
nodes.vahana: chariot, driven in his last battle by Shalya
variations: The scene in which Draupadi refuses him at her svayamvara as a charioteer's son is found in the vulgate but relegated to the apparatus of the Critical Edition.

His death is doomed by two curses: Parashurama's, that he would forget the Brahmastra at his hour of need, and a Brahmin's, whose cow he killed by accident, that his chariot wheel would sink into the earth.
Later devotional and folk retellings greatly expand his generosity, earning him the title Daanaveera.

nodes.name: Adhiratha
nodes.description: A charioteer (suta) and friend of Dhritarashtra, who with his wife Radha found and raised the infant Karna. He was Karna's foster father, and Karna honoured him as his father all his life.
nodes.story: The basket in which Kunti set her newborn son adrift floated down the rivers until it reached the Ganga near Champa, where the charioteer Adhiratha and his wife Radha found it. Inside lay a baby shining like the sun, with golden armour and earrings. Childless, they rejoiced and raised him as their own, naming him Vasushena. Years later, when young Karna entered the tournament of the Kuru princes and challenged Arjuna, old Adhiratha came into the arena trembling, his staff in hand. Karna, newly crowned king of Anga, bowed his anointed head before him, and Adhiratha embraced him as a son. Seeing this, Bhima mocked Karna as a charioteer's son, fit to hold a whip rather than rule Anga.

nodes.name: Radha (Karna's foster mother)
nodes.description: Wife of the charioteer Adhiratha and foster mother of Karna, who is called Radheya, son of Radha, after her. She is distinct from Radha, the beloved of Krishna in later Vaishnava tradition.
nodes.story: Radha had long prayed for a child. When her husband Adhiratha drew a floating basket from the Ganga and found in it a baby glowing like the sun, clad in natural armour and golden earrings, she took him to her heart as a gift from the gods. She nursed and raised him, and he grew up known as Radheya, the son of Radha. On the eve of war, when Krishna and then Kunti told Karna the secret of his birth and begged him to join the Pandavas, Karna refused. Radha, he said, had cleaned him and fed him when he was abandoned; she was his true mother, and he would not betray the love of the woman who had raised him.

nodes.name: Vrishasena
nodes.description: Eldest son of Karna and a great warrior on the Kaurava side at Kurukshetra. Arjuna killed him before his father's eyes on the seventeenth day, in revenge for the killing of Abhimanyu.
nodes.story: Vrishasena, eldest son of Karna, fought beside his father through the later days of the Kurukshetra war and was counted among the Kauravas' finest chariot-warriors. On the seventeenth day, as Karna led the Kaurava army, Vrishasena pressed the Pandava forces hard. Arjuna, still grieving for Abhimanyu, who had been cut down while surrounded by many warriors including Karna, announced before the armies that he would kill Vrishasena in front of his father, and challenged Karna and the others to save him if they could. Then he struck down Vrishasena with a volley of arrows. Karna, overcome with grief and fury, rushed at Arjuna, beginning the final duel in which he himself would fall.
variations: In the Jaimini Ashvamedha and later retellings, Karna's surviving son Vrishaketu is adopted by the Pandavas and fights beside Arjuna.

nodes.name: Upapandavas (five sons of Draupadi)
nodes.description: The five sons of Draupadi, one by each Pandava: Prativindhya by Yudhishthira, Sutasoma by Bhima, Shrutakarma by Arjuna, Shatanika by Nakula and Shrutasena by Sahadeva. They fought for the Pandavas at Kurukshetra and were murdered in their sleep by Ashwatthama on the night after the war.
nodes.story: The five Draupadeyas survived eighteen days of battle, but the war was not over for Ashwatthama. On the night Duryodhana lay dying with broken thighs, Drona's son was named the last commander of the Kauravas. Watching an owl kill sleeping crows, he resolved to strike the Pandava camp in darkness. Guarded at the gate by Kripa and Kritavarma, he entered the camp, strangled Dhrishtadyumna, and slaughtered the sleeping warriors, including the five sons of Draupadi, whom some say he mistook for the Pandavas themselves. At dawn Draupadi, mad with grief, vowed to fast to death unless Ashwatthama was punished. The Pandavas hunted him down, and in the end took from his forehead the jewel he had worn since birth.
variations: The Adi Parva says they were portions of the Vishvedevas; the Markandeya Purana explains their early deaths by a curse of Vishvamitra on those gods.
Some texts call Arjuna's son Shrutakirti rather than Shrutakarma.
The idea that Ashwatthama mistook them for their fathers comes from later retellings; the Critical Edition presents the killing as deliberate.

nodes.name: Abhimanyu
nodes.description: Son of Arjuna and Subhadra, nephew of Krishna and husband of Uttara. On the thirteenth day of the Kurukshetra war, barely sixteen, he broke into Drona's chakravyuha formation and was killed when many Kaurava warriors surrounded him together.
nodes.story: On the thirteenth day, with Arjuna lured away by the Samshaptakas, Drona arranged his army in the circular chakravyuha. Only Abhimanyu knew how to break into it, though not how to come out. Yudhishthira promised that the others would follow through the breach. Abhimanyu smashed his way in, but Jayadratha, with a boon from Shiva, held the Pandavas back at the gap. Alone inside, the boy routed warrior after warrior, until Drona told Karna that the boy's armour could not be pierced and he must first be disarmed. Karna cut his bow from behind; others killed his horses and charioteer. Fighting with a sword, then a chariot wheel, then a mace, he faced the son of Dushasana. Both fell under each other's blows, but Dushasana's son rose first and struck him on the head as he was getting up.
variations: The popular story that he learned to enter the chakravyuha while in his mother's womb, hearing Arjuna describe it, is not in the Critical Edition; there he says Arjuna taught him to enter but not to escape.
The Adi Parva says he was an incarnation of Varchas, son of the moon god Soma, who agreed to lend him to earth for only sixteen years.

nodes.name: Uttara
nodes.description: Daughter of King Virata of Matsya and Queen Sudeshna, pupil of Arjuna during his year in disguise, and wife of Abhimanyu. Widowed while pregnant, she became the mother of Parikshit, whom Krishna restored to life after Ashwatthama's weapon struck him in the womb.
nodes.story: At King Virata's court a strange dance teacher called Brihannala taught the princess Uttara singing and dancing; it was Arjuna in disguise, living out Urvashi's curse. When the Pandavas' identity was revealed, the grateful Virata offered his daughter to Arjuna. Arjuna declined, saying that he had been like a father to his pupil, and asked for her as a bride for his son Abhimanyu instead. Their marriage sealed the alliance of Matsya and the Pandavas. Months later Abhimanyu died at Kurukshetra, and after the war Ashwatthama directed his Brahmashira weapon at the wombs of the Pandava women. Uttara's son was born lifeless, but Krishna, keeping his word, brought the child back to life. He was named Parikshit, the one who had been tested.
variations: In the Bhagavata Purana the unborn Parikshit sees a thumb-sized form of Vishnu protecting him in the womb from Ashwatthama's weapon.

nodes.name: Parikshit
nodes.description: Son of Abhimanyu and Uttara, grandson of Arjuna, who succeeded Yudhishthira on the Kuru throne. Killed in the womb by Ashwatthama's weapon and revived by Krishna, he died by the bite of the serpent Takshaka; in the Bhagavata Purana he hears the whole Purana from Shuka during his last seven days.
nodes.story: Out hunting, tired and thirsty, King Parikshit came upon the sage Shamika sitting in a vow of silence and asked about a deer he had wounded. When the sage did not answer, the king in anger hung a dead snake around his neck with the tip of his bow. Shamika's son Shringin, hearing of it, cursed the king to die within seven days by the bite of Takshaka. Shamika sent word to warn him. Parikshit had a palace built on a single pillar, surrounded by guards, physicians and mantras. On the seventh day Takshaka turned back the healer Kashyapa with gifts, and sent Nagas disguised as ascetics to the king with fruits. In one fruit hid a tiny copper-coloured worm; it became Takshaka, who coiled around the laughing king and killed him.
variations: The Atharva Veda (20.127, the Kuntapa hymns) praises a Parikshit as a prosperous king of the Kurus; scholars generally connect him with the epic king, though the link is not certain.
In the Bhagavata Purana he subdues the personified Kali Yuga and, after the curse, spends seven days on the bank of the Ganga hearing the Bhagavata from Shuka.

nodes.name: Janamejaya
nodes.description: Son of Parikshit and great-grandson of Arjuna, king of the Kurus. To avenge his father he held the great snake sacrifice (sarpa-satra), at which Vaishampayana first recited the Mahabharata to him.
nodes.story: When the young king Janamejaya learned from the sage Uttanka that his father Parikshit had been killed by Takshaka, he resolved to destroy every serpent. Priests in black robes lit a great fire and chanted mantras that drew snakes of every kind from the ends of the earth to fall writhing into the flames. Takshaka fled to Indra for shelter, but the mantras grew so strong that Indra himself began to be dragged toward the fire and let go. At that moment the young Brahmin Astika, whose mother was a Naga, arrived and praised the sacrifice so beautifully that Janamejaya offered him any boon. Astika asked that the sacrifice stop. Bound by his word, the king ended it, and Takshaka was saved. During that sacrifice Vaishampayana recited the Mahabharata.
variations: The Brahmanas record Janamejaya Parikshita as a Kuru king consecrated by the priest Tura Kavasheya and a performer of the horse sacrifice; he is usually identified with the epic king.
The Harivamsha, presented as a sequel told to him, adds that he was later cursed for mistreating Brahmins at a horse sacrifice.

nodes.name: Duryodhana
nodes.description: Eldest of the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra and Gandhari and the leader of the Kaurava side in the Kurukshetra war. The Adi Parva calls him a portion of Kali; the epic also shows him as a generous friend to Karna, a master of the mace and a king who died unrepentant but, in its own words, as a kshatriya.
nodes.story: After the eighteenth day's slaughter Duryodhana hid beneath the waters of a lake, but the Pandavas found him and taunted him until he rose, mace in hand. Yudhishthira let him choose any one opponent; he chose Bhima. Their teacher Balarama arrived to watch his two disciples fight. The duel was even until Krishna reminded Arjuna of Bhima's vow, and Arjuna slapped his own thigh. Bhima struck below the navel and shattered Duryodhana's thighs, the very thigh he had once bared to Draupadi. Balarama raged at the foul blow. Lying broken, Duryodhana listed Krishna's stratagems against Bhishma, Drona, Karna and Bhurishravas, declaring that he had lived as a king and would die as one. The epic says flowers then rained from the sky upon him while celestial music sounded.
variations: Some southern and folk retellings (and the Sanskrit drama Urubhanga by Bhasa) portray him as a tragic hero reconciled in his last hours.
He is worshipped as a deity at the Poruvazhy Peruviruthy Malanada temple in Kerala and in several villages of the upper Tons valley (Uttarakhand).
Draupadi's mocking laughter at the Maya Sabha, often cited as the root of his hatred, is a later embellishment; in the Critical Edition Bhima and the attendants laugh at his fall.

nodes.name: Dushasana
nodes.description: Second of the hundred Kaurava brothers and Duryodhana's most devoted follower. He is remembered above all for dragging Draupadi into the assembly hall after the game of dice, an outrage that Bhima avenged on the seventeenth day of the war.
nodes.story: When Yudhishthira had staked and lost Draupadi, Duryodhana sent Dushasana to fetch her. She was in her season and wearing a single garment, but he seized her by her long hair and dragged her into the hall of elders, mocking her as a slave. At Karna's urging he began to strip her before the silent court, yet each garment he pulled away was replaced by another until a heap of cloth lay on the floor and he sank down exhausted. Bhima then swore a terrible oath: he would tear open Dushasana's chest and drink his blood. Years later on the battlefield Bhima brought him down, broke him, ripped open his breast and tasted his blood before both armies, crying that it was sweeter than milk or honey.
variations: In the vulgate and in devotional tradition Draupadi's endless garments are Krishna's direct answer to her prayer; the Critical Edition relegates the explicit invocation of Krishna to an appendix and keeps only the miracle.
In some retellings Draupadi vows to leave her hair unbound until she can wash it in Dushasana's blood.

nodes.name: Vikarna
nodes.description: One of the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra, celebrated as the conscience of the Kauravas. He alone among Duryodhana's brothers protested in the dice hall that Draupadi had not been lawfully won, yet he still fought for his elder brother and was killed by Bhima.
nodes.story: Dragged into the assembly, Draupadi asked the elders whether Yudhishthira, having already lost himself, had any right to stake her. Bhishma equivocated and the kings sat silent. Then young Vikarna rose. Gambling, he said, is a vice of kings; Yudhishthira was goaded by Shakuni and staked her only after he had lost his own freedom, and she was in any case the wife of all five brothers. Therefore she had not been won. The hall roared its approval until Karna rebuked him as a mere boy speaking out of turn and ordered Draupadi stripped. Loyal nonetheless to Duryodhana, Vikarna took the field at Kurukshetra and was cut down by Bhima's arrows during the fighting around Drona's array, one of many Kaurava brothers whom Bhima had sworn to destroy.
variations: Popular retellings add a lament in which Bhima grieves that he must kill the one Kaurava who spoke for dharma; the scene is elaborated in later and regional versions.
Some modern adaptations make him a larger moral voice throughout the epic, which goes beyond the textual evidence.

nodes.name: Dushala
nodes.description: The only daughter of Dhritarashtra and Gandhari, sister of the hundred Kauravas, and wife of Jayadratha, king of the Sindhus. After the war she moved Arjuna to spare her people during Yudhishthira's horse sacrifice.
nodes.story: When Vyasa divided Gandhari's hard mass of flesh into pots, Gandhari silently wished for a daughter as well, and the sage made one more portion from which Dushala was born. She was married to Jayadratha of Sindhu, who died by Arjuna's arrow. Years later Yudhishthira's sacrificial horse wandered into Sindhu with Arjuna following, and the Sindhu warriors attacked him. Hearing that Arjuna had come, Dushala's son Suratha died of grief and terror. Dushala then came to the battlefield with her infant grandson in her arms and begged her brother's foe for mercy. Remembering Gandhari and Dhritarashtra, Arjuna put down Gandiva, reproached himself for the war's slaughter, embraced the child and sent her home in peace.
variations: Accounts of how the extra portion for a daughter was created vary slightly between recensions.

nodes.name: Jayadratha
nodes.description: King of Sindhu and Sauvira, husband of the Kaurava princess Dushala. He tried to abduct Draupadi in the forest and, armed with a boon from Shiva, held back the Pandavas at the Chakravyuha on the day Abhimanyu was killed.
nodes.story: While the Pandavas were hunting, Jayadratha came upon Draupadi alone at their hermitage in the Kamyaka forest and carried her off in his chariot. The brothers pursued him; Bhima dragged him down and would have killed him, but Yudhishthira spared him for the sake of their cousin Dushala. Bhima shaved his head into five tufts and made him declare himself a slave of the Pandavas. Burning with shame, Jayadratha performed austerities until Shiva granted that he could hold back all the Pandavas except Arjuna for a single day. That day came when Drona formed the Chakravyuha: Abhimanyu broke in, and Jayadratha sealed the breach behind him. Arjuna vowed to kill Jayadratha before the next sunset or enter fire, and as the light failed on the fourteenth day his arrow took Jayadratha's head.
variations: In one version his father Vriddhakshatra had decreed that whoever made his son's head fall to the ground would have his own head burst; Arjuna therefore sent the head flying into the old king's lap.
Krishna's darkening of the sky (by yoga, or in later retellings by covering the sun with the Sudarshana) that drew Jayadratha out of hiding is told differently across versions.

nodes.name: Yuyutsu
nodes.description: Son of Dhritarashtra by a Vaishya woman who attended him during Gandhari's long pregnancy. On the eve of battle he crossed over to the Pandavas, survived the war, and was later entrusted with guarding the kingdom.
nodes.story: At Kurukshetra, with both armies drawn up, Yudhishthira took off his armour, walked across to pay respect to his elders, and then called out that anyone who wished to join the side of dharma could still do so. Of all Dhritarashtra's sons only Yuyutsu answered. As drums sounded he crossed the field to the Pandava lines, choosing conscience over kinship. He fought for them through the war and was among the very few of his father's line to survive it. When Duryodhana fell, Yuyutsu escorted the widowed royal women back to Hastinapura, and Vidura praised him for acting rightly. Decades later, when the Pandavas set out on their last journey, Yudhishthira placed the kingdom under Yuyutsu's care while the young Parikshit reigned.

nodes.name: Shakuni
nodes.description: Prince of Gandhara, son of King Subala and brother of Gandhari, who lived at the Kuru court as Duryodhana's maternal uncle and chief counsellor. A master of dice, he won Yudhishthira's kingdom, brothers and wife in the fateful game and was killed by Sahadeva on the last day of the war.
nodes.story: Consumed with envy after Yudhishthira's royal consecration and his humiliating stumble in the Pandavas' magical hall, Duryodhana confided in his uncle. Shakuni proposed a gentler weapon than war: Yudhishthira loved dice but did not know them, while he himself had no equal at the throw. With Dhritarashtra's reluctant consent the invitation was sent. In the new assembly hall Shakuni played on Duryodhana's behalf and, throw after throw, cried 'I have won!' Yudhishthira lost his jewels, his armies, his kingdom, each of his brothers, himself and finally Draupadi. Sahadeva, the youngest Pandava, swore then that he would kill Shakuni. On the eighteenth day of the war, after slaying Shakuni's son Uluka, Sahadeva struck off his head with a broad arrow, fulfilling the vow.
variations: Popular folk tales, absent from the Mahabharata, say Bhishma imprisoned Subala's family and starved them, and that Shakuni's dice were carved from his dead father's bones so that they obeyed him, making his whole life a revenge on the Kurus.
The Adi Parva identifies Shakuni as an incarnation of Dvapara, the personified age of doubt.

nodes.name: Drona
nodes.description: Brahmin master of arms, son of the sage Bharadvaja, who became preceptor of both the Kaurava and Pandava princes. Bound to Hastinapura, he commanded the Kaurava army after Bhishma and was slain by Dhrishtadyumna, the son born to avenge his humiliation of Drupada.
nodes.story: As boys Drona and Prince Drupada studied together, and Drupada promised to share his kingdom. Years later Drona was so poor that his little son drank flour stirred in water believing it was milk. He went to Drupada, now king, and greeted him as a friend, but was spurned: a king cannot be friends with a beggar. Drona came to Hastinapura, lifted the princes' ball from a well with blades of grass, and Bhishma made him their teacher. When his pupils' training was complete he asked a single fee: bring Drupada to me bound. Arjuna did so. Drona took half of Panchala and returned the rest, saying now they were equals and could be friends. Drupada left with a fire of vengeance, and performed a sacrifice for a son who would kill Drona.
variations: The Adi Parva calls him a partial incarnation of Brihaspati, guru of the gods.
His name ('born of a vessel') refers to his birth from Bharadvaja's seed caught in a drona after the sage saw the apsara Ghritachi.
In Haryana tradition Gurugram (Gurgaon) is held to be the village gifted to him by the Kurus.

nodes.name: Kripi
nodes.description: Twin sister of Kripa, born of the sage Sharadvan and raised in the palace by King Shantanu. She married Drona and was the mother of Ashwatthama.
nodes.story: The sage Sharadvan, son of Gautama, cared more for the science of archery than for the Vedas, and his austerities alarmed Indra, who sent the apsara Janapadi to distract him. At the sight of her his seed fell upon a clump of reeds, split in two, and from it twins were born. Soldiers of King Shantanu, out hunting, found the infants lying beside a bow, arrows and a deerskin and brought them to the king, who raised them out of compassion and named them Kripa and Kripi. Kripi grew up at the Kuru court and was given in marriage to the impoverished brahmin Drona. Their son Ashwatthama neighed like a horse at birth, and for his sake she endured years of poverty before Drona found favour with Bhishma.
variations: In the Bhagavata Purana Draupadi pleads for Ashwatthama's life after the night raid, not wishing Kripi to grieve for a son as she grieves for hers.

nodes.name: Ashwatthama
nodes.description: Son of Drona and Kripi, born with a jewel on his forehead and said to embody portions of Shiva, Yama, desire and wrath. He became the last commander of the Kauravas, massacred the sleeping Pandava camp and was cursed by Krishna to wander the earth; he is counted among the Chiranjivis.
nodes.story: With Duryodhana dying, Ashwatthama lay awake beneath a banyan tree and watched an owl slaughter a roost of sleeping crows. He resolved to do the same. Ignoring Kripa's pleas, he went to the Pandava camp, where a vast, terrible being barred the gate. His weapons vanished into it, so he offered himself as a sacrifice to Shiva; the god entered his body and gave him a gleaming sword. Inside, he kicked the sleeping Dhrishtadyumna awake and beat and strangled him, refusing him a warrior's death, then cut down Shikhandi and all five sons of Draupadi while Kripa and Kritavarma killed those fleeing at the gate. Pursued, he loosed the Brahmashira and turned it on Uttara's unborn child. For this Krishna cursed him to roam for three thousand years, friendless and diseased.
variations: In the Bhagavata Purana Arjuna captures him and brings him before Draupadi, who asks for his release; his head is shaved and his jewel taken instead of his life.
Folk belief holds that he still wanders, and he is said to visit places such as the Asirgarh fort in Madhya Pradesh and the banks of the Narmada.
He is listed among the seven (or eight) Chiranjivis in a popular Sanskrit verse.

nodes.name: Kripa
nodes.description: Twin brother of Kripi, born of the sage Sharadvan and fostered by King Shantanu, who became the first arms-teacher of the Kuru princes. He fought for the Kauravas, survived the war, later taught Parikshit and is counted among the Chiranjivis.
nodes.story: Born from Sharadvan's seed that fell on a clump of reeds, the infant twins were found by Shantanu's hunters and raised at Hastinapura. Their father later came in secret and taught Kripa the four branches of archery, and Kripa became teacher to the young Kauravas and Pandavas before Drona arrived. Loyal to the throne he served, he rode with Duryodhana through all eighteen days, often speaking plainly against Karna's boasts. When only three Kaurava warriors survived, Kripa begged Ashwatthama not to attack sleeping men, counselling him to consult Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Vidura. Overruled, he nevertheless stood at the gate of the Pandava camp during the massacre. After the war he returned to the Kuru court, and when the Pandavas departed on their last journey, Kripa was appointed preceptor of the young King Parikshit.
variations: The Bhagavata Purana names him as one of the Saptarishis of the future eighth Manvantara.
The Adi Parva says he was born from a portion of the host of Rudras.

nodes.name: Drupada
nodes.description: King of Panchala, son of Prishata, and father of Draupadi, Dhrishtadyumna and Shikhandi. Drona's boyhood friend turned bitter enemy, he became the Pandavas' father-in-law and chief ally, and died by Drona's hand in the war.
nodes.story: Captured by Arjuna and dragged before Drona as a teacher's fee, Drupada lost half his kingdom and all his peace. Unable to defeat the brahmin warrior in arms, he wandered among ascetics seeking a priest who would perform a sacrifice for an avenging son. The sage Upayaja refused, but his elder brother Yaja agreed. From the fire of the rite a young man rose in armour, bearing sword and bow, and mounted a chariot as a heavenly voice proclaimed that he was born to slay Drona. From the middle of the altar then rose a dark, lotus-eyed maiden, and the voice declared that she would bring about the destruction of the kshatriyas. Drupada named them Dhrishtadyumna and Krishnaa, later called Draupadi, and in time gave her in marriage to the Pandavas at her svayamvara.
variations: The Adi Parva says he was born of a portion of the Marut host.
His epithet Yajnasena is sometimes linked to his sacrifice for children.

nodes.name: Dhrishtadyumna
nodes.description: Son of Drupada, born fully armed from a sacrificial fire to kill Drona, and twin of Draupadi. He served as supreme commander of the Pandava army throughout the Kurukshetra war and was murdered in his sleep by Ashwatthama.
nodes.story: Drona knew the prophecy that Dhrishtadyumna had been born to kill him, yet he took the Panchala prince as a pupil and taught him arms, holding that destiny could not be escaped. On the fifteenth day of the war the Pandavas, desperate, let Drona hear that Ashwatthama was dead; Yudhishthira confirmed it, murmuring that it was an elephant of that name. Grief-stricken, Drona laid down his weapons and sat on his chariot in yogic meditation. Dhrishtadyumna leapt up, seized him by the hair and struck off his head, while Arjuna cried out to spare the teacher. The act divided even the Pandavas, and Satyaki denounced him. It also sealed his fate: three nights later Ashwatthama crept into his tent, kicked him awake and killed him with blows, denying him a death by weapons.
variations: The Adi Parva calls him a portion of Agni.
Retellings differ on whether Drona had already left his body in yoga before Dhrishtadyumna's blow, which some use to soften the charge of killing a disarmed teacher.

nodes.name: Shikhandi
nodes.description: Child of Drupada, born a daughter and later transformed into a man, who was the rebirth of Princess Amba. Because Bhishma would not raise arms against one born female, Arjuna shot him down from behind Shikhandi on the tenth day of the war.
nodes.story: Amba, abducted by Bhishma and then rejected by everyone, burned herself in a fire vowing to be reborn as his killer. Drupada, who had prayed to Shiva for a son, was told he would have a daughter who would become a man. The child Shikhandini was raised as a boy and even married to a princess of Dasharna, whose father, discovering the truth, threatened war. In despair Shikhandini went into the forest, where the yaksha Sthunakarna agreed to exchange sexes with her for a time; Kubera then cursed the yaksha to remain female until Shikhandi's death. At Kurukshetra Bhishma revealed that he would not fight Shikhandi, and on the tenth day Arjuna, sheltering behind him, pierced the grandsire with arrows until he fell. Shikhandi died in Ashwatthama's night raid.
variations: The Adi Parva's list of partial incarnations says Shikhandi was born from a portion of a rakshasa, alongside the fuller Amba rebirth story of the Udyoga Parva.
Modern readers have discussed Shikhandi in connection with gender identity; interpretations differ widely.

nodes.name: Virata
nodes.description: King of the Matsyas, at whose court in Viratanagara the Pandavas spent their thirteenth year of exile in disguise. His daughter Uttara married Abhimanyu, and he fought for the Pandavas until Drona killed him on the fifteenth day.
nodes.story: In the year of hiding the Pandavas entered Virata's service in disguise: Yudhishthira as the dice-playing brahmin Kanka, Bhima as the cook Ballava, Arjuna as the dance-master Brihannala, Nakula and Sahadeva as keepers of horses and cattle, and Draupadi as the maid Sairandhri. When the Kauravas raided Virata's cattle, his young son Uttara rode out with Brihannala as charioteer and returned victorious. Virata, back from fighting the Trigartas, boasted of his son; when Kanka insisted the credit belonged to Brihannala, the angry king flung the dice at his face and drew blood, which Draupadi caught in a cup. Days later the Pandavas revealed themselves. Mortified and honoured, Virata offered Uttara to Arjuna, who accepted her as a bride for his son Abhimanyu.
variations: The Adi Parva says he was born of a portion of the Marut host.
Viratanagara is traditionally identified with Bairat in Rajasthan.

nodes.name: Sudeshna
nodes.description: Queen of King Virata of Matsya, mother of Uttara and sister of the commander Kichaka. She took the disguised Draupadi into service as her maid Sairandhri.
nodes.story: When a beautiful woman calling herself Sairandhri came to the palace seeking work, Queen Sudeshna hesitated, fearing that the king himself might be captivated. Draupadi reassured her that five gandharva husbands guarded her virtue, and the queen took her in. But Sudeshna's brother Kichaka soon burned with desire for the maid and pleaded with his sister to help him. Sudeshna yielded and sent Sairandhri to Kichaka's house on the pretext of fetching wine, setting in motion the assault, the humiliation in court and at last Kichaka's death at Bhima's hands. Terrified afterwards of Sairandhri's invisible protectors, the queen begged her to leave the city; Draupadi asked for only thirteen more days, the time remaining in the Pandavas' year of hiding.
variations: She is called a Kekaya princess in the Virata Parva, while her brother Kichaka is called a suta (charioteer-caste) warrior; later retellings explain the family's origins differently.

nodes.name: Kichaka
nodes.description: The mighty commander of King Virata's army and brother of Queen Sudeshna. His assault on the disguised Draupadi led Bhima to kill him secretly in the dance hall of Viratanagara.
nodes.story: Kichaka, whose strength made him the true power in the Matsya kingdom, became obsessed with his sister's maid Sairandhri. When she came to his house he seized her; she fled into the royal court, where he kicked her to the ground before King Virata, who did nothing. That night Draupadi went to Bhima in the palace kitchen and wept. They laid a plan: she would promise to meet Kichaka alone in the dance hall after dark. Kichaka came, perfumed and eager, and found Bhima waiting in the shadows. The two wrestled like bulls until Bhima crushed Kichaka's limbs into his body, leaving a shapeless ball of flesh. When his many brothers tried to burn Sairandhri on his pyre, Bhima uprooted a tree and killed them all.
variations: Duryodhana guessed from the manner of Kichaka's death that only Bhima could have killed him, and so suspected the Pandavas were hiding in Matsya.
Kathakali and other regional theatre traditions stage Kichaka-vadha as a celebrated set piece.

nodes.name: Ekalavya
nodes.description: Son of Hiranyadhanus, chief of the Nishada forest people, who learned archery by practising before a clay image of Drona after the teacher turned him away. Drona demanded his right thumb as a teacher's fee so that Arjuna would remain unsurpassed.
nodes.story: Ekalavya came to Drona asking to be taught, but Drona, teacher of the Kuru princes, would not accept a Nishada. The boy went back to the forest, made an image of Drona from earth, honoured it as his guru and practised until he became a superb archer. One day a dog belonging to the princes' hunting party barked at him, and he silenced it with seven arrows shot into its mouth, without killing it. The princes marvelled; Arjuna, whom Drona had promised no pupil would surpass, complained to his teacher. Drona went to Ekalavya, accepted his homage, and asked for his right thumb as fee. Without hesitation Ekalavya cut it off and gave it. Afterwards, the epic says, he no longer shot as swiftly, and Arjuna's fever of rivalry passed.
variations: The Harivamsha makes him a son of Devashravas, a Yadava, raised among the Nishadas, and places him with Jarasandha against Krishna.
A passage attributed to Krishna in the Drona Parva lists Ekalavya among those he removed for Arjuna's sake; later retellings say Krishna killed him, which is not uniformly attested.
Modern Dalit and Adivasi readings see the thumb episode as a paradigm of caste exclusion; regional traditions add later lives for him.

nodes.name: Shalya
nodes.description: King of Madra and brother of Madri, and so maternal uncle of Nakula and Sahadeva. Tricked by Duryodhana's hospitality into fighting for the Kauravas, he served as Karna's charioteer, commanded the Kaurava army on the last day and was killed by Yudhishthira.
nodes.story: Shalya set out with a great army to join his nephews, but Duryodhana had rest-houses built along his route, stocked with food, wine and entertainments. Delighted, Shalya asked who had arranged them, promising a boon to his host. Duryodhana stepped forward and asked him to lead his army. Bound by his word, Shalya agreed, then went on to Yudhishthira and confessed. Yudhishthira asked one favour: if Shalya was ever made Karna's charioteer, let him sap Karna's spirit. On the seventeenth day that came to pass. As they drove to battle Shalya praised Arjuna and belittled Karna, telling him the fable of the crow who challenged the swans. The next day, as the Kauravas' last commander, Shalya faced Yudhishthira, whose hurled spear struck him in the chest and killed him.
variations: The Adi Parva says he was an incarnation of the asura Samhlada, brother of Prahlada.
Bhishma paid Shalya a rich bride-price when Madri was married to Pandu, a Madra custom the epic notes with some disapproval.

nodes.name: Bhagadatta
nodes.description: King of Pragjyotisha (in present-day Assam), son of the asura-king Naraka and a renowned elephant warrior. An ally of the Kauravas, he fought on his great elephant Supratika and was slain by Arjuna on the twelfth day.
nodes.story: Bhagadatta, old but undaunted, drove his elephant Supratika through the Pandava ranks, scattering chariots and nearly trampling Bhima. When Arjuna came against him, the king hurled his elephant-goad, charged with the Vaishnava weapon, straight at him. Krishna rose in the chariot and took the weapon on his own chest, where it turned into a garland. To the protesting Arjuna he explained that he had once given this weapon to the Earth for her son Naraka, from whom it passed to Bhagadatta; no one else could have withstood it. Freed of that danger, Arjuna shot Supratika through the temple and pierced Bhagadatta's heart with a crescent-headed arrow. The aged king fell from his elephant like a flowering tree toppled by the wind.
variations: A popular detail says he tied up his drooping eyelids with a silk band, which Arjuna cut before killing him.
The Sabha Parva calls him a friend of Indra and says he fought Arjuna for eight days during the Pandava conquests before offering tribute.

nodes.name: Bhurishravas
nodes.description: A Kuru prince, son of Somadatta and grandson of Bahlika, who fought for Duryodhana. His death on the fourteenth day, when Arjuna severed his arm and Satyaki beheaded him as he sat in meditation, became one of the war's great controversies.
nodes.story: The feud began a generation earlier, when Shini of the Vrishnis defeated Somadatta at Devaki's svayamvara and dragged him by the hair; Somadatta then won by austerity a son to avenge him. On the fourteenth day that son, Bhurishravas, met Shini's grandson Satyaki, who was worn out by battle. He threw Satyaki down, seized his hair and raised his sword. Krishna urged Arjuna to save his disciple, and Arjuna's arrow cut off Bhurishravas' sword-arm. Bhurishravas reproached Arjuna for striking a man engaged with another, then spread out arrows, sat upon them and entered meditation to die. Satyaki rose, and ignoring the cries of both armies, struck off his head. Arguments over who was in the wrong raged across the field that day.
variations: Some retellings stress that Bhurishravas was renowned as a generous sacrificer, which is reflected in his banner, the sacrificial post.

nodes.name: Satyaki
nodes.description: A Vrishni-Yadava hero, grandson of Shini, who learned archery from Arjuna and was Krishna's close companion. He was one of the few Yadavas to fight for the Pandavas, and was killed in the drunken brawl at Prabhasa after beheading Kritavarma.
nodes.story: Satyaki, also called Yuyudhana, rode at Krishna's side on the peace embassy to Hastinapura and brought an akshauhini to the Pandavas. On the fourteenth day, while Arjuna fought his way toward Jayadratha, Yudhishthira ordered Satyaki to follow and support him. He forced his way through Drona's array, fought Drona, Kritavarma and Karna's forces in turn and reached Arjuna exhausted, only to be thrown down by Bhurishravas, the son of his family's old enemy. Saved by Arjuna's arrow, he beheaded the dying Bhurishravas. Years later at Prabhasa, when the Yadavas had drunk deeply, Satyaki mocked Kritavarma for murdering sleeping men. Tempers flared, he struck off Kritavarma's head, and the Bhojas and Andhakas fell upon him and killed him, beginning the Yadavas' self-destruction.
variations: The Adi Parva says he was born of a portion of the Marut host.
Puranic genealogies give his descent from Shini, son of Satyaka, in the Vrishni branch of the Yadavas.

nodes.name: Kritavarma
nodes.description: A Bhoja-Yadava chief, son of Hridika, who led an akshauhini for Duryodhana even though Krishna fought beside the Pandavas. One of the three Kaurava warriors to survive the war, he took part in Ashwatthama's night raid and was later killed by Satyaki at Prabhasa.
nodes.story: When Duryodhana and Arjuna both sought Krishna's help, the Yadavas divided, and Kritavarma marched with a full akshauhini to the Kaurava side. He fought through all eighteen days and was among the last three standing with Kripa and Ashwatthama. On the night after Duryodhana fell he followed Ashwatthama to the Pandava camp and, with Kripa, guarded the gates, cutting down those who fled the slaughter and setting fire to the tents. He returned home to Dvaraka, but the deed was not forgotten. At Prabhasa, where the Yadavas had gone on pilgrimage and drunk heavily, Satyaki taunted him with killing sleeping men. Kritavarma retorted with the death of Bhurishravas; Satyaki leapt up and beheaded him, and the brawl that destroyed the Yadavas began.
variations: In the Syamantaka jewel episode of the Harivamsha and Puranas, Kritavarma and Akrura encourage Shatadhanva to kill Satrajit, then refuse to protect him from Krishna.
The Adi Parva says he was born of a portion of the Marut host.

nodes.name: Sanjaya
nodes.description: Charioteer, counsellor and envoy of the blind king Dhritarashtra, son of the suta Gavalgana. Granted divine sight by Vyasa, he narrated the Kurukshetra war, including the Bhagavad Gita, to the king as it happened.
nodes.story: Before the battle Vyasa offered sight to his son Dhritarashtra so that he could watch the war, but the king did not wish to see his kin slaughtered; he asked only to hear of it. So Vyasa gave Sanjaya divine vision: he would see everything, openly or secretly, by day or night, even men's thoughts, and would come through the war unharmed. From the field Sanjaya reported Bhishma's fall and then recounted the whole conflict, beginning with the dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna and the vision of the universal form. He ends the Gita declaring that wherever Krishna and Arjuna stand there will be fortune, victory and righteousness. His divine sight faded when Duryodhana died. Years later he accompanied Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Kunti to the forest and survived the fire that consumed them.
variations: Some readers treat Sanjaya's divine sight as an image for the narrator's omniscience; devotional tradition treats it as a literal gift of Vyasa's power.

nodes.name: Krishna
nodes.description: The eighth son of Vasudeva and Devaki, raised among the cowherds of Vraja, who became the prince of the Yadavas at Dvaraka, the friend and charioteer of Arjuna and the teacher of the Bhagavad Gita. Revered as the eighth (or ninth) avatar of Vishnu, and in several Vaishnava schools as the Supreme Lord himself, he is among the most widely worshipped figures of Hinduism.
nodes.story: When a heavenly voice warned Kamsa that Devaki's eighth child would kill him, he imprisoned Devaki and Vasudeva in Mathura and killed their newborns one by one; the seventh embryo, Balarama, was secretly drawn into Rohini's womb. At midnight on the eighth day of the dark fortnight Krishna was born, first revealing a four-armed divine form before becoming an ordinary infant. The guards sank into sleep and the prison doors opened. Vasudeva carried the child through a storm across the Yamuna, which gave way before him, and exchanged him for the newborn daughter of Yashoda in Gokula. When Kamsa seized the girl to dash her against a stone, she slipped from his grasp, rose into the sky as the Goddess, and told him that his destroyer was already alive and safe.
nodes.abode: Mathura, Vraja (Gokula and Vrindavan) and Dvaraka; Goloka in devotional theology
sources: Mahabharata (esp. Sabha, Udyoga, Bhishma and Mausala Parvas)
variations: Chandogya Upanishad 3.17.6 mentions a 'Krishna Devakiputra', pupil of Ghora Angirasa; whether he is the same figure as the epic Krishna is debated.
Panini's grammar (4.3.98) refers to devotion to Vasudeva, and the Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar (c. 2nd century BCE) calls Vasudeva 'god of gods', attesting an early Bhagavata cult.
Many scholars see a fusion of Vasudeva-Krishna of the Vrishni clan, the epic hero of the Mahabharata and the pastoral Gopala-Krishna of the Harivamsha and Puranas.
The Mahabharata (Adi Parva) and Vishnu Purana say Vishnu plucked a black hair and a white hair, which became Krishna and Balarama.
Gaudiya and other Krishna-centred schools, citing Bhagavata 1.3.28 ('krishnas tu bhagavan svayam'), hold that Krishna is not an avatar but the source of all avatars, including Vishnu.
The Bhagavata counts 16,108 wives (eight principal queens plus 16,100 women freed from Narakasura); other texts give different figures.
Jain tradition makes Krishna the ninth and last Vasudeva of this age and a cousin of the Tirthankara Neminatha; a Buddhist Jataka (Ghata Jataka) retells his family saga.

nodes.name: Balarama
nodes.description: Krishna's elder brother, a son of Vasudeva conceived in Devaki's womb and transferred to that of Rohini, famed for immense strength, his plough and pestle and his love of wine. He is regarded as an incarnation of the cosmic serpent Shesha and, in many lists, as an avatar of Vishnu; he taught Bhima and Duryodhana the mace and refused to fight at Kurukshetra.
nodes.story: Once, returning to Vraja and warm with the wine Varuni, Balarama wandered by the Yamuna with the cowherd women and called on the river to come near so that he could bathe. The Yamuna ignored the words of one who seemed drunk. Enraged, Balarama hooked her with the tip of his plough and dragged her towards him, threatening to split her into a hundred streams. Terrified, the river goddess appeared before him, fell at his feet and begged forgiveness, praising him as Ananta, the serpent who bears the earth. Balarama released her, and she bathed and adorned him; the Puranas say the Yamuna still bends along the course his plough carved. The episode shows the elder brother's dual nature: a rustic, hot-tempered hero who is at the same time the cosmic Shesha.
variations: The Harivamsha says the goddess Nidra (Vishnu's Sleep) transferred the embryo from Devaki to Rohini; the Bhagavata names Yogamaya.

Mahabharata and Vishnu Purana: Balarama arose from a white hair of Vishnu; elsewhere he is the incarnation of Shesha. In the Mausala Parva, at his death a great white serpent leaves his mouth and enters the ocean.
Dashavatara lists vary: some include Balarama as the eighth avatar with Krishna as the source of all, others replace Balarama with Buddha; the Gita Govinda includes both Balarama and Buddha.
In Pancharatra theology he is Sankarshana, the second of the four vyuhas; scholars link him to an early agricultural deity.
Jain tradition makes him the ninth Baladeva. The daughter Vatsala/Shashirekha of the Maya Bazaar story belongs to regional folk tradition, not the Sanskrit texts.

nodes.name: Revati
nodes.description: Wife of Balarama, daughter of King Kakudmi (Raivata) of Kushasthali, the city later rebuilt as Dvaraka. Her story, in which ages pass on earth during a short visit to Brahma's world, is one of the earliest descriptions of time dilation in world literature.
nodes.story: King Kakudmi, a descendant of Vaivasvata Manu, could find no man worthy of his beautiful daughter Revati, so he took her to Brahmaloka to ask the Creator himself. Brahma was listening to the Gandharvas sing, and the king waited politely until the performance ended before making his request. Brahma laughed: in the brief moment they had waited, twenty-seven cycles of the four yugas had passed on earth; every suitor Kakudmi had in mind, and their descendants and kingdoms, had long vanished. He advised the king to return and give Revati to Balarama, a portion of Vishnu now living on earth. Revati, from an earlier age, was far taller than the people of the new era, so Balarama gently pressed her down with the tip of his plough until she was of ordinary height, and they were married.
variations: The shrinking of Revati with the plough appears in the Vishnu Purana and later retellings but not in the Bhagavata's account.
Her sons with Balarama are named Nishatha and Ulmuka.

nodes.name: Devaki
nodes.description: Mother of Krishna, daughter of Devaka (brother of King Ugrasena) and wife of Vasudeva. Imprisoned by her cousin Kamsa, she lost six sons to him before Krishna was born and smuggled away; she is revered as the rebirth of Aditi, mother of the gods.
nodes.story: Years after Krishna had grown to be lord of Dvaraka, Devaki still mourned the six sons Kamsa had slain in the prison at Mathura. Having seen her sons bring back their guru's dead child from Yama's realm, she begged Krishna and Balarama to let her see her lost children again. The brothers entered Sutala, the underworld kingdom of Bali, who welcomed them with reverence, and brought back the six boys. They had once been sons of the sage Marichi, cursed to be born among asuras and then of Devaki. When Devaki embraced them, milk flowed from her breasts; she nursed them, and touched by the remnants of Krishna's own nourishment the boys were freed from their curse. They bowed to their parents and to Krishna and rose to the heavens, leaving Devaki consoled.
variations: Harivamsha: Aditi and Surabhi were reborn as Devaki and Rohini after Brahma cursed Kashyapa (reborn as Vasudeva) for taking Varuna's cows.
Bhagavata 10.3: in earlier ages Devaki and Vasudeva were Prishni and Sutapa, then Aditi and Kashyapa, and each time Vishnu was born as their son.
The return of her six slain sons is told only in the Bhagavata (10.85).

nodes.name: Vasudeva
