nodes.description: The Yadava (Vrishni) prince who fathered Krishna and Balarama, son of Shurasena and brother of Kunti. His epithet Anakadundubhi recalls the celestial drums that sounded at his birth; his patronymic gave Krishna the name Vasudeva (with a long a).
nodes.story: At Vasudeva's wedding to Devaki, her cousin Kamsa was driving the bridal chariot when a voice from the sky declared that her eighth child would kill him. Kamsa seized his cousin by the hair and drew his sword. Vasudeva calmly reasoned with him: killing a bride on her wedding day would bring infamy, and death comes to all in any case; the danger lay not in Devaki but in her children, and he swore to hand over every one of them. Kamsa relented. When their first son was born, Vasudeva, true to his word, carried the infant to Kamsa, who was moved and returned the child. But when Narada later reminded Kamsa that the Yadavas were gods born to destroy him, Kamsa threw the couple in chains and began killing their sons, setting the stage for Krishna's secret birth.
variations: Harivamsha: Vasudeva is the rebirth of Kashyapa, cursed by Brahma to be born as a cowherd-king for stealing Varuna's cows; Bhagavata: of Prajapati Sutapa and then Kashyapa.
Lists of his wives differ: the Bhagavata names Rohini, Devaki and several of Devaki's sisters among others.
Mahabharata, Mausala Parva: he died of grief after the destruction of the Yadavas, and four of his wives entered his funeral pyre.

nodes.name: Shurasena
nodes.description: A Yadava king of the Vrishni branch, father of Vasudeva and of Pritha (Kunti), and thus grandfather of both Krishna and the Pandavas. His name also belongs to the Shurasena country around Mathura.
nodes.story: Shura, chief of the Vrishnis, was bound by friendship to his cousin Kuntibhoja, who had no children. Keeping a promise made long before, Shura gave his firstborn daughter Pritha to Kuntibhoja to raise as his own, and so she became known as Kunti. In her adoptive father's house she served the irascible sage Durvasa so well that he taught her the mantra by which she later called down the gods and bore Karna and the Pandavas. Shura's son Vasudeva was born to great portents: the gods, knowing that Vishnu would take birth in his house, sounded their kettledrums in the heavens, and the child was named Anakadundubhi. Through this one king the two great lines of the epics, the Pandavas and the family of Krishna, are joined as cousins.
variations: The Mahabharata usually calls him Shura; Shurasena is also the name of the Mathura region and of an earlier king of the Yadu line.
The Bhagavata makes him son of Devamidha; genealogies of the Yadavas differ considerably between the Puranas.

nodes.name: Nanda
nodes.description: Chief of the cowherds of Gokula and Vraja, husband of Yashoda and foster father of Krishna. A friend of Vasudeva, he raised Krishna as his own son; in devotional traditions he embodies parental love (vatsalya) for God.
nodes.story: After fasting on the Ekadashi, Nanda entered the Yamuna before dawn to bathe, not noticing that the auspicious hour had not yet begun. A servant of Varuna, lord of the waters, seized him and dragged him down to Varuna's palace. The cowherds on the shore cried out for Krishna, who plunged into the river and came before Varuna. The god of the ocean received him with the highest worship, begged forgiveness for his servant's ignorance, and returned Nanda at once. Back on the bank, Nanda told the astonished villagers of the splendour of Varuna's court and how its lord had bowed before his little son. The cowherds began to wonder whether Krishna was really God, and Krishna, to fulfil their longing, showed them a vision of his own spiritual realm.
variations: Bhagavata 10.8: Nanda and Yashoda were the Vasu Drona and his wife Dhara, who received from Brahma the boon of pure devotion to Hari on earth.
The rescue from Varuna (Bhagavata 10.28) and the swallowing of Nanda by a python (10.34) are Bhagavata episodes.

Some Gaudiya Vaishnava commentators hold that Krishna was also born to Yashoda alongside Yogamaya, making the Krishna of Vraja truly Nanda's son (Vrajendra-nandana); mainstream texts treat Nanda as foster father.

nodes.name: Yashoda
nodes.description: Wife of Nanda and foster mother of Krishna in Gokula, to whom the infant was secretly brought on the night of his birth. Her tender, scolding love for the child-god is celebrated in the Bhagavata, Surdas and countless devotional songs.
nodes.story: One day the cowherd boys ran to Yashoda crying that little Krishna had eaten mud. She caught him by the hand and scolded him, but he denied it: they were lying, he said, and she could look for herself. Yashoda told him to open his mouth. Inside, she saw the whole universe: the heavens and the directions, mountains, islands and oceans, the moving and unmoving beings, the elements, time and nature, and even Vraja and herself standing before her child. Bewildered, she wondered whether it was a dream, a delusion or her son's divine power, and she bowed to the Lord who is beyond thought. Then Krishna spread his Yogamaya over her again; she forgot what she had seen, lifted him onto her lap and loved him as her own little boy once more.
variations: The girl born to Yashoda and exchanged for Krishna is Nidra/Ekanamsha in the Harivamsha and Yogamaya in the Bhagavata; she is later worshipped as Vindhyavasini.
Bhagavata 10.8: Yashoda was formerly Dhara, wife of the Vasu Drona.

nodes.name: Radha
nodes.description: The cowherd maiden of Vraja who is Krishna's supreme beloved, worshipped as the embodiment of devotional love (prema) and, in several Vaishnava schools, as Krishna's own divine energy of bliss (hladini shakti), inseparable from him. Radha and Krishna together are adored as the divine couple (Radha-Krishna, Yugala).
nodes.story: Jayadeva's Gita Govinda sings of a spring night in Vrindavan when Radha finds Krishna dancing and playing with the other cowherd women. Wounded, she withdraws into a bower and pines for him, while Krishna, remembering her alone among all, wanders the banks of the Yamuna repentant and lovesick. Radha's confidante goes back and forth between them bearing messages. At dawn Krishna comes to her, but Radha, still hurt, turns him away. At last, when her anger has melted into longing, the friend leads her to the bower where he waits, and the two are reunited in joy. Tradition says Jayadeva hesitated to write the verse in which Krishna asks to place Radha's foot upon his head; returning from his bath he found it written in his manuscript by Krishna himself.
symbols: blue garment (in contrast to Krishna's yellow)
nodes.abode: Barsana and Vrindavan in Vraja; Goloka in devotional theology
sources: Brahmavaivarta Purana (Krishna Janma and Prakriti Khandas)
Works of the Gaudiya Gosvamins (e.g. Rupa Gosvami's Ujjvala Nilamani)
variations: Radha is absent by name from the Mahabharata, Harivamsha, Vishnu Purana and Bhagavata Purana; devotees read Bhagavata 10.30 (the gopi Krishna takes aside during the rasa dance, 'anayaradhito') as a veiled reference to her.

Early secular references appear in Prakrit poetry such as the Gatha Saptashati (early first millennium CE); she becomes central in Jayadeva's Gita Govinda (12th century) and the Brahmavaivarta Purana.

Brahmavaivarta: Radha emerges from Krishna's left side in Goloka, is cursed by Shridama to take birth on earth, and is married to Krishna by Brahma in the Bhandira forest; it also counts her among the five principal forms of Prakriti.
Nimbarka and Vallabha schools worship Radha with Krishna; Gaudiya Vaishnavism holds her to be Krishna's hladini shakti and the source of Lakshmi, and sees Chaitanya as Radha and Krishna combined.
Traditions differ on whether her love is svakiya (as wife) or parakiya (beyond marriage); some texts give her a husband (Ayana or Abhimanyu), while others deny this.
She is often described as a form of Lakshmi; in Shakta-influenced texts as a form of the Great Goddess.

nodes.name: Rukmini
nodes.description: Princess of Vidarbha, daughter of King Bhishmaka and sister of Rukmi, who became Krishna's first and chief queen at Dvaraka and mother of Pradyumna. She is revered as an incarnation of Lakshmi and worshipped with Vithoba at Pandharpur.
nodes.story: Rukmini had given her heart to Krishna from hearing of his virtues, but her brother Rukmi insisted she marry his friend Shishupala of Chedi, and the wedding was fixed. In despair she sent a trusted brahmin to Dvaraka with a letter: she had chosen Krishna as her husband; he should come and carry her off, not from the palace, where blood would be shed, but when she went out, as was custom, to worship the Goddess at her temple on the eve of the wedding. Krishna raced to Kundina. As Rukmini stepped out of the shrine, he lifted her into his chariot before the assembled kings. Rukmi pursued and was defeated; Krishna spared his life at Rukmini's plea, shaving his head in humiliation, and the couple were married in Dvaraka.
variations: The famous seven-verse letter to Krishna is found in the Bhagavata (10.52); the Harivamsha and Vishnu Purana tell the abduction without it.
Mahabharata, Mausala Parva: after Krishna's death Rukmini, with Jambavati and others, entered the funeral fire.
A Dvaraka tradition says Durvasa cursed Rukmini to live apart from Krishna, explaining her separate temple there.
The Tulabharam story, where Rukmini's single tulasi leaf outweighs Satyabhama's gold, is a regional devotional tale.

nodes.name: Satyabhama
nodes.description: Daughter of the Yadava noble Satrajit, owner of the Syamantaka jewel, and one of Krishna's principal queens. Proud and spirited, she rode with Krishna into battle against Narakasura and demanded the heavenly Parijata tree; many traditions see her as an incarnation of Bhudevi, the Earth.
nodes.story: After Krishna slew Narakasura and returned the stolen earrings of Aditi to heaven, Satyabhama, who had ridden with him on Garuda, saw the Parijata tree growing in Indra's garden, born from the churning of the ocean and fragrant beyond any earthly flower. She longed to plant it in her own courtyard at Dvaraka. Indra's queen Shachi, disdaining a mortal woman, would not share it. Krishna uprooted the tree and placed it on Garuda's back; when Indra and the gods pursued, he defeated them. Satyabhama then told Indra that she had wanted only to humble Shachi's pride and offered to give the tree back, but Indra, acknowledging Krishna, let it go. The Parijata was planted in Satyabhama's garden, to remain on earth only as long as Krishna did.
weapons: bow (in the Narakasura battle, in later retellings)
variations: Harivamsha: Narada brings a single Parijata blossom which Krishna gives to Rukmini; Satyabhama's jealousy prompts Krishna to fetch the whole tree. Vishnu Purana and Bhagavata set the episode after the killing of Narakasura, with Shachi refusing the flower.

Bhagavata 10.59: Krishna kills Narakasura while Satyabhama rides beside him on Garuda; regional traditions (especially in the south and in Deepavali lore) say Satyabhama herself killed Naraka, since as Bhudevi she was his mother and he could die only by her hand.
The Syamantaka jewel story (Harivamsha, Vishnu Purana 4.13, Bhagavata 10.56–57) explains how Satrajit gave her to Krishna.
Mahabharata, Mausala Parva: after Krishna's death she retired to the forest as an ascetic.
The Telugu Parijatapaharanamu of Nandi Timmana and the folk Tulabharam story are later regional works.

nodes.name: Jambavati
nodes.description: Daughter of the bear-king Jambavan and one of Krishna's principal queens, mother of Samba. She came to Krishna together with the Syamantaka jewel at the end of his long duel with her father.
nodes.story: When Prasena of the Yadavas went hunting wearing the radiant Syamantaka jewel, he was killed by a lion, and the lion in turn by Jambavan, the ancient king of the bears, who carried the gem to his cave. Dvaraka whispered that Krishna had killed Prasena for the jewel. To clear his name Krishna followed the tracks into the dark cave, where he found the jewel hanging as a plaything above a child's cradle while the nurse sang of it. Jambavan rushed at the intruder, and the two fought for twenty-eight days. At last the exhausted bear-king realised that only his lord Rama could match such strength; recognising Rama in Krishna, he bowed, returned the Syamantaka, and gave him his daughter Jambavati in marriage.
variations: The duel lasts twenty-one days in the Vishnu Purana and twenty-eight in the Bhagavata.
Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva: Krishna underwent austerities to Shiva, initiated by the sage Upamanyu, so that Jambavati might bear a son, and was blessed with Samba.
Mahabharata, Mausala Parva: she entered the funeral fire after Krishna's death.

nodes.name: Rukmi
nodes.description: Eldest son of King Bhishmaka of Vidarbha and brother of Rukmini, a mighty archer who owned the celestial bow Vijaya. A friend of Shishupala and Jarasandha and an implacable enemy of Krishna, he was killed by Balarama after a quarrel over dice.
nodes.story: When Krishna carried off Rukmini, her brother Rukmi swore before the kings that he would not return to Kundina until he had killed Krishna and brought his sister back. He overtook the chariot and fought furiously, but Krishna shattered his weapons and was about to kill him when Rukmini fell at Krishna's feet and begged for her brother's life. Krishna bound him and shaved his head and beard in patches, a humiliation Balarama rebuked as unworthy of kinsmen. Unable to go home, Rukmi founded the city of Bhojakata. Years later, at the wedding of his granddaughter Rochana to Krishna's grandson Aniruddha, he challenged Balarama to dice, cheated, and mocked him as a cowherd who knew nothing of the game. When a heavenly voice declared Balarama the winner, Rukmi jeered again, and Balarama struck him dead with his club.
variations: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva: a pupil of the Kimpurusha Druma, he owned Vijaya, one of three celestial bows with Gandiva and Sharnga; he offered his army first to Arjuna and then to Duryodhana, and both refused him because of his boasting, so he sat out the war.
His daughter Rukmavati married Pradyumna and his granddaughter Rochana married Aniruddha (Bhagavata 10.61).
Accounts of the dice game differ in detail; in several versions Balarama also knocks out the teeth of the king of Kalinga, who had laughed at him.

nodes.name: Pradyumna
nodes.description: The eldest son of Krishna and Rukmini, the rebirth of Kamadeva, the god of love, after Shiva burned him to ashes. Stolen as an infant by the demon Shambara, he grew up in the demon's house, killed him and returned to Dvaraka with Rati; in Pancharatra theology he is the third vyuha of Vishnu.
nodes.story: Kamadeva, burned by Shiva's third eye, was reborn as the son of Krishna and Rukmini. The demon Shambara, who knew the child would one day kill him, stole the baby from the birthing chamber within days of his birth and flung him into the sea. A great fish swallowed the child; fishermen caught it and presented it to Shambara, and when the cooks cut it open the boy was found alive inside. Shambara's housekeeper Mayavati, who was Rati awaiting her husband and had been told the truth by Narada, raised him. When he came of age she revealed who he was and taught him the magic that overcomes illusion. Pradyumna challenged Shambara, defeated all his sorceries and cut off his head, then flew with Rati to Dvaraka, where the women at first mistook him for Krishna himself.
variations: Accounts differ on how many days old he was when stolen (six in the Bhagavata, seven in some other texts).

In Pancharatra and Bhagavata theology the four vyuhas are Vasudeva, Sankarshana, Pradyumna and Aniruddha; a 1st-century CE inscription at Mora near Mathura honours five Vrishni heroes including Pradyumna and Samba.
He also married Rukmi's daughter Rukmavati. He was killed in the drunken brawl at Prabhasa (Mausala Parva).

nodes.name: Aniruddha
nodes.description: Son of Pradyumna and grandson of Krishna, the beloved of the asura princess Usha, whose secret marriage led to a great war between Krishna and Banasura, who was protected by Shiva. In Pancharatra theology he is the fourth vyuha of Vishnu.
nodes.story: Carried by magic from his bed in Dvaraka to the inner chambers of Usha in Shonitapura, Aniruddha lived there secretly with the princess who had dreamed of him. When her father Banasura's guards discovered the prince, Aniruddha seized an iron club and cut down all who attacked him, until the thousand-armed Bana bound him with serpent-weapons. At Dvaraka the Yadavas searched in vain for four months, until Narada told them where he was held. Krishna, Balarama and Pradyumna marched on Shonitapura riding Garuda. Shiva himself came out to defend his devotee Bana with his ganas and fever-spirit, and the battle shook the worlds, until Krishna stunned Shiva with a weapon of yawning and began lopping off Bana's arms. At Shiva's plea Bana was spared, and Aniruddha and Usha returned to Dvaraka in honour.
variations: His first wife was Rochana, Rukmi's granddaughter (Bhagavata 10.61); his son Vajra survived the Mausala and was installed by Arjuna at Indraprastha.
Bhagavata 10.63 has Krishna leave Bana four arms; other texts give two.
In the Harivamsha the battle ends with Shiva and Krishna declaring their identity, a key Harihara passage.

nodes.name: Usha (daughter of Bana)
nodes.description: The daughter of the thousand-armed asura king Banasura of Shonitapura, who fell in love with Aniruddha after seeing him in a dream. Her secret union with Krishna's grandson provoked the war between Krishna and Bana; she is not to be confused with the Vedic dawn goddess Ushas.
nodes.story: Watching Shiva and Parvati together, the young Usha longed for a husband, and Parvati promised that she would meet him in a dream. One night a handsome youth came to her in sleep and vanished at dawn, leaving her desolate. Her friend Chitralekha, a gifted painter and yogini, drew portraits of every notable prince of gods, gandharvas and men; when she reached the Vrishnis, Usha blushed at the picture of Aniruddha, Krishna's grandson. That same night Chitralekha flew by her magic powers to Dvaraka and carried the sleeping prince on his bed back to Usha's palace. The two lived together in secret, hidden in the maiden's apartments, until her guards noticed the signs and informed Banasura, setting in motion a war that brought Krishna and Shiva face to face.
variations: The Harivamsha gives Parvati's promise and names the day of the dream; the Bhagavata tells the story more briefly.
Regional traditions place Shonitapura in Assam (Tezpur) or the Himalaya; in Gujarat she is Okha, and the Okhaharan is a popular folk narrative.

nodes.name: Samba
nodes.description: Son of Krishna and Jambavati, a handsome and headstrong Yadava prince whose prank on visiting sages brought down the curse of the iron pestle that destroyed the Yadava clan. Later tradition credits him with founding sun-worship at a temple on the Chandrabhaga after being healed of leprosy.
nodes.story: Some time after the great war, the sages Vishvamitra, Kanva and Narada came to Dvaraka. The young Yadavas, bent on mockery, dressed Samba as a pregnant woman and presented him to the seers: this is the wife of Babhru, who longs for a son; tell us what she will bear. The sages saw through the insult and replied that she would bring forth a terrible iron pestle that would destroy the Vrishnis and Andhakas, sparing only Balarama and Krishna. The next day Samba delivered an iron club. King Ugrasena had it ground to powder and cast into the sea, and banned wine in the city, but rushes grew from the powder on the shore. Years later at Prabhasa, drunk and quarrelling, the Yadavas snatched up those rushes, which turned into iron clubs in their hands, and slaughtered one another.
variations: Mahabharata, Mausala Parva names Vishvamitra, Kanva and Narada; Bhagavata 11.1 lists a larger group of sages at Pindaraka, including Durvasa, Bhrigu, Angiras, Kashyapa, Atri, Vashistha and Narada.

Bhagavata 10.68: Samba carried off Duryodhana's daughter Lakshmana from her svayamvara and was captured by the Kauravas; Balarama freed him by threatening to drag Hastinapura into the Ganga with his plough.

Samba and Bhavishya Puranas: Krishna cursed Samba with leprosy (after Narada engineered his presence among Krishna's wives); he was cured by worshipping Surya and founded a sun temple at Mitravana on the Chandrabhaga (associated with Multan and later with Konark).
The Mora well inscription near Mathura (1st century CE) honours him among the five Vrishni heroes.

nodes.name: Kamsa
nodes.description: The tyrant king of Mathura, son of Ugrasena, who imprisoned his own father, persecuted his cousin Devaki and tried repeatedly to kill the infant Krishna. Son-in-law and ally of Jarasandha, he was slain by Krishna in the wrestling arena of Mathura; the Puranas identify him as the reborn asura Kalanemi.
nodes.story: Failing to kill Krishna with demons in Vraja, Kamsa invited the brothers to a bow festival in Mathura, planning to finish them in the arena. At the gate the rogue elephant Kuvalayapida charged them; Krishna pulled out its tusk and killed it. Inside, the champion wrestlers Chanura and Mushtika fell to Krishna and Balarama. Furious, Kamsa ordered the cowherds driven out, Nanda arrested and Vasudeva and Ugrasena killed. Krishna leapt onto the royal dais, seized Kamsa by the hair as he raised his sword, flung him down into the arena and fell on him, crushing out his life. The Bhagavata adds that Kamsa, who had thought of Krishna night and day in fear, while eating, walking and sleeping, attained the same form as the Lord. Krishna freed his parents and restored Ugrasena to the throne.
variations: Harivamsha and Bhagavata 10.1: Kamsa was the rebirth of the asura Kalanemi, slain by Vishnu in an earlier age.
Some retellings make his real father the Danava Drumila, who seduced Ugrasena's queen in the king's form, explaining Kamsa's demonic nature.
His wives Asti and Prapti were daughters of Jarasandha, whose repeated attacks on Mathura avenged Kamsa's death.
Devaki is his cousin (daughter of Ugrasena's brother Devaka) but is often called his sister.

nodes.name: Jarasandha
nodes.description: The powerful emperor of Magadha, a devotee of Shiva and father-in-law of Kamsa, who besieged Mathura again and again and forced the Yadavas to move to Dvaraka. He was killed by Bhima in single combat with Krishna's guidance, opening the way for Yudhishthira's Rajasuya.
nodes.story: King Brihadratha of Magadha had no heir until the sage Chandakaushika gave him a blessed mango. The king divided it between his two queens, and each bore half a child: one eye, one arm, one leg. Horrified, the queens had the halves thrown out. A rakshasi named Jara found them and, to carry them more easily, pressed them together; the halves joined into a mighty, crying boy, who was named Jarasandha, 'joined by Jara'. Grown to be emperor, he imprisoned eighty-six kings to sacrifice to Rudra. Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna came to Girivraja disguised as brahmins and challenged him to single combat. Jarasandha chose Bhima. They wrestled for thirteen days and nights; on the fourteenth, as the king tired, Bhima lifted him, whirled him a hundred times and broke him, and the captive kings were freed.
variations: Bhagavata 10.72 and later retellings: Krishna signals to Bhima by splitting a twig, and Bhima tears Jarasandha into his two original halves; the Mahabharata has Bhima break him on his knee.

Bhagavata 10.50: Jarasandha attacked Mathura seventeen times and was defeated each time; on the eighteenth, allied with Kalayavana, Krishna moved the Yadavas to Dvaraka. Other texts give eighteen assaults.
Mahabharata, Shanti Parva: Karna once defeated Jarasandha in a wrestling bout and received the city of Malini from him.

nodes.name: Shishupala
nodes.description: King of Chedi, son of Damaghosha and of Shrutashrava, Vasudeva's sister, and thus Krishna's cousin. A general of Jarasandha and the rejected suitor of Rukmini, he insulted Krishna at Yudhishthira's Rajasuya and was beheaded by the Sudarshana discus.
nodes.story: Shishupala was born with three eyes and four arms, braying like an ass, and his parents wished to abandon him until a voice declared that the child was mighty, and that the one on whose lap his extra eye and arms fell away would be his slayer. When Krishna came to Chedi and took the baby on his lap, the extra limbs vanished. His aunt begged Krishna to spare her son, and he promised to forgive a hundred of Shishupala's offences. Years later, at the Rajasuya of Yudhishthira, Bhishma proposed that the first honour be given to Krishna. Shishupala rose in fury, reviling Krishna, Bhishma and the Pandavas and recounting slanders without end. When the hundredth offence was passed, Krishna released his discus and severed Shishupala's head; a radiance rose from the body and, before all the kings, entered Krishna.
variations: Bhagavata 7.1: Vishnu's gatekeepers Jaya and Vijaya, cursed by the Kumaras, were born as Hiranyakashipu and Hiranyaksha, then Ravana and Kumbhakarna, then Shishupala and Dantavakra; popular tradition identifies Shishupala with Jaya, though assignments vary.
Vishnu Purana 4.14–15 says the same being was Hiranyakashipu, then Ravana, then Shishupala, and was finally liberated by dying at Krishna's hand while thinking of him in hatred.
The Bhagavata gives him a birth tale in brief; the full account of the extra limbs is in the Mahabharata, Sabha Parva. Magha's 7th-century epic Shishupalavadha retells his death.

nodes.name: Putana
nodes.description: A demoness sent by Kamsa to kill the newborn children of Vraja, who tried to suckle the infant Krishna with poisoned breasts and had her life drawn out by him. Because she had offered him her breast, even as an enemy, the Bhagavata says she attained the realm of a mother.
nodes.story: Sent by Kamsa to kill every infant in the villages, Putana flew into Gokula and took the form of a lovely woman, her hair wreathed in jasmine. So charming was she that Yashoda and Rohini, dazzled, let her lift the baby Krishna from his cradle. She put him to her breast, smeared with deadly poison. Krishna, pressing her breast tight with both hands, sucked out her very life with the milk. Screaming 'let go, let go', she ran out, her true form bursting forth, and fell dead, her enormous body crushing trees for miles around. The terrified cowherds cut the corpse to pieces and burned it, and the smoke rose fragrant as aloe wood, because her body had been purified by nursing the Lord. The gopis then performed protective rites over the child.
variations: The Harivamsha calls her Kamsa's foster-nurse and describes her coming in the form of a bird (shakuni).
Bhagavata 10.6 describes her beauty, her giant corpse and her liberation to the destination of a mother.
Later devotional texts (e.g. the Garga Samhita) say she was formerly Ratnamala, daughter of Bali, who wished to nurse Vamana as her son.
In Ayurvedic texts such as the Sushruta Samhita, Putana is one of the grahas, spirits that afflict children.

nodes.name: Kaliya
nodes.description: A many-headed venomous naga who poisoned a pool of the Yamuna near Vrindavan, until the boy Krishna subdued him by dancing on his hoods. Spared at the plea of his wives, he was sent back to the island of Ramanaka, safe from Garuda.
nodes.story: Fleeing his enemy Garuda, Kaliya settled in a deep pool of the Yamuna where Garuda could not come, because the sage Saubhari had cursed him. The serpent's venom made the water boil; birds flying over fell dead and cows and cowherd boys who drank there collapsed. Krishna climbed a kadamba tree and leapt into the pool. Kaliya coiled around him while the people of Vraja wept on the bank. Then Krishna slipped free, sprang onto the serpent's raised hoods and danced upon them, stamping down every head that rose, until Kaliya vomited blood and was near death. His wives, the naga-patnis, came forward with folded hands and praised Krishna, begging for their husband's life. Krishna spared Kaliya and ordered him to return to Ramanaka Dvipa, assuring him that Garuda would not harm him once he bore Krishna's footprints.
nodes.abode: Kaliya's pool in the Yamuna; Ramanaka Dvipa
variations: The Harivamsha gives Kaliya five heads; the Bhagavata describes a hundred or more hoods, and iconography varies.
The curse of Saubhari on Garuda, explaining why Kaliya's pool was safe, is told in the Bhagavata (10.17).
Kaliya-mardana, Krishna dancing on the serpent, is a favourite subject of South Indian bronzes and temple festivals.

nodes.name: Sudama (Kuchela)
nodes.description: The poor brahmin schoolmate of Krishna at Sandipani's ashram whose visit to Dvaraka with a handful of flattened rice became the classic tale of friendship between God and devotee. The Bhagavata leaves him unnamed; the names Sudama and Kuchela come from later tradition.
nodes.story: Living in bitter poverty, the brahmin was urged by his wife to visit his old friend Krishna, now lord of Dvaraka. Having nothing to bring, he tied a few handfuls of flattened rice, begged from neighbours, in a corner of his ragged cloth. At the palace Krishna leapt from Rukmini's couch, embraced him, seated him on his own bed, washed his feet and sprinkled the water on his own head, while Rukmini fanned the guest. They talked of their days at the guru's ashram. Ashamed, the brahmin hid his gift, but Krishna pulled it out and ate a handful with delight; as he reached for a second, Rukmini gently caught his hand. The brahmin left without asking for anything, only to find on his return that his hut had become a palace and his wife was richly adorned.
symbols: flattened rice (poha, aval) in a torn cloth
variations: The Bhagavata calls him only a brahmin friend of Krishna; the name Sudama is attested in later devotional literature, and Kuchela ('one in poor clothes') is used in South India.
A different Sudama in the Bhagavata (10.41) is a garland-maker of Mathura, and Shridama is a cowherd friend of Krishna in Vraja; retellings sometimes conflate them.
Kuchela Dinam, the first Wednesday of Dhanu, is observed at Guruvayur; Porbandar in Gujarat claims to be his home town.

nodes.name: Akrura
nodes.description: A Yadava elder of the Vrishni line, son of Shvaphalka and Gandini, whom Kamsa sent to bring Krishna and Balarama from Vraja to Mathura. A great devotee, he received a vision of Vishnu in the Yamuna and later served Krishna as envoy and counsellor.
nodes.story: Ordered by Kamsa to fetch the brothers for the bow festival, Akrura set out for Vraja in rapture, longing to see the Lord. At dusk he reached Gokula, saw Krishna's footprints in the dust and rolled in them with tears. Next morning, as he drove the boys towards Mathura while the gopis wept at the parting, he stopped at the Yamuna to bathe and recite his prayers. Under the water he saw Krishna and Balarama, though he had left them in the chariot. He surfaced, saw them sitting there, and dived again: now he beheld the thousand-headed Ananta Shesha, and on his coils the four-armed Vishnu in yellow silk, attended by sages and gods. Overwhelmed, Akrura poured out a hymn of praise. When the vision faded, he returned to the chariot trembling, and Krishna asked innocently whether he had seen something wonderful.
symbols: Syamantaka jewel (held by him in some versions)
variations: Vishnu Purana 4.13 and Bhagavata 10.57: after Shatadhanva killed Satrajit, the Syamantaka came into Akrura's keeping; he left Dvaraka for a time, and famine followed until he returned.
Bhagavata 10.48–49: Krishna sent him to Hastinapura, where he consoled Kunti and warned Dhritarashtra about his treatment of the Pandavas.
The vision in the Yamuna is told at length in the Bhagavata (10.39–40) and briefly in the Vishnu Purana.

nodes.name: Uddhava
nodes.description: Krishna's cousin, friend and counsellor, a disciple of Brihaspati famed for his wisdom, who carried Krishna's message to the grieving gopis of Vraja. Before his departure from the world Krishna taught him the Uddhava Gita, the last great discourse of the Bhagavata.
nodes.story: Missing Vraja, Krishna sent Uddhava, the wisest of the Yadavas, to console Nanda, Yashoda and the gopis with a message: Krishna was never truly apart from them, being the Self of all, and they should meditate on him. Uddhava arrived proud of his knowledge. But when the gopis gathered around him, one, seeing a bumblebee, addressed it as Krishna's fickle messenger in a torrent of loving reproach, and all of them poured out such longing that Uddhava's learning seemed dry beside it. He stayed for months, listening to their songs of Krishna. Humbled, he prayed that in some future birth he might be a shrub or creeper in Vrindavan, so as to be touched by the dust of the gopis' feet, who had given up everything for Krishna. He returned to Mathura transformed by their devotion.
variations: Bhagavata 10.46–47 contains the embassy to Vraja and the Bhramara Gita (Song of the Bee); many devotional readers identify the gopi speaking to the bee as Radha.
The Uddhava Gita (Bhagavata 11.7–29) is Krishna's final teaching; afterwards he sends Uddhava to Badarikashrama.
Bhagavata Canto 3: Uddhava tells Vidura of Krishna's departure and the destruction of the Yadavas.
In the Mahabharata he is a minor Vrishni counsellor; his role grows greatly in the Bhagavata.

nodes.name: Sandipani
nodes.description: The brahmin teacher of Avanti (Ujjain), of the Kashyapa lineage, under whom Krishna and Balarama studied after Kamsa's death, mastering the Vedas, archery and the sixty-four arts in as many days. Sudama was their fellow student.
nodes.story: After Kamsa's death Krishna and Balarama, having received the sacred thread, went to live in the ashram of Sandipani at Avanti, serving him like any pupils. In sixty-four days and nights they learned the sixty-four arts, the Vedas and their limbs, and the science of arms. When they asked what fee they could offer, Sandipani and his wife, after consulting together, asked for their son, who had drowned in the sea at Prabhasa. The brothers went to the shore; the ocean told them a demon named Panchajana, dwelling in a conch shell, had taken the boy. Krishna dived in and killed the demon, but did not find the child in his body. Taking the conch, which became his Panchajanya, he went to Yama's city and blew it. Yama came out in reverence and returned the boy, whom Krishna restored to his guru.
nodes.abode: Avanti (Ujjain), where the Sandipani ashram is still shown
variations: Texts agree on sixty-four days of study but differ slightly in how the time was divided among subjects.
The Harivamsha and Vishnu Purana tell the recovery of the guru's son; the Bhagavata (10.45) adds the full scene at Yama's court.

nodes.name: Jara
nodes.description: The hunter whose arrow, mistaking Krishna's foot for a deer, brought about Krishna's departure from the world after the destruction of the Yadavas. His name means 'old age', and he is not to be confused with the rakshasi Jara who joined Jarasandha's two halves.
nodes.story: After the Yadavas had destroyed one another at Prabhasa and Balarama had left his body, Krishna withdrew into the forest and lay down under a tree, absorbed in yoga, one foot resting on his knee. A hunter named Jara, prowling for game, saw the reddish sole through the leaves and took it for a deer. He loosed an arrow, which, the Bhagavata says, was tipped with the last iron fragment of the cursed pestle, swallowed by a fish and found by the hunter. Running up to claim his prize, Jara saw the four-armed Lord in yellow silk and fell at his feet in horror, begging to be killed for his sin. Krishna comforted him, telling him that all this had happened by his own will, and Jara ascended to heaven in a celestial chariot. Soon after, Krishna left the world.
variations: The Mausala Parva has Jara pierce Krishna's sole; the Bhagavata (11.30) and Vishnu Purana add that the arrowhead came from the remaining piece of the iron pestle.
A popular later tradition says Jara was Vali reborn, so that Rama's killing of Vali from hiding was repaid; this is not found in the Mahabharata or Bhagavata.
The place is identified with Bhalka Tirtha near Somnath in Gujarat.

nodes.name: Subhadra
nodes.description: Daughter of Vasudeva and sister of Krishna and Balarama, who married Arjuna and became the mother of Abhimanyu. She is worshipped with Jagannatha and Balabhadra in the triad of the Puri temple.
nodes.story: During a festival on Mount Raivataka near Dvaraka, Arjuna saw Subhadra among her attendants and fell in love. Krishna, smiling, told his friend that a svayamvara was uncertain; for a kshatriya, carrying off a bride by force was an honourable way. With Yudhishthira's consent, Arjuna waited until Subhadra went to worship at the mountain, lifted her into his chariot and drove towards Indraprastha. The Vrishnis sounded the war drums, and Balarama, furious that their guest had insulted the clan, vowed to wipe the Kurus from the earth. Krishna calmed him: Arjuna had honoured them by choosing their sister and was a match for anyone in battle; better to bring him back as a son-in-law. The marriage was celebrated, and at Indraprastha Subhadra, dressed as a simple cowherd woman, won Draupadi's affection.
variations: Texts differ on her mother: Bhagavata 9.24 makes her a daughter of Vasudeva and Devaki, while other traditions make her Rohini's daughter and so Balarama's full sister.
Bhagavata 10.86: Arjuna came to Dvaraka disguised as an ascetic, and Balarama had intended her for Duryodhana.
At Puri she is sometimes identified with Ekanamsha or Yogamaya, the goddess born to Yashoda.

nodes.name: Hidimbi
nodes.description: A rakshasi of the forest beyond Varanavata who fell in love with Bhima and became his first wife. Sent by her brother Hidimba to lure the sleeping Pandavas to their death, she warned Bhima instead and later bore him Ghatotkacha. In the Kullu valley of Himachal Pradesh she is worshipped as the goddess Hadimba Devi.
nodes.story: After escaping the burning house of lac, the exhausted Pandavas and Kunti slept beneath a tree in a dark forest while Bhima kept watch. The man-eating rakshasa Hidimba, smelling human flesh, sent his sister Hidimbi to fetch them. But on seeing the mighty Bhima she fell in love, took on a lovely human form and begged him to flee with her. Bhima refused to abandon his sleeping family, and when the furious Hidimba arrived, Bhima wrestled and killed him. Hidimbi then turned to Kunti and Yudhishthira, pleading that she could not live without Bhima. Moved, they consented: she might roam with him by day and return him each night until a son was born. That son was Ghatotkacha, after whose birth Hidimbi departed, as agreed.
variations: The Critical Edition names her Hidimba, like her brother; the form Hidimbi is common in later retellings.
In Manali, Himachal Pradesh, she is venerated as Hadimba Devi, a goddess of the Kullu royal house, in a temple built in 1553; local lore says she renounced her rakshasa nature through penance there.

nodes.name: Hidimba
nodes.description: A man-eating rakshasa who ruled a forest near Varanavata and was the brother of Hidimbi. He was the first rakshasa slain by Bhima, in a ferocious wrestling match fought while the other Pandavas slept.
nodes.story: Hidimba, a huge dark cannibal with tawny eyes and long fangs, sat in a sala tree in the forest beyond Varanavata. Catching the scent of humans, he sent his sister to bring them to him. When she lingered, having fallen for Bhima, he came roaring after her and threatened to kill her too. Bhima, not wishing to wake his sleeping mother and brothers, dragged the rakshasa away. The two grappled like maddened elephants, uprooting trees and raising clouds of dust until the others awoke. Arjuna offered to help, teasing Bhima for taking so long. Stung, Bhima whirled Hidimba overhead a hundred times, dashed him to the ground and broke him in the middle like a beast, and the forest was freed of its terror.
variations: In the Vana Parva the rakshasa Kirmira, slain by Bhima in the Kamyaka forest, names himself a friend of Hidimba and brother of Baka.

nodes.name: Ghatotkacha
nodes.description: The half-rakshasa son of Bhima and Hidimbi, named for his bald, pot-shaped head. He grew to manhood the day he was born, served the Pandavas whenever they called on him, and fell on the fourteenth night of the Kurukshetra war to the Shakti weapon that Karna had reserved for Arjuna.
nodes.story: On the fourteenth night of the war, when the fighting continued by torchlight, Ghatotkacha came into his own, for rakshasas grow stronger in the dark. Swelling to monstrous size and raining rocks, trees and weapons through a storm of illusions, he broke the Kaurava lines until Duryodhana's warriors begged Karna to save them. Karna held a single unfailing dart, the Shakti Indra had given him in exchange for his armour and earrings, which he had kept for Arjuna. With no choice left, he hurled it. The dart pierced Ghatotkacha's heart and returned to Indra. Even in death the rakshasa served his family, expanding as he fell and crushing a great host of Kaurava troops beneath him. The Pandavas wept, but Krishna rejoiced, for Arjuna was now safe.
variations: His son Anjanaparvan is killed by Ashwatthama in the Drona Parva; Barbarika as his son comes from the Skanda Purana and folk tradition.
His wife is unnamed in the Critical Edition; the Skanda Purana calls her Kamakantakata (Maurvi), daughter of Mura, while folk tradition calls her Ahilawati.
In the Telugu tale Sasirekha Parinayam (the film Mayabazar) he uses his illusions to win Balarama's daughter for Abhimanyu.
In Javanese wayang, Gatotkaca is a flying hero with muscles of wire and bones of iron, among the best-loved figures of the shadow theatre.

nodes.name: Barbarika
nodes.description: The son of Ghatotkacha, a peerless archer who in the Skanda Purana and in folk tradition gives up his head to Krishna before the Kurukshetra war. He does not appear in the Mahabharata itself. As Khatu Shyam he is one of the most widely worshipped deities of Rajasthan, Haryana and north India, called the support of the defeated.
nodes.story: In the tradition centred on Khatu in Rajasthan, Barbarika, son of Ghatotkacha, was a matchless archer who had won three unfailing arrows: one to mark every target, one to destroy them all, and one to return to his quiver. Setting out for Kurukshetra, he vowed to fight for whichever side was losing. Krishna, disguised as a brahmin, tested him and saw that such a vow would make him swing endlessly between the armies until none but he survived. So Krishna asked him for a gift, and Barbarika, recognising him, offered his own head. Set on a hilltop, the head watched the whole war. Pleased, Krishna blessed him to be worshipped in the Kali Yuga under his own name, Shyam. In the Skanda Purana, Krishna instead strikes off his head to fulfil a curse from a former birth.
nodes.vahana: A blue horse (Lila) in Khatu Shyam iconography
sources: Rajasthani and Haryanvi folk tradition (Khatu Shyam)
variations: He is absent from the Mahabharata; his story is a later Puranic and folk addition.

In the Skanda Purana he is a former yaksha reborn under a curse; he worships the goddesses at a sacred site, duels unknowingly with his grandfather Bhima, and Krishna beheads him with the Sudarshana; his head later testifies that only Krishna's discus truly fought the war.
In the Khatu Shyam tradition he freely gives his head as a gift (sheesh-daan); the three arrows are a gift of Shiva, and his head was found buried at Khatu and enshrined there.
His mother is Kamakantakata (Maurvi), daughter of Mura, in the Skanda Purana, and Ahilawati in folk versions.
A Nepali tradition connects the head-giving warrior with Yalambar, the Kirata king whose head is worshipped in Kathmandu as Akash Bhairav.

nodes.name: Iravan
nodes.description: The son of Arjuna and the naga princess Ulupi, raised in the serpent realm, who fought for the Pandavas and was slain by the rakshasa Alambusha on the eighth day of the war. In Tamil tradition, as Aravan or Koothandavar, he is the hero who sacrificed himself to Kali to ensure the Pandavas' victory, and he is the patron deity of the transgender (aravani) community.
nodes.story: Iravan was born in the realm of the nagas to Arjuna and the naga princess Ulupi, and grew up there, far from his father. When he travelled to Indra's heaven to greet Arjuna, his father embraced him and asked for his help in the coming war. On the eighth day at Kurukshetra, Iravan rode out with a host of swift horsemen and cut down several of Shakuni's brothers, the princes of Gandhara. Alarmed, Duryodhana sent the rakshasa Alambusha against him. The two fought through a haze of magic; Iravan's naga kinsmen rose to aid him in serpent form, but Alambusha took the shape of Garuda and devoured them, then struck off Iravan's head. Arjuna learned of his son's death only later, and grieved bitterly.
sources: Koothandavar temple tradition, Koovagam, Tamil Nadu
variations: In Tamil tradition (Villiputturar and folk dramas), he offers himself as a sacrifice (kalappali) to Kali before the war to ensure the Pandavas' victory; his last wish is to be married, and Krishna takes the form of Mohini to marry him and then mourns him as a widow.

At the Koovagam festival in Tamil Nadu, transgender devotees (aravanis) re-enact the marriage and widowhood; his severed head is worshipped as Koothandavar and, as with Barbarika, is said to have watched the whole war.
The Bhishma Parva calls his mother a daughter of the naga king Airavata, widowed when Garuda killed her husband, rather than the daughter of Kauravya as in the Adi Parva.

nodes.name: Ulupi
nodes.description: A naga princess, daughter of the serpent king Kauravya of Airavata's line, who drew Arjuna into the waters of the Ganga during his exile and bore him Iravan. Years later she engineered and then undid Arjuna's death at the hands of his son Babruvahana, reviving him with a naga gem and freeing him from the Vasus' curse.
nodes.story: During his twelve-year exile, Arjuna came to Gangadvara, where the Ganga leaves the mountains. As he stepped into the river to bathe, Ulupi, daughter of the naga king Kauravya, seized him and drew him down to her father's palace beneath the waters. Arjuna calmly kindled the sacred fire and made his offerings, then asked who she was. Ulupi confessed that she had loved him at first sight and begged him to spend a night with her, arguing that saving a suffering being from death was itself dharma. Arjuna, bound by a vow of celibacy, yielded to her reasoning. At dawn she returned him to the riverbank and granted him a boon: he would be invincible in water, and every water creature would submit to him. Their son was Iravan.
nodes.abode: The naga realm beneath the Ganga
variations: She explains in the Ashvamedhika Parva that the Vasus (with Ganga) had cursed Arjuna for killing Bhishma through Shikhandi; she had her father intercede, and the curse was discharged when Arjuna fell to his own son.
The Bhishma Parva describes her as a daughter of Airavata and a widow whose husband Garuda had killed.
When the Pandavas set out on their final journey, Ulupi entered the Ganga while Chitrangada returned to Manipura.
The Jaiminiya Ashvamedha expands her role in obtaining the gem that revives Arjuna.

nodes.name: Chitrangada (princess of Manipura)
nodes.description: The princess of Manipura, daughter of King Chitravahana, who married Arjuna during his exile on the condition that their son would inherit her father's kingdom. She was the mother of Babruvahana. Not to be confused with Chitrangada, the elder son of Shantanu and Satyavati.
nodes.story: Wandering through the east during his exile, Arjuna reached Manipura and saw the princess Chitrangada, daughter of King Chitravahana, and at once desired her. When he asked for her hand, the king explained a family peculiarity: Shiva had granted his ancestor Prabhanjana a boon that each generation would bear a single child, and his own was a daughter whom he had appointed as a son (putrika), so that her son would continue his line. Arjuna accepted the condition, married Chitrangada and stayed in Manipura for a time. When she bore a son, Babruvahana, Arjuna embraced them both, left the child as Chitravahana's heir, and resumed his journey. Years later she lamented over Arjuna's body when their son struck him down.
variations: The epic's Manipura lies near the eastern sea coast, close to Kalinga; its identification with modern Manipur is a later tradition, embraced by the Manipuri court after its Vaishnava conversion in the 18th century.

Rabindranath Tagore's play Chitra (1892) and dance-drama Chitrangada (1936) reimagine her as a warrior princess raised as a boy, who asks Madana (Kamadeva) for beauty to win Arjuna; this is a modern literary retelling.
After the war she lived at Hastinapura in the service of Kunti and Gandhari, returning to Manipura when the Pandavas set out on their final journey.

nodes.name: Babruvahana
nodes.description: The son of Arjuna and Chitrangada, raised as heir of his maternal grandfather and king of Manipura. During the Ashvamedha of Yudhishthira he fought his own father and struck him dead, and Arjuna was revived by Ulupi's naga gem, discharging the Vasus' curse for the killing of Bhishma.
nodes.story: When Yudhishthira's sacrificial horse wandered into Manipura, young King Babruvahana came out humbly with gifts to greet his father Arjuna, who was guarding it. Instead of blessing him, Arjuna rebuked him: a kshatriya should meet an armed intruder with battle, not bows of welcome. Then Ulupi rose from the earth and urged Babruvahana to fight. He donned golden armour, mounted his chariot and met his father in a fierce duel, until one of his arrows pierced Arjuna's chest and the great archer fell dead. Babruvahana collapsed in grief, and Chitrangada wept over her husband. Ulupi then brought a gem from the naga realm and laid it on Arjuna's breast; he rose as if from sleep, and Ulupi explained that this death had freed him from the Vasus' curse.
variations: In the Jaiminiya Ashvamedha, Babruvahana beheads Arjuna, and the revival involves a gem brought from the netherworld and Krishna's intervention.
Because Chitrangada was an appointed daughter (putrika), Babruvahana counted as the son of his grandfather Chitravahana's line rather than as a Kuru heir.
Babruvahana later attended the Ashvamedha at Hastinapura with his mother and Ulupi, where he was honoured by Kunti, Draupadi and Yudhishthira.

nodes.name: Bakasura
nodes.description: A powerful rakshasa who terrorised the town of Ekachakra, demanding a daily tribute of food, animals and a human victim. Bhima killed him while the Pandavas were living there in disguise as brahmins after escaping the house of lac.
nodes.story: Disguised as brahmins, the Pandavas lodged with a brahmin family in Ekachakra. One day Kunti heard the family weeping: it was their turn to send the rakshasa Baka his tribute, a cartload of rice, two buffaloes and the person who brought them. Father, mother and daughter each offered to go in place of the others. Kunti, grateful for their shelter, declared that one of her five sons would go instead, and chose Bhima. Bhima drove the cart to Baka's forest, sat down and began eating the rice himself. The enraged rakshasa rained blows on his back, but Bhima calmly finished his meal before turning to fight. They uprooted trees and wrestled until Bhima broke Baka's back, and he left the body at the town gate, freeing Ekachakra.
variations: Kirmira, slain by Bhima in the Vana Parva, claims to be Baka's brother and seeks revenge.
Distinct from the crane-demon Bakasura killed by the child Krishna in the Bhagavata Purana.
Several places, including Ekchakra in West Bengal, claim to be the epic's Ekachakra.

nodes.name: Mandavya
nodes.description: An ascetic sage who was wrongly impaled as a thief and survived through his austerities. Learning that his suffering was punishment for tormenting an insect as a child, he cursed Dharma (Yama) to be born as a mortal, and Dharma was born as Vidura.
nodes.story: Mandavya stood in silent meditation outside his hermitage, arms raised, under a vow of silence, when thieves fleeing the king's guards hid their loot there. The guards found the stolen goods, and when the sage would not answer, the king had him impaled on a stake with the thieves. Yet Mandavya did not die; sages came to him as birds, and the king, learning the truth, begged forgiveness. Unable to pull out the stake, the king cut it off, leaving the tip (ani) inside him, which gave him the name Ani-Mandavya. The sage then went to Dharma and demanded what sin had earned this. As a child, Dharma said, he had pierced a small insect with a blade of grass. Mandavya declared that no act before the age of fourteen should count as sin, and cursed Dharma to be born as a man, the son of a shudra woman.
variations: Some retellings set the age of accountability at twelve rather than fourteen.
In the Markandeya Purana, the impaled Mandavya curses the brahmin Kaushika to die at sunrise, and Kaushika's devoted wife halts the sunrise by the power of her fidelity.
The god he curses is called Dharma in the epic; later tradition identifies him with Yama.

nodes.name: Kindama
nodes.description: A sage who had taken the form of a deer to make love with his wife in the forest, and was shot by King Pandu while hunting. Dying, he cursed Pandu to die the moment he approached his wife in desire, which led Pandu to renounce his throne and made the divine births of the Pandavas necessary.
nodes.story: Pandu, the young king of Hastinapura, loved to hunt in the forests where he lived with his wives Kunti and Madri. One day he saw a stag and a doe coupling and brought them down with swift arrows. The stag was in truth the sage Kindama, who with his wife had taken deer form so as to enjoy love freely in the wild. Dying, Kindama reproached Pandu: even a cruel man does not strike creatures in the act of love, and a king who knew the scriptures should know better. He cursed Pandu that the moment he approached a woman in desire, he too would die. Grief-stricken, Pandu renounced his kingdom for the ascetic life. Years later, overcome by desire for Madri in the spring forest, he embraced her and died at once.
variations: The Critical Edition spells his name Kimdama; many popular retellings leave the sage unnamed.

nodes.name: Nala (king of Nishadha)
nodes.description: The virtuous king of Nishadha, son of Virasena, whose love for Damayanti, loss of everything at dice under the possession of Kali, and eventual restoration form the Nalopakhyana of the Vana Parva. The tale is told by the sage Brihadashva to console the exiled Yudhishthira, a fellow king ruined at dice.
nodes.story: Twelve years after Nala won Damayanti, the demon Kali, furious that she had chosen a mortal over the gods, found his chance when Nala neglected to wash his feet before his evening prayers. Kali entered him, and Nala gambled away his kingdom to his brother Pushkara. Wandering the forest with Damayanti, half-mad, he tore their single garment and abandoned her as she slept. In a forest fire he rescued the serpent Karkotaka, who bit him, turning him into the misshapen Bahuka so no one would know him, while the venom tormented Kali within. As Bahuka, Nala served King Rituparna of Ayodhya as a charioteer, and traded his horse-lore for the king's secret of dice. With that knowledge Kali fled his body, and Nala reclaimed Damayanti and his kingdom.
variations: Shriharsha's Naishadhiya Charita, one of the great Sanskrit court epics, dwells on the courtship alone.
The gift of taste granted to him by Yama is the source of his proverbial fame as a cook; Nala-paka means a dish of rare excellence.
Distinct from Nala the vanara engineer who built Rama's bridge.

nodes.name: Damayanti
nodes.description: The princess of Vidarbha, daughter of King Bhima of Vidarbha (not the Pandava), who chose the mortal Nala over four gods at her svayamvara. Abandoned by him in the forest, she survived through wit and fidelity and contrived the second svayamvara that reunited them.
nodes.story: A golden swan carried word of Nala to Damayanti, and she resolved to marry none but him. At her svayamvara, Indra, Agni, Varuna and Yama all took Nala's form, so that five identical Nalas sat before her. Damayanti prayed to the gods by the power of her truth: if she had never strayed from Nala in word or thought, let them reveal themselves. Moved, the gods showed their divine marks: they did not sweat or blink, their garlands stayed fresh, and their feet did not touch the ground, while the true Nala cast a shadow and his garland had begun to wilt. She garlanded him, and the gods blessed the marriage. Years later, abandoned and searching, she recognised her disguised husband by his gift for commanding horses and fire.
variations: During her wanderings she curses to death a hunter who tried to assault her, and serves the queen mother of Chedi as a maid before being recognised.
Her father, King Bhima of Vidarbha, is a different person from the Pandava Bhima.

nodes.name: Savitri
nodes.description: The princess of Madra, daughter of King Ashvapati, who married the exiled prince Satyavan knowing he was fated to die within a year, and won back his life from Yama through her persistence and wisdom. Her story, told by the sage Markandeya to Yudhishthira, made her the supreme model of the devoted wife and is honoured in the Vat Savitri vow.
nodes.story: On the day Satyavan was fated to die, Savitri, who had fasted for three nights, followed him into the forest. As he split wood he was seized with pain and laid his head in her lap. Then Yama appeared, dark and red-eyed, noose in hand, and drew out Satyavan's thumb-sized soul. As he walked south, Savitri followed. Yama urged her to turn back, but she spoke so wisely of dharma and friendship with the good that he offered her boons, anything but her husband's life. She asked for sight and his kingdom for her blind father-in-law, a hundred sons for her father, and a hundred sons of her own by Satyavan. When Yama granted the last, she pointed out that it required Satyavan alive. Delighted, Yama released him.
nodes.abode: Madra; later the kingdom of Shalva
variations: Married women observe the Vat Savitri vrata in the month of Jyeshtha, worshipping the banyan under which Satyavan lay.
She was born by the grace of the goddess Savitri, whom her father Ashvapati had worshipped for eighteen years, and was named after her.
Sri Aurobindo's epic poem Savitri reinterprets the tale as a spiritual allegory.

nodes.name: Satyavan
nodes.description: The son of the blind, exiled king Dyumatsena of Shalva, who lived as a forest ascetic and was chosen by Savitri as her husband despite being fated to die within a year. Restored to life by Yama through Savitri's devotion, he lived on with her for four hundred years.
nodes.story: Satyavan grew up in a forest hermitage where his father, the blind King Dyumatsena, lived in exile after losing his kingdom. As a boy he loved to model horses in clay and paint them, and so was called Chitrashva. When the princess Savitri chose him, the sage Narada warned that, though truthful, generous and handsome, he would die in exactly one year. On that day Satyavan went into the forest with his axe to gather fruit and firewood, with Savitri at his side. Splitting wood, he felt a sudden agony in his head and fell asleep in her lap. When he awoke it was night, and he thought he had dreamed of a dark being carrying him away. Savitri told him she had brought him back from Yama.
nodes.abode: A forest hermitage; later the kingdom of Shalva
variations: Some retellings reduce the number of boons Savitri obtains or change their order.

nodes.name: Dhaumya
nodes.description: The family priest (purohita) of the Pandavas, younger brother of the sage Devala, whom they chose at Utkochaka on the advice of a gandharva. He performed their household rites, married Draupadi to them, followed them into exile and taught Yudhishthira the worship of Surya that won the inexhaustible vessel.
nodes.story: When the Pandavas left Hastinapura for exile after the dice game, Dhaumya walked before them holding blades of kusha grass and chanting the grim Sama hymns sacred to Yama. Vidura explained the omen to Dhritarashtra: one day the Kurus would lie dead on the battlefield, and their priests would chant those same hymns over them. In the forest, when brahmins flocked after Yudhishthira and he grieved that he could not feed them, Dhaumya taught him the hundred and eight names of Surya. Yudhishthira worshipped the sun with them, and Surya gave him a copper vessel that would supply food each day until Draupadi had eaten. Before the year in disguise, Dhaumya counselled the brothers on how to live unrecognised at a king's court.
nodes.abode: Utkochaka tirtha; later with the Pandavas in the forest
variations: He is distinct from Ayoda Dhaumya, the teacher of Aruni, Upamanyu and Veda in the Adi Parva (Paushya Parva).
The gandharva who recommended him to the Pandavas is Angaraparna, formerly called Chitraratha.

nodes.name: Shesha (Ananta)
nodes.description: The thousand-hooded king of the nagas, eldest son of Kashyapa and Kadru, who holds the earth on his hoods and forms the coiled couch on which Vishnu reclines upon the cosmic ocean. His name means 'the remainder', that which endures when the universe is dissolved.
nodes.story: The Mahabharata tells that Shesha, eldest of Kadru's thousand serpent sons, grew weary of his brothers' hostility toward Vinata and her son Garuda. Renouncing them, he wandered to Gandhamadana, Badari, Gokarna and the Himalayan slopes, practising such austerities that his flesh and sinews dried away. Brahma appeared, pleased by his steadiness, and offered a boon. Shesha asked only that his mind should always delight in dharma, tranquillity and austerity. Brahma granted it and gave him a great charge: the earth, with its mountains, forests, seas and cities, was unsteady, and Shesha was to hold it firm. Entering a cleft in the earth, the serpent took the world upon his head, and there he bears it still. The Puranas add that at the close of an age a destroying fire issues from his mouths, while Vishnu sleeps upon his coils on the waters.
nodes.abode: Patala, beneath the earth; the Ocean of Milk (Kshira Sagara) as Vishnu's couch
variations: Most Puranas treat Shesha and Ananta as one being; the Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas describe him beneath Patala as Ananta or Sankarshana, a tamasic form of Vishnu himself.
In the Mahabharata's account of the churning of the ocean, Ananta uproots Mount Mandara at the command of Brahma and Narayana.

Lakshmana (Ramayana tradition, especially later texts) and Balarama (Mahabharata, Mausala Parva; Puranas) are regarded as incarnations of Shesha; some texts instead make Balarama born of a white hair of Vishnu.
Shesha and Vasuki are occasionally conflated in later popular tradition, but the Mahabharata lists them as distinct brothers.

nodes.name: Vasuki
nodes.description: King of the nagas and son of Kashyapa and Kadru, famed as the living rope with which the devas and asuras churned the Ocean of Milk. He is the brother of the naga maiden Jaratkaru, mother of Astika, and is shown coiled around Shiva's neck.
nodes.story: When the devas and asuras resolved to churn the Ocean of Milk for amrita, they took Mount Mandara as the churning rod and Vasuki, king of the serpents, as the rope. Coiled about the mountain, which rested on the back of the great tortoise, Vasuki was hauled back and forth for ages; the Puranas say the asuras seized his head and the devas his tail, so that the smoke and fire of his breath scorched the demons. In the Ramayana's telling it was Vasuki who, in his agony, spewed the deadly halahala poison from his heads, threatening to burn the worlds until Shiva drank it. Earlier, fearing his mother Kadru's curse on the serpents, Vasuki had sought the counsel of the gods and learned that his sister's son would save their race, so he gave her in marriage to the sage Jaratkaru.
variations: In the Ramayana the halahala poison issues from Vasuki's heads; in the Bhagavata it simply rises from the churned ocean.
The Mahabharata names Vasuki as the naga king who crowns himself and cares for the serpents after Shesha withdraws; later popular tradition sometimes conflates him with Shesha.
Vasuki around Shiva's neck is a feature of later Shaiva iconography rather than the epics.

nodes.name: Takshaka
nodes.description: A mighty naga king, son of Kashyapa and Kadru, who killed King Parikshit and thereby provoked Janamejaya's snake sacrifice. Once a dweller of the Khandava forest and a friend of Indra, he survived the sacrifice only through Astika's intervention.
nodes.story: King Parikshit, grandson of Arjuna, once draped a dead snake around the neck of a sage who was keeping a vow of silence. The sage's son Shringin, enraged, cursed the king to die within seven days from the bite of Takshaka. Parikshit withdrew to a palace raised on a single pillar, guarded by physicians and mantras. On the way Takshaka met a brahmin healer named Kashyapa hastening to save the king; after watching him revive a tree the serpent had burnt to ash, Takshaka turned him back with riches. Then nagas disguised as ascetics brought fruits to the king. Hidden as a tiny worm within one fruit, Takshaka emerged at sunset, swelled to his true form, coiled about the king and struck him dead, an act that led Parikshit's son Janamejaya to begin the great snake sacrifice.
nodes.abode: Khandava forest; later Kurukshetra and Takshashila in some traditions
sources: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Paushya, Astika and Khandava-daha Parvas)
variations: In the Mahabharata, Parikshit retires to a pillar-palace; in the Bhagavata Purana he spends his final seven days hearing the Bhagavata from Shuka before Takshaka's bite.
At the burning of Khandava, Takshaka was away at Kurukshetra; his son Ashvasena escaped and later sought revenge on Arjuna by entering Karna's arrow.
In the snake sacrifice, Takshaka takes refuge with Indra; when the mantras draw Indra too, Indra lets him go, and Astika halts his fall.

nodes.name: Karkotaka
nodes.description: A naga king, son of Kashyapa and Kadru, best known from the tale of Nala, whom he bit in order to disguise and protect him. He is also revered as a naga guardian in Kashmir and the Kathmandu Valley.
nodes.story: Wandering in the forest after abandoning Damayanti, King Nala heard a voice calling from a blazing wildfire. It was the naga Karkotaka, cursed by the sage Narada to lie motionless until Nala should carry him. Shrinking to the size of a thumb, the serpent let Nala lift him from the flames, then asked him to walk on, counting his steps. At the tenth step, 'dasha', which also means 'bite!', Karkotaka struck. Nala's handsome body shrivelled and changed, and he became unrecognisable. The serpent explained that his venom would torment Kali, the spirit who had possessed Nala, while keeping Nala himself safe from enemies and poisons. He counselled Nala to serve King Rituparna as the charioteer Bahuka, and gave him a pair of garments that would restore his true form when the time came.
nodes.abode: Forest near Nishadha; regional traditions place him in Kashmir and in Taudaha lake, Kathmandu Valley
sources: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (list of Kadru's sons)
variations: Kashmir's Karkota dynasty claimed descent from him (Kalhana, Rajatarangini).
In Newar tradition of Nepal, Karkotaka is the naga king of the primordial lake of the Kathmandu Valley, resettled in Taudaha when Manjushri drained the lake.

nodes.name: Manasa
nodes.description: The goddess of snakes, worshipped especially in Bengal, Assam, Bihar and Odisha for protection from snakebite and for fertility and prosperity. Puranic tradition identifies her with Jaratkaru, the naga sister of Vasuki, wife of the sage Jaratkaru and mother of Astika.
nodes.story: In the Bengali Manasamangal poems, Manasa longs for worship among mortals, but the wealthy Shaiva merchant Chand Sadagar refuses her. In revenge she ruins his gardens, sinks his ships and kills his six sons by snakebite. When his last son Lakhindar marries Behula, the couple sleep in an iron chamber built to keep out every serpent, yet Manasa's snake slips through a tiny gap and Lakhindar dies on his wedding night. Refusing to give him up, Behula sets out on a raft with her husband's body, drifting downriver for months until she reaches the gods. Her dance pleases them, and Manasa agrees to restore Lakhindar and all of Chand's losses if the merchant will worship her. Chand at last offers a flower, with his left hand, and Manasa's worship spreads across the land.
sources: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Astika Parva), as Jaratkaru
variations: The Mahabharata names Vasuki's sister only Jaratkaru; the name Manasa and her full cult as a goddess appear in the Brahmavaivarta and Devi Bhagavata Puranas and the Bengali Manasamangal.
Brahmavaivarta Purana: a mind-born daughter of Kashyapa, sister of Ananta/Vasuki; Bengali Manasamangal: born of Shiva's seed, hence daughter of Shiva, and in conflict with his wife Chandi.
Her cult likely absorbed older regional and tribal snake-goddess worship; she is also linked with the Jain and Buddhist snake goddess Padmavati/Janguli.

nodes.name: Astika
nodes.description: A young brahmin sage, son of the ascetic Jaratkaru and the naga maiden Jaratkaru, who persuaded King Janamejaya to end the snake sacrifice. Serpents promise not to harm anyone who recalls his name.
nodes.story: Janamejaya, vowing to avenge his father Parikshit, began a great snake sacrifice at which the priests' mantras dragged serpents from every corner of the world into the fire. Vasuki, seeing his kin perish, sent his sister's son Astika, a young brahmin who had learned the Vedas from the sage Chyavana. Astika entered the sacrificial enclosure and praised the king, the priests and the fire so eloquently that Janamejaya offered him any boon he wished. At that moment Takshaka, who had fled to Indra, was being drawn helplessly toward the flames; Astika cried 'Stay!' and the serpent hung in the air. Then Astika asked that the sacrifice end. Bound by his word, Janamejaya agreed, and the grateful nagas promised safety from snakes to all who remember the story of Astika.
nodes.abode: Hermitage; raised in the house of Vasuki
variations: The name is explained from 'asti' ('he is'), the sage Jaratkaru's assurance that the child had been conceived.
Bengali and later Puranic tradition calls his mother Manasa.

nodes.name: Jaratkaru (the sage)
nodes.description: A severe ascetic of the Yayavara clan who married the naga maiden of the same name, sister of Vasuki, and fathered Astika. His story explains the duty to continue one's lineage for the sake of the ancestors.
nodes.story: The ascetic Jaratkaru wandered without a home, living on air and refusing marriage. One day he found his ancestors hanging head-down in a pit, clinging to a single grass root that a rat was gnawing away: without a descendant, they would fall. Moved, he agreed to marry, but only a maiden of his own name, given freely, whom he need not support. Vasuki, knowing his sister was destined to bear a son who would save the serpents, offered her; she too was called Jaratkaru. The sage lived with her on condition that she never displease him. When she woke him from sleep so that he would not miss the evening rites, he took offence and resolved to leave. Assuring her that the child she carried 'is' (asti), he departed, and that son was Astika.
variations: The Mahabharata tells the story twice, in slightly differing forms, in the Adi Parva.
Later Puranic and Bengali tradition names his wife Manasa.

nodes.name: Kadru
nodes.description: A daughter of Daksha and wife of the sage Kashyapa, mother of the thousand nagas. Her deceitful wager with her sister Vinata over the tail of the horse Uchchaihshravas began the enmity between serpents and Garuda.
nodes.story: Kashyapa granted boons to his wives, the sisters Kadru and Vinata. Kadru asked for a thousand powerful serpent sons; Vinata asked for only two, each surpassing Kadru's. Long afterwards the sisters saw the white horse Uchchaihshravas, risen from the churning ocean, and wagered on the colour of its tail, the loser to become the winner's slave. Vinata said white; Kadru said black. That night Kadru ordered her sons to cling to the tail as black hairs. Some refused, and in fury she cursed them to perish in the fire of Janamejaya's snake sacrifice. Those who obeyed darkened the tail, and Vinata was enslaved. Brahma let the curse stand, for the serpents had grown too many and too venomous. The bondage ended only when Vinata's son Garuda brought the amrita to Kadru's sons as ransom.
variations: In some Puranic versions Kadru herself blackens the horse's tail by sending serpents, without a separate curse episode.
The number and names of her serpent sons differ among the Mahabharata and the Puranas.

nodes.name: Vinata
nodes.description: A daughter of Daksha and wife of Kashyapa, mother of Garuda and Aruna. Enslaved to her sister Kadru through a rigged wager, she was freed when Garuda brought the amrita.
nodes.story: Vinata received two eggs from Kashyapa's boon and waited five hundred years while Kadru's thousand eggs hatched. Impatient and ashamed, she broke one open: inside was a son whose body was formed only in its upper half. This child, Aruna, cursed his mother for her haste: she would serve her rival as a slave until her other son freed her. Then he rose into the sky to become the charioteer of the Sun. Vinata, losing the wager over the colour of Uchchaihshravas's tail, served Kadru until the second egg hatched into Garuda, blazing like the fire at the end of an age. When Garuda learned that the price of her freedom was the amrita, he stormed heaven, seized the nectar and redeemed his mother, and the enmity between birds and serpents was born of her suffering.
variations: Some genealogies also give Vinata a daughter, Sumati, who married King Sagara (Ramayana calls Sumati the sister of Garuda).
The Ramayana and some Puranas list Vinata among the daughters of Daksha married to Kashyapa, with minor differences in the list.

nodes.name: Garuda
nodes.description: The king of birds, son of Kashyapa and Vinata, who stole the amrita from heaven to free his mother and became the mount and banner of Vishnu. Eternal foe of the serpents, he is invoked against poison and is the narrator-recipient of the Garuda Purana.
nodes.story: To free his mother Vinata from slavery, Garuda flew to heaven to steal the amrita. He scattered the gods, raised a storm of dust to blind them, quenched the ring of fire with water drawn from many rivers, and slipped through the spokes of a whirling wheel of blades. Killing the two serpents guarding the vessel, he flew off with it without tasting a drop. Pleased by his restraint, Vishnu granted him immortality without the amrita and a place above himself, on his banner; Garuda in turn agreed to become Vishnu's mount. Indra hurled his thunderbolt, but Garuda, honouring the sage whose bones had made it, merely shed a single feather. The two became friends: Garuda gave the amrita to the serpents, freeing Vinata, but Indra took it back before they could drink, and granted that serpents would be Garuda's food.
symbols: eagle or kite form, often with human torso
nodes.abode: Vaikuntha, in the service of Vishnu
variations: The Rig Veda's Suparna/Garutman, a celestial bird linked with the sun and with fetching soma, is a precursor; the explicit identification with Garuda, son of Vinata and mount of Vishnu, is later (epics and Puranas).
The Mahabharata says Garuda kills the serpent guards and gives the amrita to the nagas; in some retellings the serpents lick the kusha grass on which it was placed, splitting their tongues.
In Buddhist and Southeast Asian traditions garudas are a race of great birds; Garuda is the national emblem of Indonesia and Thailand.

nodes.name: Aruna
nodes.description: The personified red dawn, elder son of Kashyapa and Vinata, born from an egg opened too early and so lacking thighs. He serves as the charioteer of Surya and, in the Ramayana, is the father of the vulture brothers Jatayu and Sampati.
nodes.story: The Mahabharata explains why a red glow rises before the Sun. Surya, angry that the gods had watched Rahu seize him without helping, resolved to burn the worlds and blazed ever hotter. Terrified, the gods and sages went to Brahma, who remembered Aruna, the mighty son of Kashyapa and Vinata, born from an egg broken too soon: radiant, but without thighs, and so called Anuru. Brahma had Aruna placed in front of Surya's chariot as his charioteer, so that his great body would absorb the Sun's scorching heat and shield creation. So Aruna took up the reins of the seven horses, and his crimson light, going ahead of the Sun each morning, became the dawn that softens the fierce brilliance of the day.
nodes.abode: Front of Surya's chariot, in the sky
variations: The Ramayana (Aranya Kanda) makes Jatayu and Sampati sons of Aruna by Shyeni; some Puranic genealogies differ.
A late regional tale (found in some vernacular Ramayana traditions) has Aruna take a female form, Aruni, and bear Vali and Sugriva by Indra and Surya; this is not in Valmiki.

nodes.name: Nandi
nodes.description: The bull who is Shiva's mount and the chief of his ganas, guardian of the gate of Kailasa and a model of devotion. His image sits facing the sanctum in nearly every Shiva temple.
nodes.story: The Ramayana's Uttara Kanda tells how Ravana, flush from defeating his half-brother Kubera, flew over Kailasa in the Pushpaka chariot, until it suddenly stopped. Before him stood Nandishvara, Shiva's attendant, dark and tawny, dwarf-like and monkey-faced, holding a trident. He warned Ravana to turn back, for Shiva was sporting on the mountain. Ravana laughed scornfully at his monkey-like face. Nandi, angered, cursed him: since Ravana had mocked his form, beings of that same monkey form, equal to him in might and splendour, would arise to destroy Ravana and his race. Unheeding, Ravana tried to uproot Kailasa itself; Shiva pressed it down with his toe, trapping the rakshasa's arms until he howled. Nandi's curse was fulfilled when Hanuman and the vanaras laid waste to Lanka.
symbols: anthropomorphic form with bull head and four arms (Nandikeshvara)
nodes.abode: Kailasa, at the gate of Shiva's abode
variations: Nandi appears both as the bull mount and as Nandikeshvara, an anthropomorphic gana-chief; early texts do not always identify the two.
Shiva Purana: son of the sage Shilada, granted to him by Shiva; some Puranic accounts instead make the bull a son of Surabhi (Kamadhenu), given to Shiva.
Nandi is credited as the primordial teacher of Shaiva lineages (Nandinatha sampradaya) and, in the Kamasutra, as the first author of the science of kama.
In Lingayat tradition Basava (Basavanna) is regarded as an incarnation of Nandi.

nodes.name: Airavata
nodes.description: The white elephant, often four-tusked, who is the mount of Indra and the guardian elephant of the east. Most accounts say he rose from the churning of the Ocean of Milk.
nodes.story: The Vishnu Purana tells how the sage Durvasa, wandering in an ecstatic mood, received a garland of heavenly flowers from a vidyadhari.
