Meeting Indra riding Airavata, he respectfully offered the garland to the king of the gods. Indra placed it on the elephant's head; Airavata, drawn by its fragrance, pulled it off with his trunk and trampled it into the ground. Durvasa, incensed at the insult, cursed Indra that the three worlds would lose their Shri, their prosperity and splendour. The gods weakened, the asuras triumphed, and Vishnu advised the churning of the Ocean of Milk to restore what was lost. Other texts, such as the Bhagavata Purana, list a four-tusked white elephant named Airavata among the treasures that rose from that ocean, so traditions differ over whether Airavata preceded the churning or was born from it.
nodes.abode: Svarga (Amaravati), Indra's heaven; guardian of the eastern quarter
variations: Origin: from the churning of the ocean (Mahabharata, Bhagavata); from the right half of the cosmic eggshell over which Brahma chanted Samans (Matangalila and elephant-lore texts); a descendant of Iravati in Kashyapa's line (Ramayana, Aranya Kanda).
Distinct from the naga Airavata, ancestor of Ulupi's father Kauravya in the Mahabharata.
Airavata is sometimes said to have worshipped Shiva at the Airavateshvara temple, Darasuram (local sthala-purana).

nodes.name: Mushika (Ganesha's mouse)
nodes.description: The mouse or rat that serves as the mount of Ganesha, symbolising desire and restlessness brought under the control of wisdom, and the ability to penetrate every obstacle. Various Puranic and regional tales explain how a proud being became Ganesha's humble vehicle.
nodes.story: A story attributed to the Ganesha Purana tells of Krauncha, a gandharva musician in Indra's court, who carelessly trod on the foot of the sage Vamadeva. The sage cursed him to become a mouse. Krauncha became a mouse as vast as a mountain, and in his wanderings fell upon the hermitage of the sage Parashara, devouring stores of grain, gnawing clothes and books and terrifying the ascetics. Ganesha, a guest there, cast his noose; it caught the mouse by the neck and dragged him before the elephant-headed god. Humbled, Krauncha begged for mercy. Ganesha offered him a boon, but the still-proud mouse replied that he would rather grant one, so Ganesha asked him to be his mount. When Ganesha climbed on, the mouse was nearly crushed by his weight and begged him to lighten himself, which Ganesha graciously did.
nodes.abode: At the feet of Ganesha; Kailasa
variations: Mudgala Purana and South Indian tradition: the asura Gajamukha, struck by Ganesha's broken tusk, turned into a mouse and became his mount.
In Mudgala Purana, different forms of Ganesha have different mounts (lion, peacock, serpent), the mouse being one of them.
The mouse appears as Ganesha's vehicle in art from about the 6th-7th centuries CE; its symbolism (conquered desire, penetration of obstacles) is a traditional interpretation.

nodes.name: Paravani (Kartikeya's peacock)
nodes.description: The peacock who serves as the mount of Kartikeya (Skanda, Murugan), symbol of splendour and of pride and passion subdued. In Tamil tradition it is the transformed asura Surapadman.
nodes.story: In the Tamil Kanda Puranam, the asura king Surapadman, whose tyranny had enslaved the gods, faced Murugan in the final battle by the sea at Tiruchendur. Wielding sorcery, the asura changed shape again and again, and at last stood in the ocean as a gigantic mango tree. Murugan hurled his vel, the lance given to him by his mother, and split the tree in two. Touched by the god's grace, Surapadman's hostility fell away: one half became a peacock and the other a rooster. Murugan took the peacock as his mount and set the rooster on his banner, so that his vanquished foe became his devotee and eternal companion. The Sanskrit Mahabharata tells a simpler story: at Skanda's consecration as general of the gods, the peacock was among the gifts presented to him.
nodes.abode: With Kartikeya; Skandagiri / the six abodes of Murugan
variations: Mahabharata: the peacock is presented to Skanda by Garuda at his consecration; Kanda Puranam: the peacock is the transformed asura Surapadman.
Some retellings say Indra himself took the form of a peacock to carry Skanda.
The personal name 'Paravani' is used in later Puranic and popular literature; many texts simply say 'mayura' (peacock).

nodes.name: Hamsa (the divine swan)
nodes.description: The swan or wild goose that is the mount of Brahma and Saraswati, emblem of discernment, purity and the liberated soul. It is famed for its supposed power to separate milk from water.
nodes.story: The hamsa, the swan or wild goose that carries Brahma and Saraswati, is prized in Indian tradition for a single gift: it is said to be able to sip the milk from a mixture of milk and water and leave the water behind. This power of discernment, nira-kshira-viveka, made it the emblem of the wise, who draw out truth and leave illusion behind. Upanishadic seers spoke of the soul as a hamsa wandering in the great wheel of Brahman, and the highest renunciants are still honoured as paramahamsas. The Puranas give the swan to Brahma, lord of the Vedas, and to Saraswati, goddess of learning, as their mount. When the Matrikas marched against the asuras in the Devi Mahatmya, Brahmani came forth from Brahma in a celestial car drawn by swans, carrying a rosary and a water-pot.
nodes.abode: Brahmaloka; the Manasarovar lake of poetic tradition
sources: Puranic and Shilpa-shastra iconography of Brahma and Saraswati
variations: Scholars note that the bird of early texts is likely the bar-headed goose rather than the mute swan.
Saraswati is also shown seated on a lotus or with a peacock in some regional images.
Distinct from Vishnu's Hamsa avatar (Bhagavata Purana, Canto 11), and from Brahma himself taking swan form in the Lingodbhava legend.

nodes.name: Uluka (Lakshmi's owl)
nodes.description: The owl regarded, chiefly in Bengal and eastern India, as the mount of the goddess Lakshmi. It is an ambivalent bird: a watchful guardian of the night and of the granary, but also an old omen of misfortune.
nodes.story: In Bengal and eastern India, Lakshmi's mount is the owl, the lakshmi-pencha. On Kojagari Purnima, the full-moon night of the month of Ashvin, the goddess is said to descend and roam the earth asking 'Ko jagarti?', 'Who is awake?', blessing with prosperity those who keep vigil, and families stay up singing her praises. The owl, which sees in the dark and keeps watch through the night, suits this wakeful goddess; farmers also value it as a guardian of granaries against rats. Yet the bird is ambivalent: in a Vedic hymn the owl is a messenger of misfortune, and in everyday speech 'ullu' means a fool. Some modern interpreters therefore read the owl as a warning that wealth pursued blindly leads to folly, though this is a later reflection rather than a scriptural teaching.
symbols: white barn owl in Bengali images
sources: Bengali Lakshmi Puja and Kojagari vrata-katha traditions
variations: Lakshmi's mount as an owl is a regional and relatively late tradition; classical texts more often show her seated on a lotus and bathed by elephants (Gajalakshmi), and some images give her an elephant as mount.
The owl is also associated with Chamunda in some iconography.
Not to be confused with Uluka, son of Shakuni, who served as Duryodhana's envoy in the Mahabharata.

nodes.name: Dawon (the Goddess's lion)
nodes.description: The lion (or, in many northern Indian images, the tiger) that serves as the mount of Durga and of many forms of the Goddess. In the Devi Mahatmya it fights beside her against the asuras.
nodes.story: When the gods, humiliated by the buffalo demon Mahishasura, poured out their wrath, a blazing radiance gathered into the form of the Goddess. Each god gave her a weapon or ornament: Shiva his trident, Vishnu his discus, Indra his thunderbolt. Himavan, lord of the mountains, gave her a lion as her mount. Riding it, she roared with a laughter that shook the earth, and the asura armies rushed upon her. In the battle that followed, the lion, shaking its mane in fury, ranged through the enemy host like fire through a forest, while the Goddess cut the demons down with her many arms. Painters and sculptors ever since have shown the lion, or in many images a tiger, springing upon Mahishasura as Durga's trident pierces him.
nodes.abode: With the Goddess; the Vindhya and Himalaya mountains
sources: Devi Mahatmya (Markandeya Purana), ch. 2 and ch. 5
variations: The Sanskrit texts simply call the mount 'simha' (lion); the name 'Dawon' is a modern label of uncertain origin used in popular and reference works.
Lion versus tiger: the Devi Mahatmya specifies a lion; the tiger is common in later north Indian and Himalayan iconography (e.g. Sherawali Mata).
A Puranic tale has Parvati, performing austerities to become fair (Gauri), adopt as her mount a hungry lion that had waited by her in patience.
Among the Navadurga, Chandraghanta, Kushmanda, Skandamata, Katyayani and Siddhidatri are commonly shown on a lion or tiger, but Shailaputri and Mahagauri ride a bull.

nodes.name: Uchchaihshravas
nodes.description: The radiant white horse, king of horses, who rose from the churning of the Ocean of Milk and is usually said to be the steed of Indra. Later tradition gives him seven heads.
nodes.story: When the devas and asuras churned the Ocean of Milk, wonders rose one after another from the foaming waters. Among them came a white horse of dazzling beauty, swift as thought, whose name means 'long-eared' or 'neighing aloud'. Later tradition gives him seven heads. In most tellings Indra, king of the gods, took him as his steed along with the elephant Airavata; the Bhagavata Purana instead says that the asura king Bali desired the horse and received him. The same horse later became the occasion of a family tragedy: Kadru and Vinata wagered on the colour of his tail, and Kadru's deceit, making her serpent sons cling to it as black hairs, enslaved Vinata. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna names Uchchaihshravas, 'born of the nectar', as his own glory among horses.
variations: Most accounts give him to Indra; the Bhagavata Purana (8.8) says Bali took him.
Some texts associate him with the Sun (Surya), whose son Revanta is shown riding him.
The seven heads are a later iconographic development; the epic simply describes a white horse.

nodes.name: Kamadhenu
nodes.description: The divine wish-fulfilling cow, mother of all cattle, revered as a form of the sacred cow in which all gods dwell. She is said to have risen from the churning of the ocean, or to have been born of Daksha, and is the mother of Nandini.
nodes.story: The Bhagavata Purana tells that King Kartavirya Arjuna, the thousand-armed lord of the Haihayas, once visited the hermitage of the sage Jamadagni while hunting. With the help of his wish-granting cow, the humble sage feasted the king and his whole army with royal abundance. Envious, Kartavirya seized the cow and her calf and carried them off to his capital, Mahishmati, while the cow lowed piteously. When Jamadagni's son Parashurama returned and learned of the theft, he pursued the king with his axe, cut off his thousand arms, slew him and brought the cow home. This began the long feud between Parashurama and the Haihaya kshatriyas. The Mahabharata tells a similar tale, in which the king's men carry off the calf of Jamadagni's sacrificial cow.
symbols: woman's face and peacock tail with wings (later popular iconography)
nodes.abode: Goloka; the hermitages of the sages
sources: Mahabharata, Adi Parva and Anushasana Parva
Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda and Aranya Kanda
variations: Origin: rose from the churning of the ocean and was given to the sages (Bhagavata Purana); born from Daksha as he drank amrita (Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva); a daughter of Daksha and wife of Kashyapa (several Puranas); daughter of Krodhavasha (Ramayana, Aranya Kanda).
The wish-granting cows of Vashistha (Nandini/Shabala) and Jamadagni are sometimes identified with Kamadhenu herself, sometimes with her offspring.
The image of Kamadhenu with a woman's face, wings and a peacock tail is a modern popular form.

nodes.name: Nandini (Shabala)
nodes.description: The wish-fulfilling cow of the sage Vashistha, daughter of Kamadhenu (Surabhi). Kings and gods coveted her, and the attempt of King Vishvamitra to seize her set him on the path to becoming a brahmarshi.
nodes.story: King Vishvamitra, touring his realm with a great army, stopped at the hermitage of Vashistha. With the help of his wondrous cow, called Shabala in the Ramayana, the sage fed the whole host with every kind of food. Dazzled, the king demanded the cow, offering thousands of elephants, horses and gold. Vashistha refused, and Vishvamitra's men began to drag her away. Breaking free, she ran weeping to the sage and asked why he had abandoned her; Vashistha replied that he could not resist a king. She answered that a brahmin's power is greater, and at his word she brought forth hosts of warriors, Pahlavas, Shakas, Yavanas and Kambojas, who routed the royal army. Humbled, Vishvamitra renounced his throne for austerities, determined to win a brahmin's power.
sources: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Adivamsavatarana and Chaitraratha Parvas)
variations: The Ramayana calls Vashistha's cow Shabala (and also Kamadhuk); the Mahabharata names her Nandini, daughter of Surabhi.
Mahabharata: the Vasus, urged by the wife of Dyu (Prabhasa), stole Nandini; Vashistha cursed them to be born as humans, and Dyu was born as Bhishma.
Raghuvamsha: King Dilipa served Nandini and offered his own body to a lion to protect her, earning the boon of a son, Raghu.

nodes.name: Makara
nodes.description: A composite water creature, part crocodile, part fish or dolphin, with an elephant-like snout in art, that serves as the mount of the river goddess Ganga and of Varuna, lord of the waters. It is the emblem of Kamadeva's banner and the sign of Capricorn.
nodes.story: The makara belongs to the realm of the waters. Varuna, lord of oceans and cosmic order, is shown riding it holding his noose, and from the Gupta period onward temple doorways often show the river goddess Ganga standing on a makara, pot in hand, welcoming worshippers as purifying water. Its open jaws spout garlands, vines and pearls on gateways and arches, a sign of the life-giving abundance of water. Kamadeva, god of love, bears the makara on his banner and is called Makaradhvaja. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna names the makara as his glory among water creatures. Regional Ramayana traditions add that when Hanuman cooled himself in the ocean after burning Lanka, a great fish or makara swallowed a drop of his sweat and bore his son Makardhvaja.
sources: Matsya Purana (iconography of Varuna and Ganga)
variations: The makara is variously interpreted as a crocodile (mugger), a Gangetic dolphin or a purely mythical composite; its artistic form changes over time.
The Makardhvaja birth story is found in regional Ramayanas, not in Valmiki.
Makara is also the zodiac sign Capricorn, giving its name to Makar Sankranti.

nodes.name: Bhringi
nodes.description: A sage and gana devoted exclusively to Shiva, who refused to honour Parvati and is shown as an emaciated, three-legged figure beside Shiva and Ardhanarishvara. His story is a traditional explanation of the inseparability of Shiva and Shakti.
nodes.story: The sage Bhringi worshipped Shiva alone and would not honour Parvati. When he came to Kailasa to circumambulate his lord, he asked the goddess to step aside. To teach him, Parvati sat on Shiva's lap, but Bhringi became a bee and bored his way between them to circle Shiva alone. Then Shiva and Parvati fused into one body, half male and half female, as Ardhanarishvara. Unmoved, Bhringi tried to drill through the middle of that single form. Parvati then cursed him to lose all that a mother gives the body, its flesh and blood, and he collapsed as a mere skeleton, unable to stand. Repenting, he acknowledged the goddess, and Shiva, in compassion, gave him a third leg to support himself; he remained a devoted gana at Kailasa.
variations: The Ardhanarishvara episode is known mainly from South Indian Shaiva tradition and temple iconography rather than a single early Sanskrit text.
Shiva Purana and Linga Purana: the asura Andhaka, defeated and held aloft on Shiva's trident until wasted away, repented and was made the gana Bhringi (Bhringirita).
In some versions Parvati's resulting penance leads to her merging with Shiva, rather than the fusion occurring during Bhringi's visit.

nodes.name: Kamadeva
nodes.description: Kamadeva is the god of love and desire. In the Rig Veda's Nasadiya hymn kama (desire) is a cosmic principle, the first seed of mind at creation; the Atharva Veda already personifies Kama as a mighty god, and in epic and Puranic myth he is the youthful archer whose flower-arrows kindle love in gods and mortals alike.
nodes.story: When the demon Taraka could be slain only by a son of Shiva, the gods turned to Kama. Shiva, grieving for Sati, sat in unbroken meditation in the Himalaya while Parvati served him. At Indra's request Kama came with his friend Vasanta, the spring; flowers bloomed out of season and the forest hummed with bees. As Parvati drew near, Kama bent his sugarcane bow and loosed a flower-arrow. Shiva's composure wavered; he looked about for the cause, saw Kama, and a flame leapt from his third eye, reducing the god of love to ashes. Rati's lament moved the gods, and Shiva relented: Kama would live on without a body, as Ananga, the bodiless one, and in time would be born again as Pradyumna, son of Krishna.
symbols: sugarcane bow strung with a line of honeybees
five flower-arrows (lotus, ashoka, mango blossom, jasmine, blue lotus)
variations: Rig Veda 10.129 treats kama as an abstract cosmic principle (desire, the first seed of mind), not yet a personal god; Atharva Veda 9.2 and 19.52 praise Kama as a deity.

Parentage differs: born from Brahma's mind (Shiva Purana, Kalika Purana); son of Dharma and Shraddha (Vishnu Purana, Mahabharata lists Kama among Dharma's sons); in Vaishnava texts associated with Vishnu and Lakshmi through his rebirth as Pradyumna.
The Shiva Purana adds that Brahma had earlier cursed Kama to be burnt by Shiva after Kama's arrows affected Brahma himself.
Accounts differ on his restoration: bodiless (Ananga) at once, reborn as Pradyumna (Bhagavata, Harivamsha), or revived for Rati alone after Shiva's marriage to Parvati.

nodes.name: Rati
nodes.description: Rati is the goddess of love, delight and sensual pleasure, the wife and inseparable companion of Kamadeva. She is remembered above all for her grief when Shiva burned Kama to ashes and for her devotion in awaiting his return, reborn as Pradyumna.
nodes.story: After Shiva burned Kama to ashes, Rati mourned beside her husband's remains until Shiva promised that Kama would return. The Bhagavata Purana tells how the promise was kept. Kama was reborn as Pradyumna, son of Krishna and Rukmini, but the demon Shambara, forewarned that the child would kill him, stole the infant and cast him into the sea. A great fish swallowed the baby and was brought to Shambara's kitchen, where he was found by Mayavati, a woman of the household who was in truth Rati. Told by Narada who the child was, she raised him with care, in time revealed to him his true identity, and taught him the Mahamaya lore. Pradyumna slew Shambara, and the two flew together to Dvaraka, where Rukmini joyfully recognised her lost son.
symbols: mirror or bow in some icons
variations: Origins differ: daughter of Daksha, born from his sweat (Shiva Purana, Kalika Purana); in other accounts simply a daughter of a Prajapati.
In the Bhagavata she is Mayavati in Shambara's household; the Harivamsha and Vishnu Purana tell a similar tale of Mayadevi.
Kalidasa's Kumarasambhava (Rati-vilapa) gives the classic poetic lament of Rati over Kama's ashes.

nodes.name: Urvashi
nodes.description: Urvashi is the most celebrated of the apsaras, the celestial dancers of Indra's court. Her love for the mortal king Pururavas is one of the oldest love stories in Indian literature, preserved as a dialogue in Rig Veda 10.95, and through their son Ayu she is an ancestress of the Lunar dynasty.
nodes.story: The Rig Veda (10.95) preserves a dialogue in which King Pururavas begs the departing Urvashi to return, and she answers that she is as hard to hold as the wind. The Shatapatha Brahmana tells the fuller tale. Urvashi agreed to live with the mortal king on conditions, among them that she must never see him unclothed. Missing her, the Gandharvas stole by night the two lambs she cherished; Pururavas sprang up to pursue the thieves, a flash of lightning revealed him, and Urvashi vanished. Wandering in grief, he found her among other apsaras, swimming as water-birds in a lotus lake. She bade him return after a year, when their son would be born, and the Gandharvas granted him a sacred fire, kindled from ashvattha fire-sticks, by which he became one of them.
variations: Bhagavata Purana 11.4: born from the thigh (uru) of Narayana, who created her to humble the apsaras Indra had sent to disturb Nara-Narayana's penance; hence her name.
Vishnu Purana 4.6: she came to live among mortals because of a curse of Mitra and Varuna.
Rig Veda 7.33.11 calls Vasishtha born 'from the mind of Urvashi' when Mitra and Varuna beheld her; later texts extend this to Agastya.
Kalidasa's drama Vikramorvashiyam gives the lovers a happy ending, with Urvashi permitted to remain on earth.
In the Mahabharata she curses Arjuna when he refuses her, honouring her as an ancestress of the Kuru line.

nodes.name: Menaka
nodes.description: Menaka is one of the foremost apsaras of Indra's heaven, famed for her beauty and skill in dance. Sent by Indra to break the austerities of Vishvamitra, she became the mother of Shakuntala, and thus an ancestress of Bharata, from whom the land of Bharatavarsha takes its name.
nodes.story: Alarmed by the austerities of Vishvamitra, a king who strove to become a brahmarshi, Indra sent Menaka, most accomplished of the apsaras, to the sage's hermitage. The Ramayana tells that she came to bathe in the lake at Pushkara, and Vishvamitra, beholding her, invited her to stay; ten years passed as though a single day. Coming to himself, the sage saw that his long labour had been undone, yet he did not curse her, knowing she had only done Indra's bidding; he dismissed her gently and withdrew northward to resume his tapas. The Mahabharata adds that Menaka bore him a daughter, whom she left beside the Malini river, where birds (shakunta) sheltered the infant until the sage Kanva found her and raised her as his own, naming her Shakuntala.
variations: The Mahabharata presents Menaka's approach as Indra's commission and describes the wind-god lifting her garment; the Ramayana presents the ten-year union briefly and without blame on her part.
The Mahabharata also names Menaka as mother, by the Gandharva Vishvavasu, of Pramadvara, wife of the sage Ruru.
Distinct from Mena (Menaa), wife of Himavan and mother of Parvati, though the names are sometimes confused.

nodes.name: Rambha (apsara)
nodes.description: Rambha is among the most beautiful of the apsaras of Indra's court, often named as their queen. In the Ramayana she is cursed by Vishvamitra when sent to disturb his penance, and the wrong done to her by Ravana brings upon him Nalakubara's curse, which later protects Sita.
nodes.story: Rambha appears at two pivotal moments in the Ramayana. When Vishvamitra's renewed austerities alarmed the gods, Indra asked her to distract the sage. Reluctant, fearing his temper, she went nonetheless; Vishvamitra perceived Indra's design and cursed her to stand as a stone for ten thousand years until a great brahmin should release her, and then grieved that anger had once more consumed his merit. In the Uttara Kanda, as Rambha travelled to meet Nalakubara, son of Kubera, to whom she was devoted, Ravana stopped her on Kailasa and assaulted her, ignoring her plea that she stood to him as a daughter-in-law. Learning of it, Nalakubara cursed Ravana: should he ever again force an unwilling woman, his head would split into pieces. This curse later kept Sita safe in Lanka.
variations: Some traditions say Rambha rose from the churning of the ocean with the other apsaras.
Later texts and folk traditions add the Rambha-Shuka dialogue, in which the young sage Shuka resists her enticement.
Accounts differ on who released her from the stone: the Ramayana speaks only of a great brahmin; later retellings name various sages.

nodes.name: Tilottama
nodes.description: Tilottama is an apsara fashioned by Vishvakarma, at Brahma's command, from the finest particle (tila) of every beautiful thing in creation. She was created to bring about the downfall of the invincible asura brothers Sunda and Upasunda, whose tale Narada tells the Pandavas in the Mahabharata.
nodes.story: The asura brothers Sunda and Upasunda won from Brahma the boon that nothing could kill them except each other, and they began to terrorise the three worlds. Brahma summoned Vishvakarma, who gathered a sesame-seed's portion (tila) of the finest of everything in creation and fashioned from it a woman of unmatched beauty. As Tilottama circled the assembled gods in reverence, Shiva is said to have grown a face on every side and Indra a thousand eyes so as not to lose sight of her. She then went to the Vindhya hills where the brothers were revelling. Each seized one of her hands and claimed her; the inseparable brothers quarrelled, took up their maces and struck each other dead. Narada later told this tale to the Pandavas as a warning, prompting them to agree on rules for their shared life with Draupadi.
variations: The Mahabharata explains Shiva's four faces (Chaturmukha) and Indra's thousand eyes by their wish to watch her as she circumambulated them; other texts explain these features differently.
Later Puranic retellings add that Tilottama was cursed by Durvasa to be born on earth; these accounts are late and vary.

nodes.name: Chitraratha
nodes.description: Chitraratha is a king of the Gandharvas, the celestial musicians, and a friend of Kubera, whose pleasure-garden Chaitraratha bears his name. In the Mahabharata he fights and is defeated by Arjuna, then becomes a friend and adviser to the Pandavas.
nodes.story: As the Pandavas travelled by night toward Panchala, they came to the Ganga, where the Gandharva king Chitraratha, then called Angaraparna, was sporting with his wives. Angered that mortals had intruded on his hour, he challenged them and attacked. Arjuna answered with the fiery Agneya weapon learned from Drona, which burned the Gandharva's splendid chariot and struck him senseless. As Arjuna dragged him toward Yudhishthira, his wife Kumbhinasi begged for his life, and Yudhishthira released him. The Gandharva renamed himself Dagdharatha, 'he of the burnt chariot', and offered friendship: he gave Arjuna the chakshushi vidya, by which one may see whatever one wishes in the three worlds, promised the Pandavas Gandharva horses, narrated ancient tales such as those of Tapati and Vasishtha, and counselled them to take a family priest, whereupon they chose Dhaumya.
nodes.abode: Gandharvaloka; the Chaitraratha grove near Alaka
variations: Not to be confused with Chitrasena, the Gandharva who captures Duryodhana in the Ghosha-yatra episode and teaches Arjuna music in Indra's heaven.
The Brahmavaivarta Purana names a daughter of the Gandharva Chitraratha as the wife of Shani.
Several kings of the same name appear in the Vedas and epics; they are distinct figures.

nodes.name: Tumburu
nodes.description: Tumburu is the foremost of the Gandharva musicians, often shown horse-faced with a vina, singing in the courts of Indra and Kubera and in praise of Vishnu. He is the constant companion, and sometimes rival, of the sage Narada.
nodes.story: Tumburu once neglected his attendance on Kubera, lord of wealth, because of his attachment to the apsara Rambha. Kubera cursed him to be born as a fierce rakshasa, freed only when Rama, son of Dasharatha, overcame him in battle. So it was that in the Dandaka forest the monstrous Viradha seized Sita and was fought down by Rama and Lakshmana. Protected by a boon from weapons, he could not be slain by blades, so the brothers buried him in a pit; as they did so the curse ended, and he revealed himself as the Gandharva Tumburu. He thanked Rama, directed him to the hermitage of the sage Sharabhanga, and rose again to the heavens. In the Puranas Tumburu travels with Narada, the two singing the glories of Vishnu to the vina across the worlds.
symbols: tambura (the drone lute traditionally linked with his name)
nodes.abode: Gandharvaloka; courts of Indra and Kubera
variations: Puranic tales (e.g., Linga Purana and later works) make Narada jealous of Tumburu's music until humbled; the details vary.
In the Bhagavata Purana Tumburu is among the Gandharvas who sing before the chariot of the Sun in the month of Madhu.
Some South Indian traditions associate Tumburu with Tirumala (Tumburu Tirtha) and with Shiva.

nodes.name: Navagraha (Nine Planets)
nodes.description: The Navagraha are the nine celestial influences of Jyotisha: Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn and the two lunar nodes Rahu and Ketu. The word graha means 'seizer', for they are believed to grip and shape human destiny, and they are worshipped together to avert misfortune.
nodes.story: The Navagraha, the 'nine seizers', are Surya the Sun, Soma the Moon, Mangala (Mars), Budha (Mercury), Brihaspati (Jupiter), Shukra (Venus), Shani (Saturn), and the shadow planets Rahu and Ketu. The Puranas explain how the last two joined the circle. When the ocean was churned and the nectar of immortality emerged, Vishnu as Mohini served it to the gods alone. The asura Svarbhanu disguised himself and sat between the Sun and the Moon, but as he drank they exposed him, and Vishnu's discus severed his head. Made immortal by the nectar, the head became Rahu and the body Ketu, and they pursue the Sun and Moon to swallow them at eclipses. The Yajnavalkya Smriti prescribes graha-shanti rites for all nine, and temples set them together on one platform, usually arranged so that no two face each other.
symbols: nine deities on a single platform
nodes.abode: The heavens (grahaloka), in their planetary spheres
variations: Vedic texts speak of grahas and of Svarbhanu eclipsing the Sun (Rig Veda 5.40), but the fixed set of nine is post-Vedic.
Early lists sometimes count seven planets only; Rahu and Ketu were added later, Ketu originally denoting comets.
Shukra (Venus) is the planetary form of Shukracharya, preceptor of the asuras.

nodes.name: Mangala (Angaraka)
nodes.description: Mangala is the planet Mars, the fiery red son of the Earth goddess, one of the Navagraha. A martial, energetic deity, he is pictured red-bodied and four-armed, and Tuesday (Mangalavara) is sacred to him.
nodes.story: The Shiva Purana relates that when Shiva, bereft of Sati, sat in fierce austerity in the Himalaya, a drop of sweat fell from his brow to the earth. From it arose a child, red as fire, with four arms. The Earth goddess took him up and raised him as her own, so he was called Bhauma, 'son of Bhumi', and Angaraka, 'the glowing coal'. The boy went to Kashi and performed long tapas to Shiva, who, pleased, granted him a place among the planets in the heavens. Other Puranas give different origins: in the Brahmavaivarta Purana he is the son of the Earth by Vishnu in his boar form, Varaha, who raised her from the cosmic ocean. Tuesday is his day, and he is propitiated with red flowers, red cloth and coral.
variations: Born of Shiva's sweat falling on the earth and raised by Bhumi (Shiva Purana, Skanda Purana).
Son of Bhumi by Vishnu-Varaha (Brahmavaivarta Purana).
In some traditions, especially in South India, Mangala is identified with Skanda-Kartikeya, the war god.

nodes.name: Budha
nodes.description: Budha is the planet Mercury, son of Soma the Moon and Tara, and one of the Navagraha. By his union with Ila he became the father of Pururavas and so the progenitor of the Lunar dynasty (Chandravamsha), from which both the Kurus and the Yadavas descend.
nodes.story: Budha, son of Soma, was performing austerities beside a lake when a company of women passed by, among them Ila. She had been King Ila, son of Manu, who while hunting had strayed into the grove where Shiva delighted Parvati, and where every male creature was transformed into a female. Budha was struck by her grace, and she by his; they married, and in time she bore him Pururavas, founder of the Lunar line of kings. Through the intercession of sages and a great sacrifice that pleased Shiva, Ila was granted relief, living alternately a month as a man and a month as a woman. Through Pururavas, Budha stands as ancestor of the Pandavas and the Yadavas alike, and he is honoured as the wise, gentle planet Mercury, lord of Wednesday.
nodes.vahana: Lion (some icons: chariot drawn by horses)
variations: His paternity was disputed: both Soma and Brihaspati claimed the child until Tara named Soma as the father.
Accounts of Ila differ: in the Ramayana Ila becomes a woman in Shiva's grove; in the Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas Ila is first born a daughter to Manu and changed by Vasishtha's intervention.
The Vedic name Budha Saumayana ('son of Soma') appears in a Brahmana, though the planetary identity is later.

nodes.name: Shani
nodes.description: Shani is the planet Saturn, son of Surya and Chhaya and one of the Navagraha. The slowest-moving planet, whose name Shanaishchara means 'the slow mover', he is feared for his baleful gaze yet revered as a stern, impartial dispenser of the fruits of karma.
nodes.story: The Brahmavaivarta Purana tells why Shani keeps his eyes lowered. Absorbed in meditation on Krishna, he ignored his wife, a daughter of the Gandharva Chitraratha, when she came to him; slighted, she cursed him that whatever he gazed upon would be destroyed. Long after, when Parvati bore a son, all the gods came to see the child, but Shani stood with averted eyes. Parvati urged him to look, and reluctantly he glanced at the infant from the corner of his eye, and the baby's head was severed. Vishnu, riding Garuda, brought back the head of an elephant and set it on the child, who became Ganesha. Son of Surya and Chhaya, Shani moves slowest of all the planets; his gaze is feared, yet devotees honour him as an impartial judge of karma.
nodes.vahana: Crow (also vulture, or an iron chariot)
variations: His limp is explained in various ways: a blow from Yama's staff in a quarrel, or a curse from his mother.
Shani's estrangement from his father Surya is linked to Surya's rejection of Chhaya or to Shani's dark complexion, depending on the text.
Regional and folk traditions (e.g., Maharashtra, Shani Shingnapur) credit Hanuman with freeing Shani from Ravana's captivity, after which Shani promised not to trouble Hanuman's devotees.
The Padma Purana tells how King Dasharatha confronted Shani to prevent his transit through Rohini (which foretold famine) and received a boon.

nodes.name: Rohini
nodes.description: Rohini, 'the red one', is the fourth lunar mansion (nakshatra), identified with the reddish star Aldebaran, and the favourite wife of the Moon god Soma. Soma's partiality for her among the daughters of Daksha (or Prajapati) brought upon him the curse that explains the waning of the moon.
nodes.story: The Taittiriya Samhita relates that Prajapati gave his thirty-three daughters in marriage to King Soma, but Soma dwelt only with Rohini. The slighted sisters returned to their father; Soma followed to reclaim them, and Prajapati gave them back on condition that he treat them equally. When Soma again favoured Rohini, a wasting sickness seized him. The Mahabharata and the Puranas tell the tale with Daksha as father of the twenty-seven lunar mansions: Daksha cursed Soma to waste away, and the moon began to wane. At the gods' plea Daksha softened the curse; bathing in the Sarasvati at Prabhasa, Soma was restored, but ever after he wanes and waxes each month. Rohini, the reddish star, remains the moon's beloved house and an especially auspicious birth-star; Krishna was born under it.
nodes.abode: The nakshatra Rohini in the lunar path
variations: Taittiriya Samhita: Soma marries thirty-three daughters of Prajapati; epic and Puranic texts: twenty-seven daughters of Daksha, the lunar mansions.
Distinct from Rohini, wife of Vasudeva and mother of Balarama, who is named after the same star.
In the Aitareya Brahmana Rohini also appears in the myth of Prajapati and his daughter in deer form, linked with the Mrigashira constellation.

nodes.name: Tara (wife of Brihaspati)
nodes.description: Tara, 'star', is the wife of Brihaspati, preceptor of the gods. Her carrying-off by Soma led to a war in heaven, the Tarakamaya, and she became the mother of Budha, the planet Mercury.
nodes.story: Soma, radiant after performing the great royal sacrifice, grew proud and carried away Tara, wife of Brihaspati, preceptor of the gods. Brihaspati appealed for her return, but Soma refused, and the quarrel swelled into a war in heaven, the Tarakamaya: Shukra and the asuras sided with Soma, while Indra, the gods and Rudra stood with Brihaspati. At last Brahma intervened, halted the fighting and restored Tara to her husband. She was then with child, and the boy was born shining with beauty. Both Soma and Brihaspati claimed him, and Tara, out of modesty, kept silent until Brahma questioned her gently in private and she named Soma as the father. Brahma called the child Budha, 'the wise', and he became the planet Mercury. The episode is told in the Harivamsha, Vishnu Purana and Bhagavata Purana.
variations: Rig Veda 10.109 (the 'Brahmajaya' hymn), in which the gods restore a brahmin's wife taken by Soma, is often seen as a precursor of the legend.
Texts differ on Tara's role: some describe her as taken by force, others (e.g., Devi Bhagavata) as having gone with Soma of her own will.
Distinct from the Mahavidya goddess Tara and from Tara, queen of Kishkindha.

nodes.name: Dikpalas (Guardians of the Directions)
nodes.description: The Dikpalas are the deities who guard the directions of space. The epics speak of four Lokapalas (Indra, Yama, Varuna and Kubera, with Soma in some lists); later texts give eight (adding Agni, Vayu, Nirrti and Ishana for the intermediate points) or ten, with Brahma for the zenith and Vishnu or Ananta for the nadir.
nodes.story: The world-guardians play a memorable part in the tale of Nala and Damayanti. Hearing of Damayanti's svayamvara, four of the Lokapalas, Indra, Agni, Varuna and Yama, set out to win her, and even made Nala carry their suit to her. Damayanti held firm to her love for Nala, so on the day of the choice all four gods sat in the assembly in Nala's exact likeness. Praying to them, she was granted the sight to tell them apart: the gods neither sweated nor blinked, their garlands were unfaded and their feet did not touch the ground, while the true Nala cast a shadow and his garland drooped. She garlanded him, and the gods, honouring her constancy, each granted Nala two boons, among them Agni's presence at his call, Varuna's water wherever he wished, and Yama's gift of steadfast virtue.
nodes.abode: Their respective quarters; cities around Mount Meru
variations: Four Lokapalas (epics): Indra east, Yama south, Varuna west, Kubera (or Soma) north.
Eight Dikpalas: Indra (E), Agni (SE), Yama (S), Nirrti (SW), Varuna (W), Vayu (NW), Kubera (N), Ishana (NE). Nirrti is not a separate node; Ishana is a form of Shiva.
Ten Dikpalas add Brahma (zenith) and Vishnu or Ananta-Shesha (nadir).
Some lists give Soma instead of Kubera for the north, and texts vary on the placement of Nirrti and Ishana.

nodes.name: Kubera
nodes.description: Kubera is the lord of wealth and king of the yakshas, guardian of the north among the Dikpalas. Son of the sage Vishrava and half-brother of Ravana, he once ruled Lanka but lost it and his flying chariot Pushpaka to Ravana, and thereafter dwelt in Alaka near Kailasa as a friend of Shiva.
nodes.story: Kubera, son of the sage Vishrava, pleased Brahma with long austerity and was made guardian of wealth and the fourth of the world-protectors, alongside Indra, Varuna and Yama; Brahma also gave him the flying chariot Pushpaka. On his father's advice he settled in Lanka, the golden city built by Vishvakarma. But his half-brother Ravana, son of Vishrava by the rakshasi Kaikesi, grew mighty through boons and demanded Lanka. Counselled by Vishrava not to fight, Kubera yielded the city and withdrew to Mount Kailasa, where he built Alaka. When Kubera later sent a messenger urging Ravana to turn from wrongdoing, Ravana killed the envoy, marched on Alaka, routed the yakshas, struck Kubera down with his mace and seized the Pushpaka, the chariot on which Rama would one day return to Ayodhya.
nodes.vahana: A man (nara); in some traditions an elephant or the Pushpaka chariot
nodes.abode: Alaka (Alakapuri) near Mount Kailasa; formerly Lanka
variations: In Vedic texts Kubera Vaishravana is a lord of rakshasas or of hidden beings; he becomes the benign god of wealth in the epics.
His mother is Devavarnini (Ilavida), daughter of Bharadvaja in the Ramayana; some texts name her daughter of Trinabindu.
The Ramayana says his left eye turned yellow when he glanced at Parvati, winning him the name Ekapingala; Shiva nonetheless made him a friend.
The Tirumala tradition says Kubera lent wealth to Srinivasa (Venkateshvara) for his wedding to Padmavati, a debt devotees help repay.
Important in Buddhist and Jain traditions as Vaishravana/Jambhala.

nodes.name: Chitragupta
nodes.description: Chitragupta is the divine scribe who records the good and bad deeds of every living being and reads the account before Yama when souls come to judgement. Born from Brahma's body, he is revered as the progenitor of the Kayastha community.
nodes.story: The Padma and other Puranas tell that after Brahma had created the world and appointed Yama to judge the dead, the deeds of countless beings proved too many to reckon. Brahma sat long in meditation, and from his body emerged a man holding a pen and an inkpot. Because he had been conceived in Brahma's mind and long concealed (gupta) within him, he was named Chitragupta, and because he was born from Brahma's body (kaya) his descendants are called Kayasthas. Brahma appointed him to record every act of every living being. Seated beside Yama in the court of the dead, he consults his great ledger, the Agrasandhani, and reads out each soul's merits and faults so that judgement may be just. He is especially worshipped on Yama Dvitiya, soon after Diwali, when devotees honour pen, ink and account-books.
variations: Accounts of his birth differ between Puranas; some make him a son of Brahma born after long meditation, others give different parentage.
In some regions he is worshipped with his consorts and twelve sons, the ancestors of Kayastha sub-lineages.
Earlier texts mention recorders in Yama's court without the developed figure of Chitragupta.

nodes.name: Gajendra
nodes.description: Gajendra, 'lord of elephants', is the hero of the Gajendra Moksha, the Bhagavata Purana's famous tale of divine rescue. Seized by a crocodile and near death, he surrenders to the Supreme Lord and is freed by Vishnu, becoming a model of devotion in extremity.
nodes.story: On Mount Trikuta, in a lake bright with lotuses, Gajendra, lord of elephants, came to bathe with his herd. A mighty crocodile seized his leg, and the struggle between land and water lasted, the Bhagavata says, a thousand years, until the elephant's strength failed and his kin could not help him. Then Gajendra, who in a former life had been the Pandya king Indradyumna, remembered the devotion of his past birth. Raising a lotus in his trunk, he prayed to the Supreme, the cause of all causes, without naming any god. Vishnu came swiftly on Garuda, drew elephant and crocodile from the water, and cut open the crocodile's jaws with his discus. The crocodile, the Gandharva Huhu cursed by the sage Devala, regained his form, and Gajendra, freed from Agastya's curse, attained a form like Vishnu's own.
variations: The Bhagavata places the event in the fourth Manvantara (Tamasa) and ascribes the rescue to Vishnu's avatar Hari.
Temple traditions (e.g., Varadaraja at Kanchipuram, Sonpur in Bihar) localise the rescue at their sacred sites.
Gajendra's prayer, the Gajendra Stuti, is recited as a hymn of refuge.

nodes.name: Ambarisha
nodes.description: Ambarisha is a righteous king, son of Nabhaga and descendant of Vaivasvata Manu, praised as an exemplary devotee of Vishnu. His encounter with the irascible sage Durvasa, in which Vishnu's Sudarshana discus protects him, is a classic Bhagavata tale of the power of devotion.
nodes.story: King Ambarisha, who had dedicated his kingdom and senses to the service of Vishnu, was completing a year-long vow of Ekadashi fasting. As he prepared to break his fast on Dvadashi, the sage Durvasa arrived; the king invited him to eat, and Durvasa went first to bathe in the Yamuna. He lingered, and the proper moment for ending the fast was slipping away, so on the brahmins' advice Ambarisha sipped only water. Returning, Durvasa took this as an insult and from a lock of his hair created a fiery demon to destroy the king. The Sudarshana discus, set by Vishnu to guard his devotee, consumed the demon and pursued Durvasa across the worlds. Neither Brahma nor Shiva could shelter him; Vishnu declared himself bound by his devotees' love. Durvasa fell at Ambarisha's feet, and the king, who had waited a whole year without eating, prayed the discus to be pacified.
variations: The Ramayana's Ambarisha, an Ikshvaku king of Ayodhya whose sacrifice involves Shunahshepa, may be a different king of the same name.
A Vedic seer Ambarisha Varshagira appears in the Rig Veda (1.100.17); he is distinct.
The Mahabharata lists Ambarisha among great kings celebrated for their generosity and sacrifices.

nodes.name: Samudra Manthan (Churning of the Ocean)
aliases: Churning of the Ocean of Milk
nodes.description: The devas and asuras jointly churned the cosmic ocean, using Mount Mandara as the churning rod and the serpent Vasuki as the rope, to obtain amrita, the nectar of immortality. The episode yields the poison halahala, drunk by Shiva, and a series of treasures including Lakshmi, and ends with Vishnu as Mohini denying the nectar to the asuras.
nodes.story: Weakened, the gods allied with their rivals the asuras to churn the ocean for amrita. Mount Mandara was uprooted and set in the sea as the churning stick, and the serpent Vasuki was wound around it as the rope, the asuras holding the head and the gods the tail. When the mountain began to sink, Vishnu took the form of a great tortoise, Kurma, and bore it on his back. The first thing to rise was the deadly poison halahala, which threatened to burn the worlds until Shiva drank it and held it in his throat, which turned blue. Then arose the moon, the goddess Shri, the white horse Uchchaihshravas, the jewel Kaustubha, the wish-granting cow, the elephant Airavata, and finally Dhanvantari bearing the pot of amrita. When the asuras seized it, Vishnu appeared as the enchantress Mohini and served the nectar to the gods alone.
variations: The Ramayana and Mahabharata place the churning in the ordinary ocean (turned to milk by herbs in the Mahabharata); the Puranas name it the Ocean of Milk.
The Vishnu Purana ascribes the gods' weakness to Durvasa's curse on Indra; the Bhagavata names Bali as leader of the asuras.
The number and order of the treasures (ratnas) vary; later lists fix them at fourteen, sometimes including Alakshmi (Jyeshtha) as the first to emerge.
In the Ramayana Vishnu himself supports the mountain; the explicit Kurma avatar is elaborated in the Puranas.

nodes.name: Daksha Yajna
nodes.description: The Prajapati Daksha held a great sacrifice to which he did not invite Shiva, and in the Puranic versions his daughter Sati gave up her life in protest. Shiva's wrath, embodied in Virabhadra and Bhadrakali, destroyed the sacrifice before Daksha was restored and Shiva given his due share.
nodes.story: Daksha, a son of Brahma, bore a grudge against his son-in-law Shiva, whose ascetic ways he despised. He organised a grand sacrifice and invited all the gods except Shiva. Sati, Daksha's daughter and Shiva's wife, went uninvited to her father's house; insulted there, she gave up her body in the sacrificial fire through yogic power. Learning of her death, Shiva tore a lock of his matted hair and dashed it to the ground, and from it sprang Virabhadra, with Bhadrakali born of the Goddess's wrath. Their hosts overran the sacrifice: Bhaga lost his eyes, Pushan his teeth, Bhrigu his beard, and Daksha was beheaded. At Brahma's plea Shiva relented, restored the gods, and gave Daksha the head of a goat, and Daksha thereafter honoured Shiva with a share of every sacrifice.
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 66 (Shiva's bow used at Daksha's sacrifice)
variations: Vedic precursor: Rudra, excluded from the gods' sacrifice, pierces it; Bhaga is blinded and Pushan loses his teeth (Taittiriya Samhita 2.6.8, Shatapatha and Gopatha Brahmanas).
In the Mahabharata Shiva destroys the sacrifice (sometimes himself, sometimes through Virabhadra) at Uma's distress; Sati's self-immolation belongs to the Puranas.
Later Shakta texts (Devi Bhagavata, Kalika Purana) have Shiva wander carrying Sati's corpse until Vishnu's discus divides it, the pieces founding the Shakti Pithas.
In the Mahabhagavata Purana Sati manifests the ten Mahavidyas to overcome Shiva's refusal to let her go.

nodes.name: Descent of the Ganga (Gangavatarana)
nodes.description: King Bhagiratha of the Ikshvaku line brought the celestial river Ganga down to earth to purify the ashes of his ancestors, the sixty thousand sons of Sagara burnt by the sage Kapila. Shiva caught the torrent in his matted locks to spare the earth its force.
nodes.story: King Sagara of Ayodhya performed a horse sacrifice, but the horse vanished. His sixty thousand sons dug down into the earth searching for it and found it grazing beside the sage Kapila. Accusing him of theft, they rushed at him, and the sage reduced them to ashes with a glance. Sagara's grandson Anshuman recovered the horse and learned from Garuda that only the waters of the heavenly Ganga could redeem them. Anshuman and his son Dilipa died without success, but Dilipa's son Bhagiratha performed fierce austerities. Brahma granted the boon, but warned that only Shiva could bear the river's fall. Pleased by further penance, Shiva received Ganga in his matted hair, subdued her pride, and released her in streams. Bhagiratha led her across the land and down to the netherworld, where her waters washed the ashes and freed his ancestors.
variations: In the Ramayana Ganga is the elder daughter of Himavan and Mena; Vaishnava Puranas describe her as flowing from Vishnu's foot, washed by Brahma at the Vamana episode.
The sage Jahnu swallowed the river when it flooded his hermitage and released it from his ear, giving it the name Jahnavi.
In the Ramayana Indra steals the horse; some Puranas leave the thief unnamed or blame the asuras.

nodes.name: Lingodbhava (the Pillar of Fire)
nodes.description: During a dispute between Brahma and Vishnu over supremacy, Shiva appeared as an endless pillar of fire. Neither god could find its top or bottom, and they acknowledged Shiva as the supreme.
nodes.story: Brahma and Vishnu once quarrelled over which of them was the greater creator. Suddenly a blazing column of fire appeared between them, stretching beyond sight in both directions. They agreed that whoever found its end would be supreme. Vishnu took the form of a boar and dug downward for ages, while Brahma became a swan and flew upward. Neither reached the limit. Vishnu returned and humbly admitted failure, but in several Puranic versions Brahma falsely claimed to have seen the top, citing as witness a ketaki flower that had been falling from the summit. Shiva then emerged from the pillar, revealing himself as the infinite source of both. He honoured Vishnu's honesty, and in the Shiva Purana cursed Brahma to receive no worship and the ketaki never to be offered to him.
variations: Brahma's lie and the ketaki flower appear in the Shiva and Skanda Puranas, not in the earliest (Vayu, Linga) accounts.
In the Shiva Purana Shiva sends Bhairava, who cuts off Brahma's fifth head for his falsehood.
Tamil tradition locates the pillar at Arunachala, celebrated in the Karthigai Deepam festival.
Some versions add the cow Surabhi as a second false witness.

nodes.name: Tripura Dahana (Burning of the Three Cities)
nodes.description: The asuras built three fortified cities of iron, silver and gold that could be destroyed only by a single arrow when they aligned. Shiva (Rudra), using a cosmic chariot and an arrow made of the gods themselves, burnt all three at once, earning the name Tripurantaka.
nodes.story: Three asura lords, sons of Taraka, won from Brahma the boon of three cities, one in heaven, one in the sky and one on earth, built by the architect Maya of gold, silver and iron. They could be destroyed only by a single arrow at the moment, once in a thousand years, when the cities aligned. Protected, the asuras oppressed the worlds, and the gods turned to Shiva. The gods fashioned for him a chariot from the whole cosmos: the earth was its body, the sun and moon its wheels, the Vedas its horses, and Brahma its charioteer. Vishnu became the arrow, with Agni at its point and Soma at its shaft. When the three cities came into line, Shiva loosed the arrow and burnt them all in an instant, and the asuras perished within them.
symbols: Three cities of gold, silver and iron
weapons: Pashupata / the arrow formed of Vishnu, Agni and Soma
nodes.abode: The three worlds (heaven, sky and earth)
variations: In the Brahmanas the gods conquer the asuras' three forts (of iron, silver and gold) by the power of the upasad offerings, with an arrow compounded of Agni, Soma and Vishnu.
The Mahabharata (Karna Parva) narrates the cosmic chariot, with Brahma as charioteer and the three sons of Taraka as the cities' lords.
In the Shiva and Linga Puranas Mount Meru becomes the bow and Vasuki the bowstring; Maya survives as a devotee of Shiva.
Some Puranas add that Vishnu first corrupted the asuras' virtue so that they became vulnerable, and that Ganesha had to be worshipped before the chariot could move.

nodes.name: Kama Dahana (Burning of Kama)
nodes.description: Kamadeva, god of desire, disturbed Shiva's meditation with his flower-arrows and was burnt to ashes by the fire of Shiva's third eye, becoming Ananga, the bodiless one. In the Puranic and Kalidasa tradition the gods sent him so that Shiva would wed Parvati and father a son to kill Tarakasura.
nodes.story: The asura Tarakasura, invulnerable save to a son of Shiva, tormented the gods, but Shiva, grieving for Sati, sat absorbed in austerity on the Himalaya. Parvati, daughter of Himavan, served him daily in the hope of winning him. At Indra's urging, Kamadeva went with his wife Rati and his friend Vasanta, the spring, to awaken desire in Shiva. As Parvati approached, Kama drew his sugarcane bow and loosed a flower-arrow. Shiva felt a stir of longing, saw the archer, and opened his third eye; a flame leapt out and reduced Kama to ashes. Rati lamented bitterly, and Shiva, or the gods, promised that Kama would live again, bodiless or reborn. Parvati, realising that beauty alone could not win Shiva, turned to severe penance, and through it won him as husband.
nodes.abode: Himalaya; the Ramayana places it at the Kamashrama near the Sarayu-Ganga confluence
sources: Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Parvati Khanda
variations: In the Ramayana the story is brief: Kama struck Shiva during his austerities and was burnt, becoming bodiless (Ananga); Parvati and Taraka are not mentioned.
The Harivamsha, Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas say Kama was reborn as Pradyumna, son of Krishna and Rukmini, and Rati as Mayavati.
In South India Holi is associated with the burning of Kama rather than Holika.

nodes.name: Birth of Skanda and slaying of Taraka
nodes.description: Shiva's fiery seed, too potent to be borne, passed through Agni and the Ganga and was nursed by the Krittikas, giving rise to the six-faced war-god Skanda (Kartikeya). Made general of the gods, he slew the asura Tarakasura.
nodes.story: The gods needed a commander who could defeat the asuras, and above all Taraka, whom Brahma's boon made vulnerable only to a child of Shiva. Shiva's seed was so fiery that no one could bear it. Agni received it, and unable to hold it, cast it into the Ganga, who in turn deposited it among the reeds of the Sharavana on the mountainside. There a radiant child was born. The six Krittikas, the stars of the Pleiades, came to nurse him, and he grew six faces to drink from them all, earning the name Kartikeya. Only days old, he split the Krauncha mountain with his spear. Indra, fearing him, attacked and was defeated, then consecrated him as senapati, commander of the divine army. Leading the gods, Skanda slew Tarakasura with his spear, restoring heaven to the gods.
nodes.abode: Sharavana on the Himalaya; Krauncha mountain
sources: Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Kumara Khanda
variations: In the Mahabharata's Vana Parva Skanda is the son of Agni and Svaha, who took the forms of six of the seven Rishis' wives; Arundhati alone could not be imitated.
In the Vana Parva Skanda's chief foe is Mahisha; Taraka's slaying is prominent in the Shalya Parva, Kalidasa and the Puranas.
Tamil tradition (Kandha Puranam) makes the demon Surapadma his principal adversary and gives him a second wife, Valli.
Some versions have Parvati embrace the six infants, merging them into one child with six heads.

nodes.name: Kurukshetra War
nodes.description: The eighteen-day war fought at Kurukshetra between the Pandavas and their cousins the Kauravas for the throne of Hastinapura. It is the climax of the Mahabharata, ending in the near-annihilation of both armies and Yudhishthira's joyless victory.
nodes.story: After thirteen years of exile, the Pandavas' claim to half the kingdom was refused by Duryodhana, and Krishna's embassy for peace failed. Eighteen armies gathered on the plain of Kurukshetra, seven for the Pandavas and eleven for the Kauravas. Krishna, sworn not to fight, served as Arjuna's charioteer. Bhishma commanded the Kauravas for ten days until Arjuna, sheltering behind Shikhandi, laid him on a bed of arrows. Drona then led; the young Abhimanyu died in his wheel formation, and Drona himself laid down his arms on hearing the false report of Ashwatthama's death and was beheaded by Dhrishtadyumna. Karna fell to Arjuna when his chariot wheel sank, Shalya to Yudhishthira, and on the last day Bhima shattered Duryodhana's thigh with his mace. That night Ashwatthama massacred the sleeping Pandava camp. Of the vast hosts, only a handful survived.
symbols: Arjuna's chariot with the ape banner
sources: Mahabharata, Bhishma, Drona, Karna, Shalya and Sauptika Parvas
variations: Regional and folk traditions add figures absent from the Sanskrit epic, such as Barbarika (Skanda Purana, Rajasthan) watching the war from a hilltop.
Tamil tradition relates Iravan's self-sacrifice to Kali before the war to ensure the Pandavas' victory.
The Critical Edition places some passages, such as Arjuna's hymn to Durga before the battle, in its appendices.

nodes.name: The Bhagavad Gita discourse
nodes.description: The dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra, just before the war, in which Krishna teaches the paths of duty, knowledge and devotion. Narrated by Sanjaya to Dhritarashtra, it forms eighteen chapters of the Bhishma Parva.
nodes.story: As the two armies faced each other, Arjuna asked Krishna to drive his chariot between them. Seeing grandfather Bhishma, teacher Drona, cousins and friends arrayed to fight, he was overcome with grief, laid down his bow Gandiva and refused to fight. Krishna answered his despair with a teaching: the self is eternal and cannot be slain; one must do one's duty without attachment to its fruits; action offered to the divine binds no one. He explained the disciplines of action, knowledge, meditation and devotion. At Arjuna's request he revealed his universal form, in which Arjuna saw all creation and the warriors of both armies rushing into Krishna's mouths like moths into flame. Finally Krishna told him to surrender to him alone. Arjuna's doubts dispelled, he took up Gandiva again, ready to fight.
variations: The 700-verse vulgate is standard; a longer Kashmiri recension exists.
Commentators (Shankara, Ramanuja, Madhva and others) read the teaching through non-dual, qualified non-dual and dualist lenses.
The Anugita (Ashvamedhika Parva) is Krishna's later restatement when Arjuna says he has forgotten the teaching.

nodes.name: The Game of Dice
nodes.description: At Hastinapura, Yudhishthira lost his kingdom, his brothers, himself and Draupadi to Shakuni's loaded dice on Duryodhana's behalf. Draupadi's humiliation in the assembly hall, and a second game that sent the Pandavas into thirteen years of exile, set the course toward war.
nodes.story: Envious of the Pandavas' wealth after the Rajasuya, Duryodhana, with his uncle Shakuni, persuaded Dhritarashtra to invite Yudhishthira to a game of dice. Bound by honour to accept, Yudhishthira played against Shakuni and lost his wealth, his kingdom, his brothers, himself and finally Draupadi. Dushasana dragged Draupadi by the hair into the assembly. She asked whether a man who had already lost himself could stake his wife; the elders fell silent, and only Vikarna and Vidura spoke for her. Karna ordered her stripped, but as Dushasana pulled at her garment, cloth kept appearing without end. Bhima vowed to break Duryodhana's thigh and drink Dushasana's blood. Terrified by evil omens, Dhritarashtra granted Draupadi boons and freed the Pandavas, but a second game cost them twelve years in the forest and a thirteenth in disguise.
sources: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva 43-72 (Dyuta and Anudyuta Parvas)
variations: In the Critical Edition the garment multiplies without Draupadi explicitly invoking Krishna; the vulgate and later devotional retellings have her pray to Krishna, who saves her.
Popular tradition holds that Shakuni's dice were made from his father's bones and obeyed his will; this is not in the Sanskrit epic.

nodes.name: Draupadi's Svayamvara
nodes.description: King Drupada of Panchala held a contest for his daughter Draupadi's hand: the suitor had to string a mighty bow and hit a target through a revolving device. Arjuna, disguised as a brahmin, won, and by Kunti's word Draupadi became the wife of all five Pandavas.
nodes.story: Hoping that Arjuna, whom he believed dead, might still win his daughter, Drupada set a formidable test: string a great bow and shoot five arrows through a revolving aperture to strike a target above. Kings from across the land came, Duryodhana, Shishupala, Jarasandha, Shalya and others, and one after another failed. The Pandavas, living in disguise as brahmins since escaping the house of lac, sat among the priests. Arjuna rose, strung the bow in an instant and struck the target, and Draupadi garlanded him. The outraged kings attacked, but Arjuna and Bhima drove them off while Krishna, recognising his cousins, calmed the rest. Returning home, the brothers called out that they had brought alms; Kunti, unseeing, told them to share it equally. With Vyasa's sanction, Draupadi was wedded to all five brothers.
variations: In the vulgate Karna strings the bow but Draupadi refuses him as a charioteer's son; in the Critical Edition he fails by a hair's breadth and her refusal is not in the constituted text.
Later versions describe the target as a fish (matsya) on a revolving wheel, shot while looking at its reflection in water.
Vyasa justifies the polyandrous marriage by Draupadi's past life, in which she asked Shiva five times for a husband.

nodes.name: Yudhishthira's Rajasuya
nodes.description: The imperial consecration sacrifice performed by Yudhishthira at Indraprastha after his brothers subdued the kings of the four quarters. It was marked by the killing of Jarasandha beforehand, Krishna's slaying of Shishupala at the ceremony, and Duryodhana's humiliation in Maya's illusory hall.
nodes.story: Urged by Narada, who brought word that Pandu wished it, Yudhishthira resolved to perform the Rajasuya. Krishna warned that Jarasandha of Magadha, who held many kings captive, must first be removed; Bhima killed him in a wrestling match of many days. Arjuna, Bhima, Nakula and Sahadeva then conquered the four quarters and gathered tribute. At the sacrifice, with Vyasa and the great priests officiating, Bhishma advised that the first honour be given to Krishna. Shishupala of Chedi objected and heaped insults on Krishna, who had promised his mother to forgive a hundred offences; when the hundredth was passed, Krishna severed his head with the Sudarshana discus. Staying on in the wondrous hall built by Maya, Duryodhana mistook a crystal floor for water and water for floor, and was laughed at. His resentment led to the game of dice.
sources: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva 1-42 (Sabha, Mantra, Jarasandha-vadha, Digvijaya, Rajasuya, Arghabharana and Shishupala-vadha Parvas)
variations: The famous taunt by Draupadi, a blind man's son is blind, is not in the Critical Edition; there, Bhima and others laugh at Duryodhana.
Southern and vulgate recensions have Sahadeva send Ghatotkacha to Lanka to collect tribute from Vibhishana.

nodes.name: Burning of the Khandava Forest
nodes.description: To cure Agni of the surfeit caused by endless sacrificial butter, Krishna and Arjuna let him consume the Khandava forest, holding off Indra, who was protecting his friend the naga Takshaka. In return they received divine weapons, including the Gandiva bow and the Sudarshana discus.
nodes.story: Agni, sickened by the ghee of countless sacrifices, learned from Brahma that he could recover by devouring the Khandava forest, but every attempt was quenched by Indra's rains, for Indra's friend Takshaka lived there. Disguised as a brahmin, Agni approached Krishna and Arjuna on the banks of the Yamuna and asked for help. At their request he had Varuna give Arjuna the bow Gandiva, two inexhaustible quivers and a chariot with an ape banner, and Krishna the discus and the mace Kaumodaki. As the forest burned, the two warriors circled it, shooting down every creature that tried to escape and driving back Indra and the gods who attacked them. A heavenly voice told Indra that his friend Takshaka was away, and he withdrew. Only a few escaped, among them Takshaka's son Ashvasena and the asura architect Maya, whom Arjuna spared.
nodes.abode: Khandava forest (later Indraprastha), on the Yamuna
variations: The episode includes the sub-story of the Sharngaka birds, the sage Mandapala's children, whom Agni spared.
Some scholars read the episode as a memory of forest clearance for settlement and the displacement of naga peoples.

nodes.name: The War of Lanka
nodes.description: The war fought by Rama, Lakshmana and the vanara army against Ravana and the rakshasas of Lanka to rescue Sita. It ends with Ravana's death at Rama's hands, Vibhishana's coronation and Sita's ordeal by fire.
nodes.story: Having crossed the ocean by the bridge, Rama besieged Lanka with Sugriva's vanara hosts, joined by Ravana's brother Vibhishana. Angada went as envoy but Ravana refused to return Sita. In the fighting Nila slew the commander Prahasta, and Indrajit, striking invisibly, bound Rama and Lakshmana with serpent-arrows until Garuda freed them. Awakened from his long sleep, Kumbhakarna devoured vanaras until Rama cut him down. Indrajit felled Lakshmana, who was revived when Hanuman carried back a Himalayan peak bearing healing herbs; later Lakshmana killed Indrajit at the Nikumbhila shrine. Finally Ravana himself took the field. Rama, taught the Aditya Hridaya hymn by Agastya and riding Indra's chariot driven by Matali, fought him long, and slew him with the Brahmastra. Vibhishana was crowned king of Lanka, and Sita, after proving her purity through fire, was restored to Rama.
symbols: Sanjivani herbs and the mountain peak
variations: The Ahiravana (Mahiravana) episode, in which Hanuman rescues Rama and Lakshmana from the netherworld and meets his son Makardhvaja, is found in later and regional Ramayanas.
In the Adhyatma Ramayana and Ramcharitmanas the captive was a shadow Sita, and the fire ordeal restores the real Sita from Agni's keeping.
Bengali tradition (Krittivasi Ramayana) has Rama perform an untimely worship of Durga (akala bodhana) before the final battle.
Kalanemi's attempt to delay Hanuman on his way to the herbs appears in the Adhyatma Ramayana and Tulsidas.

nodes.name: Sita's Svayamvara (breaking of Shiva's bow)
nodes.description: At Mithila, Rama lifted, strung and broke the great bow of Shiva kept by King Janaka, winning Sita as his bride. The four sons of Dasharatha were then married to Sita, Urmila, Mandavi and Shrutakirti.
nodes.story: Janaka of Mithila had found Sita in a furrow while ploughing and vowed to give her only to a man who could string the mighty bow of Shiva, entrusted to his ancestors after Shiva had wielded it at Daksha's sacrifice. Many kings had failed even to lift it. The sage Vishvamitra brought the young princes Rama and Lakshmana to Mithila. At his word, Rama drew the bow from its iron chest, lifted it lightly, strung it and drew it so hard that it broke with a thunderous crash. Janaka sent for Dasharatha, and in a great wedding Rama married Sita, Lakshmana married Urmila, and Bharata and Shatrughna married Mandavi and Shrutakirti, daughters of Janaka's brother Kushadhvaja. On the journey home, Parashurama confronted Rama over the broken bow and was humbled.
variations: In Valmiki there is no assembled svayamvara: Rama breaks the bow on a visit with Vishvamitra; later versions stage a contest before many kings.
Some later and folk versions have Ravana attend the contest and fail to lift the bow.
In the Ramcharitmanas Parashurama confronts Rama in the assembly itself; in Valmiki the meeting occurs on the road back to Ayodhya.
Janaka's queen is named Sunaina only in later texts.

nodes.name: Rama's Exile
nodes.description: On the eve of his consecration as heir, Rama was exiled to the forest for fourteen years when Queen Kaikeyi claimed two boons from King Dasharatha. Accompanied by Sita and Lakshmana, he wandered through hermitages from Chitrakuta to Panchavati while Bharata ruled in his name.
nodes.story: Dasharatha announced that Rama would be made heir. Stirred by the maid Manthara, Queen Kaikeyi reminded the king of two boons he owed her and demanded that her son Bharata be crowned and Rama banished for fourteen years. Bound by his word, the king collapsed in grief, but Rama calmly accepted. Sita and Lakshmana insisted on going with him. Crossing the Ganga with the help of the Nishada chief Guha, they visited the sage Bharadvaja and settled at Chitrakuta. Dasharatha died of sorrow, recalling his curse for killing Shravana. Bharata refused the throne, came to the forest and begged Rama to return; when Rama would not break his father's word, Bharata carried his sandals back to rule as regent. The exiles moved south through the hermitages of Atri and Agastya to Panchavati.
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya and Aranya Kandas
variations: Later tradition tells that Urmila slept through the fourteen years, taking on Lakshmana's sleep so that he could guard Rama; this is not in Valmiki.
Some retellings soften Kaikeyi's role, making her act at the gods' prompting so that Rama could fulfil his mission against Ravana.

nodes.name: Abduction of Sita
nodes.description: Provoked by Shurpanakha, Ravana used the rakshasa Maricha, disguised as a golden deer, to lure Rama and Lakshmana away from Panchavati, then carried Sita off to Lanka. The vulture Jatayu died trying to stop him.
nodes.story: At Panchavati, Ravana's sister Shurpanakha tried to seduce Rama and, when rebuffed, attacked Sita; Lakshmana cut off her nose and ears. Rama then destroyed the rakshasa army of Khara and Dushana. Shurpanakha fled to Ravana and inflamed him with praise of Sita's beauty. Ravana compelled his uncle Maricha to take the form of a golden deer. Sita begged Rama to catch it; struck by his arrow, Maricha cried out in Rama's voice for help. Sita, frantic, sent Lakshmana after him. Ravana, disguised as a wandering ascetic, came to beg alms, revealed himself and carried Sita off in his aerial chariot. The aged vulture Jatayu fought him and fell with clipped wings. Sita dropped her ornaments to a group of vanaras below. The dying Jatayu told Rama what had happened, and the brothers began their search.
variations: The Lakshmana Rekha, the protective line Sita crossed, is absent from Valmiki and appears in later and popular retellings.
In the Adhyatma Ramayana and later texts Sita entrusts herself to Agni and a shadow Sita (Maya Sita), sometimes identified with Vedavati, is abducted.
In Valmiki Ravana seizes Sita by her hair and thighs; in Kamban he lifts the ground she stands on, leaving her untouched.

nodes.name: Burning of Lanka
aliases: Hanuman's leap and burning of Lanka
nodes.description: Hanuman leapt across the ocean, found Sita in Ravana's Ashoka grove and, after being captured and having his tail set alight, burnt the city of Lanka. The episode forms the heart of the Sundara Kanda.
nodes.story: Told by Sampati that Sita was in Lanka and urged on by Jambavan, Hanuman leapt across the ocean. On the way the mountain Mainaka rose to offer him rest, the serpent-mother Surasa tested him, and he killed the shadow-seizing Simhika. Overcoming the city's guardian goddess, he searched the palace, found Sita in the Ashoka grove guarded by rakshasis, and gave her Rama's ring. He then wrecked the grove and killed Ravana's son Akshayakumara. Indrajit bound him with the Brahmastra, and he let himself be led before Ravana. Vibhishana argued that an envoy must not be killed, so Ravana ordered his tail set on fire. Sita prayed that the fire be cool to him. Hanuman slipped his bonds, leapt from roof to roof and set Lanka ablaze, then, assured Sita was unharmed, flew back with her jewel for Rama.
variations: Tulsidas names the guardian of the city Lankini; in Valmiki she is the personified city, Lanka.
Regional traditions tell that Makardhvaja was born when a drop of Hanuman's sweat fell into the sea as he cooled his tail.

nodes.name: Building of Rama Setu
nodes.description: To bring his army across the ocean to Lanka, Rama had the vanara engineer Nala build a causeway of rocks and trees across the sea. The ocean god, humbled by Rama, promised to hold the materials afloat.
nodes.story: The vanara army reached the southern shore, but the ocean barred the way to Lanka. On Vibhishana's advice Rama lay on kusha grass for three days praying to the ocean for passage. When the ocean did not appear, Rama in anger aimed his arrows to dry up the sea. The ocean god rose before him, explained that he could not change his nature, but promised to bear up a bridge, and named the vanara Nala, son of the divine architect Vishvakarma, as able to build it. The vanaras uprooted trees and hurled boulders and mountain crags into the sea, and in five days Nala completed a causeway a hundred yojanas long. The army crossed over to Lanka, Rama and Lakshmana carried on the shoulders of Hanuman and Angada.
symbols: Rama's arrow aimed at the ocean
variations: Later retellings add that stones inscribed with Rama's name floated, and that Nala and Nila had been cursed so that anything they threw into water would float.
The tale of the squirrel carrying sand for the bridge, blessed with stripes by Rama, is a popular South Indian tradition.
Rama's worship of Shiva at Rameshvaram before or after the crossing is elaborated in later texts such as the Adhyatma Ramayana and Skanda Purana.

nodes.name: Janamejaya's Snake Sacrifice
nodes.description: King Janamejaya, to avenge his father Parikshit's death by the naga Takshaka, performed a sacrifice that drew serpents into the fire. It was halted by the young sage Astika, and during its sessions Vaishampayana first recited the Mahabharata.
nodes.story: Parikshit, cursed by a sage's son, died from the bite of the serpent Takshaka. When his son Janamejaya learned the truth, he resolved on a great snake sacrifice. As the priests chanted, serpents by thousands were drawn helplessly through the air into the fire, fulfilling an old curse of their mother Kadru. Takshaka fled to Indra for refuge, but the mantras dragged even Indra toward the flames, and he let Takshaka go. Just then the young brahmin Astika, son of the sage Jaratkaru and the naga woman Jaratkaru, sister of Vasuki, arrived and so pleased the king with his praise that Janamejaya granted him a boon. Astika asked that the sacrifice end, and Takshaka was saved in mid-air. During the long sessions of the rite, Vaishampayana, at Vyasa's bidding, recited the story of the Bharatas to the king.
variations: The Mahabharata is framed as recited twice: by Vaishampayana at the snake sacrifice, and later by Ugrashravas to the sages of the Naimisha forest.
Bengali and later Puranic tradition identify Astika's mother, the naga Jaratkaru, with the goddess Manasa.

nodes.name: Vamana's Three Strides
nodes.description: Vishnu, as the dwarf brahmin Vamana, asked the asura king Bali for as much land as he could cover in three steps, then grew to cosmic size and spanned the earth, sky and heaven, restoring the worlds to Indra. The striding Vishnu is praised already in the Rig Veda.
nodes.story: Bali, grandson of Prahlada, had conquered the three worlds and driven Indra from heaven. Aditi, mother of the gods, grieved, and on Kashyapa's advice performed a vow, and Vishnu was born to her as Vamana, a dwarf brahmin boy. Vamana came to Bali's sacrifice and asked only for three paces of land. Bali's preceptor Shukracharya recognised Vishnu and warned him, but Bali would not break his word and poured the water of gift. At once the dwarf grew to fill the universe: with one step he covered the earth, with the second the heavens, and there was no place left for the third. Bali bowed and offered his own head. Pleased by his truthfulness, Vishnu sent him to rule Sutala in the netherworld and returned heaven to Indra.
nodes.abode: Bali's sacrificial ground on the Narmada (Bhagavata); the three worlds
variations: In the Rig Veda Vishnu takes three strides across the worlds without any dwarf or Bali; the dwarf form (vamana) appears in the Shatapatha Brahmana, where the gods win as much land as the dwarf Vishnu can lie upon.
In the Bhagavata, Shukracharya tries to block the spout of the water-pot and loses an eye to a blade of grass.
In Kerala tradition, Mahabali was a just and beloved king allowed to visit his people once a year, celebrated at Onam.
Vaishnava Puranas say the Ganga issued from the water with which Brahma washed Vishnu's raised foot.

nodes.name: Holika Dahan
nodes.description: The demoness Holika, sister of Hiranyakashipu, sat in a fire holding the boy Prahlada, relying on her immunity to flame, but she was burnt while Prahlada, protected by his devotion to Vishnu, came out unharmed. The event is re-enacted with bonfires on the eve of Holi.
nodes.story: Hiranyakashipu could not break his son Prahlada's devotion to Vishnu.
