He had the boy thrown from cliffs, trampled by elephants and bitten by serpents, but Prahlada survived every attempt. At last the king called on his sister Holika, who possessed a boon, or in some tellings a cloak, that made her immune to fire. A great pyre was built, and Holika sat in it with Prahlada on her lap. As the flames rose, Prahlada kept chanting the name of Vishnu. The protection passed from Holika to the boy: she was reduced to ashes, while Prahlada stepped from the fire unharmed. The triumph of devotion over malice is remembered each year by lighting bonfires on the full-moon night of Phalguna, the eve of the festival of colours.
nodes.abode: Court of Hiranyakashipu (traditionally Multan, or Eranch in Uttar Pradesh)
sources: Vishnu Purana 1.17-20 (Prahlada's fire ordeal, without Holika)
variations: In the Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas Prahlada survives fire among other trials, but Holika is not named; the Holika story is found in later Puranic and folk tradition.
Some versions say Holika's immunity came from a boon of Brahma, others from a shawl given by Agni that flew onto Prahlada.
The Bhavishya Purana links the Holi bonfire to a demoness named Dhundha; South Indian tradition links Holi to Kama Dahana.

nodes.name: Slaying of Mahishasura
aliases: Durga's victory over the buffalo demon
nodes.description: When the buffalo-demon Mahishasura conquered heaven, the combined radiance of the gods took form as the Goddess Durga, armed with their weapons, who slew him after a great battle. The episode forms the middle section of the Devi Mahatmya and is celebrated at Navaratri and Durga Puja.
nodes.story: Mahishasura, lord of the asuras, defeated the gods in a hundred-year war and seized Indra's throne. The gods, led by Brahma, went to Shiva and Vishnu, whose anger blazed forth as light; from the bodies of Indra and all the gods poured further radiance, which merged into a single luminous Goddess. Each god gave her a weapon: Shiva his trident, Vishnu his discus, Varuna a conch and noose, Agni a spear, Vayu a bow, Indra the thunderbolt and Airavata's bell, Yama his staff, Kubera a drinking cup, Vishvakarma an axe and armour, and Himavan a lion to ride. Her laughter shook the worlds. She destroyed Mahisha's generals and armies, then faced the shape-shifting demon, who became buffalo, lion, man and elephant. Drinking wine, she pinned him with her foot and, as he half-emerged from the buffalo, cut off his head.
nodes.abode: Heaven and earth; traditionally the Vindhya hills or Mysore (Chamundi Hill)
variations: In the Mahabharata (Vana Parva) Skanda, not the Goddess, slays Mahisha.
The Vamana Purana names the Goddess Katyayani, born in the hermitage of the sage Katyayana.
Later Puranas give Mahisha's origin as the son of the asura Rambha and a she-buffalo.
The Kalika Purana describes three killings of Mahisha in successive ages.

nodes.name: Mausala — End of the Yadavas
nodes.description: Thirty-six years after the Kurukshetra war, a curse brought on by a prank caused the Yadavas to slaughter one another with iron-hard reeds at Prabhasa. Balarama and Krishna then left the world, and Dvaraka was swallowed by the sea.
nodes.story: Young Yadavas dressed Samba as a pregnant woman and mockingly asked the visiting sages Vishvamitra, Kanva and Narada what she would bear. The sages cursed that she would give birth to an iron club that would destroy the race. Samba brought forth a club; it was ground to powder and cast into the sea, but it grew into reeds on the shore. Thirty-six years after the war, as Gandhari had cursed, the Yadavas went to Prabhasa and, drunk, quarrelled. Satyaki slew Kritavarma, and the fight became a massacre with the reeds, which turned to iron clubs in their hands. Pradyumna, Samba and Aniruddha perished. Balarama departed in yoga, a great serpent leaving his mouth. Krishna, lying in the forest, was struck in the foot by the hunter Jara's arrow and left the world. Arjuna led the women away as the sea swallowed Dvaraka.
variations: The Bhagavata Purana inserts Krishna's teaching to Uddhava (the Uddhava Gita) before the end.
Later tradition identifies the hunter Jara as a rebirth of Vali, repaying Rama's arrow from hiding.
Puranic reckoning dates the start of the Kali Yuga to Krishna's departure.

nodes.name: Garuda Steals the Amrita
nodes.description: To free his mother Vinata from slavery to her co-wife Kadru, the eagle Garuda flew to heaven, overcame the gods and seized the amrita. On the way he won boons from Vishnu and a pact with Indra, and the serpents lost the nectar they had bargained for.
nodes.story: Vinata and Kadru, wives of Kashyapa, wagered on the colour of the tail of the horse Uchchaihshravas; Kadru's serpent sons blackened it by clinging to it, and Vinata became Kadru's slave. Her son Garuda asked the serpents their price for her freedom, and they demanded the amrita. Garuda flew to heaven, scattered the gods who guarded it, passed through a whirling wheel of blades, killed the two serpents guarding the nectar and carried it off without tasting it. Vishnu, pleased by his restraint, granted him immortality and a place above his banner, and Garuda became his mount. Indra struck him with the thunderbolt, but Garuda dropped only a feather, and the two became friends. Garuda set the amrita on kusha grass before the serpents, freeing his mother; while they bathed, Indra took it back, and the serpents licking the grass split their tongues.
variations: In the Rig Veda an eagle or falcon (shyena) steals Soma from heaven for Indra; the Brahmanas tell of the wager between Kadru and Suparni, with the metre Gayatri in bird form fetching Soma.
The full Garuda-Vinata narrative is first found in the Mahabharata's Astika Parva.
Garuda's elder brother Aruna, born prematurely when Vinata broke his egg, cursed her to servitude.

nodes.name: Slaying of Vritra
nodes.description: Indra, strengthened by Soma, slew the serpent Vritra, who had enclosed the waters, with the thunderbolt fashioned by Tvashtr, releasing the rivers to flow to the sea. It is the central myth of the Rig Veda; later versions make Vritra a son of Tvashtr and have the vajra made from the sage Dadhichi's bones.
nodes.story: The serpent Vritra lay coiled upon the mountains, holding back the waters. Indra drank deeply of Soma from three bowls, took up the vajra that Tvashtr had fashioned for him and struck Vritra, the first-born of serpents. The waters rushed over the fallen body toward the sea like lowing cows, and Vritra's mother Danu, lying above him, was struck down too. In the Rig Veda, Indra's companions the Maruts and his friend Vishnu stand beside him. In later tellings Tvashtr created Vritra to avenge his son Vishvarupa, whom Indra had slain. No weapon could harm the demon, until Vishnu advised the gods to ask the sage Dadhichi for his bones, from which a new thunderbolt was made. Burdened by the sin of the killing, Indra hid, and Nahusha ruled heaven in his place.
nodes.abode: The mountains and the cosmic waters
variations: In the Rig Veda Vritra is a serpent or dragon (ahi) withholding the waters; in the Brahmanas and epics he is Tvashtr's creation to avenge Vishvarupa.
The Mahabharata and Bhagavata have the new vajra made from Dadhichi's bones; the Bhagavata portrays Vritra as a great devotee of Vishnu.
Some Rig Vedic hymns say all the gods deserted Indra except the Maruts or Vishnu.

nodes.name: Mahaprasthana — the Great Departure
nodes.description: After Krishna's death, the five Pandavas and Draupadi renounced the kingdom and walked toward the Himalaya and Mount Meru, followed by a dog. One by one they fell, until only Yudhishthira and the dog, Dharma in disguise, reached the gate of heaven.
nodes.story: Hearing of the Yadavas' end, Yudhishthira crowned Parikshit, entrusted him to Kripa and Yuyutsu, and set out with his brothers and Draupadi, a dog following them. At the sea Agni appeared and asked Arjuna to return the Gandiva, which he cast into the water for Varuna. Circling the land, they climbed into the Himalaya. Draupadi fell first, then Sahadeva, Nakula, Arjuna and Bhima; to Bhima's questions Yudhishthira named each one's fault. Indra came in his chariot to carry Yudhishthira to heaven, but he refused to enter without the faithful dog. The dog then revealed himself as Dharma, testing his son. In heaven Yudhishthira found Duryodhana enthroned and was shown his brothers in a hell, but it was an illusion; bathing in the heavenly Ganga, he shed his human body and joined his kin in glory.
variations: The epic names the dog as Dharma, Yudhishthira's divine father; Dharma is commonly identified with Yama (Dharmaraja).
In Uttarakhand tradition the route is associated with Badrinath and the Swargarohini peak.

nodes.name: Lifting of Govardhana
nodes.description: Krishna persuaded the cowherds of Vraja to worship Mount Govardhana instead of Indra; when the angry Indra sent a deluge, Krishna lifted the mountain and held it as an umbrella for seven days. Humbled, Indra consecrated Krishna as Govinda.
nodes.story: Each year the cowherds of Vraja offered a sacrifice to Indra, lord of rain. The boy Krishna asked his foster-father Nanda why they worshipped a distant god when their cattle lived from the grass of Mount Govardhana, and urged them to honour the mountain, the cows and the brahmins instead. They agreed, and offered their feast to the hill. Enraged, Indra unleashed torrential storm clouds on Vraja. The terrified cowherds and their herds ran to Krishna, who lifted Govardhana with one hand and held it aloft like an umbrella. For seven days and nights the whole village sheltered beneath it while the rain beat down in vain. At last Indra withdrew his clouds, came down on his elephant Airavata and bowed to Krishna, and with the cow of plenty consecrated him as Govinda, lord of cows.
symbols: Mount Govardhana held on one finger
sources: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (mentioned in Shishupala's taunts)

Saranyu is the daughter of Tvashtr (Rig Veda 10.17)
Sanjna is the daughter of Vishvakarma in the Puranas
edges.variation: Vishvakarma replaces or is identified with the Vedic Tvashtr

edges.label: Sanjna created Chhaya from her own shadow to take her place
Shani is the son of Chhaya
Chhaya cursed Yama's leg when he raised his foot against her; Surya softened the curse
Chandra was born from the sage Atri (from his eyes, in the Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas)
edges.variation: Other Puranas have the Moon rise from the Churning of the Ocean

edges.label: In the Bhagavata Purana, Soma, Dattatreya and Durvasa are the sons of Atri and Anasuya
edges.variation: Other accounts give Soma no mother, born from Atri's eyes alone

edges.label: Rohini is Soma's favourite among his twenty-seven Nakshatra wives
Daksha cursed Soma to waste away for neglecting his other daughters for Rohini; the curse became the Moon's waxing and waning
Soma abducted Tara, wife of Brihaspati; she bore him Budha before being returned
edges.variation: Not a lawful marriage; Brahma restored Tara to Brihaspati (Vishnu Purana 4.6)

edges.label: Budha (Mercury) is the son of Soma and Tara
Soma's abduction of Tara led to the Tarakamaya war with Brihaspati
Shukra sided with Soma against Brihaspati in the Tarakamaya war
Chandra, the Moon, is one of the Navagraha
The waning Moon was restored by worshipping Shiva at Prabhasa (Somnath), and Shiva wears the crescent on his head
Rahu, exposed by the Moon at the Churning, swallows him at eclipses
Ketu is the Moon's shadowy foe at eclipses
Soma strengthens Indra for his battles; the two are invoked together as Indra-Soma
Some Vedic and later texts name Soma guardian of the north (or north-east)
edges.variation: Kubera is the usual guardian of the north

edges.label: Vayu is the divine father of Hanuman, born to Anjana
Vayu is the divine father of Bhima, born to Kunti
Vayu is guardian of the north-west
Vayu and Indra share the first soma as the dual deity Indra-Vayu
In a Puranic and regional tale Vayu and Shesha contested their strength over a peak of Mount Meru
edges.variation: Regional/late tradition; which peak broke off (Trikuta of Lanka, a southern hill) varies

edges.label: The Vedic Rudra is the earliest form of Shiva; the Shvetashvatara Upanishad identifies them
Puranas tell that Rudra sprang from Brahma's anger or forehead
edges.variation: Shaiva texts reverse this, making Shiva the source of Brahma

edges.label: Pashupati, lord of creatures, is one of Rudra's names in the Vedic Samhitas and Brahmanas
Rudra divided himself into the eleven Rudras (Vishnu Purana)
edges.variation: Other lists derive the eleven Rudras from Kashyapa and Surabhi, or equate them with the vital breaths

edges.label: Soma and Rudra are invoked together as a dual deity for healing (Rig Veda)
Rudra, a pupil of Angiras, fought on Brihaspati's side in the Tarakamaya war (Vishnu Purana 4.6)
Yama and Yami are twins, children of Vivasvat and Saranyu (Rig Veda 10.10)
Dharma, identified with Yama, is Yudhishthira's divine father
edges.variation: The Mahabharata sometimes distinguishes Dharma from Yama

edges.label: Vidura was Dharma (Yama) incarnate, born human through Mandavya's curse
edges.variation: The epic calls him an incarnation of Dharma; the equation with Yama rests on the Dharma-Yama identification

edges.label: Mandavya, impaled for a childhood fault, cursed Yama to be born as a shudra's son (Vidura)
Yama is guardian of the south
Chitragupta is Yama's scribe who records every soul's deeds
Yama, moved by Savitri's wisdom and devotion, restored her husband Satyavan's life (Mahabharata, Vana Parva)
Yama taught Nachiketa the knowledge of the imperishable Self (Katha Upanishad)
Yama granted Nachiketa three boons for waiting three nights at his door
As Kalantaka, Shiva struck down Yama to save his devotee Markandeya, then revived him
Yama and Shani are half-brothers, sons of Surya by Sanjna and Chhaya
As Kalindi (Yamuna), daughter of the Sun, she married Krishna (Bhagavata Purana, Canto 10)
edges.variation: Kalindi's identification with Yami is traditional but not made in the Vedic texts

edges.label: Vishvamitra composed the Gayatri mantra addressed to Savitr (Rig Veda 3.62.10)
Savitr is a son of Aditi in the Puranic lists of Adityas
Savitr gave his daughter Surya in marriage to Soma (Rig Veda 10.85)
Virabhadra knocked out Pushan's teeth at Daksha's sacrifice (Bhagavata Purana, Canto 4)
Appeased, Shiva ruled that toothless Pushan would eat through the sacrificer's teeth
Pushan is invoked with Indra as helper in winning cattle (Rig Veda)
Pushan and Savitr are closely linked solar guides in the Rig Veda
Virabhadra plucked out Bhaga's eyes at Daksha's sacrifice
Shiva granted that blinded Bhaga would see through Mitra's eyes
Bhaga sees through the eyes of Mitra after his blinding
Aryaman is invoked with Mitra and Varuna as guardians of order and covenant
Aryaman and Bhaga both preside over marriage and the sharing of fortune
Vishvarupa (Trishiras) is Tvashtr's three-headed son
Tvashtr raised Vritra from the sacrificial fire to avenge Vishvarupa (Taittiriya Samhita, Shatapatha Brahmana)
edges.variation: In the Rig Veda Vritra has no stated origin from Tvashtr

edges.label: Epic and Puranic texts often identify the Vedic craftsman Tvashtr with Vishvakarma
edges.variation: Distinct in the Rig Veda

edges.label: Nala, the vanara who built the bridge to Lanka, is Vishvakarma's son (Ramayana)
Vishvakarma built the city of Dvaraka for Krishna
Vishvakarma built Indra's city Amaravati and, in Puranic tellings, fashioned the vajra from Dadhichi's bones
The Brahmanas identify the Rig Vedic All-Maker with Prajapati
edges.variation: Vedic identification not maintained in the Puranas

edges.label: Vishvakarma, Surya's father-in-law, trimmed the Sun's brilliance on his lathe to make divine weapons (Vishnu Purana 3.2)
Later texts treat Parjanya as a name of Indra, who absorbed his rain-giving role
edges.variation: Separate deities in the Rig Veda

edges.label: Parjanya is called 'son of Dyaus' in the Rig Veda
The Atharva Veda calls Earth the wife of Parjanya, whose rain makes her fruitful
The Maruts bring on the rains with Parjanya
Tara is Brihaspati's wife
Kacha, who learned the Sanjivani lore from Shukra, is Brihaspati's son
Brihaspati is a son of the sage Angiras (Angirasa)
Brihaspati, guru of the devas, and Shukra, guru of the asuras, are lasting rivals
Bharadvaja was born to Brihaspati by Mamata, wife of his brother Utathya
Brihaspati is Guru, the planet Jupiter, among the Navagraha
With his chant Brihaspati split Vala's rock and freed the cattle and the dawn (Rig Veda 10.68)
Brahma was born on the lotus that grew from Vishnu's navel
edges.variation: Shaiva texts (Shiva Purana, Linga Purana) have Brahma and Vishnu both emanate from Shiva; Shakta texts (Devi Bhagavata) from the Great Goddess; Manusmriti has Brahma born in the golden cosmic egg.

edges.label: Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva are described as the foremost forms of the one Brahman (Maitri Upanishad; later Trimurti theology)
edges.variation: Each sect identifies its own supreme god with Brahman and treats Brahma as a created, subordinate deity.

edges.label: Saraswati, goddess of speech and learning, is Brahma's consort
edges.variation: The Pushkar tradition (Padma Purana) also names Savitri and Gayatri as his consorts.

edges.label: The Matsya Purana tells that Saraswati (Shatarupa, Savitri) emanated from Brahma's own body before becoming his consort
edges.variation: Brahmavaivarta Purana has her emerge from Krishna's mouth; Devi Bhagavata from the primordial Prakriti; many texts simply call her Brahma's wife.

edges.label: Daksha was born from Brahma's right thumb and made a Prajapati
edges.variation: Rig Veda 10.72 makes Daksha the son of Aditi; Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas give him a later birth as son of the Prachetas and Marisha.

edges.label: Marichi is one of Brahma's mind-born sons (manasaputras)
Atri is one of Brahma's mind-born sons
Angiras is one of Brahma's mind-born sons
Pulastya, grandfather of Ravana, is a mind-born son of Brahma
Pulaha is one of Brahma's mind-born sons
Kratu is one of Brahma's mind-born sons
Vashistha is a mind-born son of Brahma
edges.variation: The Rig Veda (7.33) makes Vashistha the son of Mitra-Varuna and Urvashi.

edges.label: Bhrigu is a mind-born son of Brahma
edges.variation: Some Brahmana and epic accounts make Bhrigu a son of Varuna (Varuni Bhrigu).

edges.label: Narada was born from Brahma (from his lap or mind) and learnt from him
edges.variation: The Bhagavata Purana says Narada in an earlier life was the son of a maidservant.

edges.label: The four Kumaras were Brahma's first mind-born sons, who refused to procreate
Svayambhuva Manu, the first Manu, is the son of the self-born Brahma
edges.variation: Several Puranas say Brahma divided his own body into Manu and Shatarupa.

edges.label: Kamadeva sprang from Brahma's mind at the beginning of creation (Shiva Purana)
edges.variation: Other accounts make Kama the son of Dharma, of Lakshmi and Vishnu, or self-born.

edges.label: Chitragupta emerged from Brahma's body to record the deeds of all beings
edges.variation: Late Puranic tradition (Padma, Garuda and Bhavishya Puranas).

edges.label: Jambavan, king of bears, was born from Brahma's yawn (Ramayana, Bala Kanda)
Brahma created Ahalya as the most flawless of women (Ramayana, Uttara Kanda)
The swan (hamsa) is Brahma's mount
Brahma granted Hiranyakashipu near-immortality: death neither by man nor beast, by day nor night, indoors nor outdoors
Brahma made Ravana invulnerable to gods, demons and celestial beings; he disdained to ask protection from humans
Kumbhakarna, meaning to ask for Indra's throne, asked Brahma for endless sleep because Saraswati twisted his tongue at the gods' request
Brahma granted Vibhishana unwavering adherence to dharma and later immortality
After Meghanada captured Indra, Brahma named him Indrajit and granted him a boon in exchange for Indra's release
Brahma granted Taraka that only a son of Shiva could kill him
Brahma granted Mahisha that no man or god could kill him, leaving him vulnerable to a woman
edges.variation: Details vary between the Devi Mahatmya, Devi Bhagavata and other Puranas.

edges.label: Brahma granted the three asura brothers three flying cities destructible only by a single arrow when they aligned
Brahma made Sunda and his brother immune to all but each other (Mahabharata, Adi Parva)
Brahma made Upasunda and his brother immune to all but each other
Brahma gave Durgama the Vedas, which the asura took from the world (Devi Bhagavata Purana)
Brahma blessed the infant Hanuman with invulnerability after Indra struck him down
Brahma at last acknowledged Vishvamitra as a brahmarshi after his long austerities
Brahma appeared to Valmiki and commanded him to compose the Ramayana in shloka verse
The demon Madhu attacked Brahma on the lotus at the beginning of creation
The demon Kaitabha attacked Brahma on the lotus at the beginning of creation
Shiva cursed Brahma to receive little worship for falsely claiming he had seen the top of the pillar of fire
edges.variation: Shiva Purana / Linga Purana; the Ketaki flower, his false witness, was also cursed.

edges.label: Savitri, offended when Brahma performed the Pushkar sacrifice with Gayatri, cursed him to be worshipped almost only at Pushkar
edges.variation: Padma Purana; the goddess in the story is Savitri, whom many traditions identify with Saraswati.

edges.label: Bhairava cut off Brahma's fifth head for its arrogance (Shiva Purana, Kurma Purana)
Brahma cursed King Mahabhisha, who gazed at Ganga in his court, to be reborn on earth, decreeing that Ganga would go there too and wrong him; he became Shantanu (Mahabharata, Adi Parva)
edges.variation: The curse falls chiefly on Mahabhisha; Ganga's descent is tied to it and to the Vasus' request.

edges.label: Lakshmi, goddess of fortune, is Vishnu's eternal consort, dwelling on his chest
Garuda, king of birds, is the mount of Vishnu
Pleased by Garuda's restraint in not drinking the amrita, Vishnu made him immortal and placed him on his banner
The serpent Shesha forms Vishnu's couch on the cosmic ocean and serves him eternally
Vishnu awoke from yogic sleep and slew Madhu, earning the name Madhusudana
edges.variation: In the Devi Mahatmya the Goddess as Yoganidra enables the slaying.

edges.label: Vishnu slew Kaitabha on his thighs, where there was no water
Vishnu slew the asura Kalanemi in the war of gods and asuras (Harivamsha)
edges.variation: Kalanemi is reborn as Kamsa in some Puranas; the Kalanemi killed by Hanuman in later Ramayanas is a different rakshasa.

edges.label: Vishnu severed the head of the asura Svarbhanu (Rahu) with his discus when he stole the amrita
Vishnu broke the chastity of Jalandhara's wife Vrinda by taking her husband's form, making Jalandhara vulnerable
Vrinda cursed Vishnu to become a stone (the Shaligram) and to suffer separation from his wife
edges.variation: Shiva Purana and Padma Purana; Vrinda is identified with the Tulasi plant.

edges.label: Bhrigu cursed Vishnu to be born repeatedly among humans after Vishnu killed Bhrigu's wife (Matsya Purana)
edges.variation: The Bhagavata instead tells of Bhrigu kicking Vishnu's chest to test his patience.

edges.label: Narada, humiliated at a svayamvara, cursed Vishnu to suffer separation from his wife and need the help of monkeys
edges.variation: Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita; popular through Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas.

edges.label: Pleased when Vishnu offered his own eye to complete a thousand-lotus worship, Shiva gave him the Sudarshana discus
edges.variation: Shiva Purana; the Vishnu Purana says Vishvakarma forged the discus from the sun's trimmed radiance.

edges.label: The preserver and the destroyer are complementary gods, each described as worshipping the other
edges.variation: Sectarian myths (the pillar of fire, Sharabha and Narasimha) portray rivalry; Harihara embodies their unity.

edges.label: Tamil tradition makes Vishnu the brother of Parvati (Minakshi), who gives her away to Shiva
edges.variation: Tamil temple tradition (Madurai); not found in the Sanskrit Puranas.

edges.label: Kanda Puranam says Valli was previously Sundaravalli, a daughter of Vishnu
edges.variation: Tamil tradition only.

edges.label: Kanda Puranam says Devasena was previously Amritavalli, a daughter of Vishnu
edges.variation: Tamil tradition only; the Mahabharata calls her a daughter of Prajapati.

edges.label: The elephant king Gajendra, seized by a crocodile, called on Vishnu, who rescued him (Bhagavata, Canto 8)
The child Dhruva performed austerities to Vishnu
Vishnu granted Dhruva the eternal Pole Star position
Prahlada remained devoted to Vishnu despite his father's persecution
King Ambarisha was protected by Vishnu's discus from the wrath of Durvasa
Jaya is a gatekeeper of Vishnu's abode Vaikuntha
Vijaya is a gatekeeper of Vishnu's abode Vaikuntha
The four Kumaras came to Vaikuntha to see Vishnu, and cursed his gatekeepers who barred them
Markandeya saw Vishnu as an infant on a banyan leaf floating on the waters of dissolution
Parvati won Shiva as her husband through austerity
Sati, daughter of Daksha, was Shiva's first wife
Shiva bears Ganga in his matted locks; some traditions regard her as a co-consort
edges.variation: Mainly devotional and folk traditions; the Ramayana makes her Parvati's sister, and most texts only describe Shiva catching her descent.

edges.label: Ganesha is the son of Shiva, who beheaded him and restored him with an elephant's head
edges.variation: In the Shiva Purana Parvati creates Ganesha alone; the Brahmavaivarta makes him a gift of Krishna born to Shiva and Parvati.

edges.label: Kartikeya was born of Shiva's fiery seed to destroy Taraka
Ashokasundari is a daughter of Shiva and Parvati (Padma Purana)
Andhaka was born from the sweat of Shiva when Parvati playfully covered his eyes, and was raised by Hiranyaksha
edges.variation: Shiva Purana and Kurma Purana; other accounts make Andhaka purely a son of Hiranyaksha.

edges.label: Ayyappa (Hariharaputra) is the son of Shiva and Vishnu's Mohini form
edges.variation: Kerala tradition; not found in the major Sanskrit Puranas.

edges.label: Bengali Manasamangal poems make the serpent goddess Manasa a daughter of Shiva
edges.variation: The Mahabharata and Puranas make Manasa (Jaratkaru) a daughter of Kashyapa and sister of Vasuki.

edges.label: Jalandhara was born when Shiva cast the fire of his third eye into the ocean (Shiva Purana)
Virabhadra sprang from the lock of hair Shiva tore out in rage at Sati's death
The Shiva Purana describes Hanuman as an incarnation (the eleventh Rudra) of Shiva
edges.variation: Valmiki's Ramayana makes Hanuman the son of Vayu with no Shiva connection.

edges.label: The bull Nandi is Shiva's mount and chief attendant
Shiva destroyed the three flying cities of the asuras with a single arrow
Shiva slew Jalandhara once Vrinda's chastity no longer protected him
Shiva burned Kama to ashes with his third eye for disturbing his meditation
edges.variation: Kama survives bodiless (Ananga) or is reborn as Pradyumna.

edges.label: Andhaka, lusting after Parvati, was impaled on Shiva's trident and, repenting, became a gana
edges.variation: Some versions have Andhaka become the devotee Bhringi.

edges.label: Daksha insulted Shiva and excluded him from his sacrifice
Shiva, pleased by Ravana's hymn after pinning him under Kailasa, gave him the sword Chandrahasa and his name
edges.variation: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda.

edges.label: Ravana was a great devotee of Shiva, traditionally credited with the Shiva Tandava Stotra
Shiva granted Bhasmasura the power to burn to ash anyone on whose head he placed his hand
Shiva granted Banasura a thousand arms and promised to guard his city
Banasura was a devoted worshipper of Shiva
After wrestling Arjuna in the form of a Kirata hunter, Shiva gave him the Pashupata weapon
Shiva made the boy Markandeya forever sixteen and deathless
Markandeya clung to the linga as Yama came for him
Shiva granted Amba that she would slay Bhishma in her next life (as Shikhandi)
Shiva granted Jayadratha the power to hold back all the Pandavas except Arjuna for one day
In a previous life Draupadi asked Shiva five times for a husband, and he granted her five husbands
Shiva relieved Soma of Daksha's curse at Prabhasa (Somnath) and wears the crescent moon
edges.variation: The Mahabharata has Soma cured by bathing in the Sarasvati.

edges.label: Shiva assured the grieving Rati that Kama would be restored (reborn as Pradyumna)
Shiva taught Shukra the Mritasanjivani lore that revives the dead
edges.variation: Matsya Purana; the Mahabharata has a different story of Shiva swallowing Shukra.

edges.label: Shiva taught Parashurama the arts of war and gave him his axe
edges.variation: Brahmanda Purana and later tradition.

edges.label: The sage Bhringi worshipped Shiva alone, refusing to honour Parvati
Bhagiratha propitiated Shiva to break Ganga's fall in his matted locks
The serpent king Vasuki coils around Shiva's neck
Kubera, lord of wealth, is Shiva's friend and neighbour at Kailasa
The Brahmanas identify Saraswati with Vak, sacred speech
The swan (hamsa) is also Saraswati's mount
The Brahmavaivarta Purana makes Saraswati one of Vishnu's three wives
edges.variation: Brahmavaivarta Purana only.

edges.label: In a quarrel among Vishnu's wives, Saraswati and Ganga cursed each other to flow as rivers on earth
edges.variation: Brahmavaivarta Purana.

edges.label: Saraswati cursed Lakshmi to become a plant (Tulasi) and a river in the same quarrel
edges.variation: Brahmavaivarta Purana.

edges.label: Shakta theology makes Mahasaraswati one of the three great forms of the supreme Goddess
edges.variation: Devi Mahatmya (angas) and Devi Bhagavata.

edges.label: With the Ashvins, Saraswati healed Indra in the Sautramani rite (Yajurveda, Shatapatha Brahmana)
Yajnavalkya praised Saraswati to regain his learning
edges.variation: Devi Bhagavata / Brahmavaivarta tradition.

edges.label: The Vishnu Purana makes Shri the daughter of Bhrigu and Khyati, hence Bhargavi
edges.variation: Most Puranas stress her rising from the ocean of milk.

edges.label: In the Shatapatha Brahmana, Shri came forth from Prajapati's austerity
Sita is the incarnation of Lakshmi as Rama's wife
edges.variation: Explicit in the Puranas and later Ramayanas; Valmiki's core books present Sita as born from the earth without this identification.

edges.label: Rukmini, Krishna's chief queen, is an incarnation of Lakshmi
edges.variation: Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas; the Mahabharata calls her a partial incarnation of Shri.

edges.label: Some traditions regard Radha as an incarnation of Lakshmi
edges.variation: Gaudiya and Brahmavaivarta theology make Radha the source of Lakshmi rather than her incarnation.

edges.label: Vedavati, reborn as Sita, is held to be a form of Lakshmi
edges.variation: Later tradition; Valmiki's Uttara Kanda describes her rebirth without calling her Lakshmi.

edges.label: The owl is Lakshmi's mount, especially in eastern India
edges.variation: Elsewhere she sits on a lotus flanked by elephants.

edges.label: The Mahavidya Kamala is the Tantric form of Lakshmi
Jyeshtha (Alakshmi) is Lakshmi's elder sister, who rose from the ocean before her
Lakshmi and the Moon both rose from the churned ocean, so she is called the Moon's sister
edges.variation: Other genealogies make Soma the son of Atri.

edges.label: Shakta theology makes Mahalakshmi a form, or the source, of the supreme Goddess
edges.variation: Devi Mahatmya and Devi Bhagavata.

edges.label: Lakshmi dwells on Venkateshvara's chest and incarnated as Padmavati to marry him
Parvati is the daughter of Himavan, king of mountains
Mena is Parvati's mother
After Sati's death she was reborn as Parvati to win Shiva again
Parvati fashioned Ganesha from the paste of her body
Parvati is Kartikeya's mother
edges.variation: In the Ramayana and Mahabharata he is not born from Parvati's womb (Agni, Ganga, the Krittikas or Svaha bear him); later Puranas make her his mother or adoptive mother.

edges.label: Parvati created Ashokasundari from the wish-fulfilling tree (Padma Purana)
Parvati (Uma) and Ganga are the two daughters of Himavan and Mena (Ramayana)
The mountain Mainaka is Parvati's brother
Shakta traditions regard Parvati as a gentle form of the supreme Goddess
Angered that her union with Shiva was interrupted, Uma cursed the Earth to have many lords (Ramayana, Bala Kanda)
Parvati won Shiva through years of austerity
Narada counselled Parvati to undertake austerities and gave her Shiva's mantra (Shiva Purana)
Andhaka desired Parvati and tried to seize her
Parvati drew away the flesh and blood of Bhringi when he refused to honour her
edges.variation: Mainly South Indian tellings of the Ardhanarishvara story.

edges.label: Sati is the daughter of Daksha
Sati is the youngest daughter of Prasuti
Shakta texts make Sati an incarnation of the supreme Goddess
edges.variation: Devi Bhagavata, Kalika Purana.

edges.label: The Ten Mahavidyas emerged from Sati when Shiva tried to stop her from attending Daksha's sacrifice
edges.variation: Mahabhagavata and Brihaddharma Puranas; other accounts link them to Parvati or Kali.

edges.label: Ganesha and Kartikeya are the sons of Shiva and Parvati
edges.variation: Their relative age differs: Ganesha is the elder in North India, the younger in much of the South and in some Puranas.

edges.label: Ashokasundari is Ganesha's sister in the Padma Purana tradition
Riddhi is a consort of Ganesha in popular North Indian tradition
edges.variation: The Shiva Purana names Buddhi instead; South Indian tradition holds Ganesha to be a brahmachari.

edges.label: Siddhi is a consort of Ganesha (Shiva Purana, Ganesha Purana)
edges.variation: South Indian tradition holds Ganesha to be a brahmachari.

edges.label: The mouse (or rat) is Ganesha's mount
Ganesha wrote down the Mahabharata as Vyasa dictated it
edges.variation: This episode is absent from the Critical Edition and is considered an interpolation.

edges.label: Parashurama broke one of Ganesha's tusks when Ganesha barred him from Shiva (Brahmanda Purana)
edges.variation: Other stories explain the broken tusk differently.

edges.label: Ganesha cursed the Moon for laughing at him, so it is inauspicious to see the moon on Ganesha Chaturthi
edges.variation: Popular vrata-katha tradition, with Puranic variants.

edges.label: Ganesha tricked Ravana into setting down Shiva's atmalinga at Gokarna
edges.variation: Regional temple legend (Gokarna).

edges.label: Ganga received Shiva's seed from Agni and deposited it in the reeds where Kartikeya was born
edges.variation: Valmiki Ramayana; called Gangeya.

edges.label: Indra gave Devasena to Skanda after he became commander of the gods
Murugan wooed and married the huntress Valli
edges.variation: Tamil tradition.

edges.label: Kartikeya, born for the purpose, slew the demon Taraka
In the Mahabharata Skanda slays the demon Mahisha
edges.variation: Later texts (Devi Mahatmya) attribute Mahisha's death to Durga.

edges.label: The peacock Paravani is Kartikeya's mount
As Swaminatha, the child Murugan explained the meaning of Om to his father Shiva
edges.variation: Tamil tradition (Swamimalai).

edges.label: Indra, after first fighting the infant Skanda, made him commander of the gods' army
The Matrika Kaumari is the shakti that emerged from Kumara (Devi Mahatmya)
Tamil tradition holds that Murugan taught the Tamil language and grammar to Agastya
edges.variation: Tamil tradition only.

edges.label: Ashokasundari married King Nahusha, who slew the asura Hunda (Padma Purana)
The Padma Purana makes Ashokasundari the mother of King Yayati
edges.variation: Other genealogies do not name her as Yayati's mother.

edges.label: Riddhi and Siddhi are popularly regarded as sisters married to Ganesha
edges.variation: The Shiva Purana's pair is Siddhi and Buddhi, daughters of Prajapati Vishvarupa.

edges.label: South Indian tradition makes Devasena (Deivanai) the daughter of Indra
edges.variation: In the Mahabharata Indra rescues her from Keshin and gives her away as her guardian; she is called a daughter of Prajapati.

edges.label: Tamil tradition makes Deivanai the daughter of Indra and Shachi
edges.variation: Later South Indian tradition only.

edges.label: Kanda Puranam says Devasena and Valli were sisters in a previous birth, daughters of Vishnu
edges.variation: Tamil tradition only.

edges.label: Ganesha appeared as a wild elephant to drive Valli into Murugan's arms
edges.variation: Kanda Puranam and Tamil tradition.

edges.label: Mena is the queen of Himavan
Ganga is the elder daughter of Himavan (Ramayana, Bala Kanda)
edges.variation: Vaishnava texts derive her from Vishnu's foot.

edges.label: Mena is the mother of Ganga (Ramayana, Bala Kanda)
